######## 1960-11-05 p22  [pacific\s*jazz]
ALL THAT JAZZ
Up at Blue Note Records, the last stronghold of jazz-only diskeries, we find
that Art Blakey has re-signed an exclusive pact and has been recorded “live”
at Birdland
in enough material for two
LP’s. Also under new contracts
for
Blue Note are Freddie Hubbard and Stanley Turrentine; both are featured in
new releases this month. Hubbard, formerly with
J.
J. Johnson, teamed with
Tina Brooks, McCoy Tyner, Sam Jones and Clifford Jarvis for “Open Sesame”
(4040), while Turrentine appears vdth Horace Parian, George Tucker and A1
Harewood in “Look Out!”
(4039). Forthcoming releases by Blue Note include
one by the Three Sounds, “Moods,” who’ve also been re-signed, and a package
titled
“Ti’ue Blue” by tenorman Tina
Brooks, who worked
in
the
successful
off-Broadway production, “The Connection.”
for this
is that the music
is no longer just the music of the campus and the
speakeasies. There are enough different roads
in
jazz now to
satisfy wiaely
diverse tastes. It is not one man’s right to call
all these roads wrong, for it is
too early to
tell whether jazz will take one direction
(as in the past renais-
sances)
or will continue to move out in separate areas. In speaking to Dave
Brubeck recently
(at a
cocktail party celebrating his
affiliation with WJZZ-
Fairfield, Conn.) we were never more firmly convinced that what Dave is doing
is right—^for him. Again
it becomes a matter of personal conviction and taste.
We have to laugh at Fisher’s closing paragraph
in which he urges that jazz
be allowed to shape her own future, as if his “tireless trio” are outsiders exert-
ing undue pressure on musicians and the public.
JAZZ JOTTINGS: Gloria Lynne accompanied by the Earl May Trio began a
two week engagement at Chicago’s Lake Meadows on
Oct. 26, continuing the
club’s recently initiated jazz star attraction
policy. While in Chi, Miss Lynne
and manager Monte Kay will tour radio stations in behalf of her new single for
Everest, “Dreamy” and “Condemn Without Trial.” Kay preceded his thrush to
Chicago to function as producer of the Regal Theatre’s one-week jazz package
which featured Miles Davis, Lambert, Hendricks and Ross and two of his own
clients, the MJQ and singer Bill Henderson.
.
.
. Following
its appearance for
Kay in Chicago the MJQ opens at New York’s Village Vanguard opposite the
Ornette Coleman Quartet on Nov.
1.
.
.
. Cannonball Adderley and the group
also in a Nov. 1st opening, at the Cloister Inn, Chicago. The week engagement
follows the group’s return from the West Coast. They follow Chico Hamilton
into the nitery.
.
.
. Argo releasing a new Jazztet
single, “The Cool One,” a
follow-up
to the group’s “Killer Joe”
single which broke some pop
barriers.
The label
is hoping for more pop market action on the disk. Whereas “Killer
Joe” was a musical portrait of the zoot suiter of the
’40’s, “The Cool
One,”
brings us up to date with the bopster of the ’50’s. Flipside is the Golson theme,
“Five Spot After Dark.”
.
.
. Many thanks to Bob Guthrie for his very encourag-
ing note. Bob wrote in from WOAI, San Antonio, where he spins jazz Satur-
days, 10:15 to midnight, on south Texas’ only all jazz show on AM radio.
This Week’s New Jazz Singles
DAVE BRUBECK
SARAH VAUGHAN
BENNY GOLSON
Jazz lovers “down under” got a chance
last week to hear Sarah Vaughan.
The Roulette recording star embarked Oct. 23 on a five-day whirlwind tour of
Australia and New Zealand which net her a whopping $17,500. Her lush voice
was
heard
in
Sydney,
Melbourne,
Brisbane,
Adelaide
and
Auckland. From
reports received by our Australian
representative. Miss Vaughan
is a
great
favorite in the Kangaroo country. Just before leaving for Australia, the thrush
closed out her engagement at the Cloister (Hollywood) and returned to New
York in time to cut enough sides for two albums and a multitude of singles.
We take wholehearted objection to A1 Fisher’s dissertation on the mating of
jazz
and
classics
which
appeared
in WHAT-FM’s
October
listening
guide.
Fisher
refers
to
this mating
as “The
Shotgun Wedding”
(the
title
of
the
article)
and
points
to John Lewis,
Bill Russo and Gunther
Schuller
as
the
“Tireless Trio” in this forced and unwanted marriage. Fisher even calls recent
jazz/classical concerts by Brubeck, Russo, the MJQ and Maynard Ferguson as
failures and refers to what Ornette Coleman and Cecil Taylor are doing as the
right direction. We say, to each his own—for
it’s all a matter of taste. We all
know that in all its history, jazz
is now in its most popular stages. The reason

Darin Named Variety Club's
"Personality Of The Year"
WASHINGTON,
D.C.—Bobby
Darin
has
been
selected
by
The
Variety
Clubs of America as the “Personality
of the Year,” according
to Hirsh De
La
Viez,
chairman
of
the
organiza-
tion’s award committee.
The
award
is
presented
annually
to the outstanding personality
in the
world
of show business,
as
voted by
members of the Variety clubs. Previ-
ous recipients have included A1 Jolson,
Arthur
Godfrey,
Perry
Como
and
Eddie Fisher.
In
citing Darin as this year’s win-
ner,
De
La
Viez
said
that
“at
24,
Darin
possesses
a
degree
of
stage
presence
and
a
flair
for
showman-
ship
that
some
performers
never
achieve
in a
lifetime.”
Darin
will
accept
the award
at a
formal
dinner
at
the
Statler
Hotel,
this
city, on November
19. He
is cur-
rently
in Rome making
his
first fea-
ture-length
flick, “Come
September.”

MOA Expands Exec Staff;
Ratajack To New Post
MIAMI BEACH, FLA. — In
one
of
the most dramatic announcements
in
years emanating from the music ma-
chine industry, George A. Miller, pres-
ident and executive director of Music
Operators
of
America
(MOA),
an-
nounced
last week that the organiza-
tion’s Board
of Directors, meeting in
executive session at the Deauville Ho-
tel, this
city, October 31 to November
2, had authorized an expansion in the
executive
staffing.
Edward
R.
Ratajack,
one
of
the
coin machine industry’s leading execu-
tives, has accepted the newly created
post
of managing
director and
coor-
dinator. Ratajack will headquarter
in
the Chicago
office of MOA. His duties
will
be
similar
in
scope
with
those
of
Miller.
The
new
offices
will
be
opened in Chicago approximately Feb-
ruary
1,
and
Ratajack
will
assume
his
duties
at that
time.
Ratajack,
at present
is
vice
presi-
dent of AMI (Automatic Music, Inc.),
music machine manufacturers; execu-
»
tive vice president of Rowe-AMI Sales
,<
Company; and president of AMI Sales
%
Company
(Chicago AMI
distributing
firm). He will continue with his pres-
ent affiliation until February, at which
time he
will
devote
his
full time
to
i
MOA.
MOA’s
11th Annual
Convention
is
I
scheduled
to be held
in the Deauville
y
Hotel, Miami Beach, Florida, May 15,
16 and 17, 1961. With Ratajack work-
ing with
Miller on the plans for
this
,
convention, it is expected that the 1961
show
will
surpass
by
far
anything
ever held
in previous years.
Dimitri Mitropoulos Dies
NEW YORK — Dimitri Mitropoulos,
an
all-time
great among
conductors,
died in Milan last week
(2)
after ap-
parently being
stricken with
a heart
attack while rehearsing for a concert
there.
Mitropoulos, who was
64-years
old
at his
death, was familiar
to Ameri-
can concert-opera lovers as conductor
of the Minneapolis Symphony Orches-
tra, The New York Philharmonic Or-
chestra and
as an
orchestra
director
for the Metropolitan Opera House.
He was
scheduled
to conduct four
operas for the Met this season, begin-
ning in the middle of Dec.
Mitropoulos made
his
first appear-
ance
in the
U.S.
in
1936, conducting
the
Boston
Symphony
and
other
American
orchestras. He became
di-
rector of the Minneapolis the follow-
ing
year,
succeeding
Eugene
Or-
mandy,
and
headed
the
Minneapolis
for twelve
years. He became director
of
the
New
York
Philharmonic
in
1951. Leonard
Bernstein, the
orches-
tra’s current conductor, took over the
post last year. Mitropoulos was often
a guest conductor at the Philharmonic
before assuming
its
directorship.
Mitropoulos was born
in Athens on
Feb.
18, 1896. He studied composition
for
a
while, but took an
interest
in
conducting
and
after
studying
with
Erich
Kleiber
he
became
assistant
conductor
of
the
Berlin
Staatsoper
from 1921-24. He returned
to Athens
to
become
the
permanent
conductor
of
the Athens Symphony
for
twelve
years, also making frequent guest ap-
pearances
in Europe.
Mitropoulos was invited to the U.S.
by
the
late
conductor
of
the
Boston
Symphony, Serge Koussevitsky.
He became
a U.S.
citizen
in
1946.
He never married.

Supreme Court 
Upholds Bourne; 
Rejects Rose's "Gang" Appeal 
NEW YORK-The 
U.S. 
Supreme 
Court has just denied Billy Rose's ap- 
plication to have the Court review the 
decision of the U.S. Court of Appeals 
which had previously unanimously af- 
firmed a judgment in favor of Bourne, 
Inc., 
judicially 
determining 
that 
Bourne was the owner of the renewal 
copyright of the oldie, "That Old Gang 
Of Mine," of which Rose was one of 
the writers. 
The long-standing suit involved a 
test of the principal holding that a 
writer may assign his interest in the 
renewal term of his copyright at any 
time prior to the commencement of the 
renewal period, the prerequisite to the 
effectiveness of such assignment being 
that the writer be alive at the com- 
mencement of the renewal period. 
Rose not only challenged the princi- 
pal, but claimed that an assignment of 
the renewal, prior to the commence- 
ment of the renewal period, did not 
embrace new discoveries, such as radio 
and TV, or any other means not in 
existence at the time of the original 
assignment. 
The District Court as well as the 
U.S. Court of Appeals, and now the 
U.S. Supreme Court, have all rejected 
this contention. 
The District Court had awarded 
Bourne the sum of $7,500 toward the 
fees of its attorneys, Phillips, Nizer, 
Benjamin, Krim & Balton, for their 
services in the trial. The Court of Ap- 
peals not only approved this award, 
but permitted an application for a 
further award for Bourne's attorneys' 
services on Rose's appeals to the Court 
of Appeals and to the Supreme Court. 
The amount of such additional award 
has not yet been fixed by the Court.

ALL THAT JAZZ 
Atlantic's second group of jazz singles will be released this week it was dis- 
closed by label topper Ahmet Ertegun. He said the release was prompted by the 
success of the first batch of singles issued last month. Among the new disks are 
Charlie Mingus' "Saturday Night Prayer Meeting," Slide Hampton's "Sister 
Salvation," Ornette Coleman's "Una Muy Bonita" and Herbie Mann's "Uhuru" 
and "High Life." Of these four records, all except Mann's are two-part'ers. This 
points up the opposing views of diskeries in regards to jazz singles. Whereas 
some (as Atlantic) prefer not to edit down performances, others such as Blue 
Note and Verve do edit the original LP tracks and offer the consumer two differ- 
ent tunes per disk. The fact that heavy issuance of jazz singles is a relatively 
recent trend and no consumer preference has yet been voiced, it will be inter- 
esting to see which school of thought will prevail in the future. Some people 
look to this divergence as a future battle between the artistic and commercial 
viewpoints, yet can it be argued that release of jazz singles is alone a very 
commercial endeavor? 
We focus attention this week on the release of the Columbia package "Thes- 
aurus of Classic Jazz," a four disk set of reputedly classic jazz performances 
culled from the now historic catalogs of Perfect, Harmony, Okeh, Pathe, Dom- 
ino, Actuelle and Velvet Tone. The four disks come boxed with a comprehen- 
sive sixteen page booklet (notes by Richard DuPage and Frank Driggs) and in 
total contain fifty-two previously unavailable tracks from the Twenties by such 
figures as the early Dorsey Bros. ork, Frankie Trumbauer, Miff Mole, Joe 
Venuti, Eddie Lang, Adrian Rollini, Red Nichols, Arthur Schutt, Wingy Ma - 
none, and many others. According to introductory notes by John Hammond, 
this four volume release represents "the cream of early improvised jazz in one 
of the most comprehensive collections ever published on long playing records." 
After sampling some of the treasures in the package, we heartily concur. 
Our sincerest apologies to Geoff Edwards. Seems that several weeks after we 
inaugurated this column, Geoff informed us that he'd been sending out a news- 
letter for over a year under the heading, "And All That Jazz." Anyway, Geoff 
has more important things to say. His "Grotto" show, broadcast nightly over 
KFMB-San Diego, is now rated number one by Pulse, beating all others in 
every quarter hour from 8 PM to midnight. We quote Geoff, "who says jazz 
doesn't build audience?" Now if only others will wake up to this fact! Geoff 
lays claim to the only "formula" jazz show in the country and he's sure that 
this is the reason for his success. 
While in Nashville covering the Country Music Festival, we discovered that 
not only has that city moved to virtual domination of the pop music scene but 
it is now extending its tentacles into the jazz world. First came the RCA Victor 
LP, "After the Riot at Newport," which featured a group of Nashville country 
musicians that were invited to display their brand of jazz at the Newport Festi- 
val. Unfortunately the cancellation of the festival prevented the "cowboys" 
from performing. But Victor was on hand to tape the boys' work. Now we dis- 
covered that Don Law, Columbia's country music A&R head has recorded 
guitarist Hank Garland in a jazz album. Don even flew Joe Morello and Joe 
Benjamin in for the session. Hank, we learned, has been jazzing it up after 
hours at the clubs along Printer's Alley for some time, so it was inevitable that 
someone would have the foresight to preserve his work on disk. We're looking 
forward to the release of this session. 
Roulette continues to cash in nicely on the Basie 25th ann'y special. The 
label is now offering consumers one free LP with the purchase of any two from 
its catalog, which include the three new Basie packages. 
Chris Connor's next album for Atlantic will be her first with a string accom- 
paniment. The set will be titled "Portrait of Chris" and feature arrangements 
by Jimmie Jones. 
Reggie Lavong, WWRL's "Dr. Jive," premiered a new jazz program for 
WRFM in New York. The show, tagged "Jazzville, U.S.A.," is a two hour stint 
heard each Saturday from 4 to 6 PM over the FM outlet. 
JAZZ JOTTINGS: Miles Davis brings his quintet into the Village Vanguard 
on Nov. 15 for a two week stand that will be the group's only New York nitery 
booking of the season. The group is recently returned from a highly successful 
tour of Europe... Alternating with Davis will be the Bill Evans Trio.. 
. 
Following his smash engagement at the Cloister, Cannonball Adderley and the 
Quintet embark Nov. 16 for an eighteen day European tour. The first nine 
days will be spent on the continent, the second nine in England. They arrive 
back in New York Dec. 4.... Herbie Mann opens at Birdland Nov. 10 with his 
Afro -Jazz group. As with his recently -released Atlantic LP, "The Common 
Ground," Mann will augment his group with four trumpets for the occasion. 
Also into Birdland the 10th is vocalist Gloria Lynne. She is skedded for an ap- 
pearance on the Nov. 20th Harry Belafonte TV spectacular.... The Belafonte 
spec will also feature the Modern Jazz Quartet.... Gene Krupa and his trio, 
currently at Chicago's London House through Nov. 20th, open the following 
night at Ft. Wayne's Embers for a week.

"THE COMMON GROUND"-The Herbie Mann 
Afro -Jazz Sextet plus 4 Trumpets-Atlantic 1343 
Mann's preoccupation with rhythmic experi- 
ments of African and Afro-Cuban music has made 
him a popular favorite and led to a State Dept. 
tour of Africa, which culminates in this album. 
The regular Mann group is enlarged to include 
four trumpets as a "kicker" for the session. Se- 
lections 
include 
"Baghdad," "Walkin'," 
"St. 
Thomas," "High Life" and "Night In Tunisia." 
Exciting music, with a passion not heard much 
in modern jazz. 
"STRING ALONG WITH BASIE"-Count Basie 
-Roulette SR 52051 
The easy-going Basie piano is surrounded by 
a full string complement in a relaxing, enjoyable 
album. Additional highlights of the session are 
Ben Webster, Illinoin Jacquet and Andy Fitzger- 
ald solos and Quincy Jones and George "The Fox" 
Williams arrangements. Among the tunes are 
"Summertime," "Stringing the Blues," "Poor But- 
terfly," "Sweet Lorraine" and "Blue and Senti- 
mental." 
"COOL VELVET"-Stan Getz and Strings - 
Verve MG VS -68379 
The warm tone and graceful manner of the 
Getz style fits well into the string -accompaniment 
arena. There is no friction between the two as 
with many such endeavors. Here the Getz horn 
is in smooth -flowing harmony on "The Thrill is 
Gone," " 'Round Midnight," "Early Autumn" and 
"Whisper Not." Excellent jazz offering. 
"MARIAN McPARTLAND PLAYS THE MUSIC 
OF LEON %RD BERNSTEIN"-Time S/2013 
The vet jazz pianist takes easily to the music 
of Bernstein, which has already been proven to be 
of facile adaptation to the jazz idiom. Working 
with a trio, she improvises freely on such items 
"It's 
" "Lonely 
" 
as 
t s Love, 
Town,""Tonight,"I 
Feel Pretty" and "Somewhere." Sound is excel- 
lent; music is enjoyable. 
"THE BLUES MESSAGE" - Curtis Amy and 
Paul Bryant -Pacific Jazz PJ-9 
Amy and Bryant might well be to the West 
Coast what Eddie Davis and Shirley Scott are 
to the East. Playing tenor and organ respectively, 
they delve into the low-down funky blues area 
in stirring terms. They allow themselves plenty 
of stretch -out time on "Searchin'," "The Blues 
Message," "This Is the Blues" and two others. 
Good, solid stuff. 
"A.MBNSS%DOR OF JAZZ"-Max Kaminsky- 
Westminster WST-15060 
Kaminsky, holdover from the Chicago era of 
jazz, still thrills audiences with his eloquent 
trumpet playing and his adaptability to many 
styles. Here he relies on a swing basis for his 
band's playing of "Henderson 
Stomp," "The 
Song Is Ended," "Bye Bye Blackbird," and "The 
Preacher."

"THE MOODS OF TAFT JORDAN"-Mercury 
SR 60101 
Jordan employs an almost strict melodic ap- 
proach, prefering to use smears and innuendos 
within the notes to express his feelings for the 
music. His support includes drums, bass and gui- 
tar (all unidentified) who each get some solo 
space, but most of it is reserved for Jordan's 
"different" style. He plays 'When Your Lover 
Has Gone," "My Man," "It's The Talk Of The 
Town" and six others including a couple of orig- 
inals.

"et SWINGING CHRISTMAS"-Ella Fitzgerald 
-Verve MG VS -64042 
The first lady of song conjurs up a delightful 
season with a package bursting with amiability. 
Frank DeVol's ork is her comrade on such sunny 
songs as "Jingle Bells," "Sleigh Ride," "Winter 
Wonderland," 
"White 
Christmas" 
and 
"The 
Christmas Song." Strong end -of -year package. 
"CHRISTMAS TIME"-The Pete King Chorale 
and Orchestra-Kapp KS -3214 
The smoothly -blended, well -disciplined King 
Chorale makes its offering for Christmas. It con- 
sists of medleys of seasonal favorites, both re- 
ligious and popular. Highlights of the set are 
"My Favorite Things" (from "Sound Of Music"), 
and "The Christmas Song" and "Have Yourself 
a Merry Little Christmas," both featuring the 
solo voice of Beth Adams. 
"SING THE SONGS OF CHRISTMAS"- Guy 
Lombardo 
and the Royal Canadians -Capitol 
STAO 1443 
Recorded "live" at Town Hall, Stoneham, Mass., 
the set features Lombardo, the band, vocalist 
Kenny Gardner and a chorus of 100 children's 
voices, in a presentation of familiar Christmas 
items. The reverent and the popular are combined; 
included among them "It Came Upon A Midnight 
Clear," 0 Little Town Of Bethlehem," "Winter 
Wonderland" and "Jingle Bells." Book type liner 
includes the lyrics to sing along with. 
"CHRISTM &S CAROLS"-Temple Church Choir, 
London, directed by Dr. George Thalben-Ball- 
Angel S35834 
The historic Temple Church plays host to an 
excellent boy choir. It's recorded here in one of 
the better albums this year. Among the selections 
are "While Shepherds Watched," "Unto Us A 
Boy Is Born," "The Holly And The Ivy" and 
"In Dulci Jubilo." Stirring religious album. 
"HARK! THE HER 1LD ANGELS"-Virgil Fox, 
organ-Capitol SP 8531 
Internationally known organist Fox delivers an 
exemplary Christmas program. The lineup are 
the usual familiar favorites-"Joy To The World," 
"O Sanctissima," "Gesu Bambino"-and they're 
played with reverent spirit. Stereo sound is an 
asset. 
"O TANNENBAUM"-Christmas On The Rhine 
-Mixed Chorus and Orchestra under the Direc- 
tion of Werner Muller-Decca DL -78388 
Though this album contains German Christmas 
songs, its appeal is universal. There are a few 
familiar items but most are relatively unknown 
here, making this set even more of a treat. Among 
the dozen selections are "Vom Himmel Hoch," 
"Kling Glockchen" and "Kommet, Ihr Hirten." 
The Cash Box-November 19, 1960

BENELUX 
Cees Hundepool, Bovema's label manager of Capitol, told The Cash Box that 
Holland is really Frank Sinatra -crazy, as a result of the recent Edison 1960 - 
Award which the famous singer won for his LP "Only The Lonely." Bovema's 
tie-in with this Sinatra -madness is underlined by the release of a single fea- 
turing "Ebb Tide" and "Blues In The Night," two numbers of the record. 
Also the presentation of three singles from Sinatra's "Come Dance With Me" 
-album will certainly prove to be a great commercial success," said Hunde - 
pool. Many preparations are being made for the big event of the Show busi- 
ness -year in Holland: An Evening With Judy Garland in Amsterdam, on De- 
cember 10 next. The star will be brought to this area by impresario Lou van 
Rees in close cooperation with L.C. Bovema's Capitol label. It is to be expected 
that Judy's personal appearance will give a tremendous up -lift and support 
to the popularity of American showbusiness in Holland. 
The Dutch Swing College Band, traditional jazzband with more than Euro- 
pean fame, has a new single record released on the Philips label (L.C. Phono- 
gram) with an unusual number, featured in the new Heidi Brühl-picture, "Im- 
mer Will Ich Dir Gehoren" (I Want To Be Yours Forever). This piece, called 
"Erzherzog Johann-Jodler" (The Yodling Duke), is heard played by this band 
in the picture just mentioned. Flipside of the new single is "Bei Mir Bist Du 
Schün," a steady favorite ever since it was first sung by the still active An- 
drews Sisters, way back in the late thirties. 
Willeke Alberti, charming 15 years old daughter of Willy Alberti (known in 
the States too, since his hit recording of "Marina"), sings the Dutch version 
of a popular German hit on her latest Philips single. This very catchy song, 
"Midi-Midinette," will no doubt become another big success for this promising 
new songstress (L.C. Phonogram). 
Bovema's MGM label will soon release a series of singles from the Benny 
Goodman Treasure Chest Performance 1937-38, featuring the original orchestra, 
quartet and trio which broke up the Swing Era. The singles are presented in 
a specially designed cover by the publicity dept. of Gramophone House. 
The French label Pathé already scores a tremendous amount of enthusiasm 
in Dutch record buying circles.. Dutch people are, besides American, also very 
French -minded, which is quite logical because of Holland's multi-linguitism. 
The Pathé label, managed by Bovema in Holland, just released a new record 
of the French songster Line Renaud, from the Paris -musical "Plaisirs," well 
known to all Americans who visited the French capital this year. Also featured 
on the record is the Golden Gate Quartet. Furthermore Pathé's most important 
highlights are: "Quand Le Valse Est Lá" (When The Waltz Is Here) by René 
Louis Lafforgue, famous for its magnificent music and lyrics, interpreted by 
the composer, André Claveau and the French accordeonist Yvette Horner. 
The Ozek's recently made their first recordings. This vocal -instrumental trio 
features brothers Frans and Hans Ozek and William Paffen. They are all coal - 
miners in Limburg (the mining district of Holland) and are very well known 
in that part. Frans and Willem play the accordion, Willem plays the drums. 
These musical miners write most of the songs they sing as well, both words 
(in German) and music. Their debut record is "Nur Ein Wandersmann" and 
"Die Blauen Matrosen," on L.C. Phonogram's Philips label. Also debuting on 
Dutch Philips label this month are The Yellow Rocks, who sing two novelty - 
songs by Dutch orchestra leader Frans Kerkhof: "De Kat En De Hond" (The 
(The Cat And The Dog) and "Engeltjec-Rock" (Angels -rock) on their first 
single release. These "Rocks" certainly have a new, fresh sound and L.C. 
Phonogram is expecting big sales of this hit -to -be. 
From the first LP by Bing Crosby on the MGM label, "Bing and Satchmo," 
the well known version of "Muskrat Ramble" has been released, also "Ruby 
Douby Du" from the motion -picture "Key Witness" played by Charles Wolcott. 
Great sellers in the current MGM repertoire are a religious treat by Hank 
Williams, "Jesus Is Calling" and Connie Francis' "White Christmas." Also the 
sales of Jimmy Jones-and Five Saints-recordings are doing very well. 
The original Dutch version of Loewe & Lerner's "My Fair Lady" has just 
been released by L.C. Phonogram on a 12" LP. The same songs as on the 
Broadway version LP are heard, in the same order of course. "On The Street 
Where You Live," "The Rain In Spain," "With A Littl Bit Of Luck" and all 
the other big hits are enthusiastically sung by well known Dutch artists like 
Wim Sonneveld, Margriet de Groot. Dutch lyrics were written by twenty-one 
year old student Seth Gaaikema. Dutch premiere of "My Fair Lady" at Rot- 
terdam's Luxor Theatre was reported in The Cash Box of October 29. Dutch 
interest is so great that the first supply of this Philips LP was out of stock 
within two days. 
Bovema's Columbia label provides the European premiere of the new Bobby 
Rydell-record, "Sway" and "Groovy Tonight," also the Hucklebuck" by Chubby 
Checker. Both records are making headway promotion in The Cash Box lists. 
There's a great demand for Dixieland -versions of oldtimers in the European 
market. This fact explains the popularity of bands like Acker Bilk's, Chris Bar- 
ber's and Papa Bué s in Europe. Acker is now high in the charts with his 
"White Cliffs Of Dover"-Dixieland-typed number, according to Robert Oeges, 
Bovema's Columbia label manager. 
Just released on the Philips -label is the hit version of "The Green Leaves Of 
Summer" from the film "On The Alamo," beautifully sung by the vocal -instru- 
mental quartet The Brothers Four. This version is, as USA Cash Box -readers 
know, coupled with the oldie "Beautiful Brown Eyes," one-time hit of Rose- 
mary Clooney. 
The latest activities of L.C. Bovema in the home-made recording field are 
represented by a single of singer Mary Scotti, entitled "Lief Zusje" on the 
Imperial -label and the release of a brandnew Toon Hermans-LP and EP of his 
famous "One Man Show 1958." Toon is one of the best entertainers in the 
comedy -field today. His appearance in Vienna, Austria, is a real gasser. Her - 
mans is to be heard on the His Master's Voice -label. 
Last Saturday evening Corry Brokken was for more than one hour the guest 
of Dutch most popular TV -hostess, Mies Bouwman. During this program every- 
thing she wished, could be realized. For instance she acted "La Dame Aux 
Camelias" with one of our young actors, Maxim Hamel. Also she disguised as 
a clown, but the highlight was the discussion about her job and her family. 
Gerry Mulligan and his big band are playing concerts in Amsterdam and 
The Hague, followed on November 19 by "Jazz At The Philharmonic" -concerts, 
also in Amsterdam and The Hague. J.A.T.P. will feature the Cannonball Ad- 
derly Quintet, Dizzy Gillespie, J. J. Johnson, Roy Eldridge, Coleman Hawkins, 
Ben Webster, Stan Getz. On November 27 Art Blakey's "Jazz Messengers" 
are expected in Brussels; this group will play in Holland in December. 
C 
GERMANY 
Ralph Maria Siegel reports that he thinks that "My Heart Has A Mind Of 
Its Own," the Connie Francis hit, will be even bigger here than "Everybody's 
Somebody's Fool" which is high on the charts. The song has been recorded by 
Gina Dobra, the 20 year old Polydor newcomer, Nana Gualdi, on Phillips, and 
Swedish star Siw Malmquist on Metronome. Ralph did the lyrics on both of 
the tunes and also publishes them. 
Hazy Osterwald is still a young man, but his life story is already being 
filmed for TV. Hazy with his sextet specializes in comedy presentations. The 
50 minute TV show will be broadcast on December 28. Hazy's latest hit is 
"Tango Bombastico." 
Rudy Von Der Dovenmuehle from Minerva Music reports that the Tommy 
Sands hit, "That's Love," has been recorded in German by English sensation 
Billy Saunders, Les Paul & Mary Ford's "Wonderful Rain" has been covered 
by the Darling Sisters, and the Australian top hit which also made time on the 
English charts, "Tie Me Kangaroo Down Sport" is being done by the Nilson 
Bros. All will be released on Electrola. 
The singles market here is getting tighter and tighter. Right now, it's neces- 
sary to have two "A" sides in order to really move a record. One example took 
place recently when Polydor called back the latest two Ted Herold records, 
cut out the "B" sides, and re-released the "A" sides back to back. Ted is a top 
teenbeat star, but has recently specialized in sweet numbers. Electrola pro- 
ducer Nils Nobach also says that he has quit looking for a strong "B" side and 
tries to produce only top sides so the public and the music boxes can take 
their choice. 
Music publisher Melodie Der Welt reports that they have the following 
Cash Box Top 100 tunes for Germany: "Twist," "Chain Gang," "Never On 
Sunday," "Diamonds And Pearls," "Move Two Mountains," "Poetry In Mo- 
tion," "Dreamin'," "Pineapple Princess," "Finger Poppin' Time," "Temptation," 
"If She Should Come To You," "The Girl With The Story In Her Eyes," "Wait 
For Me," "Night Theme," and "Yes Sir That's My Baby." 
Camillo, the top D.J. at Radio Luxemburg reports that his two top tunes are 
"Everybody's Somebody's Fool" sung by Connie Francis in German, and "Never 
On Sunday" sung by Lale Anderson. It takes over 2000 written requests to 
make the number one spot on his show. 
German Baritone Fischer Dieskau has just won the Edison Prize in Holland 
as the most popular classical singer there. 
Gerry Mulligan and his new Big Band will make their first appearance in 
Germany on November 9. Gerry is still quite popular here because of the old 
sides he made with his pianoless quartet featuring Chet Baker. Chet's living 
in Italy at present. 
Also from the world of European Jazz, French critic Charles Delauney is 
privately producing an LP with Lucky Thompson, Kenny Clarke and Bud Pow- 
ell. This LP will be distributed through indie channels throughout the world, 
and all profits will go to the family of the late great bass player, Oscar Petti- 
ford. 
It looks like our predictions of the top version of "Never On Sunday" are 
correct. Lale Anderson has already sold 120,000 copies of the top hit. 
Electrola star Ruth Fischer is becoming a top star in E. Germany. The com- 
munist radio there is playing the wax off her records. 
Sir John Barbirolli, from the Hallé Orchestra in London, is conducting a con- 
cert with the orchestra from the Bavarian State Opera on March 6. There's 
still time to get tickets. 
The newly formed Pye-Vogue record firm here has picked up distribution 
of the Mexican label Orfeon and the N.Y. based Latin American -jazz firm 
Seeco. One of the top selling LP's for the firm is the new Diana Dors record. 
The publicity reads "She sings like she looks." 
French star Jacky Noguez who hit the charts on the Jamie label stateside 
a few months ago has adopted a bit of the Ray Conniff sound. He's also got a 
big vocal group singing wordless phrases on his new EP. It's moving well in 
Germany. 
The manager for Della Reese, Lee Magdid, was in Berlin to line up TV shots 
for his star and is setting publishing rights for his firm. He had talks with 
Gerd Hammerling of Peter Schaeffers Music Peter Meisel, and Paul Siegel. 
Germany is finally giving a try to the old method of covering standards in 
new pop arrangement style. Philips has released a new Peter Biel single fea- 
turing "I Walk Alone," and Polydor has released Billy Buhlan with "As Time 
Goes By." 
Capitol record executives Gordon Fraser and Richard Rising visited the 
Electrola offices in Cologne for talks with Dr. Veder, and export manager 
Herr Wirtz. 
Vico Torriani, who smashed with his French based song "Kalkutta Liegt 
Am Ganges," is releasing another song along the same line. It's named "It 
Only Happens In Paris." 
Caterina Valente has an invitation to appear on the Perry Como show next 
year. She'll leave in January for Mexico, and then appears in Israel for a tour. 
Baden-Baden TV is also planning to film the "Caterina Valente Story" for re- 
lease next fall.

Capitol Sets Bjoerling
Disk Releases For '61
HOLLYWOOD — Four new albums
featuring
the

of

late
Swedish tenor, Jussi Bjoerling, will be
released
next

by

Rec-
ords,

According to Dunn, Capitol will re-

of
Puccini’s “Madame
Butter-
fly” with Victoria de Los Angeles

Also

on Jan.
3
is the

of three albums
collec-
tively
tagged
“The
Beloved
Bjoer-
ling,”

by

in

by

C.
S-honberg,

which ran
in the Times last
Sept.
18.
MGM's Jules Rifkin Marries
NEW YORK—Jules Rifkin, MGM
la-
bel’s national radio promotion rep, was
married here
last week
(16)
to Elea-
nor Levin, a member of Dave Garro-
ways’ TV production
staff. They were
married
in
the Boulevard Restaurant
in Rego Park, Queens. Miami Beach
is
the
site of the couples’ honeymoon.
With
Atlantic’s
portable
recording
equipment at his disposal, Lomax was
able
to record
in both monaural and
stereo.
Each of the LP’s contains a booklet
describing the music being heard.
In recording more than eighty hours
of
material—involving more
than
a
hundred
different
individuals
and
groups—Lomax ranged over the Blue
Ridge Mountains, the Ozarks and the
foothills
of Alabama and Mississippi.
He went
into
prisons
to record
con-
victs
singing
at
their
labor, and
he
went
to
the
Georgia
Sea
Islands
for his materials.
The packages are: “Sounds Of The
South”—Survey and general
intro
to
the series; “Blue Ridge Mountain Mu-
sic”—Featuring
the
Mountain Ram-
blers
of
Galax,
Va.;
“Roots Of The
Blues”—Negro
country
blues,
field
holders, and
levee camp
songs from
Alabama,
Mississippi
and
Arkansas;
“White Spirituals”—Sacred songs and
hymns of white backwoods people
of
the South, some of them dating back
to
frontier
times;
“American
Folk
Songs
For
Children”—Including
twenty-one songs that make-up “The
People’s
Mother
Goose”;
“Negro
Church Music”; “The Blues Roll On”
—Supplements “Roots Of The Blues”
volume.
Atlantic
said
it
would
conduct
a
“heavy”
advertising
and
promotion
campaign of the
series. Besides trade
paper advertising, the set is being ad-
vertised
in High
Fidelity,
The New
York Times, Down Beat, The
Satur-
day
Review,
Little
Sandy
Review,
Journal
of
American
Folklore
and
“Sing Out” and other publications.
A special effort is being made to in-
terest
libraries,
music
schools
and
universities
in
the
educational
and
cultural values of the
set.

‘JUST A CLOSER WALK WITH THEE”—Patti
Page—Mercury SR 60233
The
thrush’s
last LP
outing was
a
collection
of
gospel
songs, some
of which
she
performed
in
the
“Elmer
Gantry”
flick.
Here
she
is
con-
cerned with spirituals which have been arranged
to
fit into her vocal style—soft and gentle. With
full chorus and soloists in accord with her, Miss
Page
offers
stirring
readings
of
“Steal Away,”
“Little David,” “Gi-eat Gettin’ Up Mornin’,”
“It’s
Me Oh Lord” and “Were You There.”
Illllllllllllllllllililllllllllllll
“PHILLY JOE’S BEAT ’—Philly Joe Jones—At-
lantic
1340
Jones’
beat
is
the most
articulate
in modern
jazz drumming. A master of polyrhythmic
solos,
he
is also most
reliable and consistent
in
laying-
down
a strong rhythmic
line which
can’t
fail
in
propelling the most lethargic member of his cur-
rent
group.
Working
the
rhythm
section
with
Jones here
is Paul Chambers and Walter
Davis,
while
newcomers
cornetist
Michael Downs
and
tenorman
Bill
Barron
work
the
horn
line.
Of
course
lots
of
solo
space
is
given
to
Jones.
Se-
lections include “Salt Peanuts,” “Two Bass Hit.”
“Dear
Old
Stockholm”
and
four
others.
“AN AMERICAN IN ROME”—Phil Brito—War-
wick W 2017
A
sightseeing
visit to
this
Italian
city
is
tied
up
in
the
liner notes
with
Brito’s performances
of a dozen American pops. The singer translates
such
sturdies
as
“Cherokee,”
“Jersey
Bounce,”
“Perdito,” “Misty” and “Undecided”
into
Italian
language vehicles. He has a warm, pleasing voice
and
accounts
nicely
for
the
bi-lingual
etchings
here.
“THE AMAZING PAUL RENARD PLAYS THE
ALL
AMERICAN
MUSIC
OF
GEORGE
M.
COHAN ON THE WURLITZER PIPE ORGAN”
—Riverside RLP 845
Somehow
the
endearingly
cornball
music
of
George M. Cohan seems
so much
at home being-
played
on
an
organ.
And
Renard’s
masterful
technique on the huge Wurlitzer
is matched with
an
affection
for
the
beloved
music,
resulting
in
an enjoyable LP. Among the selections are “Har-
rigan,”
“Forty
Five
Minutes From
Broadway,”
“Mary’s A
Grand
Old Name,”
“Nellie
Kelly,
I
Love You” and “Give My Regards To Broadway.”
“BE MY GUEST”—Rolf Kuhn—Panorama PLPS
—2008
Kuhn, a young German clarinetist now making
his
indelible mark on
the American
jazz
scene,
is
surrounded
by
several
outstanding American
jazzmen here for a musical trip to distant lands.
With Kuhn
for
performances
of
such
items
as
“Istanbul,” “South of the Border,” “Atlanta, Ga.,”
and
“Chicago,”
are
Don
Lammond
(or
Ray
Mosca), Jim Hall
(or Chuck Wayne) and others,
each adding
to
the
total;
but
it
is
the
tasteful,
melodic, inventive
(in a Buddy De Franco
style)
and
relaxed work
of Kuhn
that
is up
for
scru-
tinization. He passes this test with flying colors.
“ONE FOOT IN THE GUTTER”—A

in

which

in the

“TRAD
.JAZZ”
Volume
1—Chris
Barber’s
Jazz
Band—Laurie 1903
Barber,
of
“Petite
Fleur” fame, heads one
of
England’s
leading
traditional
jazz
bands.
His
group
has
been
recorded
here
in
a
mixture
of
vintage tunes, pop items and some originals. Each
is handled in the New Orleans style regardless of
their
origin, but there can be detected
traces
of
more recent jazz leanings
in the band’s playing.
Clarinetist Monty
Sunshine
takes
the most
solo
time
and
he
has
a
pleasant,
melodious
tone.
Among the tunes are “Swannee
River,” “Golden
Striker,” “I Remember When” and “Creole Song.”
"DANCES
OF
PORT
SAID”—Mohammed
El
Bakkar & His Oriental Ensemble—Audio Fidelity
AFSD 5922
The
late El Bakkar reigned
in the U.S. as the
foremost
interpreter
of
the
pulsating,
sensuous
music
of the Middle
East. This
fifth album
for
AF contains a dozen tracks featuring El Bakkar’s
forceful
tenor
voice
over
a
chorus
of
strident
voices and the contagious music spilled out ener-
getically by the instrumentalists. He has a faith-
ful
following.
“LET’S GO LATIN”—Herb Zane and his Orches-
tra—Tico SLP
1073
A happy album
of
cha cha chas
for dancing.
Zane
uses a pleasing mixture
of brass and
per-
cussion instruments entwined
in imaginative but
uncomplicated
arrangements, with
the
sole
pur-
pose
of
providing
easy-to-follow
Latin
danee-
ables. Stereo is used effectively but not religiously
so
as
to
diverge from
the
primary
purpose
of
musicality.
The
tune
program
is
a
mixture
of
American
pops,
classical
themes
and
authentic
Latin
songs—“Frenesi,”
“Espana
Cani,”
“The
Speak Up Mambo” and
“Sentimental
Journey,”
among them.
“ART BLAKEY AND THE JAZZ MESSENGERS
AT THE JAZZ CORNER OF THE WORLD”—
Blue Note 4016
This
is the
second volume of Blakey perform-
ances
cut
at Birdland
earlier
this
year.
This
is
one
of the hardest striking groups
in
jazz,
pro-
pelled by Blakey’s relentless rhythmic drive. Lee
Morgan,
Hanks
Mobley,
Bobby
Timmons
and
Jymie
Merritt,
all
disciples
of the funky Blakey
school,
complete
the
picture.
Selections
include
“Chicken
An’
Dumplin’s,”
“Hi-Fly”
and
“Art’s
Revelation.” This
is strong
stuff.

Concertos
1-6—Herman

Orchestra—Westminster
14114,
14115,
14116
Scherchen
repeats
for
Westminster
in

his three

session
of the complete Branden-

An acknowledged great interpreter of Bach, the
conductor now has the facilities of stereo for even
fuller appreciation of the works and he takes ad-
vantage
of breadth and
vividness.
“THESAURUS OF CLASSIC JAZZ”—Columbia
C4L 18
Columbia
has
scoured
its
jazz
catalog
of

cordings from the Twenties and has found enough

of

and

labels for four

Mole,

Rollini, Wingy Ma-
none
and many
others.
Of
immense
historical
interest!
“KLEMPERER
CONDUCTS WAGNER”—Otto
Klemperer conducting the Philharmonia Orchestra
—Angel 3610 B
In celebration of the distinguished conductor’s
75th birthday he has recorded for this Angel re-
lease two disks of Wagnerian operatic orchestral
music. The set includes readings of overtures for
“Rienzi,” “The Flying Dutchman,” “Tannhauser,”
“Die Meistersinger,” preludes to “Lohengrin” and
a
couple
of other
pieces,
all
magnificently
per-
formed in the superb Klemperer
tradition. A re-
cording milestone for the artist.

ALL THAT JAZZ
ABC-Paramount Records has re-united J. J. Johnson and Kai Winding on rec-
ords. Th^e trombone team were a fantastically commercial success a few years
back when they were
cutting
for
Columbia,
but
gone
their separate ways
for the past several years. Their first session fof Paramount is already in the
can and will be released in LP form after the holidays.
Gerry Mulligan’s Concert Jazz Band, fresh from a three week tour of West-
ern Europe, returns to the Village Vanguard this week for a two week stand.
This will be the fourth time in six months that the Mulligan aggregation has
played
the
club.
Opposite them
will
be
the
cerebral
Bernard
Peiflfer, who
alternated with Mulligan in their last previous Vanguard date. The
initial im-
pact and growing success of the Mulligan Band is regarded as a healthy omen
and a trumpet call for the return of the big bands. But these same people were
heralding this cry when Quincy Jones scored on tour with the ill-fated “Plain
and Fancy.”
Individual success
can, but not necessarily mean
a new trend.
So tread lightly.
Leave it to Martha G^ser to come up with the exciting information that her
Erroll Garner and pop singer Adam Wade are both alumni of Pittsburgh’s West-
inghouse High School. The angle is that Wade has recorded Garner’s composi-
tion of “Dreamy” for release by Coed Records. They’re all hoping for another
“Misty.”
Plans for Japan’s
first festival of American modem jazz were revealed by
Monty Kay, producer of the four-city event. This initial festival, part of a series
of four which Kay will present in Japan during 1961, will premiere at Sankei
Hall in Tokyo on Jan. 2 and continue through Jan.
15 with performances
in
Osaka, Kobe and Nagoya. The perfomiers
will be Art Blakey and
his Jazz
Messengers—with Lee Morgan, Bobby Timmons, Wayne
Shorter and
singer
Bill Henderson. Subsequent festivals are planned for March, May, and Sep-
tember. Artists for these dates will be announced at a later date. According to
Kay, extravagant attendance at these festivals
is virtually assured based on
the fact that the Japanese people’s interest in modern jazz has reached con-
siderable proportions in the past few years. Kay quotes reports in Japan’s lead-
ing newspapers which point up the enthusiasm and respect for American jazz,
particularly among
the
country’s
youth. Kay expounded
the importance
of
jazz as “the nations’ strongest link to mutual goodwill” and is urging the in-
auguration of an
official governmental agency for the purpose of exporting
modem jazz
artists. He quotes ANTA figures relating to entertainment sent
abroad pointing out that for the five year period 1954-59, out of 105 entertain-
ment units sent abroad, only six were in some way related to jazz and only
three of the six were representative of modern jazz. Kay said that his own pro-
motional activities abroad are aimed at accelerating an international cultural
exchange program that will
fill the demand for modern jazz.
Kay has arranged to video tape the festival’s tour and
is negotiating with
several TV networks for the sale of the film. Expressed purpose of this
film,
said the producer, is to serve as documentary verification of the personal and
working relationships between the American jazzmen and their audience.

billy
“BILLY BLOWS HIS HORN”—Billy
Butterfield
and his Orchestra—Columbia CL 1514
The accent
is on melody and a danceable beat
and Butterfield proves
gifted
in both
endeavors.
The session, not unlike the brightly swinging Con-
niff and Jonah Jones hit albums, features the jazz
trumpeter
leading
his
ork-chorus
crew
through
mainstays “It’s Easy To Remember,” “Narcissus,”
“The Donkey Serenade,” “Tuxedo Junction” and
“Sunrise Serenade.” Very commercial date.
UKE
’Eft
“FOR YOU, FOR ME, FOR EVERMORE”—The
Anita Kerr Quartet—Decca DL 4061
Probably the most
active vocal group on
rec-
ords
(they’re heard on innumerable
sessions out
of Nashville), the Kerr Quartet emerges every so
often from the background
to
do
a turn them-
selves. Here
their smooth blend gently
caresses
such stalwarts as “Till The End Of Time,” “Ev-
eryday,” “Twelfth Of Never” and others
in
this
love-forever idiom. Excellent
vocal mood
setter.
“BROADWAY IN BRASS”—Eric
Johnson
and
his Orchestra—^Westminster WP-6126
Although brass
is the dominant
characteristic
of the music, Johnson has also used large quan-
tities of percussion in setting this danceable mood
of music from the B’way stage. The selections are
outstanding—“They
Say
It’s
Wonderful,”
“To-
night,”
“Bewitched,
Bothered And
Bewildered,”
“I Get A Kick Out Of You”—and “Smoke Gets In
Your Eyes.” Enjoyable instrumental package.
“LIKE ’ER RED HOT”—Various Artists—Duke
DLP 73
Duke has packaged a dozen previously released
singles by
its
stable of artists under one
cover.
Artists
include
Bobby
Bland,
Clarence
“Gate-
mouth” Brown, Johnny Ace, the
Casuals,
Little
Junior Parker and Paul Perryman, and they offer
their performances of “Pledging My Love,” “Far-
ther Up The Road,” “Slop Time,” “Tell Me Why”
and others. Should go well in R&B markets.

“MOODS”—The Three Sounds—Blue Note
4044
The
Three
Sounds
become
more
adventurous
here, doing unusual things to such tunes as “Love
For Sale,” “Things Ain’t What They Used To Be,”
“L’l Darlin’ ” and “Sandu.” The spirited cohesive-
ness
in which
they work
continues
to
fascinate
audiences of their disks and this date should ex-
tend their popularity even further among the jazz
pui'ists.
“TAL FARLOW PLAYS THE MUSIC OF HAR-
OLD ARLEN”—Verve MG V-8371
Guitarist
Farlow, though
not
a “commercial”
jazz name
has demonstrated
through numerous
LP’s that he
is an
artist
of the highest quality
with uncompromising taste. He leads three groups
here
in easy going,
lightly swinging
interpreta-
tions
of eight Harold Arlen
tunes, among them
“Blues
In
the
Night,” “Between
the
Devil
and
the Deep Blue Sea” and “Petticoat High.” Far-
low’s solos are in accord with the solo work here
of Frank Wess
(flute & tenor) and Dick Hyman
(piano). Reliable pleasant listening.
“MUSIC FROM THE CONNECTION’ ’’—Howard
McGhee Quintet—Felsted FL 7512
Freddie Redd’s music for the avante garde, suc-
cessful off-Broadway
play, “The
Connection,”
is
played here with aggressive spirit by the McGhee
group; which includes Tina Brooks, Milt Hinton,
Ossie Johnson and
I.
Ching. The music
is emo-
tional and striking and solidly in the blues groove.
Will vie strongly with the original “cast” waxing.
“PERCUSSIVE
BIG
BAND
JAZZ”—Bobby
Christian—Audio Fidelity DFS 7005
Heading up a large studio ork, Bobby Christian
has supplied them with crisp, crackling arrange-
ments of twelve pop tunes. Such tracks as “Ev’ry-
thing’s Coming Up Roses,” “Glory Of Love,” “Wil-
low Weep For Me” and “Did
I Remember”
are
representative
of
Christian’s
swinging
scoring
with an added
stereo percussion
sidelight. Good
big band music for the sound enthusiasts.
“THE
LONG
ISLAND
SOUND”—The
Volpe
Quintet—K-P Records LP 1240
The
Volpe
Quintet,
all
Long
Islanders,
play
dance music
in a relaxed, unhurried vein. Their
reliance
is on the melody coupled with a consist-
ently danceable beat. Here, on their first date they
offer such sturdies as “You’re Devastating,” “The
Breeze And I,” “I’ve Told Ev’ry Little Star” and
“Together Wherever We Go.”
“A DATE TO DANCE”—Charles Turecamo and
his Society Orchestra—Winston 1000
Society dance music in the smooth, sugary Lom-
bardo manner is presented by Turecamo through
extended medleys
of pop
sturdies.
Side one has
the full ork sound while side two brings
it down
to a softer, bluer cocktail bar style. Both halves
maintain the
light dance beat which adults
will
appreciate.
Selections
include
“By
Myself,”
“Witchcraft,” “A Foggy Day,” “Easter Parade”
and others.
JAZZ PICKS
OF THE WEEK
“A PORTRAIT
OF
DUKE
ELLINGTON”—
Dizzy
Gillespie
and
His
Orchestra—Verve MG
VS-68386
One
jazz
great
pays
tribute
to
another
but
throw
sentimentality
to
the
winds,
for
what
emerges
is a dazzling modern ork date. Gillespie
helms an
unidentified assemblage
of
musicians,
handling first solo himself, in all-Dix treatments
of such sturdies as “In A Mellow Tone,” “Chelsea
Bridge,”
“Sophisticated Lady” and “Do Nothin’
Till You Hear From Me.” The session
is respect-
ful, colorful, vibrant and inventive. Tops for the
jazz trade.
“THE CONTEMPORARY JAZZ CLASSICS OF
THE PAUL MOER TRIO”—Del-Fi DFLP 1212
Pianist Moer has
a
delicate
but
definite and
unhesitating touch. His bass and drum men also
fit into this subtle groove and together they ease
through a lineup of mostly Moer originals with
clever performances. Noteworthy tracks in the 10
tune set include “Azure Blues,” “Short Politician,”
“Moer Or Less” and “We’ll Be Together Again.”
CLASSICAL PICKS OF THE WEEK
MASCAGNI :
“Cavalleria
Rusticana”—Giuletta
Simionetta, Mario Del Monaco,
Corbel MacNeil,
Chorus and Orchestra
of L’Accademia
di Santa
Cecilia, Rome, conducted by Tulio Serafin—Lon-
don OSA 1213
Simionato Del Monaco and Serafin, all of whom
have recorded the short one-act opera (complete
on three sides)
before for other labels, combine
here for a thrilling stereo recording of the work.
Takes its place as a definitive version. Side four
is an interesting Italian song recital by Del Mon-
aco
in which he
sings
“Dicitencello Vuje” and
“Torna A Surriento” among others.
BEETHOVEN: Concerto in D Major
for
Violin
and Orchestra—Yehudi Menidiin,
violin. The Vi-
enna Philharmonic Orchestra conducted by Chn-
stantin Silvestri—Capitol SG 7229
Menuhin's long association with the Beethoven
concerto culminates in
this
stereo remake which
makes his mastery of the piece seem even more
remarkable. His full flowing tone
is enhanced by
the new stereo sound and it obsoletes his previous
mono recording of
it, A staple classical item.

Newport Must Decide
By Dec. 20 On '61
Festival
NEW YORK—Whether there
will be
a Newport
Jazz
Festival
next
year
rests in action by the city of Newport
by
Dec.
20. At
a meeting
with
city
officials last week, Louis L.
Lorillard,
the
tobacco-heir who
is
president
of
the
festival,
set
the
deadline
as
the
last
possible
date
to
start
planning
the
’61
fete.
After
college-youth
rioting
during
the
festival
last
July
4th
weekend,
the city revoked the festival’s license,
ending the
festival before
its
sched-
uled
completion
and
bringing
public
pressure against another festival.
The
festival
instituted
a
$450,000
damage
suit
against the
city for
its
action. The suit, however, was not dis-
cussed at last week’s meet.
Lorillard
and
festival
treasurer
James
P. Maloney also gave the
city
a
financial
report which
stated
that
$142,000 was needed
to meet the fes-
tival’s
obligations.
According
to
Lorillard,
$45,000
is
needed for ticket refunds to those who
could not attend the canceled perform-
ances; $72,000 for commercial obliga-
tions
including payment
to
perform-
ers
under
contract
who
did
not
perform due to the canceled perform-
ances;
$25,000
to
start
next
year’s
festival.
The
council
promised
Lorillard
it
would
hold
further
meets—including
a possible public hearing—on return-
ing the festival.

Elektra Inks Bob Gibson
NEW YORK—Folk singer Bob Gibson
has been signed to an exclusive long-
term
contract with
Elektra
Records,
it was
disclosed
last week. The pact
calls
for
a minimum
of two albums
per year over the term of the agree-
ment.
Gibson
has
concertized
widely
and
has made
a
successful
previous
recording for Elektra of “Ski Songs.”
Elektra president Jac Holzman and
chief
engineer Mark Abramson
will
fly to the west coast in mid-December
to
supervise
the
first
sessions.
Ex-
pected release date
is March, 1961.
novations
in
merchandising
and
an
aggressive distributing organization.”
The
re-organization
also
involves
the
appointment
of
Albert
Fishman
as
Epic’s
national
sales
manager.
Fishman* previously with Columbia as
branch manager, district
sales mana-
ger,
and
most
recently
as
Master-
works
sales manager, will be respon-
sible for Epic’s
field sales efforts and
sales
administration. He
reports
di-
rectly to Gallagher.
Continuing
in
their
Epic
positions
are Charles
Shicke,
field
sales mana-
ger; Herbert Linsky, national promo-
tion
manager;
Ricky
von
Seekman,
sales administration manager. All re-
port directly
to Fishman.
William
Levy,
formerly
with
Col-
umbia, has been appointed Epic direc-
tor
of A&R
and
merchandising,
re-
porting directly
to
Gallagher.
In his new responsibility. Levy will
coordinate the activities of the label’s
A&R
staff
consisting
of
Miss
Jane
Friedman,
classical
A&R;
James
Fogelsong, popular A&R; Mike
Ber-
niker, pop A&R;
C. Snyder, interna-
tional A&R.
Levy will also be responsible for the
coordination
of
Epic
merchandising
programs with the label’s department
of
creative
services and manufactur-
ing. He
will
also work
directly with
Fogelsong and Berniker in producing
and
acquiring
Epic
singles
product.
Gallagher
said
that Epic would
rely
on
independently
produced
masters
for many of their singles releases.
Fishman and Levy will also be
re-
sponsible
for
the
development
of
monthly
release
schedules
and
mer-
chandising programs with the
assist-
ance
of
Epic’s
complete
sales
and
A&R departments.
“In addition
to the Epic
field
staff
as
outlined,”
Gallagher
said,
“I
will
also make available the assistance of
Columbia’s
field
sales force of twelve
men whenever their services can pro-
vide efficiencies and economies toward
Epic’s future success.”

######## 1960-12-10 p44  [jazz\s*messengers]
SWEDEN
SCANDINAVIA
BFB has prolonged
its contract with
singer Gunnar Wiklund
for another
3-year period. The same label has also inked Ingeborg Nyberg. Ake Wassing,
who is well known here for two novels of a biographical type, has recorded his
own song, “Du Inspirerar Mig” (You’re Inspiring Me)
for BFB. Wassing, be-
fore he became famous as an author, had
several songs on the Swedish
hit
parade. His new song
is published here by Reuter & Reuter, and according to
Lennart Reuterskiold, the song has great possibilities in the world market.
Scandinavian Record Clompany
(Sonet,
Storyville,
Roulette,
Colpix,
Gazell
and other labels)
brings Art Blakey and The Jazz Messengers to Stockholm,
where they will give concerts in the Concei't Hall on December 6. According to
Gunnar Bergstrom, head of the company, Sonet’s next great hit here will be
Umberto Bindi’s Italian recording of “11 Nostro Concerto.” Southern Music js
the Swedish publisher of this song. A Swedish lyric has been written by Karin
Wollgast.
Stig Andersson, composer and writer of “Klas-Goran,”
told The Cash Box
that he now handles a music publishing firm, Bens Music, which handles Paul
Anka’s music company, Spanka, in Scandinavia. Bens also brings out some Con-
tinental songs. Bens expects a
lot from the Greek song “Hyssos”
(Love) by
Manos Hadjidakis, writer of “Never On Sunday.”
Helge Roundqvist of Cupol Records said that his company will release Tobin
Matthews’ hit “Ruby Duby Du” in Scandinavia. The
original recording
is
re-
leased in the U.S. by Chief Records.
The Dutch singing brothers Blue Diamonds, singing on Philips, might come
to Sweden for TV appearances
in near future. Philips also reports that they
have
contracted
a new
singing Swedish group
calling themselves Four Hits.
Anders Holmstedt of EMI reported that MGM just released the original ver-
sion of the theme music from the TV serial “Bonanza,” played by David Rose
and his orchestra. This melody has quickly become a bestseller here where the
show
is one of the most popular of the Swedish TV viewers. Another record
which looks like a
hit here
is Frank
Sinatra’s “OT MacDonald” on
Capitol.
Since there’s no doubt that “Save The Last Dance For Me” will become a hit
here, EMI has rushed out
its answer, Damita
Jo’s version
of
“I’ll Save The
Last Dance For You” on Mercury and the sales figures look very good already,
reports Holmstedt.
Ivar Nordstrom of Edition Odeon, EMI’s publishing house, reports that the
firm has had great success with a French song, “Rose” written by Henri Salva-
dor. Three Swedish recordings, and several French versions, are already avail-
able here. Nordstrom has just returned from a visit in Oslo, where he discussed
the Norwegian release of some new songs by Swedish singer-composer Thore
Skogman.
There will not be any strike in Swedish radio and TV. The negotiations ended
the
other day with both
parties coming
to an agreement,
just a few hours
before the
strike would have
started.
Swedish TV presented a new serial the other day “Plattparaden”
(Disk Pa-
rade), a Swedish version of the British TV program “Disc Jockey Jury.” In the
program, records are played for a jury of four which after listening are sup-
posed to say if they think they will be hits or not. According to a newspaper
interview with some record executives, trade people liked the program and the
idea behind
it.
NORWAY
The sale of “Froken Johansen Og Jeg” (Miss Johansson and I), the Swedish
song which has been topping the Norv/egian best sellers during the last weeks,
continues satisfactory, reports Rolf Syversen of Iversen & Frogh A/S in Oslo.
The record has already been awarded a silver disk after the sale of 25,000, but
there
is great chance that
this record
also
will get a golden
disk, when the
50,000 peak has been reached. These awards are in Noinvay distributed by the
daily paper Arbeiderbladet and started January
1 this year. So far, the paper
has given out eight silver awards but there has not yet been any gold award.
EMI expects Inger Jacobsen to become the first gold disk winner—if the present
sale of the record continues, and
it might do so now when the Christmas sales
start.
A Norwegian record of a Norwegian song appears on the
best-sellers here
this week. It is “Hjemlandets sang” (The Song Of My Country), sung by Bjorg
and Per Gunnar on Triola. According to J6rg.-Fr. Ellertsen of Egil Monn Iver-
sen A/S, it is something of a sensation when a record which has not appeared
among the top twenty of Radio Luxembourg becomes a best seller at the Nor-
wegian market.

GERMANY
Heidi BruhTs first English record will be released in England on January
2,
just in time for her TV appearance there. It will be an English version of her
big
hit, “Wir Wollen Niemals Auseinander Geh’n,” which went far over the
half million mark here.
Lale Anderson has passed the 300,000 mark with her recording
of “Never
On Sunday,” which
still tops the charts here.
Marlene Dietrich’s new LP
is moving well here. She wrote
2
of the texts
herself under the name Max Kolpe. Not only
a pseudo-name, but a pseudo-
gender.
Germany finally has
its Brenda Lee. Fourteen year old Gitte from Denmark
has done a terrific job on the Lee
hit, “I’m Sorry,”
in German.
Gitte, a jazz-
loving
youngster,
is
at
present
filming
in
Scandinavia. Lou Von
Burg,
the
Dutch quizmaster with the big voice,
is giving up
his German speaking ver-
sion of “A Dollar A Second”
this year.
He’ll open up next year with
a new
show
called “Music, Music, Music” which
is probably a takeoff on the “Stop
The Music” quiz
idea. Lou
is also selling like wildfire with his new Electrola
records.
English
star
Laurie London, who topped
the
charts with
“He’s
Got The
Whole World In His Hands” a few seasons ago,
is concentrating hard on the
German market. He’s set for a TV shot in Zurich along with other stars on a
show
called “Show Boat.” A few days ago in
his hotel room, the telephone
rang. Laurie picked
it up and said “Here
is London.” The voice at the other
end
said “No, No, No,
I
didn’t want a long
distance
call,
I
just wanted
to
speak
to room 408.”
The Quincy Jones Big Band will be presented on German TV on December
5
in a program presented by jazz
critic Joachim Ernst Berendt. The German
public will be treated to a full half hour of the Jones brand of music. Lolita,
whose “Sailor” is in the top 20 in The Cash Box charts, has her first LP on the
market.
Polydor
is
featuring many
of
its
artists
on
single
LP’s, which
is
really
something new for Germany. Peter Alexander, Peter Kraus, and several other
pop stars now have LP’s under their own names.
“Mustafa”
is leading the charts in Yugoslavia. This song
is getting plenty
of “behind the iron curtain”
action.
Polydor has signed the Paraguay-Argentina group “Los Amigos Del Amam-
bay”
to an
exclusive
contract.
There’ll be an LP on the market here
soon.
They have
also recorded an LP with the South Rhodesian group “The
City
Quads.”
Rainer Bertram has been signed to sing “Itsy Bitsy” in a new film here.
Elvis Presley sang in German and the wheels started turnin’. Elvis’ recording
of “Wooden Heart,” based on an old German folk song, with one chorus sung
in German has been culled from the LP, “GI Blues” and has been released as
a
single by RCA. Polydor followed immediately by cutting the record com-
pletely in German by former GI Gus Backus, who recorded lead with the Del
Vikings
in the states and
is
currently making chart action with
his version
of Johnny Preston’s “Running Bear.”
Sam
Cooke’s “Chain Gang”
is being recorded by the Teddies
on
Polydor.
Ralph Maria Siegel’s Jupiter Records has released an instrumental version of
the Udo Jurgens hit “Jenny” featuring trumpet player Roy
Etzel. Ariola
is
starting something new. On its record jacket is a printed juke box strip ready
for the box. The operator has just to buy the record, cut out the strip and set
it and the record in the machine. The first record with the new cover is “A Fel-
low Can Dream What He Wants” from Danish teen duo Jan and Kjeld.
Germany’s biggest record firm, Deutsche Grammophon, has formed
its own
distribution organization. The firm has always been represented by the parent
firm, the Siemens Corporation. Label feels that it will now have better control
over the sale of its product.
Ralf Bendix moved into 2nd place in the Stuttgart “Schlager Scala” show
after one play on his new recording of “Venus Waltz,” reports Peter Rebhuhn
from Rolf Budde Music.
The trade
is
still talking about
the romance between Connie Francis and
German teenage
idol Peter Kraus.
It seems that Vienna was the focal point
of the romance, but when the ocean separated the two youngsters, the romance
cooled
off considerably.

Radio

or for the German
speaking
lands.

held
a

Gina Dobra, the young Bulgarian

many,

ALL THAT JAZZ
Cadence Records
is finally getting set to launch its Candid jazz label
affiliJ
ate. Candid topper Bob Altshuler said that the label will be handled through thel
regular Cadence distributors but introduction of the
line
will involve a novel!
promotion. The initial release, skedded for January, will be sent to jazz dealers
in a package
similar
to
Atlantic’s
recently-issued “Southern
Folk
Heritage
Series,” each album
in
its regular jacket but the entire release enclosed in a
special package, the liner of which will detail the label’s ideals and directions.
Altshuler again reiterated the Candid recording program
: to record in all fields
of jazz—modern,
swing,
blues,
etc.;
something
for
every type
of
jazz
fan.
Altshuler
said
that any
jazz
dealers who
would
like
to
receive
the
initial
presentation package, and all jazz disk jockies wishing to be put on the label’s
mailing list, to write him c/o the Cadence address.
Shelly Manne
(drums). Red
Mitchell
(bass)
and Pete Condoli
(trumpet)
have been added to the orchestra now scoring the “West Side
Story” sound-
track. The
trio, under the
direction
of Johnny
Green,
will
provide
specialljl
written backing for three of the film’s numbers, as well as
fill in intermittently
throughout the score. The hope from this end is, that the great Leonard Bern-
stein
score, which does provide some touchy problems for
film producing,
is
not tampered -with too much.

Everest Records has been awarded the Grand Prix Du Disque De Jazz 1960
by the Hot Club of France, the country’s leading jazz organization. The award
is for the company’s recording of the Jo Jones
'Trio, and also for the best jazz
soloist
release—Charlie
Shavers. Everest seems
to be
really
cleaning up
in
France
this
year,
as
they were
also awarded Le Grand
Prix
National Du
Disqu from the Academy of French Recordings
(classical)
for
its release
of
Lili
Boulander’s works
performed by
Igor
Markevitch
and
the Lamoureux
Orchestra.
Another new label to bow soon
is ABC-Paramount’s Impulse jazz
line. The
line brings AmPar back into the jazz
field, in which
it was pretty active sev-
eral years ago. Heading up the label will be AmPar A&R man. Creed Taylor,
who already has cut sessions with Ray Charles,
J.
J. Johnson & Kai Winding
and the
Gil Evans
ork. The albums, each
in a double-fold “deluxe” package,
will
hit the market next month under price tags
of $4.98
(mono)
and
$5.98
(stereo). A
special feature of the Impulse schedule
will be the
release of a
33
1/3 stereo single for juke boxes from each album. Unlike the above men-
tioned
Candid
outlook.
Impulse
will
concentrate
on
recording modern
jazz
artists only. According to the company’s advance notices,
it will operate as a
completely separate
enterprise from ABC-Paramount,
so
as
not
to
confuse
the consumer with the AmPar pop
line. It was just this type of disassociation
which was behind the setting up of a completely separate corporate image for
AmPar’s highly successful Grand Award and Command labels.
The Modern Jazz Quartet again take to the stage of Carnegie Hall to pre-
sent
its case for the blending of jazz and classical influences. On
Dec., 14, the
Quartet will take part in the Orchestra
of America’s presentation of George
Antheil’s “Jazz Symphony,” Arthur
Kreutz’s
“Dixieland
Concerto
for Sym-
phony Orchestra” and Gunther
Schuller’s “Concertino
for Jazz Quartet and
Orchestra.” The performance of this last piece will be the first New York per-
formance of
it; continuing
Schuller’s exploration
into
his
“third stream”
of
American music. The piece
is planned for 75% improvisation for the quartet
but contains completely written out parts for the orchestra.
Atlantic’s Gary Kramer was given the duty of ushering eight young Ger-
man amateur jazz musicians around New York during their tour of the coun-
try. The musicians, winners of the German Amateur Jazz Festival in the tra-
ditional and modern categories, were feted
to a reception at Birdland while
they were in this city, on the first leg of their journey. Quipped Kramer, when
informed of his being picked as host, “I guess I’m the only jazz figure in the
city who can speak German.”
Prestige Records admits to varying degrees of reception to
its new Swings-
ville, Moodsville and Bluesville
series, but states that overall acceptance has
been very gratifying. In response to measured research, the similarity among
the
jacket designs
of
the
three
labels
will
soon
cease. Work has bgun
on
changing the Swingsville covers to a basically photo-dominating cover, while
design work is under way to give Moodsville a new look
too. Also, the com-
pany disclosed
it will step up activity of its Prestige International
line, pro-
viding increased opportunities for new domestic and foreign folk artists to re-
cord. Folklorist Ken Goldstein
is currently seeking out talent in this
field.
JAZZ JOTTINGS.

.
. Lambert, Hendricks & Ross swing
into the
village
Vanguard Dec. 13 for a three-week holiday gig. They’ll alternate with the Ray
Bryant Trio. L, H & R have now taken to Ellington with a new Columbia LP
of the great man's music. ... We record with deepest sympathy, the loss
of
Gerry Mulligan’s father.

. Gene Quill, reed man with Mulligan, was mai-ried

song-and-dance
act.

.
. Max Roach
takes
his
Quintet
into

Cloister Dec. 12 for two weeks.
.
.
. Gene Krupa, stricken with a slight heart
attack during his last week at the London House, had to cancel all engagements
for the rest of the year on doctor’s orders.

piano, Teddy Wilson, finishing up three weeks at New York’s Composer East.

Sets 3 Album Issue
HOLLYWOOD—Indigo

of

level.
MRIA Committees To
Watchdog Standards
CHICAGO — Ten
subcommittees
to
watchdog standards for magnetic tape
recorders were named
last week by
the Magnetic Recording Industry As-
sociation.
C.
J. LeBel of New York, chairman
of MRIA’s standards committee,
said
that the “tremendous strides made by
manufacturers
to tape recording ma-
chines
in
the
past
two
years
have
pointed to the need for a constant re-
view
of standards to assure the con-
tinued growth of tape music systems
for
the home
and
for
tape
in
audio
visual education.”
Engineers have been named
to
the
following
subcommittees:
measure-
ment of frequency response, distortion
&
signal
to
noise
ratio, wow &
flut-
ter &
speed
tolerance, power output,
stereo
characteristics
(crosstalk,
dif-
fei'ential phase
lift), head
character-
istics, standard reproducing character-
istics,
head
dimensions,
track
dimensions and tape and
reel dimen-
sions.

a

No '60 WB Xmas Product
Explained By Conkling
BURBANK, CALIF.—In an effort not
to “further satiate” the record market,
Warner
Bros.
Records
will
not
re-
lease any pop singles or LP’s on Yule-
tide themes, prexy James B. Conkling
announced
last week.
“Our
decision
not
to
release
any
Christmas,”
Conkling
explained,
“is
influenced
by
our
policy
to
release
only
a few
selected albums we
feel
our distributors can adequately devote
some promotional
effort
to.”
This
policy, the exec
said, appears
to have met with
the
“wholehearted
approval” of WB’s thirty-two distribs
thi'oughout the country.
“Distributors have
told
us,”
Conk-
ling concluded, “that the largest per-
centage
of sales comes from popular
material
not
devoted
to
the
holiday
season except for that rare occasional
Christmas
hit. We want
to keep our
distributors
and
all
dealers
happily
occupied with a greater rate of turn-
over on the entire Warner Bros, cata-
log,
rather
than
relegate
special
ef-
fort to seasonal material.”

porary
injunction
against

Hampton’s Glad Records.

Reviews
vnspH
“A SWINGIN’ DANCE DATE”—Peter
Palmer
and His Orchestra—Mercury 60166
The Palmer ork in an infectious dance session.
Set to a catchy shuffle-beat, the ork and blended
wordless voices perform such standards as “Blue
Moon,”
“Heart
and
Soul,”
“The
Continental,”
“They Didn’t Believe Me” and “But Not For Me.”
This
is music much
in the Ray
Conniff manner
and should have substantial commercial appeal.
“THE TIMELESS ONES A LA TOUZET”—Rene
Touzet—GNP 52
One of the few remaining orks catering to cha
cha cha disk fans, Touzet’s ensemble offers pleas-
antly danceable cha cha cha arrangements
of a
dozen “timeless” sturdies. Included in the set are
“September Song,” ’’Poinciana,” “Stardust,” “My
Reverie” and “Bewitched.” A chorus adds
lyrics
to many of the tracks. Colorful dance session.
’’CHUBBY’S
RASCALS”—Chubby
Jackson—
ABC-Paramount ABC-370
Top-rated
jazz
basist turned TV
kiddie show
host. Chubby Jackson brings
his
antics
to
disk
with
the
help
of
Barbara
Lyons
and
the
Jack
Halloran
Singers. They
all contribute
to produc-
ing
an
effectively
entertaining
kiddie
session
which
features
a
dozen
original
tuneful
ditties
angled at the moppets.
“TELL THE WORLD ABOUT THIS”—The Tar-
riers—Atlantic 8042
The
Tarriers are one
of the most electrifying
ensembles in their idiom. Much of excitement they
generate
arises
from
their
choice
of
material,
which leans heavily on Negro spirituals and blues.
And their dramatic, jazz-like interpretations
are
arranged
to
get
the
biggest impact
out
of
the
work. Here they indulge themselves in readings of
“Bald Headed Woman,” “This Train,” “Lonesome
Traveler,” “Jordan’s River” and “Take This Ham-
mer.” Solid folk-singing offering.
“GOIN’
PLACES”—Casey
Anderson—Elektra-
192
Anderson’s
Elektra
debut
immediately
elicits
the truth that the lad
is definitely “goin’ places.”
He has a strong, rich attractive voice and a dy-
namic vocal personality which he invests into this
program
of
self-penned
and
otherwise
gathered
folksongs. Among them
are “900
Miles,” “Wait-
ing For Jo Johnny,” “Pastures of Plenty” and the
inevitable “John Henry.”
“IRELAND, MY IRELAND”—Eileen Donaghy—
Epic LF 18004
As
pert
a
coleen
as
ever sang
of
Ireland
is
Eileen Donaghy. With a cute brogue and an
at-
tractive
soprano
voice
she
renders
such
senti-
mental
delights
as “Homes
of
Donegal,”
“Girld
With the Brogue,” “Let Mister Maguire Sit Down”
and
“Rose
of Aranmore.”
Will
appeal
to many
more than just those of Irish descent.
“HYMNS
OF
THE
CATHOLIC
CHURCH”—
Choir of St. Patrick’s Cathedral, Melbourne, con-
ducted by Rev. Dr. Percy Jones—ABC-Paramount
ABC-349
The
St. Patrick’s “a capella” choir, composed of
48 boys and
12 men, has a distinguished history
dating back
100
years.
In
this album,
the
choir
sings 14 famous Catholic hymns, including “Holy
God We Praise Thy Name,” “Soul of My Saviour,”
“Faith of Our Fathers,” “Hail Queen of Heaven”
and “Lourdes Hymn.”
Excellent recording;
par-
ticularly timely for the Christmas season.
JAZZ
PICK
OF THE WEEK
“MUDDY WATERS AT NEWPORT”—Chess LP
1449
It was an afternoon blues concert which closed
out the ill-fated 1960 Newport Jazz Festival and
the
big
attraction for that
concert was the ap-
pearance of Muddy Waters’ band. In these return-
to-roots days
in
jazz, here
is
a man who never
left the roots—he drives home the soulful, unvar-
nished messages of both the country and big-city
blues
scenes
in a passionate, earthy fervor. The
recorded performances include
“I Got My Brand
On You,” “Tiger In Your Tank,” “I Feel So Good,”
“Got My Mojo Working” and four others. Of infi-
nite interest to jazz and blues buffs.

“THE RAMSEY LEWIS TRIO IN CHICAGO”—
Argo LP 671
Chicago’s Blue Note
Club, where
this
set was
cut, played host to the Lewis Trio just before it
shut
its doors. A warm, personal, friendly place,
it was easy to quickly establish rapport with the
audience, which is just what Lewis does here. The
group
lends
its sunny disposition
to “Old
Devil
Moon,”
“I’ll Remember April,” “But Not For Me”
and
“What’s
New.”
Good,
listenable,
uncompli-
cated trio jazz.
“BILL HOLMAN’S GREAT BIG BAND”—Capi-
tol ST 1464
Holman turns in his best writing for disks yet;
a
great
big swinging
session
in which
he
calls
upon his talents to invest a bunch of oldies with
modern new life. This is hot stuff for both pop and
jazz buyers. Notice the unusual section writing in
“Shadrack,”
“The
Moon
is
Blue,”
“Old
Man
River,” “June
Is Busting Out
All Over” and “In
a Sentimental Mood.”
“SINGIN’ &
SWINGIN’ ’’—Betty
Roche—Pres-
tige LP 7187
Betty Roche marks her return from retirement
with this recording. Vocalist with many bands of
the
’30’s,
lastly with
Ellington
in the
’40’s,
she
transcends
the
interim
years with very modern
performances of a collection of standards. Accom-
panied by a
solid small combo, she tears
it up, in
the upbeat and on
ballods, with “Come Rain Or
Come Shine,” “Day By Day,” “Where Or When”
and “Billie’s Bounce.” Jazz purists will appreciate
the talent here.
“THAT’S RIGHT!”—Nat Adderley
and the Big
Sax Section—Riverside 9330
Nat, now drawing raves with big brother’s Can-
nonball’s quintet, heads this date here, which finds
his
lyrical cornet superimposed over sax
section
work by Cannonball, Jimmy Heath, Charlie Rouse,
Yusef Lateef and Tate Houston. A bright, free-
wheeling blowing date. Credit Jimmy Heath with
the bulk of the writing. Tunes include “The Old
Country,” “You Leave Me Breathless” and “That’s
Right!” Has the Adderley name drawing power.
“SPEAKIN’ MY PIECE”—Horace Parian Quintet
—Blue Note 4043
Pianist
Parian,
with
the
Turrentine
brothers
completing
the
front
line,
works
in
various
grooves, the most satisfying being the blues-roots
area.
This
quintet
session, Parian’s
second
date
for the label, upholds the pianist as being one of
the brighter new talents on the scene. It’s a swing-
ing,
striking
session.
Tunes
include
“Wadin’,”
“Ratsus,” “Borderline” and other originals.

“THE FRANK WESS

This Prestige series offers the most consistently
