The Controversial Mr. Coleman
CHICAGO—Ornette Coleman and his Quartet, shown here
in performance at
New York’s
Five
Spot where
the group
first
attracted
attention
in an
ex-
tended engagement
last
year, has
just completed
a
rai’e,
nine day
Chicago
appearance at the
Cloister. The controversial Coleman
is shown
playing
his
white plastic
alto
sax, along with Don Cherry and his pocket-sized
Pakistini
trumpet, Eddie Blackwell on drums and Scott LaFaro on bass.
Charlie Byrd, unamplified guitar virtuoso, has been
set for
a twelve week
tour of South and Central America under the auspices of the President’s Spe-
cial International Program for Cultural Presentations. The Program, admin-
mtered by the American National Theatre and Academy (ANTA) for the State
impartment, has slated Byrd to leave March 15th accompanied by Keter Betts
(bass) and Buddy Deppenschmidt
(drums). Byrd, who
has won wide
critical
and public accolades for his jazz and
classical work on Washington Records
and
his consistent work
at Washington,
D.C.’s Showboat Lounge
(his home
base), was selected for the tour “because of the feeling that his ability to per-
form with equal mastery in both classical and jazz styles, makes him a perfect
arnbassador of good will, enabling him to reach the natives of
all these coun-
tries m programs that will combine the music of the old world with that of the
n^.
’ This quote, corny as it may appear, actually does make sense
if you con-
sider that jazz had made
little headway with our South American neighbors,
and that the unamplified guitar, a very popular instrument in these countries,
seems a
logical way of introducing the medium. Previous to Byrd’s
tour, he
will journey to New York for a one-week engagement at the Village Vanguard,
opening January 3rd. He has also just cut his fourth jazz album for Washing-
ton Records.
Ever hear of a Jazz Tree? Well New York City has one! The tree, a Ginkgo
by species, was donated to the city by the Modern Jazz Quartet for planting
on 57th Street as part of the city’s
official “Salute to Seasons” project.
It will
thrive on 57th St. (between 6th & 7th Aves.) as “a living symbol of the growth
of jazz as an American art form.” It was donated by the MJQ at special cere-
monies Dec. 12th as one of twelve trees to be planted on the same
site—the
center of the international music scene—donated by various representatives of
the music world.
Candid Records, Cadence’s soon-to-bow jazz affiliate, is busy signing up talent.
Latest to be inked is the Toshiko-Mariano Quartet. The Quartet, headed by new
star Japanese pianist Toshiko and husband Charlie Mariano, former lead
alto
with Stan Kenton, has already cut one LP for the label, skedded tentatively for
February release. Also
pacted
is tenorman Booker
Ervin,
a member
of the
Charlie Mingus group, whom Candid’s Bob Altshuler calls 'The New tenor star.
He is currently in the process of preparing his first starring LP, though he has
already been cut on the “Freedom Now Suite” LP. Others being recorded for
future Candid release include Steve Lacy,
in a program of Cecil Taylor and
Thelonious Monk tunes; Don
Ellis, Clark Terry and Benny Bailey, trumpeter
with the Quincy Jones ork. Of particular interest
is a forthcoming album by
Lightning Hopkins, believed to be the first studio recorded work by the great
blues singer. Candid cornered him while he was
in New York recently for a
concert appearance.
NPA (Nordisk Polyphon Aktieselskab), Copenhagen, Denmark, which handles
distribution of the United Artists, London, Fontana (Columbia), Decca, Coral
and Brunswick
lines, has issued a catalog titled very idiomatically American:
“Nothin’ But Jazz,” which lists all its albums available. An interesting facet of
the catalog is that it is divided into sections labeled traditional, modern, swing,
blue, and Louis Armstrong. The old man rates a section all to himself.
The Jazz Arts
Society, an incorporated non-profit educational organization,
presented
its Inaugural Concert Dec. 4th
at Hunter College Assembly
Hall.
Performers were the Cannonball Adderley Quintet, Lambert, Hendricks & Ross
and the John Handy Quartet with Leonid Hambro. The Society has set as
its
purpose to establish a center to “foster and promote the understanding, crea-
tion and study of jazz as an American art form;
to house and provide mate-
rials—historical and
current—such
as
manuscripts,
books,
recordings,
sheet
music, photos and films in permanent archives; to encourage talented scholars,
students and musicians; to further harmonious intergroup relations through the
art of jazz which appeals to people of all groups and ages; and (what we think
the most important) to provide a means of reaching the teen-ager through the
medium of jazz on the basis of which both the juvenile and society can find a
common ground of acceptance.” The Society’s address
is 20 West 43rd
Street,
New York 36, N.Y.

An open house celebration was held Dec. 15 at the Presidential Arms Hotel
in Washington,
D.C.
to
honor WWDC
personality
Art Brown’s
twenty-five
years in radio. The party took place during Art’s broadcast hours to
let listen-
ers unable to attend in on the festivities. Brown has consistently maintained a
top rating for his morning show and continues to receive letters from persons
who have been faithful listeners for the quarter century.
.
.
Also from WWDC
comes the news that ten radio and television stations throughout the country
have joined
in WWDC’s
editorial campaign
to procure the right to vote for
President of the U.S. for District of Columbia residents. The campaign, initiated
by WWDC president Ben Strouse, is urging stations to promote the passage of
The happy combination of four boys
and a girl that makes up the Miracles
came
about by
accident.
The
group,
originally
an
all
male
quintet,
had
been singing around its native Detroit
when
a
split-up was
inevitable upon
the
draft
of
one
member
into
the
Army.
It was at that time that a friend of
the group had arranged for them
to
audition for Berry Gordy,
Jr., Tamla
Records head. Pressed for time and a
fifth member, the four needed a Mira-
cle. They came up with Claudette Rog-
ers, sister of the Army-bound former
member. Out of this meeting and sub-
sequent
hearing by Gordy came
the
group’s
recording
of
“Bad
Girl,”
which
started
them
on
their
way.
“Shop Around” has garnered them na-
tional
recognition
as an up-and-com-
ing vocal group.
The
individual members
are:
Bill
Robinson,
Ronald
White,
Warren
Moore, Robert Rogers and
Claudette
(Mrs.
Bill
Robinson).
All
natives
of
Detroit,
their average age
is
19.
The
Viscount's
The
Viscounts
are
another
local
group that made good—all five mem-
bers
hailing
from
New
Jersey.
Groundwork for the current setup was
laid by Bobby and
Joe
Spivak, who
had a guitar-novelty instrumental act
going
when
they
were
only
seven
years old. Later on they added Harry
Haller
(sax),
Clark
Smith
(drums)
and Larry Vecchio (organ and piano).
The
boys
were
discovered
playing
in
a
local
club
by
Madison
Records
prexy Larry
Uttal who
immediately
signed them to a disk pact. This part-
nership
resulted
in
“Harlem
Noc-
turne,” “Night Train” and now “Wa-
bash Blues.”
An
exciting
in-person
attraction,
the
Viscounts
spend
most
of
their
time
now
on
personal
appearance
tours throughout the country in clubs,
concerts and
hops.

. WLEE-Richmond, Va. jockies Art Lane, Mickey Kahn, Gene Lov-
ing and Dave Lyman recently staged the
First Annual Grand
National
Tri-
cycle Race before cheering thousands
in Richmond. The race, held
in behalf
of the Marine Reserve Toys for Tots campaign, found Loving streaking across
the finish
line
in
first place. The tricycles used
in the race, plus thousands of
other toys, were donated by WLEE listeners for the drive.
.
.
. KDKA-Pitts-
burgh
is once again conducting
its Penny-A-Month fund drive for Children’s
Hospital. Listeners are asked to contribute 124 for the charity. This phase of
the
Pittsburgh
Press
Old Newsboys
drive
for
crippled
children
has drawn
nearly $18,000 over the past two holiday seasons.
Cleveland’s
first building designed and
built
exclusively
as
a radio
station
opened last week as
the new home
of WERE AM and FM. The
building,
a
$500,000
two-story
structure
located
at
1500
Chester
Awe.,
contains
10,()00
square
feet
of space featuring the most advanced developments
in
radio.
It
includes
four
studios
with
individual
control rooms
and
a
custom-designed
audio
system,
built by General
Electric,
allowing
for AM-AM
stereo
(com-
patible single sideband) and FM-FM stereo (multiplex)
to be broadcast simul-
taneously. A weather tower
is mounted atop the building and connected
elec-
tronically with
a
panel
in
the newsroom
to
give
up-to-the-minute weather
readings. The design also allows for expansion.
.
.
. WDON-Washington, D.C.
has announced plans for a $50,000 expansion plan which includes the installa-
tion of a new, more powerful transmitter and the transfer of the studios and
exec offices to larger facilities after Jan.
1.
.
.
. With the blizzard that hit the
eastern part of the U.S. last week there was at least one person who retained
a sense of humor. Among the numerous announcements of cancellations, post-
ponements, school closings and road
closings, WWDC disk jockey Fred Fiske
noticed
one
devilish memo which
read:
“and
due
to
the
inclement weather,
Christmas has been postponed
until Jan.
1.”
.
.
. Harry Neumann, WAAT-
Trenton, broadcast his show for an
entire week from a
local bomb shelter
in
behalf of a
civil defense campaign.
(Actually he was just hiding from record
promotion men.)
.
.
.
Joel Sebastian reports great reception
to
his work
at
WXYZ-Detroit. Membership
in his Hi-Fi Club, which he emcees over the
air,
has snowballed to 30,000 card-carrying members.
.
.
. WALG-Albany, Ga., the
Johnny Reb
Station,
is charging
listeners
five
cents for each record
request
made. The money
will be used
to purchase food for needy people.
.
.
. Rick
Shaw,
disk jockey at WCKR-Miami,
is
capitalizing on some
station
errors.
When
printing
their weekly record
survey, numerous
errors were made,
so
Rick is now offering complete stereo rigs to the three people who come up with
the most complete
list of mistakes. Everybody’s got a gimmick.

Chuck Daugherty moves from
the
all-night show
at WXYZ-Detroit
to
an
early morning stint at WQTE, the same city.
.
.
. Singer-pianist Page Morton
brings her radio show into New York via WOR. Show’ll be heard every
Sat.
nite beginning Dec.
24.
.
.
. WCUE-Akron, Ohio has reshuffled
its
staff to co-
ordinate
with
its new programming
concept.
They
call
it
“Million
Dollar
Music”-—a middle
of the road pops with accent on gold
records. The
station
originally went with a top
40 format. Newcomers are Mark
Scott, formerly
of WADC-Akron, Bob Martin,
recently released from
the Army,
Joel
Rose,
late
of KYW-Cleveland, and Ken
Court wright, from WERE-Cleveland.
.
.
.
Bob Holmes
is
the new program
director for KLIV
(formerly KSJO), San
Jose, Calif.
.
.
. Bob Powers
is hosting the 3-7 PM stint at WYDE-Birmingham.
Ala. He comes from WGST-Atlanta.
.
.
. We have discovered that there
are
two
jockeys named
Johnny
Bell.
There’s
one
at WINZ-Miami
and
one
at
WHPL-Winchestei’. End
of confusion!
.
.
. Ted Work has rejoined WWDC-
Washington, D.C. as music director. Joe O’Neil, who currently heads the music
dept., is assuming new duties as editorial assistant in the station’s news dept.
.
.
. Effective Jan.
1, WARL-Arlington
will become WAVA (AM & FM) and
will establish formal operation of its new 20,000 watt FM transmitter. No im-
mediate format changes are contemplated.

######## 1960-12-31 p29  [capuchin|blue\s*note\s*40\d\d]
Album
Reviews
“DANCING ON THE SUNSET STRIP”—Eddie
Cano & Jack Costanzo with Tony Martinez and his
Orch.—GNP 44
“Live” recorded at the Crescendo, the package
presents a danceable Latin session with the Mar-
tinez ork featuring Eddie Cano
at the piano and
hongo-conga drummer Jack Costanzo. A pleasant
dance album. Tunes
include “Blue Moon,”
“Bes-
ame
Mucho,”
“The
Continental,”
and
“Babalu.”
“HARMONICA
PERFORMANCES
OF
ALL-
TIME FAVORITES”—Danny Welton—Coral CRL
57347
Among the “all-time favorites” played by Wel-
ton
are
“Tammy,”
“Night
Train,”
“Boogie
Woogie,” “Ruby” and “Peg
O’ My
Heart.” The
harmonicist
is
supported
in
various
ways,
in-
cluding lush strings, bright ork-chorus, and teen-
beat insistency. An enjoyable
disk.
“THE HOTTEST MARIACHI IN MEXICO” —
Mariachi Santana—Request RLP
8041
The Mariachi, native Mexican street troubadors
and musicians who roam the
streets playing na-
tional
(folk)
music, are among the most colorful
Mexican
customs.
Here,
Request
has
recorded
one of these groups in a typical program of songs
and
it
is
a
delightful change
of
pace from
the
usual. Selections include “La Maruca,” “El Jarabe
Tapatio,” “El Borracho,” “La Mancormadora” and
“Espana Cani.”
“FOLK SONGS OF FRANCE”—Monitor MF 339
A valuable
addition
to Monitor’s
extensive
in-
ternational folk catalog
is made by this recording
of French folk songs. Various choruses are used
to
display
the
ancient
songs
representing
the
sections
of
Provence,
Lorraine,
Normandie,
Basque, Champagne,
Languedoc
and
Catalogne.
A treasury of fascinating music. Lyrics and trans-
lations are
gratuitously provided.
“A MUSIC TRAVELOG OF EUROPE”—Arturo
Chaite and his Continental Orchestra—Seeco SP-
4001A
three-disk
set
offering
a musical picture
of
France, Spain and Italy. The Chaite ork
is
effec-
tive in
all three areas, playing the popular music
of each of the three countries on each disk. First
in a series of Seeco travel packages, retailing at
$9.95,
it could prove a sales-getter.
“HALL OF FAME”—Winifred
Atwell—London
LL 3178
Miss
Atwell,
an
accomplished
pianist
in
her
own style, pays tribute to famous pianists of the
past
and
present by
emulating
their
keyboard
style
in tunes associated with them. Her recrea-
tions are amazingly accurate and provide a pleas-
ant
listening
session.
Set includes Fats

Note 4038

“INTRODUCING ROLAND KIRK”—Featuring
Ira
Sullivan—Argo LP 669
Kirk plays tenor sax and two other woodwind
instruments known as the manzello and the strich
(resembling
in tone, soprano and

spectively). These are not used as gimmicks but
as honest media for expression. And the expres-
sion is of the “down-home” soul blues. A convinc-
ing performer. Should interest many jazz fans.

ALL THAT JAZZ
Jazz comes
to
ballet. Or vice-versa. Gunther
Schuller’s composition “Vari-
ants,” commissioned by choreographer George Ballanchine for the New York
Ballet Company will be premiered by the Modern Jazz Quartet with the New
York City Center Ballet Company and orchestra in a series of six performances
beginning January 4th at the City Center.
Schuller’s “Variants”
is
in seven movements, consisting
of an introduction
for orchestra, solo variations for each member of the MJQ, a fifth variation for
ensemble quartet, and the finale with quartet and orchestra. Schuller will con-
duct the orchestra and Melissa Hayden, Diana Adams, and Arthur Mitchell are
among the principal dancers for the jazz-ballet production. This venture
into
the
merging
of
traditional
ballet
and
modern
jazz
represents
a
profluent
achievement in John Lewis’ efforts to extend modern jazz beyond
its present
boundaries.
Freddie Redd, Jackie McLean, Larry Ritchie and Michael Mattos are recreat-
ing their original stage roles
in the film version of “The Connection” for pro-
ducer Lewis Allen. The four musicians, who play piano,
alto, drums and bass
I
respectively, won plaudits for their work
in Jack Gelber’s award-winning
off-
Broadway stage success which deals with junkies and jazz. The
film, shot en-
tirely in New York
(and now being
edited), was
directed by
Shirley Clarke
from Jack
Gelber’s
screenplay.
-
1
Don Elliott (Nutty Squirells, etc.) composed two campaign songs which were
used by winning candidates
in
the recent
elections. He composed
songs
for
Governor-elect Terry Sanford of North Carolina and one for Senator Kennedy
(lyrics by Steve Allen and Jane Harvey). Don has been invited to give a com-
j
mand performance of the Sanford song at the Governor’s Inaugural. So far, no
invitation yet from the White House.
Band
Business bad? You
couldn’t prove
it by Warren Covington and
the
Dorsey Band—either from the bookings or the crowds they draw. Concluding a
1
successful return engagement at New York’s Roosevelt Hotel, the band went
into the studios for five dates for Decca to provide a backlog of material while
they’re out on the road. And they’ll be on the road for quite a while, looking at
their booking dates.
CORE
(Congress of Racial Equality)
is sponsoring the premiere public per-
,
formance of the “Freedom Now” Suite written by Max Roach and Oscar Brown,
j
Jr. The
suite, already recorded for release on Candid Records
(Cadence), will
be heard in concert on Jan. 15th at Art D’Lugoff’s Village Gate with the follow-
ing featured personnel:
the Max Roach Quintet, vocalist Abbey
Lincoln, Ni-
gerian drummer Olatunji (whom Herbie Mann brought back from Africa) and
dancers Helena Walker and Jerome Jeffery. Coleman Hawkins
is featured on
the recorded version of the work, which
is titled “We Insist!”
Candid Records continues to build up
its catalog
of
artists and recordings
while not having even one
release
on
the
market.
Currently, the
label
has
signed Abbey Lincoln;
is preparing to record a program of original albums in J*.
Europe by Lucky Thompson, Kenny Clark, Martial
Solal and Peter Trunk;
is
completing negotiations to release the “Treasury of Field Recordings”
in the
"
best recordings of traditional music); and arranging to record albums by such
artists as Paul Bley, Pee Wee Russell, Phil Woods, Buell Neidlinger and Danny
Barker. From the first views of what the label
is doing we must conclude that
they have made the strongest attempt to have a well-rounded, versatile catalog.
Jack Teagarden was honored Dec. 10th by his home town of Vernon, Texas.
“Jack Teagarden Day” featured a parade and a
civic luncheon headed by the
-
mayor. The real highlight of the day occurred when the grand old man of the
;
trombone sat in with the high school band (which he graduated from) followed
by a two hour concert by Teagarden and his group at the Wilbarger Memorial
Auditorium. Teagarden
is
currently appearing
at
the
Tidelands Motor
Inn,

ALLENTOWN, PA.—A recent edition of WAEB disk jockey Kerm Gregory’s
regular Saturday hop, Castle Rock, saw more than 2,000 teenagers turn out to
welcome Bobby Vee and Zacherley. Vee performed his latest Library hit, “Rub-
ber Ball,” and Zacherley did some of the bits which he does on his Elektra LP,
“Spook Along With Zacherley.”

Engemann Upped
In Capitol A&R;
Wyatt Named Assoc. Producer
HOLLYWOOD—Karl Engemann, for-
merly an associate A&R producer for
Capitol Records, has been named ad-
ministrative
assistant
to
Francis
Scott,
album
director
for
the A&R
division
of the
label.
Announcement
of Engemann’s
ap-
pointment
was
made
last
week
by
Scott, who stated that Engemann will
move
immediately
into
the
newly-
created
post from
his
current
duties
as an associate producer under execu-
tive A&R producer, Ken Nelson.
It
was
also
announced
that
Paul
Wyatt,
formerlv
Capitol’s
editing
supervisor, would
replace Engemann
as
associate
producer under
Nelson.
Engemann, who joined
Capitol
last
March, will take on broader A&R
re-
sponsibilities
under
Scott.
Among
various
duties, Engemann
will
serve
as
album-planning
committee
secre-
tary.
Before
joining
Capitol, Engemann
was
an A&R
producer
for
Warner
Brothers
Records, where
he
handled
most
of
the
film
and
television
per-
sonalities who recorded for that label.
Among his
artists were Connie
Stev-
ens, Edd (“Kookie”) Byrnes, and Clint
Walker.
Wyatt, who joined Capitol last Jan-
uarv, has a broad background
in both
singing and songwriting around Nash-
ville.

Ogden Nash Cuts
Capitol Album
HOLLYWOOD—Poet-social
observer
Ogden Nash has recorded his
first
al-
bum
for
Capitol
Records
after
sign-
ing
an
exclusive
contract
with
the
label,
it was announced
last week by
Alan Livingston, Capitol’s Vice-Presi-
dent
for
Creative
Services.
The album, “Ogden Nash Reads Og-
den Nash.” was recorded in New York
recently under the supervision
of ex-
ecutive A&R producer Andy Wiswell.
Nash reads humorous selections from
his anthology of poems, “Verses from
1929 On.”
According
to
Wiswell,
arranger-
conductor Glenn Osser will provide an
off-beat musical setting for the Nash
readings,
and
the album
will
be
re-
leased later this year.
Ogden Nash’s highly inventive and
American rhymes have become
a na-
tional
institution
since
his
first
col-
lection, “Hard Lines,” put a smile on
the
face
of
the
Depression
in
1931.
The
flood of Nash verse
in both book
and
magazines
has
continued
doing
unorthodox
things
to
and
with
the
English language
for an
entire
gen-
eration.
Nash’s
recording
activities
are added
to a heavy schedule of lec-
ture
appearances
and magazine
con-
tributions.

ing

-

pearances on

the major television

HERE AND THERE:
PHILADELPHIA—Bob Heller and Gene Canter, operators of Flying Record
Dist. Company here, have hired Rothstein Advertising Agency to come up with
a new promotion-exploitation scheme every month of the year. The entire plan
is designated “New Frontiers Of Record Distribution.” For January, the plan
centers on the idea of building a new artist, particularly a female
artist,
HOUSTON—Loads
of
activity for the new year
goin’ on
at Don Robey’s
Duke-Peaeock-Backbeat outfit. A&R chieftains Ed Franks and Joe Scott work-
ing over-time prepping for new James
Little Booker, Clarence “Gatemouth”
Brown,
Little Buck and Bobby Bland
sessions.
Folk-singers Abner &
Linda
(Abner Jay and Linda Sender) have been signed to a long-term pact with the
label. Robey adds that the hottest LP in the catalogue is the Allen Drew comedy
package, “Mr. Speaker.”
LAS VEGAS—Johnny Mathis (and his revue), at the Sahara Hotel for a one
month stint, marks his first date at the Sahara and the first time he had head-
lined a Vegas Show.
.
.
. Singer-pianist Frances Faye, recently pacted by Verve
Records, bowed
at the Flamingo
last week.
MONTREAL—New promotion man for the Canadian diskery, Compo Rec-
ords,
is former CJQC-Quebec deejay Hal Ross.
DETROIT—Berry Gordy, Jr. has hit the answer trail with two new releases,
one by the Satintones, “Tomorrow And Always”—the answer to the Shirelles’
smash, and one by Debbie Dean, “Don’t Let Him Shop Around,” the answer to
the big Miracles deck. Both are on the Motown banner.
.
.
. Leo Cheslak an-
nounced several changes at Cadet distribs. Prexy Harry Levin appointed Alfred
Truax as sales mgr., and has hired two additional salesmen, Morrie Horowitz
and Cy Rott.
PULASKI, TENN.—James Brown, prexy of the Chanson diskery, announced
that he has turned over his hot master of “If I Could Pretend,” by Clentt Gant,
to Leonard Chess’ Chess outfit. Brown adds that he has just signed a wax pact
with
organist—Johnny
Bridgeforth and
that the
label
is on
the lookout for
female singers. Demo’s and photo’s should be sent to the 410 N. 1st St. Pulaski
address.

“YOU ’N ME”—A1 Cohn & Zoot Sims—Mercury
Emarcy SR 60608
In the modern history of jazz, there have been
no two
careers
that have
paralleled
each
other
so
closely,
or have been
so mutually
beneficial
than the careers of A1 Cohn and Zoot Sims. Since
the historic days
of the Herman “Second Herd,”
they have worked
together
so
closely that they
have attained an almost unbelievable understand-
ing and cohesiveness, despite the disparity in their
tenor
styles. Again, on
this record they demon-
strate their solidarity in
a thoroughly enjoyable
blowing date. Selections include “On The Alamo,”
“Angel Eyes,” “You’d Be So Nice To Come Home
To”
and
a
eye-opening
“Improvisation
for Un-
accompanied Saxaphones.”
“CURTIS FULLER”—Blue Note BLP 1583
Fuller, member
of the fantastically successful
Jazztet and one
of
its important cogs,
is
finally
gaining the recognition he deserves as one of the
leading
trombonists
on
the
scene.
This
session
finds
him
leading
a
group
comprised
of
Art
Farmer,
Sonny
Clark,
Louis Hayes and George
Tucker
in
a
consistently
interesting
program.
He
displays
earthiness
_ and
soul
and
a
vital,
surging immediacy to his statements. Farmer
is
a natural standout here too, as
in everything he
does. One of the label’s best in recent issues.
“TENDERLOIN DIXIELAND” — Phil Napoleon
and his Memphis Five—Capitol ST 1535
The
lusty earthiness
of many
of the songs
in
the “Tenderloin”
score make appropriate
fodder
for
the
cannons
of Napoleon’s
two-beat
troupe.
The
trumpeter
leads
the way
in
high-stepping
fashion through
“Artificial Flowers,” “The Army
Of The Just,” “Little Old New York,” “My Gen-
tle
Young
Johnny”
and
eight
others.
For
the
traditionalists.
Hill
“DISCUSSION IN PERCUSSION”—Mike Simp-
son and Orchestra—Mercury PPS 6004
Mercury’s
Perfect
Presence
Sound
Series
is
kicked
off with an
invigorating
display
of
per-
cussion.
Simpson’s
arrangement
of
the
various
assorted
percussion
instruments used
takes
full
advantage of the sound expanse with which Mer-
cury
engineers
have accommodated
him.
Tunes,
mainly
in
the
Latin
style,
include “Say
Si
Si,”
“Three
Little
Words,”
“Listen To The Mocking
Bird” and “What
Is There To Say.” Will
excite
the
stereo
bugs.
“BLUES, CANDY AND
BIG MAYBELLE”—
Savoy MG
14011
The
singer’s
repertoire
runs
from
the
low-
downest meanest blues wails to
the rafter-shak-
ing contagiousness
of
a rhythm &
blues
shout.
This
set includes excellent examples of her mas-
tery of both techniques through a compilation of
some
of
her
big
single
hits.
Lineup
includes
“There, I’ve Said It Again,” “Blues, Early Early,”
“Pitiful,” “Mean to Me” and “Tell Me Who.”
“BLUE & SENTIMENTAL”—Lurlean Hunter—
Atlantic 1344
First Atlantic outing for the songstress pleas-
ingly maintains an unhurried blues pace inclined
toward
the pop-style
area. The only out-and-out
“jazz”
track
is
a
rapid-fire
vocal
exercise
on
Kern’s
“The
Song
Is
You.” Jimmy
Giuffre
ar-
ranged
(and
conducts)
the
cozy
septet
setting.
Tasteful program
of plaintive
vehicles.
“ITALIAN
SONGS AND DANCES”—Monitor
MF 345
A unique look
at the music of Italy
is offered
in
this
collection
of
folk
songs
and
dances.
To
the
folklorist,
this music
is
rich
in
the heritage
of ancient origins, and, as presented here, should
provide fascinating
listening
to those with wide
musical
interests. The disk contains instrumental
and vocal tracks of tarantellas, mazurkas, quad-
rilles,
stornellis and waltzes.

“GOLD DIGGERS
IN DIXIELAND” —
Matt)
Matlock and
the Paducah
Patrol—Warner
Bros
B
1374
Remember those “Gold Diggers”
flicks
of
the
Thirties? Well Matlock digs back to those gaudy
films for some of the tunes they contained, some
good, some
bad, but the struttin’ Paducah Patrol
gives
them
all
a
rousing
two-beat
sendoff
into
the
present.
Tunes
include
“Lullaby
of
Broad-
way,”
“We’re
In
The
Money,”
“Painting
The
Clouds With
Sunshine,” “Tip-Toe Thru The Tu-
lips
With Me”
and
several
non-entities.
Enjoy-
able
Dixie
jass.
“A TASTE OF HONEY”—Bobby Scott—Atlantic
1355
Bobby
Scott’s
incidental music
for the Broad-
way show “A
Taste
Of
Honey”
is
in
the
jazz
idiom. Here, the composer-pianist offers his own
performances
of
the
music.
Assisted
by
two
groups, one a combo, the other string-augmented,
Scott
barrels
his way
through
the
various
de-
scriptive themes. Good showcase for
the
pianist
and
his music.
“JAZZ OF THE FORTIES”

FJ
2841
For
its initial issue of dated jazz. Folkways has
come up with
a
series
of cuts made

Russell,
Art
Hodges,
Mezz
Mezzrow,
Pops
Foster, George
Wettling. Tunes
played
in-
clude “Royal Garden
Blues,” “China Boy,”
“Sis-
ter
Kate,”
“Jazz Me
Blues”
and
“Maple
Leaf
Rag.” Though sound
is poor, jazz historians will
cherish
these
relics from
the
past.

BEETHOVEN:
“Wellington's
Victory” “Leonore
Overture” “Prometheus Overture"—Antal Dorati
conducting
the
London
Symphony
Orchestra
Mercury LPS 9000
Dorati kicks off the “Victory” with a bang! Just
as
the
conductor
took
cannon
to
Tchaikovsky’s
most hackneyed work, the “1812
Overture,” and
made
it
into one
of the
best-selling
classical
al-
bums
of
all
time,
he
now
brings
musket
and
Howitzer
to Beethoven’s corny glory-tune, “Wel-
lington’s Victory,” and
could easily do the same.
Dramatic
emphasis
on
sound
effects
will
leave
stereo
pop
fans
agog. Two
more
popular,
but
higher level Beethoven pieces
fill out side two.
PUCCINI: “Madame Butterfly”—Victoria de Los
Angeles, Jussi Bjoerling. Orchestra and chorus of
the Opera
House, Rome,
conducted
by
Gabriele
Santini—Capitol SGCR 7232
Competing for
the
stereo
sales
of
this
opera,
Capitol
issues
its
second
“Butterfly”
with
Los
Angeles. This time around Jussi Bjoerling plays a
vital
role
in
this, one
of
his
last recordings
be-
fore his death. A fine addition to an already over-
crowded
catalog.
Bjoerling’s name
is the big
at-
traction here.
MOZART: “The Marriage
of Figaro”—Eberhard
Wachter,
Fllisabeth Schwartzkopf, Gieseppe Tad-
dei, Anna
Moffo, Carlo Maria Giulini conducting
the
Philharmonic
Orchestra
and
Chorus—Angel
3608 D/L
Mozart’s “Figaro”
is performed
in
its entirety
(four disks) by a distinguished cast directed im-
maculately
by
Carlo
Maria
Giulini.
Each
per-
former,
particularly
Mdmes.
Schwarzkopf
and
Moffo, turn in handsome performances of the long
work. Assumes an important position in the “Fig-
aro” catalog.
MOZART: Concerto No. 24 in
c minor; Rondo in
a
minor—Artur
Rubinstein,
pianist,
Orchestra
conducted by Josef Krips—RCA Victor LM-2461
Rubinstein’s
pianistic genius
is
the ingredient
needed
to
successfully perform
these two
great
Mozart
works.
His
grasp
of
the
nuances
and
meanings
in
the
music,
coupled
with
his
great
technical
skill, overshadows pianists who have at-
tempted Mozart with just virtuosity. A true art-
istic triumph.

A Feather
In Arlen’s Kapp
NEW YORK—Roger Williams
is flanked by Dave Kapp
(left), president of
Kapp Records, and Harold Arlen discussing Roger’s new Kapp album, “Roger
Williams Invites You To Dance.” The album includes one of Arlen’s greatest

is currently witnessing renewed
disk interest in his work.
Capitol Realigns
Int’l Dept.
HOLLYWOOD—Motivated by a “con-
tinuing
expansion”
of
its
overseas
marketing
activities,
Capitol
Records
has
realigned
executive
responsibili-
ties
within
its
international
depart-
ment,
according
to an announcement
last
week
by
Lloyd
C.
Dunn,
vice-
president for marketing.
Dunn announced the following
ap-
pointments:
Sandor
A.
Porges, who
joined Capitol in Feb., 1947, and who
has served as an administrator of the
international
department
since
that
time, has been named to the new post
of
executive
consultant
of
foreign
markets. He will continue to report to
Dunn.
Gordon
R.
Fraser,
who
was
ap-
pointed
director
of
the
international
department in Jan., 1960, will assume
complete
executive
responsibility
for
the
department
and
will
report
di-
rectly
to Dunn.
Fraser
formerly
re-
ported to Porges. Fraser will also as-
sume
the
post
of
vice-president
and
general manager
of
Capitol
Records
International
Corp., a Capitol
subsid.
Richard
J.
Rising, who has served
as
assistant
director
of
the
interna-
tional department since August, 1960,
has been
appointed
international
de-
partment manager. He
will
continue
to report to Fraser.
Julius
Varady,
who
has
been
a
member
of the
international
depart-
ment’s New York staff since 1950, has
been named export order service man-
ager. In his new
post, he
will be
re-
sponsible
for
supervision
of
the
de-
partment’s New York staff, as well as
functional
direction
of
the
depart-
ment’s
Scranton,
Pa.
export
order
service.
Bob Klein, former pop records mer-
chandising manager
of
Capitol
Rec-
ords Distributing Corp., has resigned
his CRDC post in order to become in-
ternational
promotion
manager,
re-
placing King Lane, who has resigned
from
the company.
In
his new
post,
Klein
will
report
to
international
marketing manager Rising.
Also
reporting
to
Rising
will
be
James
R.
Winfree,
who
has
been
named to the post of international ad-
ministrative
service manager.
According
to Dunn,
all moves
are
effective Jan.
16. With the exception
of Porges and Varady, who
will
re-
main
in New York,
all personnel
in-
volved in the present moves
will con-
tinue
to
be
headquartered
at
the
Capitol
Tower
in
Hollywood,
Dunn
said.

Cates’

in

include “Now

“A

LPBR-9004
Nelson Eddy has
retained much
of
the

that made

a

in

of
the

Screen. With

offers dramatic read-
ings
of
“Tonight We
Love,”
“ ’Till

Time,” “Full Moon and Empty Arms,” “Stranger
in Paradise” and others well suited for his
style.
A program that many adults will appreciate.
“PAUL

Character

in

interpreting

Mingus’ new

to

“WE
INSIST!—MAX
ROACH’S

NOW SUITE”—Abbey Lincoln, Coleman Hawkins,
Olatunji, Max Roach—Candid CJM-8002
Roach’s

Suite”
is
an

compelling

that
tells
musically
of
the

in

and

Its

Benton,

Little
and

Polhe News, 245 W. 55

(Special

“The Return
of Dexter Gordon” would seem an appropriate
title
for the
tenorman’s
first Blue Note album. Frank Wolf and A1 Lyons
disclosed
last
week that they had signed the vet jazz star to a recording contract and will
soon release his initial session. Dexter, who has been relatively inactive for the
past few years, was with Lionel Hampton from 1940 to 1943; spent six months
with Louis Armstrong in
’44, and then moved into the tenor chair with Billy
Eckstine where he recorded his
first solo on “Blowing the Blues Away.” After
18 months with Eckstine, Dexter gigged around New York and the west coast,
recording intermittently for Dial, Savoy, Prestige, Victor, Apollo, Emarcy and
,
King. His
first album on Blue Note
is being awaited impatiently by the many
jazz fans who remember his fine work in the early
’40’s.
The
Messrs. Wolf and Lyons further
reiterated
their
belief that
it
takes
time to produce good jazz records. They cannot understand how small or new
t
jazz labels can hit the market with numerous recordings, stating that a good
catalog can be attained only through years of thoughtful cutting and thorough
planning, as they have been doing at Blue Note for twenty years. This stand
makes sense when considering what Wolf and Lyons have done for Blue Note.
They
still continue
to
personally supervise each
session,
edit
carefully, and
basically follow the recording right through each process to its final stage.

CHARLIE BYRD

four trumpets, singer Gloria Lynne with the

“SPIRITUALS AND BLUES” — Josh White —
Elektra EKL-193
Longtime vet of the folk blues trail, Josh White
appears in a newly recorded program of his most
remembered songs. Accompanying himself on gui-
tar and with rhythm combo
assistance, the
per-
former
sings
of
“Southern
Exposure,”
“Black
Snake,” “I’ve Got That Pure Religion” and “Just
A Closer Walk With Thee.” Of infinite interest to
blues and jazz markets.
“YUK-A-PUK”—Morey
Amsterdam—Signature
SM 1023
The vet comedian joins the ranks of his fellow
laffsters who
have
set down
their
routines
on
disks. Amsterdam
is a pro at the quip game, and
delivers
his
lines
in
both monologues
and
song
(his
famed
“Yuk-A-Puk”
song
is
included).
Chances are that many have waited for Amster-
dam
in LP form; he won’t disappoint them.
“AN
EVENING
AT THE
CAFE
CARLYLE
WITH GEORGE FEYER”—Cadence CLP 3051
Cocktail pianist George Feyer
is showcased
in
a program
that
consists
of such
easy-listenable
items as “The Sound of Music,” “Hi-Lili, Hi-Lo,”
“Gigi,” “The Apartment” and
“Mademoiselle
de
Paris.” The presentation
is soft and unobtrusive,
making
it
ideal
as background
for
special mo-
ments.
“MUSIC OF KERN, GERSHWIN, YOUMANS,
ARTHUR SCHWARTZ”—With
Milton
Retten-
berg
at the
piano—Folkways FS 3857
In
a
rare
pop
showing
for
the
folk-inclined
label,
pianist and
musicologist
Rettenberg, who
was the
first piano
soloist to give
a public
per-
formance
of
Gershwin’s
“Rhapsody
In
Blue”
other than the composer himself, gives
rich, but
melody-conscious
keyboard
readings
of
mostly
ballads by five masters of musical-comedy songs,
some
of whom
are
partly represented by some
of their lesser known gems. A very attractive set.
“THE RESURGENCE OF DEXTER GORDON”
—Jazzland JLP 29
Absent
from
the
jazz
spotlight
for
several
years, Dexter Gordon
returns
to
the
disk
scene
via an enormously gratifying session for the Riv-
erside subsid label. He has an earthiness and driv-
ing temper
that hadn’t been matched
until' the
current renewed interest in “soul music,” but now
that this branch of jazz has reached a high point
of popularity it was only a matter of time
till he
was recorded
again.
Five
pieces, none
outstand-
ing, accompany him in readings of “Home Run,”
“Affair In Havana,” “Field Day” and three other
numbers. The tenorman
will
be welcomed back
with open ears.
“MOON-FACED, STARRY-EYED”—Max Roach
plus 4 featuring Abbey Lincoln, vocals—Mercury
SR 60215
The always-exciting Max Roach group takes off
in a thrilling display of moody effectiveness here.
They play such sentimental ballads as “Never Let
Me
Go,”
“You’re Mine You”
and “Wild
Is The
Wind,”
while
chirper Abbey
Lincoln
adds
vocal
spice
to
“I
Concentrate
On You”
and
“Never
Leave Me.” Roach has a big loyal following that
will appreciate this change of pace by him.
“I DIG DANCERS” — Quincy Jones & Band —
PJercury SR 60612
The precision engineered Jones band
is a jazz
dancer s
dream,
for
it main cains
the
beat
con-
sistently
while remaining an invigorating swing
machine with imagination of presentation.
Selec-
tions
include
such

as
“Pleasingly
Plump,” “Tone Poem” and “Chinese Checkers” as
well as evergreens “Moonglow,” “Love
is Here to
Stay” and “A Sunday Kind of Love.” A band with
a message.
“SUNNY SIDE UP”—Lou Donaldson—Blue Note
4036
Altoist Donaldson is a hard-biting musician, re-
lying on a driving blues vein for most of his ex-
pression. An accompanying group of Horace Par-
ian, Sam Jones,
Bill Hardman, Laymon Jackson
and A1 Harewood are also in this groove and the
close
cooperation shows
in
the
fine results they
achieve with such material as “The Man
I Love,”
“Goose Grease,” “Softly As
In A Morning Sun-
rise” and “The Truth.” Session packs a wallop.
“OTIS SPANN
IS THE BLUES”—Otis
Spann
and Roberta Lockwood, Jr.—Candid 8001
Spann, pianist with Muddy Waters’ band and a
tremendously

“CHAMPION JACK’S NATURAL & SOULFUL
BLUES”—Champion Jack Dupree—Atlantic 8045
Dupree is an extremely soulful and earthy blues
singer, especially doing such material as his trib-
ute to his friend
Bill Broonzy, “Death of Big Bill
Broonzy,” “How Long
Blues,”
“Seafood

“PERCUSSION AND BASS”—Jo Jones and Milt
Hinton—Everest LPBR 5110
The two jazz
vets, Jones
(drums)
and Hinton
(bass),
relinquish

usual
venture
into
experimental

for
the
sound enthusiast. Hinton’s bass carries whatever
melody there
is in striking solos, while Jones adds
pungent effects on various drums.
It succeeds to
a point but
it’s a case of either too much album
or not enough musical interest to maintain
it.

Competition among
Canadian
distribs
for
U.
S. masters
has
reached
its
highest peak in the past few weeks. The new distributors have acquired lines
from the established distribs by offering attractive deals to the U.S. companies.
Big percentages and front money are no longer uncommon on the Canadian
scene. Also, the increased promotion being given by the distribs plays a major
role as to which company acquires the U.S. master. Most
of the distributors
have arranged their release schedule in order to coincide with the U.S. release
dates. In the past the local distrib would wait until a favorable reaction was
first shown in the U.S. before releasing in Canada. What has changed this pat-
tern of thinking was the new policy of radio stations. Stations previously pro-
grammed the Top Forty exclusively, not giving a chance to new records unless
they made the U.S. charts. Distribs now feel a record has a fair chance to break
here at the same time as it does in the U.S., if not before. This has come about
since stations are spinning material which they feel has a chance to become a
hit.
Don Passerby, who has recently exited CFOX Lakeshore radio to become a
touring impressario, is packaging the giant show coming to the Show Mart in
Montreal on Feb. 10 and
11. The show includes Bobby Vee, Buddy Knox, The
Ventures, Dion, Michael Louvain, and The Beaumarks.
Shelly Berman
is booked for Feb. 5 at Her Majesty’s Theatre. He had pre-
viously cancelled a S.R.O. engagement because of illness. Appearing along with
him will be The Cumberland Three.
Buck Lacombe, chief A & R man at Apex Records, has left the company to

his own

a
total
of
six
singles to be
released. The French
label has not been named
at the time

Buddy Knox preparing for an 18 week swing through Canada.

FRENCH NEWS:
The past five years have proven to be a fantastic period of growth for French
Canadian
labels. No
less than twenty companies operate on a regular release
schedule. A new French distributorship headed by Tony Choma will handle the
Fleur De Lys, Meteor, Adanac, and Reel labels. The company will be known as
Adanac. Jean Paul Rickner of Trans Canada Distributors has begun their own
label bearing the same name. Four records were released on the
first release
date, three of these became great
hits. One, “Pourtant Je L’aime” by Claude
Vincent reached the No. 1 spot, another “Tu Mens” by Fernand Gignac hit the
No. 2
spot. Gaston Charette at Centrodisc has another hot record by Andre
Lejeune. The song,
“I’ll A
Suffit De Peu De Choses,”
is a cut from
his new
album, “Andre LeJeune Chante.” Yvan Dufresne recently named A and R head
at Apex Records. Michael Louvain, French Canada’s singing idol, had his com-
plete wardrobe and music material stolen from his hotel in Paris while home
for the holidays.

Disk
Sales
Bowing
To Winter's Cold
NEW YORK—Old man winter
is
evi-
dently not too sympathetic to the rec-
ord
industry’s
sales problems. Heavy
snows and
temperatures
consistently
below freezing have taken their toll in
disk sales, particularly in the east and
mid-west.
The
cold snap—which
at presstime
had shown no signs of abating—comes
at a time when labels are putting their
best-foot foward in terms of product.
But, to take rack sales as an example,
the bad weather keeps
traffic
out
of
supermarkets
and
other
establish-
ments that have a rack section. Many
of the
latter stores
offer a telephone
delivery service whereby the customer
can
phone
his
purchases
(i.e.
food)
and
thereby
avoid
facing-up
to
the
weather.
The
record
dealer,
of
course,
also
suffers from potential customers who
spend most of their free time in-doors
during
unfavorable
weather.
If
not
actually
intending
to
venture
into
a
disk shop, the house-bound consumer
doesn’t even get a chance to see an at-
tractive
dealer
window-display
that
could draw him into the store.
Major
markets
most
seriously
af-
fected by the
cold snap
include New
York, Baltimore. Washington, Cincin-
nati,
Buffalo, Kansas
City,
St. Louis,
Cleveland and Nashville.

DENMARK
Swedish jazz musician Lars Guilin, who has been touring Denmark for some
time, is now returning to his native Sweden where some jazz club engagements
in Malmo are waiting for him. Jens Lawaetz, head of Danish State TV Co., on
business visits to Stockholm, Helsinki, and Oslo.
“West
Side Story”
will be produced on Scandinavian
stages
this autumn,
according to theatre publisher Lars Schmidt. Record companies, most of which
have released one
or another album from
the
show,
are
carefully watching
this event, which is expected to first take place in Copenhagen.
A Danish
operetta,
“Farinelli,” composed by Emil Reesen with
lyrics by
Mogens Dam, has been recorded on an LP by Nordisk Polyphon AS. Singing
on the LP, on which 12
of the most popular songs appear,
are
Else
Mariel
Gardelli, Grethe Mogensen, Lise Panduro, Poul Bundgaard and Hans Kurt.
Scandinavisk Grammophon AS (SGA) has released a Danish version of the
Swedish song, “Froken JohansenogJeg,” sung by Raquel Rastenni. This song,
composed by Thore Skogman, has for long time been topping the Norwegian
best sellers, and is now reported starting to grow big also in its native Sweden.
According to Danish publisher Imudico, it might very soon be a bestseller also
in Denmark. SGA promoted the record over the commercial radio station Radio
Mercur on February
1.
Starting on Feb.
1, a strike was expected among the artists in Danish radio
and TV. This
is probably of very
little importance
to radio
listeners
in
the
Copenhagen neighborhood, where the commercial Radio Mercur has for long
time been much more popular than the Danish government controlled
radio.
Representatives
for Radio Mercur refuses
to comment on
the
situation, but
it is known that any strike of this kind
is among the best that
c-ould happen
to stimulate their popularity.
Danish jazz clubs have presented their 1960 award
to Metronome Records
for
its release of “Giant Steps” on Atlantic with John
Coltrane. Metronome
in Copenhagen was very happy to notice that “Apache” with Jorgen Ingmann
is doing well on The Cash Box Top 100. Some Danish newspapers have discov-
ered
that
the
Danish
recording
is
finding most
of
its American
buyers
in
the Indian districts.
SWEDEN
Hasse Eson
is the name of a 32 year old debutant on records. He has cut
first EP
for RCA. Eson
is, however, well known
as pop song composer and
several of his compositions have been recorded by various artists here. This is
the first time he
is giving his own presentation of his songs.
Knappupp Records have presented the
first Swedish-language recording
of
the English hit, “Goodness Gracious Me,” titled “Oj Da, Kara Nan!” The artists
singing the song are Hans Alfredsson and Brita Borg. It
is also reported that
Felix Alvo, head of Knappupp Organization
is leaving for a biz
visit
in the
United States one of the next days.
Jack
Kotschack, prexy
of
the
so-called
pirate
radio
station
Radio
Nord,
reports that why the station has not yet begun its activity because of sabotages
against the ship from which the station will operate. Radio Nord
is reportedly
financed by some American businessmen, who
recently
visited
Stockholm
to
study the
situation. According to
reports
here,
the European
oil
millionaire
Edmund Nichols-Roth, now living
in Rotterdam, Holland,
is negotiating with
Radio Nord which he is supposed to join on financial basis.
A Swedish composition “Symphony No. 3” by Rune Wahlberg, will have
its
world release when played by Canadian Broadcasting
Co. on March
6.
This
symphony was composed back in 1948.
“Bonanza,” the theme music from the American TV
serial, has now placed
itself high on the best-sellers here. At the same time, Swedish Broadcasting-TV
Co. (SBC) reports that
it aired the
last film
in the serial on Saturday
(Jan.
28th). SBC has some more films in this series, which undoubtedly is one of the
most popular TV programs
in Sweden, but those
films has been banned
as
being “too cruel with too much killings.”
Valentina Levko, opera
singer, will be a member
of an
artist group from
URSS who
will tour Sweden
during August.
There
will
probably
be
some
Swedish artists touring URSS
in exchange, but so
far, no names are known.
Olof Rydbeck, prez of SBC, off for business visits in Brussels and Paris.
Music publisher Lennart Reuterskiold of Reuter & Reuter back from
busi-
ness visit in Helsinki. He reports good success for the song “Goodness Gracious
Me,” which
is doing very well here.
The Henning Hendrix Orchestra will tour Finland during Feb. Singer Towa
Carson, an RCA artist, will join the orchestra as vocalist.,
Some years ago,
it was of greatest importance to a record company to get
their records aired over the Swedish radio stations. Today, this
is of very little
importance, while a TV presentation has become the biggest help to the record

FRANCE
It’s in
all
the newspapers, the radio and
television are humming with the
story—the new “Adagio” attributed to Albinoni and recently recorded on the
Barclay
label by the Symphonia
Orchestra conducted by Jean Witold
really
from the pen of Albinoni, or is
it a hoax? Eddie Barclay and Jean Witold de-
clare that the work was discovered
lately among the composer’s manuscripts
and present guarantees
of
authenticity but
in
such
cases
absolute
certitude
can never be established. Meanwhile, the record
is moving towards the
best-
seller class.
Roquiere and his “plugger,” Soula, are working hard to make “Exodus” into
a
hit here. The French version has been waxed by singers Edith Piaf (EMI)
and Rika Zarai
(Bel-Air). Raymond Lefevre will do an orchestral version for
the Barclay
ticket. Cuco Erminio
(Ducretet-Thomson)
will balance
off Dario
Moreno’s recording
of
“Soleil de Lima” by cutting
his interpretation
of
the
tune. Annie
Fratellini
(Decca)
is
getting
“C’est
Tout,
C’est Tout”
(“That’s
All”) on the market in her special style. “Compagnons” by Pierre Lucky has
been chosen by Michele Arnaud (Dueretet)
for her next session. Los Matecoco
(Bel-Air)
and
Aimable
(Vogue)
have
waxed
“Annette,
Brigitte
Et
Cie.”
A.
Salvet and
L. Morisse have
signed
the French adaptation
of “Poetry
In
Motion” and Jacqueline Danno’s (EMI) next recorded tune
will be “Au Petit
Bal.”
Salvet Editions awaits with impatience release in France of the Elvis Presley
film “G.I. Blues”
in order to launch the original musical track for which they
have
rights. While waiting, Salvet’s “Le Joie D’aimer”
is coming up
strong.
Rieordi
Editions
is
specializing more and more
in publishing
film
music.
Aniinollah
Hossein’s
score
for
the
movie
“La
Menace”
belongs
to
Rieordi.
Fontana
will market the record
of the original track. Rieordi
will release the
music from “Les Menteurs” and “Le Gout De La Violence” on
its own
label.
G. Delerue will write the music for the film, “Une Aussi Longue Absence” and
the main
tune, “Trois
Petites Notes De Musique,”
will
be recorded by Cora
Vaucaire for Pathe-Mareoni.
A. Segal has the rights to Aznavour and Gavarentz’ song “J’aime T’aimer”
1
and Ricordi’s new singing discovery, Jocelyne Andret, will record the tune on

label. “Napoli Cha Cha Cha”
is the
title
of an
original recording by Jo
i
Sentieri. Monsieur Arduino
is pleased with the
sales
progress
of the Count
Basie and Cannonball Adderly albums.
Vogue’s Leon Cabat has auditioned the original tapes
sent to Paris by
his
agencies
in Dakar and Abidjan. They contain modern African music, national
marches and war dances and ought to
sell well throughout the world. Johnny
Halliday’s “Kiliwatch” on the Vogue label is breaking sales records—more than
200,000 sold to date accoi’ding to Monsieur Cabat. Johnny’s next tune—“Nous
Les Gars, Nous Les Filles”
(Jil & Jan), published by Alpha.
M. Ferreri has
left for Italy to represent Vogue at the San Remo festival.
Leon Cabat is off to Milan. What a traveller!
Abe Olman
is passing through
Paris
at
this
writing.
Rudi
Revil, having
established
his reputation as a publisher, will try
his hand
at recording. His
first orchestral record will be distributed by Arteco.
Leo Missir of Bel-Air continues
to bet on Paul Mauriat and
will have the

at

jl

Artec-o’s Taylor continues his work of reconstructing the famous recordings

Theatre where he will co-star with Josephine Baker in “Violettes Imperiales,”

######## 1961-02-18 p31  [blue\s*note\s*40\d\d]
Album Review
lllilllllllllll
THE HOMEY BEES
“TIME OUT FOR TEARS”—Savannah Churchill
—Jamie JLP—70—3016
Savannah
Churchill,
one
of
the
pioneers
of
rhythm & blues and one of its great artists, moves
expressively through a lineup of pop ballads and
blues ballads. This down to earth soulful display
is an important commodity on the blues markets.
She
offers
her
classic
“Time
Out
For
Tears,”
which just recently witnessed a revival, plus “Be
Anything,”
“I Almost Lost My Mind,”
“I Want
To Be Loved” and “Summertime.”
“GREAT AMERICAN HITS”—The Honev
Bees
—Everest LPBR 5111
Three femme
songstresses tagged
the Honey
Bees prettily do up a passel of country standards
in sweet harmonic tones. Reaching back through
the years they come up with “Bouquet of Roses,”
“In The Jailhouse Now,” “I Don’t Hurt Anymore,”
“Slowpoke” and “Roly Poly.” A permanent part
of musical Americana delightfully surveyed.
“THE BOLD HUMOR OF DAVEY BOLD”—
—Norman NL-100
St. Louis comic sensation Bold has been cut in
performance
at
his
own
Celebrity
Club
there
doing
his regular routine
of stand-up jokes and
patter. His repertoire runs the normal gamut of
his ilk with special emphasis on the risque. Bold
has a huge fount of stories, and though many are
old his casual, well-modulated delivery gives them
new life. Can be a successful comedy disk.
“HAWAII
WITH
A
BONGO
BEAT”—LeRoy
Holmes, His Orchestra and Chorus—MGM E3874
The LP is entirely different from the usual run-
of-the-mill
Island
sessions. Holmes
has
dressed
up
a dozen hula favorites with an exciting beat
and sans-lyric chorus chanting (something in the
Conniff manner)
and
the
music becomes
fresh,
friendly and especially easy to take. A veritable
boon to this music that could witness chart reac-
tion.
Selections
include “Hawaiian War
Chant,”
“Pagan Love Song,” “Song Of The Islands” and
“Lovely Hula Hands.”
JAZZ
PICKS
OF THE WEEK
“THE
PROVOCATIVE
ERROLL GARNER”—
Columbia CL
1587
Seven extended tracks by Garner, among them
“Holiday
For
Strings,”
“Love
For
Sale,”
and
three
originals—“Margin
For
Erroll,”
“Blue
Ecstasy” and
“Look, Ma-All Hands!”
Indeed,
a
provocative session, but more so an exciting and
thrilling
session. Has
a
tremendous
market.
“WILD WOMEN DON’T HAVE THE BLUES”—
Nancy Harrow—Candid 8008
It is unusual to find a jazz vocalist’s first album
in which an attempt hasn’t been made to emulate
a current singer
or fad. And Candid has neatly
avoided
this
cliche
to
intro Nancy Harrow.
She
has a
style
strongly reminiscent
of the
earliest
blues singers and to showcase this style the label
has
put her
in
a Buck
Clayton-led
swing band
setting that firmly establishes the mood. Even the
material chosen for the date furthers the stand;
Ida
Cox’s earthy
title tune;
Ellingtonia
such
as
“All Too
Soon,”
“I
Don’t Know What Kind
of
Blues I’ve Got.”
“SON OF DRUM SUITE”—RCA Victor LSP-2312
A sort of sequel to the label’s highly successful
“Drum Suite”
is
this new “suite” created by A1
Cohn. Under his aegis are five top jazz drummers
plus a full 19 piece ork in a performance of Cohn’s
new
suite.
Besides
being
a
vigorous
display
of
drumanship, there is also plenty of solid jazz ork
work here in the melody dept. Could be the label’s
biggest jazz LP of the year.
HOME COOKfN
THE INCREDIBLE JIMMY SMITH
“HOME COOKIN’”—Jimmy Smith—Blue
Note
4050
Album is aptly titled for the down home cookin’
organ playing of Smith. In this
all blues date he
is accompanied lustily by tenorman Percy France,
guitarist
Kenny
Burrell
and
drummer
Donal
Bailey in what amounts
to
a healthy serving of
soul blues, with each contributing large portions.
Selections
include
“See
See
Rider,”
“I
Got A
Woman,” “Messing Around” and “Come On Baby.”
One of the most evocative of jazz organs.
joe moretlOr drums
9ary burton, vibes
joe benjamin, tmss
hank garland
CLASSICAL
“JAZZ WINDS FROM A NEW DIRECTION”—
Hank Garland—Columbia CL 1572
One
of
Nashville’s
top
guitarists
on
country
music recording dates, Garland has also achieved
local prominence as the city’s leading jazz guitar-
ist. Columbia now proves this with his
first jazz
LP
in which they’ve gathered Joe
Morello, Bru-
beck’s
exciting
drummer,
Joe
Benjamin
(bass)
and youngster Gary Burton
(vibes)
for the
ses-
sion. Not only is the work of Garland appealing,
but
Burton
bears watching
as
a
comer
in
the
field. Of the six tracks, “All The Things You Are,”
“Riot-chorus”
and
“Relaxing”
are
the
best. A
couple
of new names
for jazz prominence.
“EXPLORING THE SCENE”—The Poll Winners
—Barnev
Kessel,
Shelly
Manne—Contemporary
M
3581
'
Kessel, Brown and Manne, consistent jazz
poll
winners
in
their
respective
categories, band
to-
gether for a swinging
trio tour
of modern
jazz
classics. They offer interesting,
quietly evocative
readings of “The Duke,” “Doodlin’,” “The Golden
Striker,” “This Here” and four others. Good jazz
date.
“LOUIS HAYES”—Vee Jay LP-3010
Hayes’ quick-tempered drumming has sparked
the Horace Silver group and now is the rhythmic
drive
behind
the
Cannonball
Adderley
quintet.
Here,
with
the
Adderley
personnel
minus
the
altoist, but with Yusef Lateef’s
scorching tenor
as a replacement, Hayes keeps things moving at
a torrid clip. The music is right in the “soul blues”
groove, with Nat Adderley again distinguishing
himself
on
cornet.
Selections
include
“Hazing,”
“I Need You,” “Sassy Ann” and three more origi-
nals. Driving, hard-hitting jazz date.
“SCREAMIN’ THE BLUES”—The Oliver Nelson
Sextet—Prestige/New Jazz 8243
The
searing,
literally
“screaming”
tenor
sax
statements
of Nelson are spotlighted
in yet an-
other
powerful
Prestige
session.
Standout
per-
formers with Nelson are trumpeter Richard Wil-
liams, pianist Richard Wyands and drummer Roy
Haynes, who
lays down
a
non-pretentious
but
constantly
reliable rhythm
pattern. Among
the
six tunes are “The Meetin’,” “March On, March
On” and “Three Seconds.” For the strong-hearted
jazz fans.
“DANUBE
WAVES”—The
Hollywood
Bowl
Symphony Orchestra conducted by Miklos Rozsa
—Capitol P 8540
Film track composer Rozsa (“Ben Hur”)
is also
a well respected conductor. Here, fronting Capi-
tol’s
ubiquitous
Hollywood
Bowl
ork, he
offers
pleasant, unpretentious, carefully paced readings
of symphonic war horses. Among them are Sme-
tana’s “Bartered Bride”
overture,
Strauss’
(Sr.)
“Radetzky March,” and Liszt’s “Hungarian Rhap-
sody” No. 14. An enjoyable light classical listen-
ing
session.
“BERLIOZ OVERTURES”—Charles Munch con-
ducting
the
Boston Symphony
Orchestra—RCA
Victor LP-2438
Munch, acknowledged Berlioz master, has been
recorded in a series of the composer’s most
stir-
ring overtures. The emotional music is translated
into
passionate
ork terms by an understanding
and
intense
display
of
conducting
facility. The
overtures
include “The Roman
Carnival,” “Ben-
venuto
Cellini,” “The
Corsair” and two
others.
The Cash Box—February
18,
1961

Novelty Hit
Is Child's Play
NEW YORK—Money earned by John-
ny Parker for writing the years-back
hit, “Tra La La,” eventually led to the
current Buzz Clifford hit on Columbia,
“Baby Sittin’ Boogie.”
With his royalties, Parker invested
in
Ampex
tape
equipment.
Subse-
quently, he married and had two chil-
dren. From their birth, he constantly
had
a
microphone
placed
over
their
cribs, taping
their
gurgles,
laughter,
and eventually taping over a 100 baby
sounds. Later, he wrote a song, “Baby
Buggy Boogie,” which he brought
to
publisher Herb Reis. Parker’s tape of
the tune had some of his baby sounds
inserted
throughout,
and
the
whole
idea of song and baby sounds “flipped”
Reis. The
publisher
tried
to
sell
the
master
to
Columbia,
but
the
label
agreed that while the idea was good,
it would like to re-record the novelty.
The
result was
a
new
version—the
word “Buggy” being changed to “Sit-
tin’ ”—and
a
big Top
100 waxing.

######## 1961-02-25 p24  [jazz\s*messengers]
ALL THAT JAZZ
Bob Altshuler told us about a recent studio session with Abbey Lincoln that
turned into a meeting of jazz giants. Bob was overlooking Nat Hentoff’s super-
vision
of Abbey’s
first solo LP
for Candid, a sort of sequel
to the “Freedom
Now”
date
tagged
“Straight
Ahead,” when
Charlie Mingus
dropped
in
to
listen followed by Thelonious Monk who stopped in to give approval of Abbey’s
lyrics
to
his famed “Blue Monk” opus. Max Roach
did the charts for the
ses-
sion.
Minton’s, the “place where modern jazz was born,” has become a famed and
fabled place
to
jazz fans and musicians
alike. And throughout
its years
of
importance as a jazz experiment mecca, not one commercial recording had ever
been made in
it. Never, that is, until Jan. 6th this year, when Prestige Records
went in to tape a “live” session by the Eddie Davis-Johnny Griffin Quintet. The
place, known
as
the Playhouse Restaurant
(208 W.
118th
St.)
to
non-jazz
buffs,
still has
live jazz—the Davis-Griffin Quintet
is there now—but has
lost
much of its fame in recent years. Prestige intends to revive interest in
it as an
offshoot to the recording of “The Tenor Scene,” the title given the set recorded
there. Advance reports
indicate
that though these men
are not pointing
the
way in modern jazz there, they sure can blow up a storm.
TERI THORNTON
SAMMY JAY
AHMAD JAMAL
Gene Ammons, absent from the New York scene for several years, returned
to the
city for a week date at the Apollo Theatre as co-headliner with Nina
Simone,
Horace
Silver, James Moody
and
Eddie
Jefferson
in
disk
jockey
(WEVD) Mort Fega’s jazz show. The show closed out a successful week Feb.
20th. While in N.Y., Ammons did a studio session for Prestige which will be on
LP in March.
Monte Kay has put together his second theatre jazz package in a month. The
new one
is set for a week at Washington,
D.C.’s Howard Theatre
(beginning
Feb. 24th)
and features Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers, Herbie Mann’s
Afro-Jazz
Sextet augmented with four
trumpets, and
Gloria
Lynne accom-
panied by the Earl May
Trio. This
is Blakey’s
first bug date
since returning
from Kay’s jazz festival
in Japan
in January.
Songstress Teri Thornton
is being groomed as a new jazz star by Riverside
Records. The thrush, who boasts
a
rich contralto
voice, was pacted by Orin
Keepnews, Riverside’s A&R topper, who has already cut her
initial LP,
titled
“Devil May Care.” The
gal had been doing
club dates
in
Montreal, Chicago
and Cleveland
until a shot on
the Dave Garroway TV’er
attracted
attention
to her talents. Keepnews signed her on recommendations by Cannonball Adder-
ley and Johnny
Griffin.
The Modern Jazz Quartet has established some sort of “first” in jazz by hav-
ing three
of LP’s released simultaneously
in one week by
Atlantic
Records.
The LP’s are “European
Concert,” a double-disk
set, and “The Modern Jazz
Quartet &
Orchestra.” The “European Concert” package was recorded
“live”
in
Copenhagen
last year
by
the
label’s Nesuhi
Ertegun
during
the
MJQ’s
triumphal European
tour. The other set follows the pattern
set by the group
on
its previous “Third Stream Music” LP, combining a blend of classical and
jazz elements.
Opening of Ahmad Jamal’s Chicago
nitery, the A1 Hambra, has been post-
poned for
several weeks because
of construction
difficulties, but barring any
further delays, the spa will open sometime in April. Jamal’s been doing- a series
of concerts in the area and is skedded for a date at McCormack Place on March
18. Argo’s just released a new LP by the pianist, “Listen to The Ahmad Jamal
Quintet.”

Album Reviews
“PORTRAITS IN BRONZE”—Bessie
Griffin and
the Gospel Pearls—Liberty LMM-13002
As one of its first “Premier Series” deluxe LP’s,
Liberty has recorded an exciting gospel concert
with
the
intensely
driving
spirit
of
the
Gospel
Pearls. The group’s repertoire consists
of
spiri-
tuals,
jubilees,
gospels
and
even
pop
inspira-
tionals,
the
latter sung
with more
fervor than
any pop artist can muster. It’s a joyous, electrify-
ing listening experience which fits excellently into
stereo sound medium.
Selections
include “Swing
Low,” “I Believe,” “Bye And Bye,” and “Lord, In
The New Jerusalem.”
“LET’S HAVE A BLAST WITH THE GONDO-
LIERS”—Ric
RLP-2001
The
Gondoliers,
six
musicians-singers-com-
edians, have been cut “live” in a typical perform-
ance
of their
nitery
act, which includes
musical
numbers, satire and largely risque material. Their
are some funny moments
here but presentation
is unprofessional.
JAZZ
PICKS
OF THE WEEK
“GENIUS + SOUL = JAZZ”—Ray
Charles—
Impulse A-2
As one of the kickers in its new Impulse series,
Am-Par has recorded Ray Charles
in a
jazz, an
idiom
in which
he’s
previously
displayed
profi-
ciency but has been somewhat neglected by
his
pop
success.
In
this
field
too,
Charles
draws
largely
on
gospel
elements
for
communication.
He
plays
the organ,
sings
a
couple
of
striking
blues, and generally has a romping time with the
vivid Quincy Jones arrangements. Hot item
for
both pop and jazz markets.
"LISTEN TO THE AHMAD JAMAL QUINTET”
—Argo LP 673
Another superlative session of commercially at-
tractive jazz by the
pianist. To
his popular trio
setup, Jamal has added guitar and violin and
in-
dulges in some experimentation with the arrange-
ments. But the same swinging feeling
is retained
throughout. Selections include
“It’s A Wonderful
World,” “Lover Man,” “Who
Cares”
and
“Val-
entina.”
“STAN GETZ
AT LARGE”—Verve MG
VS-
68393-2
Still America’s favorite tenor sax jazz musician
despite years of expatriation, Getz has been
re-
corded in his “native” Copenhagen in a tremend-
ously appealing two-disk album. This
is a more
mature, years-wiser Getz but with the same high
degree of communication as early Getz. The bal-
lads
and
light
swingers
are
his
best
tracks:
“Night And Day,” “Folks Who Live On The Hill,”
“Younger Than Springtime” and “In Your Own
Sweet
Way.”
Compelling
recording.
Big
sales
attraction.
“THE GREAT KAI AND J.J.”—Kai Winding &
J.J. Johnson—Impulse A-l
Am-Par unveils its new Impulse jazz line with
the wonderful reuniting of the popular trombone
duo of a few years ago. If billing means anything,
the
group’s
title
should be
reversed
(as
it was
originally)
for Johnson
is
still by far the most
articulate
and
original
trombone

in

Together,
and

Bill

Paul

Roy
Haynes
and
others,
they
provide
exciting
jazz moments
on
“Georgia
On My
Mind,”
“Just
For A
Thrill,”
“Trixie” and eight others. Should be a top-selling
item.

MAKE

O’Day—Verve MG VS-62145

gal’s

“Mad About The Boy” and “Yesterdays.”

companies. The RCA

•of their singles.
Local singer Bruce Gillespie

gagements following the success of

in

in Melbourne. The Four Lads
are

single
of “Standing On The

probably the biggest hit from the show.
Bookings are open for The Shirley Bassey Show which hits here mid-Febru-
ary. This will be the second visit to this country by Miss Bassey; her supporting-
acts are Norman Erskine, The Hoganas, The Rivieras, The Tropinos and com-
pere Johnny Lockwood.
Everything is progressing according to schedule for the tour by The Kings-
ton Trio; this group should be a real knockout here as they are very popular-
on disks. Supports to the trio will be Max Geldray, popular English star from
“The Goon Show”; The Howard Morrison Quartet; John Daley; Wilma Reading
and The Bryce Rohde Quartet.
With the demand for comedy records at a new high, Warner Bros,
shoirld
hit the top again with Bob Newhart through his “Strikes Back!” album. New-
hart is now firmly established as a comedy star here as a result of the great
success of his
first album which
is
still a best seller
in this country. Warner
Bros, has also hit the high spot with the album “Sing Along With Bing.” Peter
Sandford of Australian Record Company (who handles Warner Bros, here)
in
Melbourne reports that the Crosby disk is one of the hottest he has handled for
a long time and says the response is
still as strong as ever.
The Festival group has
issued—on

by, Steve

in this country.

“Bye
Bye
Birdie,” which begins
its Australian season early
in March at Her Majesty’s
Theatre in Melbourne, headquarters of the
J. C. Williamson Ltd. circuit.
Falling
in with the policy of many overseas companies, Australian
Record
Company (Coronet (Columbia) and Warner Bros, labels)
has decided to move
onto a monthly release schedule as against
its weekly
plan. The new scheme
will operate from next month and from there on ARC releases
will be made
on the first calendar day of each month. The announcement of the change was
made by Jim
Sutton, general
sales manager for ARC.

Co-Ro S.A.
is also very important in the record business of Mexico. It does
its own records with the Co-Ro label and the president of the company
is Jose
Riojas with his son Federico Riojas as general manager and Enrique Cantu as
A & R man. Firm represents MGM and United Artists.
Gabriel Mendoza
is the owner

is the

sentative of Decca, Coral and Vocalion.
Another important man
in the record busines of Mexico
is Mario Friedberg
who makes

called
Tizoc and has the
exclusivity
of
sale
of
Somerset,
Hi-Fi,
Fantasy, GNP and

And so goes the records business
in Mexico. Hundreds of different labels to
attend the buyers, and a market with a great future. In this, my first column,
as I told you before,
I just want to situate you in my country, musically speak-
ing. In future columns,
I will write about recordings, programas, visitors,
etc.

Victor Reorganizes
Special Market Div.
Under Irwin Tarr
NEW YORK—The RCA
Victor Rec-
ord Division has reorganized
its spe-
cial markets
organization
under
the
direction of Irwin Tarr,
special mar-
kets
sales
manager.
In
order
to
broaden
its
activities
and
consider
new areas, Tarr announced last week
the
following
promotions
and
reas-
signments:
W.
H.
O’Dell
has
been
appointed
manager
of
the
rack
merchandiser
and
syndicate
sales
department.
O’Dell
is a veteran of twelve years in
Victor’s
field
sales
organization.
Re-
porting
to him
will be the
following
special markets
regional
representa-
tives:
Paul
Sklar,
eastern
division;
Charlie Boyd, central division; Charlie
Hall,
western-central
and
southeast
division;
Allan
Clark,
western
divi-
sion; and
Bill Graham, southern
divi-
sion—the latter formerly record sales
manager for Victor’s Memphis distrib.
Ray
Sacher
has
been
appointed
manager of educational sales. Sacher,
formerly part of Victor’s special mar-
kets
field organization,
has
also had
extensive
experience
with
Victor’s
activities
in
the
educational market.
His new
duties
will
include
the
ex-
ploration
of new methods
to
extend
the
record
market
for
educational
sources and
the development of new
products. Reporting to Sacher will be
Anne
O’Keeffe,
educational
services
assistant.
R.
J. Clarkson has been
appointed
manager of Premium Records. Clark-
son, formerly with
the RCA Custom
Records department, will explore new
avenues
to
expand
activities
in
the
premium
field. Reporting to Clarkson
is C. C. Crumpacker A&R director of
special markets.
O’Dell, Sacher and Clarkson will re-
port directly to Tarr.
“Today, more than ever,” said Tarr,
“the
record
business
offers
tremen-
dous
growth
and
profit
potential
to
record manufacturers, as well as
dis-
tributors,
dealers and rack merchan-
disers. Each of course, has
to devel-
op
his own method
to meet
the
op-
portunities and
challenge
of
today’s
market.”
“RCA
Victor’s
reorganization
of
special
markets,”
Tarr
concluded,
“will
be, we
hope,
a major
step
to-
ward the development of new and vi-
tal areas
in our industry.”

Columbia Records has embarked on a campaign to
sell
J.
J. Johnson. They
are escorting the trombonist on disk jockey visits,
etc., and are giving him the
general build-up that usually applies
only
to their pop
artists. According
to
one Columbia promo
exec.,
J.
J. has been something
of an enigma
since he
joined the
label several years ago after the Kai Winding
split, for, although
his stature as a jazz
artist
is
still high with the public as well as musicians
(witness his poll-winning habit), his records have not sold as well as Columbia
thinks they could. Hence the campaign.
Johnson himself said that he
still hasn’t been disassociated from the J.
J. &
Kai tag despite the years apart, and he’s continually being besieged by public
inquiries as to when they’ll team up again. Not that J. J. is trying to live that
reputation down,
it's just that he feels that his work with Kai Winding was
less artistic than his real capabilities. We at The Cash Box feel that if this
is
the case, then
it was a mistake for J.
J.
to do the recently-released Impulse
album with Winding, because all
it can do
is revive public interest in the asso-
ciation.
Now Johnson disclosed that he’ll soon begin getting a new group together.
Rumor has
it that Miles Davis would like him to join his quintet, but nothing
is definite here. Teo Maeero takes
J.
J.
into session soon for another LP
re-

Polka Popularity Up,

NEW
YORK—The
popularity
of
polka music
is growing, feels Walter
(L’l Wally)
Jagiello, polka artist and
president
of
the
big Jay Jay
polka
label
of
Chicago.
Jagiello, who announced a tour
of
one-night
stands
in
fifteen mid-west
and
eastern
cities from
April
11-29,
said that his group, as well as other
successful
polka
bands
have
been
performing
before
SRO
crowds
in
many of the ballrooms
in which they
have been booked.
“One
of
the
greatest
tributes
to
polka
music we
experienced was
a
night
several
months
ago
at
the
famed Aragon
Ballroom
in
Chicago,
when
we
played
before
more
than
4,000 happy
people
.
.
.
this was on
a normal
off night—Wednesday
eve-
ning,” Jagiello
said.
“And
yet,
radio
station
disk
jockeys,
with
few
exceptions,
prac-
tically refuse
to expose polka music
along the
nation’s airwaves. The
air
exposure
is
sorely
needed,
as
the
average
record purchaser makes
his
selections
according
to
the
sugges-
tions offered by the deejay.”
Jagiello
urged
radio
personnel
to
delve
further
into
the
“ever-grow-
ing”
popularity
of polka
music. He
believes that a greater acceptance of
this
“pleasant,
joyous”
music
will
quicken the return of “beautiful dance
music.”

ENGLAND
Official Board of Trade figures just issued confirm that the production and
sales of records for 1960 reached an all-time high. Total manufacturers
sales
for the year at £15,000,000 were 10% more than in 1959 and greater than the
previous best year
1957. Export sales of £3.2 million were, however, 7%
less
than in 1959. Taking the year 1960 as a whole, production-wise, the greatest
increase was in
45’s. These were 20% up on the previous year and accounted
for 71%
of the total number of records produced
in
1960. Production
of
33’s
also increased and was 11% more than
in
1959, accounting for 23%
of
the
total. Production of 78’s continued to decline being 53%
less than a year earlier
and accounting for only 5%
of the total production of 1960.
Central Record Distributors has signed an agreement with America’s oldest
independent jazz
label, Blue Note
to distribute
in
this country. CRD already
handles the famous Riverside catalog as well as Doug Dobell’s Seventy Seven
Records and Folklore Records. The most topical Blue Note release
is “Music
From The Connection” by Freddie Red and
his Quartet with Jackie McLean
(alto sax). Both men appear on stage in the London production of “The Con-
nection,” which, following its successful off Broadway run, opened at The Duke
of Yorks Theatre to a stormy and controversial press. Five other Blue Note
releases
include
recordings by
Art
Blakey,
Cannonball
Adderley
and
Miles
Davis, Horace Silver and George Lewis.
Another jazz show “King Kong”—the all-African musical presented by Jack
Hylton at The Princess Theatre also just opened. After a warm reception and
excellent press,
it looks certain of a long run. The original cast LP,
is released
by Decca. Music published by Burlington Music.
May 17
is the date
set for the opening
of the
first “Centre Of Sound”
in
London.
Sponsored by Audio
Industries
Club
Ltd.
in
conjunction
with The
British Recording
Club,
this new
six story
building
centrally
situated near
Piccadilly
Circus,
will
contain
a
theatre
fully
equipped with
recording and
sound reproduction apparatus, closed circuit TV, a theatre for showing 16mm
and 35mm
films
and
libraries
stocked
with
technical
information
on
sound
recording and reproduction, plus a restaurant, bars and lounges. Designed as
‘An International Rendezvous Of Sound,’ the club will provide a meeting place
for artists, advertising agents, film personnel and
all those, both professional
and amateur, connected with sound whether on tape, film or record.

“JACK HASKELL SWINGS FOR JACK PAAR”
—Strand SL 1020
Haskell is a very capable “legit” singer with an
agreeable, well-modulated
voice.
In
this
first
al-
bum for Strand he gets swinging assistance from
the A1 Cohn arrangements for brisk, bubbly per-
formances
of “Moonlight
Saving
Time,” “Make
Someone Happy,” “Make Believe,” “I Hadn’t Any-
one
Till You” and other superior melodies. Good
taste reigns throughout.
“AS
TIME
GOES
BY”—Vera
Lvnn—MGM
E 3889
Miss Lynn, one of England’s top
entertainers,
has a
rich,
colorful
voice matched to a
flawless
delivery. Here she’s at her most romantic and the
deep
expressiveness
with which
she
sings
is
a
refreshing breeze. Among the songs are “Young
At
Heart,”
“It’s Easy To Remember,”
“I’ll
Re-
member April,” “In the Wee Small Hours
of the
Morning” and the cherished title tune. An enter-
tainer of stature
in a wonderful album.
“AZURE”—King
Curtis
and
his
Orchestra
Everest LPBR 5121
The blue mood is woven here by the threads of
the King
Curtis tenor
sax,
string backdrops by
Samuel
Lowe
and
soft
voices
of
the
Malcolm
Dodds Singers. Curtis’ soulful solo work is super-
imposed
over
lush
strings
and
now-and-then
voices
in dreamy performances
of
“Off
Shore,”
“The Nearness
of You,” “When
I
Fall
In Love”
and “Our Love
Is Here To Stay,” among others.
“UP IN THE AIR WITH OSCAR BRAND”—
Songs For The Madcap Airman—Elektra EKL-
198
Having destroyed the Air Force in song, as well
as
other Armed
Services
and
hobbyists,
Brand
now
takes on
the
private
fliers
in merry
song.
Calling upon his usual collection of P.D. melodies,
he
has
fitted them
with
appropriate
lyrics
and
they now come
out “When
I
First
Set Out To
Fly,”
“The A
&
E
Mechanics,”
“Passenger’s
Lament” and “Teterboro Tower.” Though the set
has particular appeal to
fliers, Brand has a wide
following.
“GRIMM’S HIP FAIRY TALES”—As Dug
By
Don Morrow—Roulette R 25146
Like when Hansel and Gretel, two hip kids with
square handles, met up with a sexy witch with a
twitch, well
.
.
. Grimm never sounded
like
this
when we were kids. But Don Morrow, with crea-
tive assists from Andy Doyle and Mort Lindsey,
put his imagination to work to come up with these
hip,
beat
translations
of
Gi'imm’s
fairy
tales.
Here
are Hansel &
Gretel,
Rumpelstiltskin,
the
Shoemaker and
the Elves and others done
to
a
crisp
hip
turn. A
swingin’
jazz combo
accom-
panies Morrow’s narration. Not for the squares.
“EL
MARIACHI”—Mariachi
Monumental
De
Silvestre Vargas—Orfeon LP 12-119
The usual complement
of
Mariachis
has
been
doubled by Silvestre Vargas, one of the founders
of the genre, for a “monumental” reading of some
of Mexico’s classic songs. With spirit and obvious
devotion they perform such cherished melodies as
“Alla En El Rancho Grande,” “Cielito Lindo,” “La
Bamba,” “La Negra” and
Guadalajara.” Enjoy-
able listening.
