PICK
OF THE WEEK
MT BUKEV &
THEJ4ZZKSS
ENCERSiM
IHIWtKIM
“A NIGHT IN TUNISIA”—Art Blakey
and the
Jazz Messengers—Blue Note 4049
The
Dizzy
Gillespie
jazz
classic
has
always
been a showstopper in the Blakey book.
It’s now
the highlight of this album, which even takes
its
name from
it. The fiery, pulsating, poly-rhythmic
“Tunisia”
stands out particularly as a showcase
for Blakey’s drumming, and he
pulls out
all the
stops on
this
studio
session. Other
selections
in
the
set
are
“Sincerely
Diana,”
“So
Tired,”
“Yama” and
“Kozo’s
Waltz,” but “Tunisia”
re-
mains the major attraction.
VOL. 2
PERCUSSIVE
“MAYNARD ’61”—Maynard Ferguson—Roulette
R 52064
Some of the newer items in the Maynard Fer-
guson book are presented here. These are not the
dance
date
tunes, but
the more
ambitious
jazz
undertakings of the band and reveals its direction
toward wider communication with
its
audiences.
Throughout,
there
is
a
vital
enthusiasm
that
sparks the band in whatever
it’s playing.
Selec-
tions here include “The
Pharaoh,”
“Ole,” “Ulti-
mate Rejection” and “Blues for Kapp.” Has wide
appeal.
“THIS
IS OUR MUSIC”—The Ornette Coleman
Quartet—Atlantic 1353
The
controversy
still rages and Coleman con-
tinues to play “his” music—heralded by some as
the “new”
jazz, laughed
at by many as “junk”
music. The safest stand to take is that ultimately
Coleman might have a strong hand in forming an
important new direction in jazz. As yet, his music
remains unlistenable
to most. Here he plays
six
originals and one standard (“Embraceable You”)
with
his usual devoted
passion.
It
is a
striking
display of originality, to say the
least.
“PERCUSSIVE
JAZZ”
Vol.
2—Arranged
by
Sidney Cooper—Audio Fidelity DFS 7007
Hip,
swinging
jazz
directed
at
the
big
pop
stereo market. Cooper’s arrangements make use
of
a
variety
of interesting instrumentation and
with brisk percussion effects combine in tight-knit
ensemble work on such melodic tunes as “Every-
thing’s Coming Up Roses,” “I’ve Heard That Song
Before,” “If
I Were A Bell” and
“It’s All Right
With Me.” Stereo separation
is at
its maximum.
Sales
should be
too.
“DIXIELAND
LEFT
AND
RIGHT”—Johnny
Best
and
Dick
Cathcart
and
their
All-Stars
Mercury PPS-6009
The Dixie bands of Best and Cathcart are pitted
against each other in a stereo battle of the bands.
With
Best’s
ensemble
emanating from
the
left
speaker and the Cathcart group at the right, they
swing
vigorously
through
a
bill
of
standards,
several
of which are ideally
suited for the two-
band
arrangement:
“Little
Sir
Echo,”
“Sam’s
Song,” “You’re Just In Love.” A bright swinging
semi-jazz outing with strong pop appeal.
CLASSICAL
PICKS
OF THE WEEK
VERDI:
“La
Traviata”—x\nna
Moffo,
Richard
Tucker, Robert
Merrill, Fernando
Previtali
con-
ducting
the Rome Opera
House
Orchestra and
Chorus—RCA Victor LM-6154
This new “La Traviata” from Victor, aside from
being
an
exquisite
stereo
production,
reaffirms
American pride in
its opera star-producing capa-
bility, for its three principals are U.S. born. Each
performs with brilliance. Although
it’s the third
“Traviata” in the Victor catalog,
it’s the
first in
stereo. This plus Victor’s low opera package price
makes it a handsome, appealing set.
WAGNER:
“The
Flying
Dutchman”—Dietrich
Fischer-Dieskau, Gottlob Frick, Marianne Schech,
Chorus
and
Orchestra
of German
State
Opera,
Berlin, conducted by Franz Konwitschny—Angel
3616 C/L
Richard
Wagner’s
eerie,
despairing
operatic
version of the famed legend
is put
to disk with
great care and
sensitivity.
It
is a richly colorful
work and
is performed with amazing intensity by
the
principals. The recording
itself
is extremely
well-balanced with realistic depth and movement.
Only the third complete recording in the catalog,
this three-disk
set should receive a big welcome
in the market.

A hard driving, indeed fiery tenor man, Forrest

to
appeal
to
a
wide
audience.

“GILBERT & SULLIVAN FOR ORCHESTRA”
—Eric Johnson and
his Orchestra—Westminster
XWN-18952
A delightfully enjoyable music pageant of
Gil-
bert & Sullivan
is offered by the Johnson ork as
it
plays
medleys
of
the
songs from
G&S’s
six
most
famous
operettas.
Cherished
melodies
abound
here
in
overture-like
essays
of
“The
Mikado,”
“H.M.S.
Pinafore,”
“Pirates
of
Pen-
zance,” “The Yeoman
of the Guard,” “Patience”
and “The
Gondoliers.”
Excellent
musical
show-
piece.
“MURIEL ANGELUS EXPRESSES THE LYR-
ICS OF OSCAR HAMMERSTEIN II”—Strand
SLS 1022
The late Oscar Hammerstein was recognized as
a poet
of
lyricists, and with
single-minded pur-
pose of transmitting happiness through his work.
Here, one-time actress Muriel Angelus takes the
Hammerstein lyrics out of their Richard Rodgers
musical surroundings and reads them as poetry.
Paul
Lavalle
supports
with
soft-string
back-
grounds
of the Rodgers music. The result
is en-
chanting and
inspiring. Selections include “Hello
Young Lovers,” “A
Fellow Needs A
Girl,” “My
Favorite Things” and “You’ll Never Walk Alone.”
!
miikLdjis
S-iH
0
“POTENT PERCUSSION”—Don
Catelli and
the
All-Stars—Directional Sound DS 5010
An
enjoyable
session
of
easy-swing,
oriented versions of such tunes as “I Love Paris,”
“Manhattan,” “My Heart Belongs To Daddy” and
“Always True To You.”
Solo work
is admirable
and the ensemble works with crackling precision.
Percussive
accents add
an
interesting
flavor
to
the date.
“BALALAIKA”—Sasha Polinoff and his Russian
Gypsy Orchestra—Elektra EKL-194
One of the very few balalaika virtuosos outside
of Russia, Polinoff (an emigree living here)
puts
on an amazing display of
skill on the instrument.
Not
at
all
lacking
is
his
deep
feeling
for
his
native music. Lovers of Russian music will cherish
Polinoff’s
readings
of
“Meadowland,”
“Dark
Eyes,” “Moscow
Evenings,”
“Hussar’s
Drinking
Song” and
others.
“WOODWINDS & PERCUSSION”—Hal Mooney
and
his Orchestra—Mercury PPS 6013
With
an
all-star
cast
of
the
leading
studio
musicians
playing
his
arrangements,
Mooney
comes up with
a
scintillating display
of
stereo-
oriented
music. A
10 man woodwind
ensemble,
playing
melody,
provides
the
base
for
the
per-
cussion
accents.
Selections
include
“Baby,
It’s
Cold
Outside,”
“Tonight,”
“Old
Devil
Moon,”
“Holiday For Strings” and “Swampfire.” Has very
strong appeal.
“FREDERICK FENNELL CONDUCTS GERSH-
AVIN”—Mercury PPS 6006
A dozen Gershwin standards
are
displayed by
an ork of symphonic proportions under the expert
guidance of maestro Frederick Fennell. A distinct
classical atmosphere pervades the
entire record-
ing, giving it a distinct flavor from the usual such
offerings.
Selections
include
“Love Walked
In,”
“But Not
For
Me,” “Oh
Lady
Be
Good,” “The
Man
I
Love”
and
“Embraceable
You.”
Sound
quality
is
excellent.
“AROUND THE WORLD IN PERCUSSION”—
Billy Mure and
his Orchestra—Strand SLS
1021
Mure,
in
capacity
as
arranger-conductor-solo
guitarist, takes
a
musical journey that
includes
such interesting places as “In A Persian Market,”
“Pink Hawaii,” “Petticoats of Portgual,” “Mana-
gua
Nicaragua”
and “The Japanese
Sandman.”
It’s an enjoyable trip, for Mure has put together
a
fascinating
array
of
melodic
and
percussive
sounds.
JAZZ
“BLUE HOUR”—Stanley Turrentine with
the
3
Sounds—Blue Note 4057
With the
3 Sounds providing a
solid rhythmic
foundation
(as well as vital solo work, especially
by
pianist
Gene
Harris),
tenorman
Turrentine
moves soulfully through an earthyblues program
of
“Please
Send Me
Someone To
Love,”
“Blue
Riff,” “Since
I
Fell For You” and
others. A real
“low-down” mood
concert
that
dredges
up
the
rawest
of
feelings. A full-bodied, adventuresome
jazz date.
“COLLABORATION”—Johnny
Dankworth
and
His
Orchestra
with
The
London
Philharmonic
conducted by Hugo Rignold—Roulette R 52059
This album
is a result of a “collaboration” be-
tween the London Symphony and Dankworth for
several
concex’ts
in England and
is
another
ex-
tension
of that “third stream” music gaining
in
popularity
here.
Salzedo and
Lindup’s “Rendez-
vous,”
a
five-part
rondo
for
jazz
quartet
and
orchestra depicting various music types, abounds
in
fascinating
explorations
into
music
combina-
tions. Stravinsky’s “Ebony Concerto”
is a rhyth-
mically engrossing
piece and
Dankworth’s
“Im-
provisations
For
Jazz
Band
and Symphony”
is
virtually
all experimentation, and the most jazz-
iest. Of
significant modern music
interest.
CLASSICAL
PICKS
OF THE WEEK
inTin
3RRSS
“LATIN
BRASS”—John
Evans
Orchestra-
Directional Sound DS 5001
Debut
disk
of
the new
“deluxe” sound
series
fits into the already-established pattern for such
albums. A brass choir flares out in bright melody
over
infectious
back-and-forth
percussion.
Gui-
tars, organ, and various other instruments set the
particular mood of the piece. Evans has arranged
with precision and color. Tunes include “April
In
Portugal,”
“Gualione,”
“Tequila”
and
“Mambo
Jambo.” Danceable and very
listenable.

DONIZETTI:
“Lucia
Di
Lammermoor”—High-
lights Giuseppe Di Stephano, Renata
Scotto, Et-
tore Bastianini, Orchestra and Chorus of La Scala
conducted by Nino Sanzogno—Mercury SR 90261
Donizetti’s romantic opera is presented through
its highlights, culled from the label’s outstanding
complete
recording
package.
Standout
perform-
ances are turned
in by the principals, who reach
a superb climax with the popular “sextet.” This
single disk version should enjoy a brisk
sale.
SHALL WE DAiCE?
“SHALL WE DANCE?”—Jack Jones with
Billy
May and His Orchestra—Kapp KL-1228
Jones, a songster with a decidedly more
legit
outlook
on
music
than many
of
his
contempo-
raries, takes
easily
to
this program
of assorted
Broadway and
Tin Pan
Alley
items. With
Billy
May guiding him with musical efficiency, he proves
a

Wins Western Award

Western Heritage Awards recognize
achievement
in
western
motion
pic-
tures, television, magazines and music.
They
are
designed
to encourage
au-
thenticity in western fact and fiction.
“The
Alamo
Soundtrack”,
the
judges commented,
“captures
a
gen-
eral feeling of Americana. Outstand-
ing is the ballad ‘The Green Leaves of
Summer’ which has a definite, nostal-
gic folksong quality.”
Copies of
the trophies—replicas

Russell’s

re-

of

since

of Sum-
mer”, a

single
this year,

of the Year.”

######## 1961-04-08 p24  [teddy\s*edwards|pacific\s*jazz|jazz\s*messengers]
Stan Getz’s opening performance at the Village Vanguard was disappointing.
Though many
discarded
the
proceedings
as
“just
the
first
set,”
Getz’
on-
stand behavior indicated he’s
still a problem
child. His disinterested attitude
and
continual absence from
the stand
to wander
aimlessly around
the club
during the quartet’s performance was a disservice and an insult to those who
came to cheer him. Now that that’s taken care of, a visit to the club later in
the week proved that he had settled himself somewhat more comfortably for
the week’s run and was playing much more
efficiently, expressively and ma-
turely than in past years. Denmark has been good to his playing, mellowing it
quite a
bit. There’s very little stridency left in his statements.
The rest of the quartet was comprised of Roy Haynes (drums), Jimmy Gar-
rison (bass) and Steve Kuhn (piano), who had his hands full filling in for the
missing Getz. The other half of the
bill presented pianist Junior Mance with
Buddy Catlett on bass and Paul Gusman displaying a particularly effervescent
style on drums.
With Getz’s week-long date, the Vanguard’s Max Gordon announced a star-
studded Spring lineup of talent set for the club. Following Getz into the place
was the Modern Jazz Quartet and the Don Ellis Trio.
Ellis, trumpet graduate
of the Ferguson,
Thornhill and Barnet
organizations, makes
his nitery bow
with the date. April 4-16 brings Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers into the
club
alternating with the
International Jazz
Quartet, representing members
from Hungary, Belgium, the Netherlands and the U.S. April 25th finds genial
vet Jack Teagarden disturbing the modernists who usually inhabit the Van-
guard with his likeable Dixie melodies. But Junior Mance will soothe the dis-
comforted as he returns once more, to alternate with Teagarden. On May 9th
Oscar Brown, Jr., returns for an unusually long four-weeks booking. This lad
is really on the move upward—even plans a Broadway musical, “Kicks & Co.”
for fall opening.
Franklin Geltman boasting that this Summer’s Randall’s Island Jazz Festival
has now become the largest of its kind in the world. At the same time, producer
Geltman announced the dates for the fest: August 25-26-27. A complete list of
the performers is forthcoming from the Geltman office.
The
Cannonball Adderley
Quintet embarks
April
6th
for
three weeks
in
Europe. The tour commences in Amsterdam and
is followed by dates in Ham-
burg, Stockholm, Helsinki, Copenhagen, Oslo, Gothenburg, Cologne, Dusseldorf,
Berlin, Munich, Vienna and Frankfurt. Cannonball’s personal manager, Chuck
Taylor, will be accompanying them on the tour.
Les McCann recently completed his
first vocal recording session for
Pacific
Jazz Records. He was backed on the date by a big band playing charts by Ger-
ald Wilson. It was also learned from the label that Richard “Groove” Holmes, a
discovery of McCann’s, has been pacted by them. McCann “discovered” Holmes
while on a recent eastern tour and persuaded him to come west. McCann will
produce Holmes’
first album.
Dan Terry and his “Big Band On Campus,” which has been playing jazz con-
certs and proms on the east coast college circuit, is being paged to headline the
Virginia Beach Jazz Festival. Tom Gwaltney, chairman of the fest, will brings
the group of youngsters to a festival which last year_ featured Maynard Fer-
guson’s band and the year before starred Count Basie. Pretty big shoes for
Terry to
fill.

.

.
Braving the riots
at Ft. Lauderdale (which made Newport seem like a soft summer breeze)
are
Chris Connor, the Hi-Los and Gerry Mulligan, all headlining the Ft. Lauderdale
Jazz Festival (March 24-29). Following the fest, Chris continued on her south-
1
ern concert tour which began at Wake Forrest March

THE
MUSIC COES
ROUND AND ROUND
LEO ADDEO
“DANCE BY THE LIGHT OF THE MOON”—
The Olympics—Arvee A 424
The
Olympics
have
racked
up
an
impressive
string of
hits. Here in their second LP they per-
form
hits “Dance By The Light Of The Moon,”
“Shimmy
Like
Kate” and
“Little
Pedro,”
their
cui'rent chart success, and several new hard rock
originals. An infectious, contagious session by one
of the better proponents
of the teen beat idiom.
“SPECTACULAR PERCUSSION GOES LATIN”
—Roger King Mozian and
his
Orchestra—MGM
E3921
The
arranger-conductor-trumpeter
shattered
speakers
first
with
“Spectacular
Brass,”
then
took
it
to
the
cha
cha
cha,
and now
ventures
forth
in
a
sparkling
Latin
concert.
Various
rhythms
(easily
accessible
for dancing)
set the
pace for bristling lively treatments of “Put On A
Happy Face,” “The Sound of Music,” “Softly As
In A Morning -Sunrise” and “What’s New At The
Zoo” among
others. A
contagious
interplay
be-
tween the brass and percussion keeps things zing-
ing along at a sunny
clip.
“THE MUSIC GOES ’ROUND AND ’ROUND ”—
Leo Addeo and
his Orchestra—RCA Victor LSA-
2353
Indeed, the music goes
’round and
’round, for
Victor’s engineers have made it so for this “Stereo
Action”
release.
Addeo’s
unusually-instrumental
ork features
his
harmonica, four
ocarinas, four
guitars,
a
bass
accordion
plus
assorted rhythm
and percussion. In total they produce an unusual
ensemble sound that makes merry with such
se-
lections
as
“Let’s
Take A
Walk
Around
The
Block,”
“You’d
Be
Surprised,”
“Then
I’ll
Be
Happy” and “Don’t Fence Me In.”
GIRLS OF
IV]Y DREAMS
“GIRLS OF MY DREAMS”—Frank
Barcley &
Harry Arnold—Atco 33-127
The
cocktail-ish
piano
mannerisms
of
Frank
Barcley
is superimposed over the fragrantly
ro-
mantic settings of Harry Arnold’s ork in a liquid
expression
of
sentimentality. Mood music
lovers
will treasure
this
session
as one
of the best
in
recent
months.
Selections
include
“Laura,”
“Ramona,”
“Louise,”
“Linda,”
“Cecilia”
and
“Nancy.”

“EVOLUTION OF THE BLUES SONG”—Jon
Hendricks—Columbia CL 1583
Jon
Hendricks
earned
international
accolades
for
his performance
of “Evolution
of the Blues
Song” at
last year’s Monterey Jazz Festival. An
original rhyming narrative
directed
basically
at
children for
effect but actually a pointed
lesson
for
adults,
the work
traces
the
beginnings
of
music through the
spirituals, gospels,
blues and
jazz.
Specific
points
are
illustrated by perform-
ances by Hannah Dean, Big
Miller, Pony
Poin-
dexter, Jimmy Witherspoon, the Ike
Issacs
Trio
with Ben Webster and
Hendricks
himself. Over
44 minutes of stimulating listening and learning.
“THE SOUL OF JAZZ PERCUSSION”—War-
wick W5003
Unlike
previous
attempts
to
mate
jazz
with
percussive effects, this album comes
off as an ex-
cellent
jazz
session,
with
percussion from
the
normal range of instruments enhancing the music
in
the
same way
that
any
fine
jazz drummer
dresses up a band with more than just timekeep-
ing. Three different groups play a series of seven
specially composed numbers
(plus two
others).
Don Ellis and Pepper Adams contributing superb
solo work.
Finally,
a
superior
stereo production
for the jazz fans.

FREDDIE
REDD
QUINTET
“SHADES OF REDD”—Freddie Redd Quintet-
Blue Note 4045
Redd
earned
accolades
for
his
music
for
the
long-running off-Broadway hit, “The Connection.”
Here, with Jackie McLean
(also of “Connection”
fame),
Tina
Brooks,
Paul Chambers
and
Louis
Hayes, Redd contributes more of the earthy blues
passion that stood him in good stead for the show.
The ensemble passages
are
stirringly portrayed
in one-ness by the front
line thespians and each
displays
a
searching,
soulful
view
solo-wise.
Tunes are
all Redd originals and include “Thes-
pians,” “Shadows,” “Just A Ballad For My Baby.’
“BIG BRASS”—Benny Bailey—Candid 8011
From the sounds of this album, Benny Bailey
is sorely missed on the American jazz scene. (He
resides permanently in Europe.) He
is extremely
articulate, relying on a variety of natural devices
for expression. His tone, open and muted, is well
controlled
and
there
is
a
completely
relaxed
naturalness
in
all
his work. Though not intense
and
searching,
he
manages
to
be
thoroughly
original and inventive in his conceptions. Accom-
panied by sextet of top jazz musicians, he plays
“Hard
Sock
Dance,”
“Alison,”
“Tipsy”
and “A
Kiss To Build A Dream On.” A delectable change
of pace here.
“A RARE BATCH OF SATCH”—Louis
Arm-
strong—RCA Victor LPM-2322
A
dozen
Louis Armstrong
recorded
perform-
ances from the early
Thii’ties have been dug up
by
Victor and
re-packaged
here. The
numbers,
recorded with
three bands—Chick Webb’s, Mike
McKendriek’s and a pick-up group—shows Louis
in various settings as an outstanding trumpeter,
a great singer, a showman and sometimes comic.
In
all,
it’s a look at the entire personality of one
of the greatest. Selections include “I Gotta Right
To Sing The Blues,” “Basin Street Blues,” “High
Society” and a rare, informal
session, “Laughin’
Louie.” Collectors will be interested.
“THE
HAP’NIN’S”—The
Gigi
Gryce
Quintet
featuring Richard
Williams—Prestige/New
Jazz
8246A
solid swinger with an uncompromising ven-
turesome outlook on whatever he does, Gigi Gryce
has
been
recorded
here
with
his
quintet
in
a
vibrant blowing session. Trumpeter Richard Wil-
liams
is featured
and
together, Gryce and Wil-
liams cut a neat figure on the ensemble passages
as well as establish their fervent blues approach
in
solo
work.
Selections
include
standards
“Frankie and Johnny,” “Lover Man,” and “Sum-
mertime.”
“THE WARM MOODS”—Ben Webster—Reprise
R-2001
The most
satisfying
ballad
artist
in
jazz
for
many years has been Ben Webster. His fat, warm,
fog
horn-like
tone
is
a
sheer
delight
on
the
moodier
pops. Here he once again displays
this
forte in a program that includes “Stella By Star-
light,”
“Time
After
Time,”
“It’s Easy To
Re-
member” and “Nancy.” The string quartet accom-
paniment provided by arranger Johnny Richards
is excessively saccharine and muddles the session
but Webster manages
to
cut through the smog
and emerge on top.
“THE CONTEMPORARY JAZZ CLASSICS OF
THE PAUL MOER TRIO”—Del-Fi DFLP 1212
This album intros the fresh pianistic and writ-
ing
talent
of
Paul Moer. He
is
extremely
eco-
nomical
in his
playing, seemingly choosing only
the choice notes for expression, and favors under-
statement
in
setting
the mood. With brass and
drums
accompaniment
acceding
to
his
sparse
style, he offers improvisations of “I Love Paris,”
“We’ll Be Together Again,” “Azure Blues” and
a handful
of
original compositions.
CLASSICAL
PICKS
OF THE WEEK
“THE FOUR BRAHMS SYMPHONIES”—Otto
Klemperer conducting the Philharmobia Orchestra
—Angel 3614 D
An ultra deluxe package
(similar to the Soria
productions) houses an equally outstanding set of
four disks on which are recorded Otto Klemperer’s
superb interpretations
of the four Brahms sym-
phonies.
It
is
a masterful achievement
in every
aspect as Klemperer once again displays his pene-
tration
of
Brahms’
work.
The
“Tragic”
and
“Academic
Festival”
overtures
fill
out the deck
nicely. A choice classical item.

&

this new package.

WB's Weiss Goes To Oviert
For License Appointments
HOLLYWOOD—Robert B. Weiss,
in-
ternational
director of Warner
Bros.
Records,
following meeting and
dis-
cussions with prexy James
B.
Conk-
ling and WB
staffers, planed out for
the Far East last weekend
(8), as he
continues his round-the-world tour in
behalf of the
label appointing global
licensees.
Enroute to his Paris headquarters,
Weiss will stop
off for meetings with
disk executives in Japan, Hong Kong,
the
Philippines,
Viet Nam,
Malaya,
Thailand, Burma, Ceylon, India, Pak-
istan,
Israel and
Greece. During
his
jet tour
of the Far
East, Weiss
will
review
future
plans
with
current
Warner
Bros
Records
Licensees
in
Tokyo and Manila as well as appoint
new
distributors
in
the
remaining
areas.
In
Tokyo,
he
will
meet
with
the
directors of Nitchiku Industrial Com-
pany, Ltd., and in Quezon City
(Phil-
ippines)
with
L. Villar and
his
staff
at Mareco
Co.,
Inc. One
of the
dis-
cussion
points
will
cover
the
release
of local language records by Japanese
and
Philippine
artists
on
the WB
label, in an effort to enhance the value
of
the
American
record
trademark
in the respective countries.
Weiss expects
to make
the
trip
in
four weeks, returning
to
Paris
early
in May.
Following
his
Paris
return,
he will plane to London for meetings
with WB
licensee, Decca/England,
to
discuss
immediate
plans
for
new
singles promotion plus the scheduling
of LP
and EP
product
for
the
fall
season.
During
the
time
of
his
Burbank
visit, Weiss reviewed all international
matters with president Conkling-, and
they outlined future operational plans
in
the
continued
expansion
of
the
label
via
its
foreign
manufacturing
and
distributing
organizations.

last

BENELUX
Mariano Rapetti, manager of pop music
of Ricordi-Milano, visited Editions
Altona,
Amstei’dam,
and
congratulated Wim
van
Vught
on
the
wonderful
Dutch recording on
the Polydor
label
of “Mais
Oui,” waxed by well-known
Marcel Thielemans. Although
this
title
is recorded
all
over Europe, Rapetti
preferred the Dutch version in spite of the fact that he only could understand
these two words: “Mais Oui!”
Music publisher Joop Portengen rejoices on the fast growing international
interest in
his Dutch production:
the song “Amore Mia (Wann Kommst Du
Wieder)” was
recorded by Scandinavian
top-star Siw Malmkvist
last week;
“The Amsterdam Waltz” was inserted in the French motion picture “Marche
Ou Creve (Go Or Die)”, which
will be released
all over Europe.
Meisel Ver-
lag, Berlin and Southern, London, bought the rights of another Portengen-hit,
“Ay Ay Caballero,” both publishers expecting great possibilities on this song.
Both
winning numbers
of
the
Eurovision
Song
festival
are
published
in
Holland by Editions Altona. “Nous Les Amoureux” will be recorded in Dutch
by Jan van der Most for L.C. Phonogram. A & R-manager Jan de Winter has
chosen the big German title “Jenny” for the flip-side. This
title
is also a pub-
lication of Editions Altona. The original recording of the winning song “Nous
Les Amoureux” by Jean Claude Pascal was brought on the mai’ket by
L.C.
Bovema within two days after the Cannes contest. “Are You Sure,” Englands
winner, number two
in Cannes,
is already released by
L.C. Phonogram and
A & R manager Jan de Winter
is preparing a Dutch cover record by a new
young
couple. The
song
will
be
recorded
in German
by
the
famous
Blue
Diamonds. “Non
Je Ne
Regrette
Rien,”
published
in
Holland
by
Editions
Altona,
is climbing up in the charts. The original Edith Piaf recording
doing-
solid
sales.
Dutch
cover
recordings were made
by
Corry Brokken
and
Rie
Helmig, and both are getting action.
The
old German
hit
song
“Erst Schwort Man Treu
(The
First
Oath
Is
Fidelity)” will be republished by Bassart in a new version. Bassart has many
of these
old German evergreens on
its
repertoire and once republished
in
a
new
version,
they seem
to
have
great
possibilities.
Artone
purchased
the
Laurie master
“Little Lonely One” by The Jarmels
for immediate
release.
Phonogram Director Theo Van Der Meer just
left for Milan.
Old
timer Pee Wee Erwin
with The
Dixie
Strutters
go “Down By
The
Riverside” on his new LP on the London label. Wonderful versions of “Swing
Low, Sweet Chariot,” “When The
Saints Go Marching
In,” “Careless Love,”
“Just A
Closer Walk With Thee” and some
other
steady
favorites
are
on
this jazzy LP
(L.C. Phonogram). On “Great Golden
Hits,” Billy Vaughn and
his
orchestra
swing
the
great
instrumentals
of the
late
thirties and
early
forties. Quite a
different sound
for those who know
Billy from
“Sail Along
Silv’ry Moon” and other hits with his sax gimmick. Favorites from the band
books of Glenn Miller, Artie Shaw, Glen Gray’s Casa Loma Orchestra, Tommy
Dorsey and Charlie Barnet are
included, such
as “Little Brown Jug,” “Opus
One,” “No Name Jive” and “A String Of Pearls” (London).
Three
records
with
selections from
famous
operettas were
released
last
week on the Decca
label:
“Grafin Mariza” by Emmerich Kalman, “Der Bet-
telstudent” by Carl Millocker and “Der Graf Von Luxemburg” by Franz Lehar.
These operettas are
still beloved in the low countries and are released by L.C.
Phonogram.
A happy swinger in the Warner Bros, repertoire
is “Swing Fever” by Ham-
mond organ-player Buddy Cole. “I certainly expect to get a
lot of demand for
this album,” says
C. Pompe, Bovema’s Warner
Bros,
label manager.
Bovema was the first
in Europe to release the Dutch
(national)
version of
the current German success “Drei Weisse Birken,” sung by Uschi und Peter on
the Imperial-label. New releases of the
Impeidal-label in Holland are “Parijs
Ligt Aan De Seine” by De Vrolijke Zangers and the Dutch version of the well-
known
hit “Sucu Sucu.”
Pete
Felleman, manager
of Funckler Records—a
division
of Artone—told
The Cash Box that his current top-selling singles include: “Kili-Watch” (The
Cousins), “Hava Nagila”
(The Barry
Sisters), “You Talk Too Much”
(Joe
Jones), “Kana Kapila” (The Cousins), and “Tumbala-Lika” (The Barry
Sis-
ters). John James Vis told The Cash Box
that Artone’s
top
five
singles
in-
clude: “Sucu Sucu” (Eddy Christiani), “Carolina Dai” (Rocco Granata), “The
Story Of My Love” (Paul Anka), “Vaya Con Dios” (The Virtues) and “A1 Di
La” (Milva).
Hot news from Bovema’s Columbia-label: Edith Piaf’s “Non Je Ne Regrette
Rien” reaching the 60,000 sales figure Robert Oeges, Columbia label manager,
believes that the record
will
beat the results
of “Milord,” which was
Piaf’s
big
hit one year ago.
Famous Dutch comedians, De Wama’s, have a new record that
is bound to
become a big seller: “Doet U Mee Met De B.B.?” and “Striptease Blues,” on
the Decca
label. Also on Decca
is a new 45
single
record
of the now world
famous Blue Diamonds. Two more good old songs in the Diamonds way, with
orchestra directed by their coach Jack Bulterman: “In A Little Spanish Town”
and
“I’m
Forever
Blowing
Bubbles.”
Another
“Ramona”
is
expected
and
Dutch record buyers will soon make this record the number one
seller on the
Best
Sellers
is the general
belief.
Teenage music
is always present on the London
label. “Baby, Oh Baby” by
The Shells and “Wait A Minute” by The Coasters are among the latest addi-
tions. This week we welcome Eydie Gorme on the London
label, who
joines
her husband in “The Facts Of Life” and “I’m A
Girl, You’re A Boy.” Other
single releases worth mentioning are “Theme From Exodus” by Ferrante &
Teicher and “The Exodus Song” by Pat Boone.
Artone’s A & R Chief Lion
J. Swaab just recorded Rijk de Gooyer, one of
Holland’s prominent radio- and tv-personalities for the
label. Rijk de Gooyer
is currently active on the German movie
scene.
In this years’ internationally famous festival at the
little village of Blokker,
the
following
artists
are
exnected among
others: Rex
Gildo, Jan &
Kjeld,
Louis Armstrong All Stars, Heidi
Briihl, The Blue Diamonds, Conny Froboess
and Connie Francis. In the near future, jazz-concerts will be given in Amster-
dam by the Thelonious Monk Quartet (15th April) and Mahalia Jackson (22nd
April). The Cannonball Adderley Quintet recently appeared there.
There’s an extremely great demand for the full-color Capitol-catalog, which
was offered by Mr. Hundepool, Bovema’s Capitol-captain, for Dutch consumers.
Thousands
of cards and requests were received at Gramophone House.
Frank
Visser,
MGM’s
label
manager
for
Bovema,
told
The
Cash
Box
that Mark Dinning
is making a wonderful comeback with “Top
Forty, News
And Sports” in the novelty field. MGM’s newest release is the mono-and stereo-
version
of Leroy Holmes, LP, containing
his own composition “Tara Lara.”
Holland also releases a Dutch manufactured Conway Twitty
hit, “Sorry” with
“Pretty Eyed Baby” on the
flipside.
Latin-American
singer
Carmela made
a
wonderful
impression when
she
sang recently at the International Culture Centre in Amsterdam and on Dutch
TV the following day. Her first LP, just released,
is already in high demand;
it
is released by L.C. Phonogram, on the Fontana
label.
“Paris Jam Session,” a live recording (December 18th, 1959) of Art Blakey’s
Jazz Messengers with Bud Powell and Barney Wilen,
is a welcome new
re-
lease for
all modern jazz fans, on Fontana
(L.C. Phonogram).

ALL THAT JAZZ
Randy Weston
joins the growing
list
of jazz composers who have drawr
inspiration from the African freedom movement for an extended
jazz work
Weston’s “African Suite” has been recorded by Roulette and will be released
this month as part of the “Uhuru Afrika” (Freedom Africa) album. The suite
features lyrics by Langston Hughes, a spoken narration by Tuntemeke Sanga,
of Tanganyika,
baritone
vocal
solos by Brock
Peters
and
soprano
solos
by
Martha Flowers. The arrangement is by Melba Liston, who also conducted the
twenty-six piece ork on the date. The list of musicians who participated in the
recording
reads
like
a
who’s who
of
jazz: Max
Roach,
Olatunji,
Candido,
Armando Peraza and Charlie Persip form the percussion line; others featured
include Kenny
Burrell, Clark Terry, Benny Bailey, Richard Williams, Jerome
Richardson,
Gigi
Gryce,
Les
Spann,
Yusef
Lateef,
Slide Hampton,
George
Duvivier, Jimmy Cleveland, Cecil Payne and Freddie Hubbard.
The album also debuts a new Roulette “sound”
series which will emphasize
Afro-percussion.
Teddy Wilson’s current engagement at New York’s Embers is being used by
the pianist to mark his thirtieth year in jazz. The thirty years dates from an
engagement
in April 1931 at Chicago’s Gold Coast Club where Wilson played
for six weeks as part of a dance sextet. Actually, Wilson’s music career pre-
dates 1931, but it was this year that started him on his way. For the next few
years he gigged around Chicago with Louis Armstrong, Jimmy Noone, Erskine
Tate and others. Then joined Benny Carter in New York in 1933. After playing
with Willie Bryant’s band in 1934-35 he made jazz history by recording with
and touring as part of the Benny Goodman Trio—the swing
era’s
first inter-
racial
act.
International prominence with the Goodman groups
firmly estab-
lished Wilson as
a top name. His
precise, economical, gently swinging^ style
proved an innovation on jazz piano and influenced countless other musicians.
Today Wilson is considered one of the all-time greats of the instrument.
Charlie Mingus was guest of honor (even wore a tie and jacket)
at a press
party jointly hosted by Candid Records and the Copa City nitery at which the
bassist introduced his “Rotary Perception” new jazz conception. The idea is one
of complete
individual
improvisation within
the
group,
with rhythm
cycles
determining the
limits.
(That’s the way we understand
it.)
Appearing with
Mingus were
regulars Dannie Richmond,
Eric
Dolphy, Ted
Curzon, Jimmy
Knepper and Charlie McPherson, Britt Woodman, Lonnie Hilyer and Paul Bley.
Max Roach showed up and proved the high point of the
evening’s
activities
when he and Mingus improvised several duets together. The party also
cele-
brated
the
extension
of
Mingus’ engagement
at
the
club
for
an
indefinite
period. When Charlie finds a place he likes, he stays there!
Jordan
Ramin,
indie
record
producer,
has
produced
for Argo
Records
a
satirical LP on the old Norman Granz Jazz At The Philharmonic concerts. Re-
leased last week under the title “Morris Grants Presents J.U.N.K.,” the album
features
imitative sounds
of some
of the top names
in jazz represented by
such new names as Morris Brewbeck, Sol Desman, Miles Morris with Can-E-Bal
Naturally, Morris Garner, Ornette Morris and Thelonliest Plunk. The package
is complete right down to the liner notes by Ira Morris (“America’s Foremost
Liner-Note Writer”). Obviously, not too much good taste was present when the
LP was conceived
and, obviously, Ramin has a
fixation
(or fetish?)
on the
name “Morris.”

“AMERICA’S GREATEST MUSIC MAKERS”—
Decca DL 74126
Excerpts
from
12
new
Decca
instrumental
packages
provide
not
just
a sampler but a
de-
lightfully
diverting
dancing-listening
date.
The
tracks range in taste and tempo from the sweet-
ness of Guy Lombardo, Liberace and Jan Garber
to the more compelling entertainment provided by
Henry Jerome (“Brazen Brass”), Pete Fountain,
Ralph Flanagan and Warren Covington. Diversity
is the big attraction.
“1961 ITALIAN SONG HITS FROM THE SAN
REMO FESTIVAL”—London TW 91255
Through the
11 years of its existence the San
Remo Festival has accounted for many fine pop-
ular songs as well as numerous International hits.
A dozen entries in this year’s fest have been as-
sembled in their original diskings by London and
released in this package. It includes performances
by
Italy’s
biggest
stars,
Flo
Sandon’s,
Aurelio
Fierro,
Little Tony, Julia De Palma and
Achille
Togliani. A charming songfest.
“MOTION PICTURE THEMES CHA CHA CHA”
—Tito Rodriguez Orch.—Ultra Audio WWS 8507
The
usual Rodriguez combo
is augmented
by
additional
brass, woodwinds and percussion, and
with Teddy Randazzo arrangements, offers easily
danceable Latin-ized slicings of such flick themes
as “Exodus,” “Never On
Sunday,” “A Summer
Place,” “The Apartment” and “The Unforgiven.”
Sound, in the “deluxe” idiom, is good—well-modu-
lated, never blaring. Rodriguez has a multitude of
fans.
“CHARANGA!”—Seeco SCLP 9216
Seeco capitalizes on the mushrooming charanga
craze by culling from its vast Latin dance archives
a compendium of pachangas performed by select
native Cuban aggregations. Portraying the dance
authentically are La Sonora Matancera, Orquesta
America Del ’55, Estrellas Cubanas and Hermanos
Ferreira. This
is the real thing—to be especially
appreciated by students of the dance.
“CHARANGA & PACHANGA”—Hector
Rivera
and His Orchestra—Epic LN BN 599
Though the Rivera ork adheres to the pachanga
rhythms its sound is not true charanga. Whereas
the correct sound
is that of flute (s) and strings,
Rivera’s complement is the usual American-styled
brass
band.
In
this
idiom
it
portrays
a
dozen
danceables,
among
which
is
the
popular
“La
Pachanga.” OK dance wax.
“LA PACHANGA”—Rene Touzet—GNP 57
Touzet also
suffers from unfaithfulness to the
proper
charanga
sound,
leading
his
regular
strong-rhythmed,
brass-based
ensemble.
Tune
lineup features “La Pachanga” and eleven others,
including several Touzet originals.

“DOUBLE

and

The

Ferguson band provides Chris Connor with

include “Two Ladies In De Shade of De Banana
Tree,”
“All

the Most” and “Summer-

“GERRY MULLIGAN AND THE CONCERT
JAZZ BAND AT THE VILLAGE VANGUARD”
—Verve V 8396
The immense success of the new Mulligan band
is obvious upon one hearing of this album. Mul-
lingan has tooled a group
of mainly youngsters
into an
efficient swing machine
that plays with
emotional
intensity and
stirring
urgency,
over-
shadowing whatever technical shortcomings youth
and inexperience may find. Taken from a Sunday
afternoon
session
at
the New York
nitery,
the
album showcases the band in six pieces from
its
standard
repertoire,
notably
“Blueport,”
“Black
Nightgown” and “Come Rain Or Come Shine.”

Once

Especially tailored for jazz tastes, the set should
also be gratefully appreciated by pop buyers.

“LEE-WAY”—Lee Morgan—Blue Note 4034
This is essentially a Jazz Messengers’ date with
an expanded spotlight on Lee Morgan. Blakey
is
here
to
lay down
a vitally compelling beat and
front-liners Morgan and Jackie McLean also get
uncompromising
support
from
Paul
Chambers
and
Bobby
Timmons.
All
solo
effectively
with
Morgan leading the way displaying his constantly
increasing
proficiency. A
spirited,
dynamically
satisfying LP.
“BOSS OF THE SOUL-STREAM TROMBONE”
—Curtis Fuller—Warwick W 2038
The best of the new trombonists, and the most
exciting new
star on the instrument
since J.
J.
Johnson’s emergence years ago, Curtis
Fuller
is
growing by
leaps
and bounds
as
an
important
new voice in jazz. In this Warwick date he plays
with more
economy
than
is
customarily
heard
from him, yet thrillingly puts across
his soulful
blues statements
in
effective terms. Sidemen
in-
clude
Yusef
Lateef,
Freddie
Hubbard,
Walter
Bishop,
Stu Martin
and Buddy
Catlett. Among
the tunes are “If
I Were A Bell,” “But Beautiful”
and “Do I Love You.”
“JUG”—Gene Ammons—Prestige 7192
Gene Ammons moves freely and easily between
the most
soulful “low-down”
blues
to
a
bright,
gently swinging pop and
is equally comfortable
in each
situation—which he has proven
consist-
ently on previous dates. Here, once again his re-
laxed manner takes charge
as he communicates
pure jazz feelings on “OP Man River,” “Exactly
Like You,” “Tangerine” and five others. Support
is sympathetic to the Ammons groove. Artist
is
building a loyal following.
“THE ORIGINAL MUSIC OF THRILLER”—
Pete Rugolo and his Orchestra—Time S/2034
Rugolo’s score for the Tuesday nite TV offering
is another example of the vital importance music
has
in advancing a particular theme. In
this
al-
bum
of
selections from
various
“Thriller”
epi-
sodes, Rugolo creates vivid musical images which
can
stand
apart from
the
show
as
fascinating
musical
diversion. Apart from
the main theme,
the LP
contains
such
appropos-titled
tracks
as
“Voodoo Man,” “Tvristed Image” and “Finger of
Fear.”
CLASSICAL PICK OF THE WEEK
WAGNER: “Tristan Und Isolde”—Birgit Nilsson,
Georg
Solti conducting the Vienna Philharmonic
Orchestra—London OSA 1502
In
the
grand
tradition
of
its
opera
catalog,
London has created another outstanding disk pro-
duction—the elaborate “Tristan Und Isolde.” Bir-
git
Nilsson’s
Isolde,
acclaimed
at
the Met and
heard temptingly on the excerpts disk released last
year,
is
a rewarding
experience, and
Solti
cap-
tures the spirit of the work in his faithful direc-
tion. Support is uniformly excellent. The opera is
complete on five disks, while the package offers an
additional one disk bonus of rehearsals and
dis-
cussions
in
preparation
to
the
final
recording.

Album Reviews
“ONE EYED JACKS”—Original Film Soundtrack
—Liberty LOS
17001
With “One Eyed Jacks”
doing-
big box
office
now,
sales
of
this
track
release could
put
it
in
best-selling- contention. Hugo
Friedhofer’s
sensi-
tive
score
is
a
coloi-ful panorama
of
the
Cali-
fornia-Mexico situation in the 1880’s, scene of the
flick, combining areas of boisterousness with deli-
cate Spanish guitar passages. Serves an interest-
ing mood
listening purpose.
“ACCENT!”—Latin
Piano
by
Jan
August
Mercury SR 60618
Pianist August, renowned
for
his
hit
stylings
of Latin tunes, energetically approaches a lineup
of Latin and American pop sturdies and interprets
them
in
his
stylish
concertized manner.
It
pro-
vides an enjoyable instrumental interlude wherein
melody receives topmost consideration. Offered are
“El Cumbanchero,” “Green Eyes,” “I Concentrate
On Y'ou,” “Siboney” and “Two Guitars.” August
is
still an adult favorite.
“SIZZLING
STRINGS-CASTANETS-PERCUS-
SION
’—Don Luis Quintero and the Madrid Festi-
val Orchestra—Directional Sound DS 5007
The
fiery music
of
Spain,
in
either
origin
or
intent,
is a proven international LP commodity.
Here maestro Quintero directs his ork in particu-
larly
authentic
readings
of
such
favorites
as
“Espagna”
(Chabrier),
“Capriccio
Espagnol”
(Rimsky-Korsakov),
“La
Paloma,”
“Estudian-
tina” and “Granada.” The Mario Valero Dancers
and guitarist Jose Alvarez are heard on two ad-
ditional
flamenco
tracks.
Percussion,
mainly by
castanets, is an inherent part of the music rather
than an added attraction.
“VIVA LA PACHANGA”—Joe Sherman and
his
Pachanga-Charanga Kings—Kapp KL-1241
Arranger-conductor
Joe
Sherman
has
trans-
posed
the
original
Latin-American
Charanga
sound into a pop composite that should serve as
appealing fare to the increasing number of Pach-
anga
dance
followers
in
the
U.S.
Most
of
the
tracks
follow
the
“authentic”
sound
faithfully,
complete with
Spanish language
vocal
choruses
over
the
strings-flute instrumental
backing, but
Sherman
has
also
added
brass, woodwinds
and
stronger rhythms. Selections include some trans-
lated pop
hits among Latin
originals.
“GLENN
MILLER
MEETS
THE
DORSEY
BROTHERS
IN
PERCUSSION” —
Warwick
W5007 ST
Tunes from the
Miller and Dorsey Swing
era
books have been
re-arranged
for
stereo
percus-
sion listening retaining the basic
flavor
of
their
original sound and are assembled here
in an
en-
tertaining package. The Dorsey contributions in-
clude “Boogie Woogie,” “Green Eyes” and “Ama-
pola”;
the
Miller
book
serves
up
“Moonlight
Serenade,”
“In
The
Mood”
and
“Little
Brown
Jug.” Good listening for big band buffs.
“CARMEN CAVALLARO PLAYS
HIS SHOW
STOPPERS”—Decca DL
74018
Musical selections—classical, semi-cla.ssical and

Cavallaro

PIC K

“TWO’S COMPANY”—Maynard
Ferguson
and
Chris Connor—Roulette R 52068
The reciprocal Connor-Ferguson dates for At-
lantic and Roulette prove a boon for both artists.
Here the Roulette package
follow's basically the
similar path established by the Atlantic date
(re-
viewed last week)
in that Chris
if provoked into
vigorously swinging performances with
a sunny
outlook by a brignt, heady Ferguson band. Both
artists’ performances are inspired by the presence
of each
other. Selections
here include
“I
Feel A
Song Coming On,” “Something’s Coming,” “New
Yoi'K s My Home,” and “Send For
IMe.”
Terrific
entertainment.
“AROUND THE WORLD IN PERCUSSION”—
Louis
Bellson—Roulette R 65002
Bellson has proven innumerable times through
the years that he can be a one man whiz at per-
cussion. Here,
his drums are augmented by two
additional percussion men, and with Bellson’s
big-
band in tow, they drive headlong into a vibrantly
exciting series of performances. The date can be
taken at stylish big band jazz or as jazz-oriented
pops, and in this way works toward a wider sales
outlook. Deserves
it
too. Tunes
include “Brazil,”
“Loch Lomond,” “Sabre Dance” and
a
collection
of various
oldies and
originals.
“BEV KELLY IN PERSON”-Riverside RLP 345
Despite the similarity
in
vocal tone and
style
between Bev Kelly and Anita O’Day, Miss Kelly
communicates
a
decidedly
personal
attachment
to the songs she sings. She has a glowing warmth
in
her
voice
and
she
colors
her
performances
with
subtle
shadings
of
feelings and
moods.
In
this “live” date (San Francisco’s Coffee Gallery)
this personality
is much more evident than
it has
been
in
previous
studio
sessions.
Material
runs
to
the
best
of the pops, “Then
I’ll Be Tired
of
You,”
“It Never Entered My Mind,” “Falling
In
Love With Love” and “Body and
Soul.” Superior
jazz vocal entertainment.
“ANOTHER
OPUS”—Lem
Winchester-Pres-
tige/New Jazz 8244
At
the
time
of
Lem
Winchester’s
untimely
death
in January
of this year he was an
estab-
lished new star on vibes and had been developing
into
a
personal
musician.
This
last
session,
in
which he appeared with Frank Wess, Hank and
Eddie Jones and Gus Johnson, goes a long way in
proving the
artist’s growth
out from under the
Milt Jackson wing. Wess’ flute talks business too
in
its
usually
precise
swinging
manner.
Good
jazz
here.
“US THREE”—Horace
Parian,
George
Tucker,
A1 Harewood—Blue Note 4037
Solid new
talent
to
arise
out
of
the
Mingus
Workshop,
pianist
Parian
has
demonstrated
on
two previous Blue Note leader dates that his de-
velopment is continuing at a fast pace and on an
original path. Tucker and Harewood provide the
two other parts of the cohesive unit that
is heard
on
“I Want
To
Be
Loved,”
“The
Lady
Is A
Tramp” and
the
groovy
title
tune.

HARM Means Business At Miami Meet
MIAMI BEACH, FLA.—A
business-
like attitude keyed last week’s confab
of the National Association of Record
Merchandisers (NARM)
here
at
the
Eden Roc Hotel.
With
registration
activities
out-of-
the-way after Monday
(24), the meet
got down to real business on Tuesday
morning (25) at the first business ses-
sion.
Following
prexy
Harold
Gold-
man’s welcoming address, Jules Mala-
mud,
NARM’s
executive
secretary,
traced NARM’s
brief
history
which
began at a 1958 Toiletries Convention.
Via
speeches
by
James
J.
Tiedjens
(“Promotion &
Sales Aids—Merchan-
dising & Packaging Techniques’’) and
George
E.
Kline
(“Progressive
Gro-
cer’s” Rack Merchandising Study)
at
the
first workshop the same morning,
the point of maturity, NARM’s desire
for
“adult”
recognition
of
problems
that
must
be
faced
in
unity,
was
stressed.
Tiedjens’
talk,
with
assistance
by
Donald Van Gorp, both of Musical Isle
Corp.,
covered
packaging
techniques
and such pooints as poly-bagging ma-
chines, proper
identification
of mono
or stereo packages, positions of
titles
on
covers,
importance
of
sleeves
on
singles,
sales aids and merchandising
and promotion.
Each day from 2-5,
all rack-jobbers
were assigned to visit the record com-
pany rooms.
The second workshop
session
(26),
featuring Harold Goldman
(“Aspects
of
Discounting”)
and
Earl M.
Fore-
man
(“History &
Functions
of
Fair
Trade Commission”),
delved
into the
aspects
of
discounting,
which
was
summed-up by Dave
Miller
of Miller
International,
manufacturers
of
the
Somerset
label. Miller said that there
couldn’t be any price fixing because of
federal
legislation,
discounting stems
from overproduction and that unreal-
istic disk pricing
is the practice, and
that
it will be maintained because of
record
clubs.
At
a Wed.
(27)
panel
discussion,
moderated
by
Bob
Rolontz
of
Bill-
board Music Week, various aspects of
rack-jobber
merchandising were
dis-
cussed. Ed Mason said the best mer-
chandising
aid
is
good
product,
and
that too many displays sent to rack-
jobbers were too big, being meant for
music
stores
where
large
displays
were
possible. Ken
Sachs noted
that
price
alone was not
sufficient promo-
tion, but
that promotion needed pur-
pose.
Ed
Snyder
said NARM
could
help
in setting rack-jobber standards
for design and type of displays needed
in rack sales. Larry Rosmarin pointed
out
that because
rack-sales were
no
longer strictly impulse purchases, buy-
it-here displays were required for cus-
tomers
who
now
look
for
specific
things.
Irwin
Tarr,
of RCA
Victor,
said that point-of-sale merchandising
should not be
standard, and that im-
pact
depends
on
being
unique
and
evolved
individually.
Others
in
the
discussion included Mike Maitland
of
Capitol
Records,
Lee
Hartstone
of
London
Records
and Dave
Miller
of
Miller International.
A
panel
discussion
on
Thursday
(27), moderated by Jerry
Shifrin
of
The Cash
Box, turned
to such
topics
as trends toward full-line rack-jobber
record departments and the
effect on
the
supermarket
department,
the
33
single and the future of the EP, “low-
end
line”
(88(S
to
$1.98),
the
rack-
jobber
and
stereo,
cut-outs
and
dis-
counted
LP’s
and how NARM,
with
the advent of an executive secretary,
can create a better liaison of informa-
tion directly between the record manu-
facturer and the record merchandiser,
particularly
in
respect
to
sales,
aids,
programming
and
advertising,
the
manufacturer in regards
to inventory
protection, the problem of singles
re-
turns and how an equitable
situation
for
all can be achieved, use of racks
for
new
promotions,
manufacturer-
distrib-rack relationships and discount
houses vs. rack-jobbers.
Associate members participating
in
the second panel discussion were Wil-
liam Gallagher of Columbia
Records,
Claude
Brennan,
of
Decca
Records,
A1
Bennett
of
Liberty
Records
and
Randy Wood of Dot Records.
The
meet
was
capped-off
by
a
formal
dinner-dance
and
NARM
Awards were presented for label-art-
ist
achievements
in
1960
(see
last
week’s issue for winners).
Reprise
In Tape
Deal
With
United
Stereo Tapes
SUNNYVALE, CALIF.—Reprise Rec-
ords and United Stereo Tapes, a divi-
sion
of Ampex Audio
Co., have
con-
cluded an exclusive agreement where-
by UST will produce
Reprise
record-
ings on 4-track stereo tape. The pact
was concluded by Herbert
L. Brown,
Ampex vice president and manager of
Ampex Audio Co., and Moe Ostin, vice
president
and
general
manager
of
Reprise.
In
announcing
the
agreement.
Brown
said,
“We
are
extremely
pleased
to
be
able
to make
Reprise
recordings available on tape and have
pledged ourselves to doing everything
we
can
to
help
this
aggressive new
company become an outstanding
suc-
cess.”
UST marketing manager
Bill Mus-
ter said that the
first Reprise release
is a rush 4-track version of the Sinatra
album “Ring-A-Ding-Ding!” It will be
followed
closely by
tape
releases
of
tbe album
“Mavis,”
featuring Mavis
Rivers, and Sammy Davis’ “The Wham
of Sam.”
Muster added, “UST intends to work
closely with Reprise in issuing 4-track
tapes as
close
as
possible
to
the
re-
lease date of the equivalent LP. This
will give tape dealers a better oppor-
tunity
to
tie
in with
the
promotion
and DJ
air play surrounding
the
re-
lease
of the LP.”
Muster added that UST
is currently
revamping
its
national
distribution
network
to
improve
availability
of
tape. “When UST
first introduced
4-
track tape there were only a handful
of
dealers
and
the
company
could
adequately serve them through factory
representatives and UST depots on the
two
coasts,”
he
noted.
“Now,
with
thousands of dealers actively stocking
and
selling
4-track
tape,
there
is an
ever increasing need for wider
distri-
bution
and
better
local
representa-
tion.”
Announcement
of
new
UST
distributors
and
representatives
will
be made
shortly. Muster stated.
“Stereo
tape
is
a
specialized mar-
ket,”
concluded
Muster,
“but
a
very
encouraging one. In spite of a slightly
depressed
economy
the
tape
market
has
continued
to grow
steadily
with
retail tape sales currently at the high-
est peak since 4-track was
first intro-
duced.”

Prado Debufs "La Chunga"
NEW YORK—A
new
Latin
dance-
step, “La Chunga,” has bowed
via
a
new RCA
Victor
Records
single
by
Perez
Prado,
“Ritmo
de
Chunga”
(Rhythm of the Chunga). An album
is in the works for release soon.
The dance, created by Kathryn and
Arthur Murray,
is based
on
a game
that
children play
in Cuba
in which
they have to bend their knees to keep
hitting a
ball with a stick.
The Murray’s are now teaching La

the
country.

liner
notes
for
Prado’s
La
Chunga LP
will
feature
special
instructions on how
to dance
it.
Victor and the Murray’s
are plan-
ning
a
joint
advertising and promo-
tion campaign for the dance and the
new Prado single. Both the single and
the album
will be packaged
in
four-
color
sleeves
that
feature
both
the
Murray’s
and
the
Prado.

Philips Records

introduction of a new series of 12" LP’s “Masters Of Art” for release on Fon-
tana. The

is designed

is reproduced one

The death occurred in London last week of Eddie Standring. A well known
figure
in the publishing world for over 30 years he was general manager
of
Campbell Connelly until
ill health forced him to retire in 1959.

the chart topping “Sailor.” With an eye
to the
international market Pet has
cut one side
in English “W’elcome Home” and one side
in French “Les Gens
Deront.”
The Thelonious Monk Quartet and Art Blakey’s Jazz .Messengers arrived for
two London concerts and a nationwide tour of one-nighters. Monk’s Riverside
recordings
are
released here by

and

Album Reviews
“THE WONDERFUL TEENS”—Dick Powell and
the Joe Leahy Orch. & Singers—Record Producers
RPC-M105
In “The Wonderful Teens,” Dick Powell takes
the
listener back
to
the
days
of
the
“Roaring
Twenties,” when he himself was a teenager and,
according
to
the
disk,
acted
no way
different
than
today’s
teenagers.
Through
narration
by
Powell and songs by the Leahy ork & chorus, a
personal glimpse
of
the era
is
neatly
achieved.
Performances by Leahy, several vocal groups and
especially Linda Wells are
authentically charac-
teristic of the time.
“2 ORGANS AND PERCUSSION”—Sy Mann &
Nick Tagg—Grand Award GA 256 SD
Mann and Tagg, at the Hammond and Lowery
organs, and
assisted by
a
variety
of percussive
accents, perform in sparkling duet a program
of
pops. Moods range among the
romantic,
lightly
swinging, and
Latin
dance
beat.
Tunes
include
“Sweet And Lovely,” “I’ve Got The World On
a
String,” “Get Me To the Church On Time” and
“Three Coins In the Fountain.”
“BIRD WATCHING”—The Nutty Squirrels—Co-
lumbia CL 1589
Those
hip,
jazz-oriented
squirrels
pop
up
on
Columbia
with
another
charming
journey
into
jazz, bringing
a
light touch
to
a
field that can
sometimes get too heavy and serious about itself.
The
program
includes
several
Don
Elliott
and
Sascha Borland originals as well as some proven
pops, all delightfully transformed to the world of
speeded-up-voices
in
scat
singing
improvisation.
Among them are “Skylark,” “Bye Bye Blackbird,”
“Yardbird
Suite” and “Didee Bird.”
“WINE WOMEN AND WALTZES”—The Sound
of The Blue Danube—Eric Vaughn, The Medal-
lion Strings and
Percussion—Medallion ML-7519
The charm and
lilt of the Viennese waltz turns
up in full, rich orchestral tapestries woven faith-
fully by arrangers Emanuel Vardi and Jack El-
liot. Melody,
of prime importance
in
this music,
is
strictly adhered
to,
yet
the
addition
of
per-
cussive
coloring becomes
a
vital
ingredient
for
the enjoyment of the LP to set it aside from other
such
endeavors. Among the
selections
are “The
Blue
Danube
Waltz,”
“The
Emperor’s
Waltz,”
“The
Skater’s Waltz”
and
“The
Merry Widow
Waltz.”
“KAKO Y SU COMBO”—Alegre LPA
803
Originally limited in appeal
to Spanish-speak-
ing audiences, this album of authentic Latin dance
music takes on a wider commercial attitude con-
sidering
the
current
renewed
interest
in
Latin
dance
bands.
The
music
is
authentic
in
every
aspect, with a strong spark
of sensuous
excite-
ment running throughout
the
twelve
selections.
Rhythms include mambos and pachangas.
Could
do well in selected locations.
“THE SOULFUL MOODS OF MARVIN GAVE”
—Tamla 221
Gaye,
a
jazz-inflected
vocalist,
intros
on LP
turning in a good performance. Choice
of mate-
rial runs
to
the
better pop
tunes—“My Funny
Valentine,” “How Deep Is the Ocean,” “Love For
Sale,” “Always”—and they’re delivered
in a late-
hours
soulfulness
with
sympathetic combo
sup-
port. An honest effort.
JAZZ
PICK
OF THE WEEK
“NOT SO DUKISH”—Johnny
Hodges
and
his
Orchestra—Verve MG VS-68355
Although
at
first glance
the
title might
indi-
cate something different, this LP
is all-the-way a
very “Dukish”
set. Nothing wrong with that, for
Hodges
has
been
a main
cog
in
the
Ellington
wheels almost since they began to turn, and one
of the early developers of the alto sax. He is
still
one
of the most respected names on
the
instru-
ment, playing
in a mellow, melodic manner. The
accompanying
small
band
here
is
also
mainly
from the Duke and together they make pleasing,
very enjoyable sounds. Top notch date by one of
jazz’s most consistent purveyors.
“FLIGHT
TO
JORDAN”—Duke
Jordan—Blue
Note 4046
Jordan, an early disciple of the bop revolution
and now a solidly entrenched pianist in the New
York “hard bop” scene, has displayed signs in the
past
of being
a
first-rate composer
(“Jordu”
is
the most famous example). Here, commanding a
group comprised
of
relative
youngsters
Stanley
Turrentine, Dizzy Reece, Reginald Workman and
Art Taylor,
six Jordan compositions are treated
with musical sympathy and understanding. Tunes
include the warm melodic ballad “Starbrite,” the
spiritual-like
“Flight
to
Jordan”
and
the
low
moaning “Deacon Joe.”
“UHURU, AFRIKA” (Freedom, Africa)—Randy
Weston,
music,
Langston
Hughes,
lyrics—Rou-
lette R 65001
The Randy Weston-Langston Hughes
collabo-
ration
is an extended
suite commemorating and
displaying
militancy
for,
the
African
freedom
movement.
It
is
a particularly pungent piece
of
music with explosive, and at times, touching lyr-
ics. A host of jazz’s best names have been gath-
ered for the
date,
especially the rhythm
section
which
includes
Olatunji,
Candido, Armando
Pe-
raza, Max
Roach,
Charlie
Persip,
G.
T. Hogan.
Narration
is by Tuntemeke Sanga of Tanganyika
and vocal soloists include Brock Peters and Mar-
tha Flowers. Musicianship all-around is outstand-
ing.
Should
witness
a
tremendous
reception
in
Negro markets.
“RANDY WESTON LIVE AT THE FIVE SPOT”
—United Artists UAS 5066
Randy Weston, a capable if uninventive pianist,
gets
lead
billing here
but
it
is
the
presence
of
Coleman Hawkins and Kenny Dorham solos and
the inclusion of one vocal track by Brock Peters,
a rich, sensitive baritone, that make this LP. Cut
during performance at N.Y.’s Five Spot Cafe in
a warm, relaxed atmosphere, the group
(also
in-
cluding Roy Haynes, Wilbur
Little and
Clifford
Jarvis)
runs
through
five
Weston
originals
(“High Fly,” “Lisa Lovely”) and one Billy Stray-
horn composition, “Star Crossed Lovers,”
all ar-
ranged by Melba Liston,
in the easy-going man-
ner that the club induces to all who appear there.
mmm
“PERCUSSIVE SOUND OF THE BIG BAND”—
John Evans—Directional Sound DS 5003
John
Evans
has
molded
a
fairly
clean
crisp
ensemble sound here. He
is mostly partial toward
the reed section laying down the basic
line over
which individual and grouped brass voicings are
used
for further theme development and
to
cre-
ate
musical
excitement.
The
selection
of
tunes
includes a handful
of Swing oldies among whicji
are “American Patrol,” “Blue Skies,” “Strike Up
the Band” and
“St. Louis Blues March.” Enjoy-
able
listening.

Lehar’s

ALL THAT JAZZ
The Modern Jazz Quartet has embarked on
its
first Far Eastern
concert
tour, beginning in Japan, May
1 through
15, and continuing to Australia and
New Zealand. As in their four major tours of western Europe during the past
five years. International popularity has preceded the MJQ
to the Far
East,
where they’ve won recent polls in Japanese and New Zealand magazines. And,
as they’ve broken precedents by appearing at European classical music festi-
vals, the MJQ
is the only jazz group invited to participate in the 1961 East-
West Music Encounter in Tokyo. Another highlight of the tour will be a TV
appearance with the Tokyo Symphony Orch. over JOKR-TV-Tokyo
in which
they will preem such “third stream” offerings as Gunther Schuller’s “Concer-
tino
for Jazz
Quartet and
Orchestra,” Andre
Hodier’s “Around
the
Blues,”
Werner Heider’s “Divertimento” and John Lewis’ own “England’s Carol,” which
they’ve
played with
the
Cincinnati and
Minneapolis Symphonies and which
appear on their new Atlantic LP, “The Modern Jazz Quartet and Orchestra,”
with
the
Stuttgart Symphony.
The MJQ jaunt marks the
second jazz tour
of Japan arranged by Monte
Kay.
Earlier
this year Kay
scored an impressive triumph by bringing Art
Blakey and the Messengers to the Orient.
West
Coast promoter Jimmy
Lyons
is
hoping
to
stage
a two-day
Erroll
Garner Festival in Carmel, Calif, following the pianist’s June Crescendo date
in Los Angeles. Plans are contingent on Garner’s being able to
fit
it in with
his summer tent sked, which
is set to kick
off July 3 at the Westbury Music
Fair. He closes out at the Crescendo June 25. Most jazz fans remember Carmel
as the scene of the artist’s now-famous “Concert By The Sea” LP, which, since
its release in 1955, has become his best-selling album, and one of the biggest of
all-time.
Sid Bernstein presented the city fathers of Newport with a check for $10,000
with which they’ll provide extra police protection during the four-day “Music
At Newport” fest, of which Bernstein is co-producer along with John Drew and
Abe Margolies. Additional contractual stipulations which Bernstein has directed
include that no parking lots be located near Freebody Park, ticket booths to be
some distance from the park, beaches to be lighted
all night and no drinking
on the
streets.
Bernstein, who’s had immense success
in the past producing
rock and
roll theatre shows, apparently knows how
to handle unruly crowds
of youngsters, the non-jazz cause of Newport’s past troubles.
Benny Goodman
is reactivating his big band (14 pieces) for a series of five
dance dates at Disneyland—starting May 27. BG’s book will include many of
the original Fletcher Henderson charts that initially sparked the BG band in
the
30’s. The final night, June
15, will climax the
series with a giant gradua-
tion prom comprised of thirty high schools from the southern California area.
Should be the biggest prom blowout of all-time.

Caterina
Valente—the famous European
artist—was
well
appreciated by
the Argentine public. Her performances (Opera Theatre and Channel 9), were
considered very good. On May
5, she flew to Santiago de Chile for a show on
Radio Mineria.
Dean Reed—the North American teen
singer—spent a few days in Buenos
Aires after his smash success in Chile and Peru. Although he isn’t well known
in the States, in Chile he was the greatest hit of recent years, and
will return
soon to shoot a picture. Currently, he is in the States recording “Runaway” and
“La Novia” for Capitol.
Baby
Bell returned from
a two week tour
of Mendoza, reporting that the
songs the public
liked best were “Put Your Head On My Shoulder” and “My
Home Town,” two Paul Anka tunes sung in Spanish. She also told us that her
waxing “Fantastico” has been released
in Japan.
Billy Cafaro will act in “Tbe Show of Andy Russell,” a TV program starting
next month. Cafaro’s last record, “Mon Amour,”
is selling well.
Ricardo
Garcia, one
of
Chile’s top
disk jockeys, came
to Buenos
Aires
to
invite the recording industry to the International Festival that will take place
in Vina del Mar in February, 1962. This song contest will include tunes from
all Latin American countries.
Channel
9, CADETE,
signed
a
contract
with
four
well known
musicians,
Juan
Carlos
Correa, Freddy
Lipesker, Jorge
Buonsanti
and
Alberto
Alcala.
This quartet had formerly performed on Hugo Guerrero’s program.
Venezuelan magazine, “Canciones,” considered Roberto Yanes the best for-
eign singer in that country. Yanes’ last recording,
“11 Nostro Concerto,”
will
be put on sale very soon.
RCA
is releasing the fourth LP of
its “Explosivos”
series, containing what
the
label
considers are
or
will
be
16
hits. The
first three “Explosivos”
sold
about
112,000 copies.
Yuyu Da
Silva, Brazilian singer currently living
in Argentina,
is going
to
Europe. Will work in Spain, Italy, France and Germany. Her last recording is
“Cara De Payaso” (“Face Of A Clown”)
for RCA.
Lucio Milena, well known musician and arranger, has already
finished the
music for the picture “El Rufian.” The main song of the film
is called “Tengo
Para Ti.”
Teddy Martino recorded “Makin’ Love” and “Vuelve Primavera” for Odeon
Pops. Both are currently hits. Los Juveniles waxed “Greenfields” and “It’s Time
To Cry” (both in Spanish)
for the same
label.
Los Tres Sudamericanos started their own TV program. They recently waxed
“Pissi Pissi Bao Bao” and “Que Facilidad” for Columbia, and now are prepar-
ing a new LP.
Two of the TV Channels, 9 and
13, will work as radio stations from 10 AM
to noon, running disk jockey programs. As Buenos Aires has already 600,000
installed TV
sets, this could
affect very much regular deejays’ popularity.
Mario
Clavell, showman and composer, will
start a new biz trip next July,
including Uruguay, Chile, Peru, Colombia and Venezuela. Clavell cut recently
“Yo Soy El Novio” (I’m 'The Bridegroom), satirizing “La Novia” (The Bride).
A new vocal
quartet. Las Cuatro Plumas,
will
record
for
Philips.
Santos
Lipesker
is
its director.
Julio Korn publishers
issued
a song book with tunes composed by

Blasquez,
including
“Novelera,” “Humo
y
Alcohol,” and
eleven more
titles.
Eladia’s last song, “Doce Meses de Amor” (Twelve Months of Love) has been
recently recorded by Marty Cosens.
Peppino de Capri, famous Italian artist, will perform here in July. Although
he is very popular in Italy, his records haven’t been released here yet.
RCA
is putting to sale lots of waxings by the “Nueva Ola”: “The Story of

Capitol Rushes Out
Harper ”AI Di La”
NEW YORK—Capitol
Records
last
week rush-released
songstress Janice
Harper’s English lyric version of “A1
Di
La,” which was
the
top
song
at
this year’s San Remo fete
in
Italy.
The overwhelming predominance
of rock
’n’
roll
over
all
other types
of
popular music in France today
is a phenomenon worth noting once more. This
trend was scarcely discernible a year ago, but asserted itself with a vengeance
with the advent on the music hall stage and on records of Johnny Hallyday.
Practically
overnight,
Johnny
became
the
idol
of
the
teenagers
and
the
Blousons Noirs,” who consider him as their spokesman and their incarnation.
The rage spread to other sections of the younger generation and Johnny might
be
considered today as a
reflection
of “La Jeunesse.”
It
is amusing
to note
that even
in
certain
schools run by
religious groups, young boys and
girls
gather for their record sessions of Hallyday and, more recently, Les Chausettes
Noires. Net result of all this is that sales of other pop categories are suffering
and music
hall programs must be modified. A&R
directors
of
all the record
firms have hastened to sign up rock
’n’ roll groups and the popularity of Les
Chausettes Noires on the Barclay
label has followed
closely on the
heels
of
Hallyday’s. Interesting that the national firms reacted swiftly and successfully
to the developing trend and that by the time the extra-national firms got mov-
ing the
ideal moment for rock
’n’
roll star-making seemed about over. Rocky
Volcano
(Philips), Frankie Jordan
(Decca) and even Hedika
(Festival), w'ho
got strong promotional backing from
these
labels,
can’t seem
to
usurp
the
place of the established
idols.. The story has been a
little different for EMI’s
A&R man, Gerard
Cote, who went
to get
in England what he
couldn’t
find
here in France. He brought back Les Travellers, and English-language duo with
talent—and
a French
past. Les Travellers had
spent
practically
all
of
1960
vegetating in
Paris, looking for a contract. At the time, only Unidisc’s A&R
man, Pirard showed some interest in them but the label belonged to a Catholic
publishing firm. Rue de Fleurus, in Paris and scarcely seemed the type of label
to put the rock
’n’
rollers on the map. Les
Travellers’
45
single on Unidisc
got a chance to be heard on the juke boxes but the promotional utility of juke
boxes hadn’t yet been accepted by the big commercial companies and certain
international firms have
still
to learn
the
lesson. The music publishers make
almost
exclusive
use
of
the medium
for
their
promotion
and
the
younger
firms (Vogue, Barclay, Festival), whose freedom of movement and willingness
to taks
risks are greater, have found that juke box promotion pays
off—for
their rock
’n’ roll stars and their other artists too.
Had trouble reaching Phil Boutet
(Barclay Editions)
who’s hard
at work
preparing for the “Coq de la Chanson” contest at the end of this month. We
learned however that the third song which
his
firm will present
in the com-
petition will be “Je Suis le Risque” by Mireille and Contet, to be sung by Paola.
Since her recording of “Si t’as ete a Tahiti” two years ago, Paola had practi-
cally disappeared from the record scene.
Latest tune waxed by Les Chausettes Noires is a free French adaptation of
“Everybody’s Got a Date but Me,” called “Fou
D’elle.”
Olympia projects:
it seems more than
likely that the opening program for
the autumn season will star Gilbert Becaud and Les Djinns. Becaud will sing,
accompanied by Les Djinns and may even record with “the heavenly voices”
(as Trent
calls them).
Edith
Piaf
used
this same formula many years ago
when she used to sing to the accompaniment of Les Compagnons de
la Chan-
son, who were then just starting their career. Their early collaboration with
Piaf helped the Compagnons on their road to success but
it was not
difficult
for the famous singer to tour with the 10 Compagnons. We don’t quite see how
things will work out with the Djinns, who comprise more than 30 singers!
Another
Pathe
operation
is Gerard
Cote’s
launching
of
a
Becaud-penned
“rock,” which

publicist

Arteco reports that three Blue Note
artists, Jackie McLean, Freddie Redd
and Arthur Taylor, are playing at Paris’ “Au Chat Qui Peche”
club. The
lat-
ter seems to have become the jazz center of the
left bank and even of Paris
in general. The Blue Note label was foi-merly distributed by Vogue here, but
Arteco has taken over. The label did much to make modern jazz known to the
French. Two leading jazz radio programs use Blue Note recordings as theme
tunes—Art Blakey’s “Paper Moon” and Horace
Silver’s “Come On Home.”

IRMA Agrees To Join ARMADA;
Members Can Join On Own
NEW YORK — Following
a
confer-
ence
between
Art
Talmadge,
presi-
dent
of
the American Record Manu-
facturers
and
Distributors
Associa-
tion (ARMADA)
and
Milt
Gelfand,
president
of
the
Independent Record
Manufacturers
Association
(IRMA),
and
a
special
exec board meeting
of
the
latter
organization,
Gelfand
an-
nounced that
it has been unanimously
agreed by the IRMA board to recom-
mend
to the membership
that IRMA
join ARMADA as an affiliate member.
The recommendation
also stated that
any IRMA member was free
to
join
ARMADA on
his own as an
affiliate.
During
the
meeting
between
the
two
top
association
execs,
the
need
for close relationship between the two
organizations was stressed, especially
in
the
area
of
counterfeiting where
both have been
active
independently,
and where IRMA was very closely as-
sociated with the recent
trial
in Ber-
gen County.
“Our many areas
of mutual
inter-
est,” Gelfand
said, “make
it most ad-
visable
that we
effect
a
closer
rela-
tionship.
To
this
end
our
executive
board,
at
a
specially-convened
ses-
sion,
unanimously
agreed
to
recom-
mend
that IRMA become an
affiliate
member
of ARMADA and
that
indi-
vidual members could join ARMADA
on their own.”

“PACHANGA AT THE CARAVANA CLUB”—
Charlie Palmieri and his Charanga La Duboney
Alegre LPA 804
Palmieri’s Duboney Orchestra
is
credited with
being the first charanga band
in the U.S., having
entertained
with
this brand
of
authentic Cuban
music
at N.Y.’s Caravana Club for the past sev-
eral years. Now that this style
is
in
its national
ascendancy, Palmieri takes
his
place among the
leaders. The music is fresh and invigorating, lend-
ing
itself
infectiously
to dancing
or
to
exciting
listening. Undoubtedly, one of the best charanga
LP’s
on
the
market. Mark
it
for
solid
sales
in
the right markets.

ALL THAT JAZZ
The hallowed walls of the rather sedate Waldorf Astoria
will be reverber-
ating for the next three weeks from the swinging sounds served up by Woody
Herman. The old Woodchopper himself takes a new aggregation into the hotel
May 31 with a book augmented by such titled tunes as “Shakespeare With a
Beat,” “Rock And Roll Satire,” and “The U.N. Beat,” and other special mat^
rial. In a throw-back to the early 40’s, Herman will also provide dance music
for the less inhibited attendees.
Richmond, Va.
is now getting jazz via
disk jockey Joe Murray. Murray’s
hosting the jazz portion of WLEE’s Weekend Hall of Hits, Sunday mornings,
midnight to 2 AM. A long-time jazz fan and collector of disks, Murray draws
from
his own collection in presenting a highly listenable program which has
already attracted a large and
enthusiastic following.
Ft.
Lauderdale
is
also
getting
the
good
sounds,
there
via
Billy
Crisp’s
“Cool Corner” on WWIL and WWIL-FM, aired nightly from
7 PM to mid-
night. With the station’s forthcoming power increase to 10,000 watts and the
subsequent extension to 24 hour broadcast day, they plan to add more jazz air-
time for the late, late hours.
Old Town Records finally got out
its
initial release in
its long-planned jazz
line. Best of the
lot
is “Plenty of Horn” by Ted Curson, itinerant trumpeter
with Charlie Mingus. Kudos to Stan Free for turning out a really fine product.
Actually, with
the huge amount
of
jazz
records
being turned
out—some
good, many bad—it is disheartening to realize that United Artists has alrnost
completely de-emphasized
its jazz product. Before the label’s present regime,
a
class
jazz catalog was being
built up—mainly through the
efforts of Bob
Altshuler
(now
with
Candid)—which
included
such
outstanding
artists
as
Art Farmer, Gerry Mulligan, Benny Golson, and with such outstanding LP’s
as “The Jazz Soul of Porgy & Bess” and “Brass Shout.” Unfortunately, busi-
ness sense has to prevail over artistry, and once more jazz
is the loser.

Garner’s
first
record
date
in almost three years
is what AmPar’s
heralding to introduce the pianist’s
first LP under their new agreement
.
.
.

McClintic.
Looks

shows.

disk

to share emcee chores during the fest. Bernstein
is falling into the

“JIMMIE THE
KID”—The
Legendary
Jimmie
Rodgers—RCA Victor LPM-2213
As the liner notes point out, Jimmie Rodgers is
the “patron saint” of country music. Though now
dead for 28 years,
his records
(in numerous
re-
issues) remain outstanding favorites
in the
field.
Here
Victor has
assembled
16 Rogers
sides
cut
between
1927 and
1933, the
six years before
his
death
in which
he made
all
his recordings and
established his musical immortality. A collector’s
item for folk and country music fans.

“Songs

JAZZ
PICKS
OF
THE WEEK
“IN THE PURPLE GROTTO”—Old Town LP
2001
A1
Collins’
Purple
Grotto,
a
habitat
of

“cool,”
inoffensive,

jazz/pop
sounds, has determined the course taken here by
a fine group of studio musicians under pianist Lou

These

“It

Mean
a

“When Your Lover Has Gone” and

lins-Stein

ground jazz.
“THE NEW SOUND OF COLLEGE JAZZ”—
Chuck
Speas
and
the
American
Jazz
Septet
Carlton STEP 12/135
Liner note-wise,
this “new” sound
is supposed
to
be
the
ability
to combine
Traditional, Swing
and Modern influences. Actually, this sounds like
just
another
group
of
young
jazz
enthusiasts
who, in groping for an identity, have relied on
all
the
old, time-worn cliches to attract attention of
youngsters. When they play Traditional, they have
the studied stagnace of the Dukes
of
Dixieland,
likewise
the
derivativeness
of
their Swing
and
Modern
tracks.
Probably
teeners
getting
their
first taste
of jazz
will
like
this
set.

“ZUNGO!” — Afro-Percussion — Olatunji — Co-
lumbia CL 1634
Twenty-five musicians and singers collaborated
to provide the musical excitement in
this record,
all under the direction of Nigerian tribal drumrner
Olatunji. For followers of the African percussion
and vocal sound, this
is about the nearest to the
real thing. Drummers
flail, the brass shouts and
the 13 member chorus chants with fervor. There’s
a magnetic
attraction here
that
will be hard
to
resist by jazz fans.
“JACKIE’S BAG”—Jackie
McLean—Blue
Note
4051
Jackie
McLean’s
spirited,
swashbuckling
alto
sax work is heard on this LP in two different ses-
sions, but both achieve the same swinging results.
One finds him in company of Donald Byrd in the
front
line and the other with Blue
Mitchell and
Tina Brooks. Actually, the Byrd date
is
slightly
better, due to the nresence of the trumpeter and
Philly Joe Jones. But only slightly, for both pro-
vide
pure
listening
pleasure.
Five
of
the
six
tracks are McLean originals.
“TONIGHT ONLY!”—The Dave Brubeck Quartet,
giiest star Carmen McRae—Columbia CL 1609
The Brubeck Quartet
is joined by Carmen Mc-
Rae
for a performance
of mostly Dave Brubeck
originals
(plus
one
standard
and
one
each
by
Desmond and Wright). The lark
is in
fine voice
as usual and the quartet does well by her in sup-
port, and also on 'the instrumental passages, but
the songs
don’t really rate
the
quality
of talent
and amount of work expended on them. A better
choice of material should have been made. Luckily
(as the title indicates)
it’s just a one-night stand.
“THE ISLANDS CALL”—The Surfers—Hifi R427
The Surfers are a rare exception among those
who perform Hawaiian music in that they neatly
avoid most of the cliches that have cheapened the
music
in recent years. Rather, these four young
men
work
up
fine
harmonic
patterns
of
both
authentic Island music and mainland songs which
retains the enchanting flavor inherent in them but
with an entertaining, listenable freshness. A zest-
ful enthusiasm for their work
also
help
greatly.
In
this newest LP
session
they perform “Keep
Your Eyes On The Hands,” “J’etendre,” “Sophis-
ticated
Hula,”
“Far Away
Places”
and
“Sand
And the Sea.”
“BYRD OF PARADISE” — Jerry Byrd — Monu-
ment SM 14003
Jerry Byrd has tuned
his
steel guitar here
to
the
flavorsome,
languidly
exotic mood
of
Poly-
nesia. In a most relaxed and gently-flowing man-
ner he expertly interpretes a dozen
lesser-heard
Hawaiian made
melodies
including
a
couple
of
his
own. Accompaniment
includes
some rhythm
and an occasional chorus chant. Good mood music.
“PALMER
-
HUGHES
ACCORDION
SYM-
PHONY”—Capri
The
Palmer-Hughes
Accordion
Symphony
numbers 40 strong who, from Houston, Texas, are
dedicated
to the
uplifting of the recognition
ac-
corded
the
instrument.
Judging from
this
first
record they have succeeded at least in displaying
the
ability of the instrument more
so than
ever
before. Vivid imagination and firm musical knowl-
edge have been used in orchestrating the instru-
ments on this disk. Pieces performed range from
the
classical, “Carmen

“Bolero,”
to
the
popular,
“Granada,” “Arkansas

Lots
