JAZZ
PICK
OF THE WEEK
“FORBIDDEN FRUIT” — Nina Simone — Colpix
CP 419
An
unusual
vocal
style
has
brought her
pop
acceptance but Nina Simone has artistic attributes
that transcend just uniqueness of sound. She has
a quickness of mind that gets right to the heart
of the song, a strong feeling for blues and spirit-
uals, and a fertile interpretive mind that can turn
(in this LP) an ordinary love song such as “Where
Can
I Go Without You”
into
a dramatic
experi-
ence.
Other
outstanding
examples
of
her
vocal
art
include
“Rags And
Old
Iron,”
“Gin
House
Blues,” “Work Song” and “Forbidden Fruit.”
“SHIRLEY’S SOUNDS”—Shirley Scott—Prestige
7195
In her latest session for Prestige Shirley Scott
maintains
the
consistency
of
performance
that
had
first established her on the organ jazz scene.
In typical fashion she swings hard and furious on
“It Could Happen To You” and “Indiana’^ and ^is
softly appealing on “Summertime” and
S posin
.
Should do well with jazz organ fans.
CLASSICAL PICK OF THE WEEK
ALBENIZ: “Iberia”; RAVEL: “Rapsodie Espag-
nole”—Jean Morel conducting the Paris Conserva-
toire Orchestra—RCA Victor LM-6094
Two distinct views of Spain and
its rnusic are
presented here. One, Ravel’s “Rapsodie”
is of the
early Twentieth Century school of Parisians who
became enamored with Spanish music. The other
is Albeniz’
“Iberia,” a
series
of twelve
intricate
portraits of his country, which took almost
years
after
his
death
to
be
orchestrated when
finally
completed
in
1955.
Morel’s
direction
is
precise, allowing the
full orchestral
color of the
works
their
total impact upon the
listener,
ihe
“Iberia”
is of particular significance.
“BEETHOVEN: Sonata No. 5 in F, Sonata No. 9
in A”—Yehudi Menuhin, violin, Hephzibah Menu-
hin, piano—Capitol SG 7246
The two most popular Sonatas in the Beethoven
catalog. No. 5 “Spring” and No. 9
‘ Kreutzer,
in
striking virtuoso performances by Yehudi Menu-
hin. The exacting and demanding
“Kreutzer
is
an especial delight in this recording as the violin-
ist brings
it calmly under his wing. Piano accom-
paniment by sister Hephzibah proves totally ade-
quate to the job. Artistically rewarding recording.
“FRENCH
OVERTURES”—Ernest
Ansermet
conducting L’Orchestre de
la
Suisse Romande —
London CS6205
.
The variety of moods and feelings expressed in

collection
of French

are

met. He

“La

Helen”
and
“Orpheus
in
the Underworld,” Auber’s “Fra Diavolo” and “Le
Domino Noir,” Lalo’s “Le Roi d’Ys” and Zampa s
“Herold.” A strongly appealing classical
release.

LOUISIANA MAN
,
HICKORY #1137
ALL THAT JAZZ
“It sure
is a mess!” This was Stan Kenton’s answer when asked to comment
on the contemporary music scene. The place was the Capitol Records studio on
West 46th Street in New York; the occasion, a one-day respite from the road
when
this reporter had an opportunity to ask Stan about his new band and
for a few words on his celebration of twenty years as a bandleader.
It’s been a long haul since that summer day in 1941 when at the Rendezvous
Ballroom
in Balboa Beach,
Calif., Kenton unveiled
his
first band, a
14 piece
organization which resulted from Kenton’s
artistic restlessness and powerful
drive to create something new.
Still, after twenty years and innumerable re-
organizations, Kenton’s drive hasn’t diminished much and he’s
still searching
and reorganizing. The present band, tagged “The New Era In Modern Ameri-
can
Music,”
is
comprised
of
five
trumpets,
five
trombones,
five
saxes, two
drums, bass and four mellophoniums, a brass instrument resembling a French
horn and keyed
in F which was designed specifically for Kenton (by Conn)
to
fill what Kenton describes as a coloration void between the trumpet and trom-
bone. Almost all of the band members are youngsters, many just out of school
and
still clutching their music degrees. By filling many of his positions with
youngsters, Kenton
is recognizing the effectiveness
of music
school
training,
an area in which he
is
particularly
active. He
strongly advocates the wider
hiring
of these “superbly” trained musicians
in
all bands and
believes they
comprise the best crop of ready musicians available for band work.
Back to Stan’s comment on the music scene. Stan feels that there is not at all
enough
originality
in current music. He said
it seems as
if people are afraid
to
try new things on disks and that they rely on the
old, established
tricks.
Especially with pop music, he thinks that record companies should pay more
attention to artists who have a reasonable validity of talent and can produce
in person. They should try to build a talent rather than grab the quick buck
on a one-shot deal.
In regards to
his new band, Kenton said that he
is
still trying
to explode
something fresh
in music. Before organizing the new band he junked every-
thing and
built a fresh book with
40 new charts. Again, concerts
will make
up the bulk of the band’s work. To introduce the sound of the band
to
disk
audiences, a Capitol LP
titled “The Romantic Approach of Stan Kenton” will
be released
in early fall. Already in the can
is his
first Christmas album and
a version of the Leonard Bernstein score from “West Side
Story.” In refer-
ence to “West Side Story,” his first show score, Kenton said he felt
it was the
first such score that fit well into his concept of music. A preview listen of the
disk at the studio confirmed Kenton’s feeling for
this reporter, who thinks
it
is the best work Kenton has done on records for several years.
It will be re-
leased
in conjunction with the
film.
In summing
up, Kenton
said that he
feels he has captured
a fresh sound
with the new band and feels
it will go a long way
in reestablishing
his con-
tact with youngsters. At
least he appears more enthusiastic
about
this new
venture than he has for anything in quite a while.
JAZZ JOTTINGS: Upon the signing of Chris Connor and Herbie Mann to
exclusive booking contracts with Joe Glaser’s Associated Booking Corp., Monte
Kay, manager of both
artists, was overheard saying, “Associated
is the best
agency in the business and they don’t charge any more than the worst, so why
not.”
.
.
. The MJQ
leads
off the Berkshire Music
Barn’s summer season
in
Lenox with a July 2nd concert. They’ll appear together with the Contemporary
String Quartet.
.
.
. This week finds Lambert, Hendricks & Ross, Joe Williams
and Gloria Lynne in a series of concerts at Chicago’s Tivoli Theatre. L, H & R
exit Tuesday for an opening at NY’s Village Vanguard opposite the Bill Evans
Trio. Closing out the Vanguard are Stan (jetz and pop singer Gene McDaniels.
.
.

a talent
bill
of $155,000 for

can deliver.

with
just
trio
backing,
plus
Eddie
Jefferson’s
vocals.

former trumpeter with

Brown’s youth
bands,
is
rehearsing
a
17-

.

Mancini To Tour S.A. For “Peter Gunn” Music
LOS
ANGELES—In
a
significant
tribute to the importance of music to
a
television
series,
Sparton
Produc-
tions
and RCA
Victor
will
shortly
sponsor a
series
of personal appear-
ances in South America by composer-
conductor Henry Mancini.
The first such tour by an American
composer
will
be made
in
behalf
of
the
“Peter
Gunn”
series,
for
which
Mancini
wrote
and
conducted
the
score.
Sparton
Productions
produces
the
series. The music, to which Man-
cini
also
holds
all
publishing
rights,
caused
a
sensation when
the
series
first went on the air and was largely
responsible
for
an
entire new
trend
in
jazz-type
background
music.
Vic-
tor albums
of the
score were smash
sellers.
Mancini will
fly to Hawaii
in about
two weeks
to
initiate
a
promotional
campaign there. Shortly after he will
kick
off
the
tour
of South
America,
where
the
series
is being introduced
in
Mexico,
Argentina,
Venezuela,
Guatemala, Nicaragua, Costa Rica and
Panama, as well as in the Dominican
Republic and Puerto Rico.
In
addition
to
projected
p.a.’s
on
Latin-American TV and
radio, Man-
cini will set up branches of his music
publishing firm, Northridge Music, in
countries he
will
visit.

JAPAN
CANADA
JAPAN—We continue with the story from our previous issue on the Colum-
bia IMP-WB
film meeting. The meeting
is held every month
to
discuss what
measures should be taken in order to promote Warner Bros. Records business.
Columbia
Records
is assuming WB’s
distribution,
although
Nitchiku
is
the
directly
contracted
party. IMP
(International Music
Publishers)
is
the
firm
that publishes
all of WB tunes. This meeting came
into existence at the pro-
posal of Robert B. Weiss, international director of WB, who was in Japan re-
cently and
is now visiting Asian and European nations. In this country, musi-
cal scores used to be published after the release of the film involved, or after
the tune made
a
clear
hit. Weiss
tried
to change
this
trend. IMP promptly
agreed on his idea, as the firm was established just to follow the “publication
before the release of disk-or-film system,” Yokichi Kitagawa, executive director
of IMP, stated to The Cash Box. Only Columbia balked at Weiss’ offer that
it
should
release any WB
repertoire
before
the
film’s
opening. The
“release-
before-film’s-opening system
is very dangerous for Columbia’s record business,
because no one can
tell
if the tune
will
sell
well, the
firm
said. At the
final
stage, Columbia then said okay on Weiss’ proposal. This okay does not mean
accep^nce,
but
it
only means
“I
See,”
according
to
the Japanese way
of
speaking. So
it
is not sure that Columbia
will carry out this plan. Neverthe-
less, the meeting will be held regularly.
Sachiko Nishida, Gramophon’s songstress, cut her first 10" LP, “Akashiya-no
Amega
Yamutoki.”
“Never On
Sunday,”
“Where
The
Boys
Are”
and
the
tune which carries the same
title are featured. Nishida
is now one of the top
selling
artists
as far
as Gramophon
is
concerned.
A strong selling campaign to boost Hawaiian records was just put in force,
lasting until August 20, by Toshiba. The firm released
3 LP’s
(one on stereo)
and 6 singles as
its June issue. “Li’l Brown Gal” by Esel Nakada and 5 others
by Webby Edwards
and
the
Hawaii
Calls
Orchestra
are
available
on
45’s.
Customers who
pick up
Toshiba’s Hawaiian
tunes
at record
stereos
will
be
given three
or one
lottery
tickets for every LP
or
45 RPM. Toshiba
Stereo
Sound Box, Type 202 for 10 persons and Toshiba Stereo Player-TPS for
100
persons
ax’e the
first and runner up prizes
respectively.
The Japanese Best Sellers Chart has been changed as of this week.
It has
been divided into two
sections—local popular tunes and international popular
tunes with the publishers of
all the songs included. This
classification
is very
important. These two are completely different in their background, stratum of
listening
people,
style and
others
just
as
top
100 tunes and down
to
earth
country music
is. Furthermore, Japanese publishers usually do not
cari’y re-
cording rights, which undoubtedly belongs to a particular diskery by contract-
ing with authors and composers. This
is why the same tune
is not recorded on
different labels
usually.
Japan Phonograph Record Association (JPRA)
offered
a
conciliation
plan
with BIEM only to gain no substantial outcome. At the meeting with BIEM’s
Tokyo rep, JPRA stated
it wanted to renew
its contract with BIEM
at
exist-
ing rate of use. The Japanese side feels that the Educational Ministry
is
still
reserving its decision against BIEM’s requisition, and affiliated firms of JPRA
cannot release any tunes under BIEM’s control. This
is a troublesome condi-
tion for both parties. Therefore we are willing to enter a new pact on the con-
dition that w'e pay for BIEM’s tunes at the existing rate of use until the Edu-
cational Ministry issues
its decision on
this matter. BIEM’s representative
in
Tokyo said
it understood Japanese situation and hoped for a new pact. Rep of
BIEM replied
it would give further comment after contacting
its head
office in
Paris as long as the rate of use was concerned. Verbal conflict between BIEM
and the Japanese parties has been exchanged for over six years. The Japanese
side says the existing 29r
or 7.20 yen per tune as the rate of use
is proper,
w'hile BIEM claims 4% should be
paid. As this matter
is very important, but
complicated, we will try to give more details as to the progress of the problem
next week.

moters included

######## 1961-06-24 p41  [jazz\s*messengers]
JAPAN
AUSTRALIA
JAPAN—The Japanese record industry and BIEM (head office in Paris), have
been quarreling for 6 years on the matter of ratio to be paid as the rent for
tunes under BIEM’s
control,
as we
reported
last week. To
begin
with,
our
domestic law regulates that the ratio
of the rent be 2%
of the tax excluded
retail price or
7.20 yen, on each tune. But BIEM
is requesting 4%. This was
the cause of the hard to resolve debate. The Japanese side says
“all other na-
tions
are
also paying
the rent
in
accordance with
its
domestic
law,
act
or
regulation and more remittance than our law permits
is substantialy impos-
sible for us to send and we can’t enter the contract.” Japanese diskeries asked
the Educational Ministry to talk with BIEM, leaving the existing contract ex-
pired, but continuing
it automatically for another year. This provisional con-
tract was, to be accurate, the state of no contract. Further,
it was again ex-
tended automatically starting January
1, 1961 thru March 31 by the proposal
of the Japanese side. On BIEM’s side, it also asked the Educational Ministry of
Japan to mediate the debate. Japan Phonograph Record Association (JPRA)
backed this plan up ardently. But the ministry failed to make any decision on
this matter before the
contract expired. The proceedings
of the negotiations
were reported to BIEM’s head
office by JPRA on March
22. Along with
this
report, JPRA
proposed
the
prolonging
of
this
pact
starting
April
1,
1961.
BIEM replied in
its ultimatum to JPRA (dated March 31)—“No recording of
tunes under BIEM's control should be made in Japan from now on. No tunes
of BIEM’s
control should be distributed
affective April
1,
1961.”
(But those
which have already been released before March 31, 1961 will be allowed to be
used 2 years from now). This makes Japanese labels unable to use any tunes
of European origin. But, as one quarter points
out, “no severe attack”
is ex-
pected for the Japanese
side because
it
still can use German tunes through
GEMA. GEMA seceded from BIEM last January. Moreover, BIEM nowadays
doesn’t occupy the important role
it had before. Out of the whole remittance
paid by Japanese
diskeries for foreign material, only 13%
or
so
is
paid for
BIEM. This
is a declining figure for BIEM. For
all
that, both
parties have
again started
conciliation talk. We might add that the U.S. and Canada pay
only 2%
as
the rent for BIEM
(cheaper than
that
of Japan). The matter
should have been reported before the general meeting of International Federa-
tion
of
Phonograph
Industry
(IFPI)
which
met
at
Copenhagen May
30
through June
3.
Shujo Muto,
president
of Japan’s
King, remained
as
president
of JPRA
when the following directors were also put into their former posts, respectivly,
no May 27. Yonezo Hata (Columbia), Hitoshi Momose (Victor), Shigeji Nanko
(Teichiku), Nobusuke Izawa (Toshiba), and Kei Hoashi (Shin-Sedai). And was
re-elected executive director, as well. Secretaries are Kiyonari Nara
(Colum-
bia)
and Michio Sakakibara, both newly elected. The board
of directors who
voted the above-mentioned
people,
also heard how
the
debate on the BIEM
problem was going on.
The Victor
sales campaign
in commemoration of the opening
of the Hiro-
shima and
Sendai branches has
started. This
is the campaign
for the
firm’s
specially contracted stores. The stores in the business district of the Hiroshima
branch will be classified into three (“A,” “B,” “C”) groups, according to their
selling results
of May through June. All
of them
will be invited to
the
spa
where they will discuss how to increase record sales of Victor. Sapporo (in the
northern-most island, Hokkaido) branch, is also doing just what the Hiroshima
branch
is doing.
Meanwhile Columbia started
its sales campaign, too. Both dealers and
cus-
tomers will share the favor given by the
firm. This campaign, “DSC Golden
Sale”
is connected wth the
firm’s phonographs. Anyone who buys “Columbia
Stereo Phonograph-DSC System” will be given a special record. 100 men will
be chosen in the middle
of October to get
12
stereo
LP’s, 50 men
to receive
6 stereo LP’s and
1,000 people to obtain three stereo compact
33’s each. The
stores from which the
first prize winners are chosen will be qualified to take
10 stereo LP’s.
The Nishinomiya plant of the defunct Nippon Mercury Records will start to
work again in the near future. Kenji Hasegawa, composer formerly with Nip-
pon
Mercury, Fusami Yamazaki and Masato Sugawara, purchased
the
long
closed plant and -established Mercury Co. Ltd. The new company has nothing
to do with the disbanded Nippon Mercury Records. Victor
is helping to reset
up the revived plant. After the completion of the adjustment, the factory will
work
as the pressing
plant
for
Victor,
as
the
first
step
for the
first
three
months or so. Then,
if things go well, the firm will embark on producing and
distributing
its own records.
2,319,780 copies of records (996,098,017 yen at producers sale; tax excluded)
were produced by 9 diskeries during last April, according to the statistics re-
leased by JPRA. This shows 9%
in number or 22%
in dollar value above last
April. Production of stereo versions are going up—243,199 copies were put out
during May, 1961 (226,015 during last April).

In a shock announcement that took the entire trade by surprise, Ken Taylor
has
resigned
his
position
of
general
sales manager
and A&R manager
of
Festival Records. 'Taylor has held this position with the Festival Group for a

of years and

is

some difference of opinion on policy matters within the company. The Festival
Company
is now fifty per cent owned by Am-Par Record Co. of the U.
S. At
the time of writing, Taylor had not divulged what his future plans would be.
The death occurred recently of Sir Richard Boyer who, until his death, was
Chairrnan
of the Australian Broadcasting Commission
for sixteen years. The
Commission controls a network of Government-operated radio and
television
stations throughout the Commonwealth. Sir Richard was greatly respected by
the
entire trade
as a man
of great knowledge and
first-class
administrator.
His funeral was attended by hundreds of his personal and business friends and
associates who paid their respects.
American comic Bobby Sargent currently doing
well
in

in Aus-
tralia.
Jim
Cuff,

manager
of
the

Division
of RCA
of
Australia, reports that the firm is enjoying a good run with the soundtrack al-
bum from “The World Of Susie Wong”; both film and stage production of the
show are currently running in this country. Jim reports that RCA has a good
tie in with the film company and dealers are giving maximum support to this
exposure.
Also from RCA comes news of Elvis Presley’s new single “I Feel So Bad”
c/w “Wild
In The Country.” Advance orders have been
so

so

in order to

If anything,

is becoming even more
popular here and he never seems to be without at least one best-selling single,
EP and album.

After having been on the market for a couple of weeks—and already show-
ing on charts—EMI suddenly held the Andy Williams single

French singer Vicki Renet is at present in Australia for television and club

The new Ampar label, nationally distributed through the Festival group, has

Nat “King” Cole’s brother Ike Cole, is due to arrive in Australia next month
for

Album Reviews
“SOMETHING FOR EVERYBODY”—Elvis Pres-
ley—RCA Victor LPM-2370
The “something for everybody” aspect of Pres-
ley’s latest LP
is devoting one entire side to bal-
lads, the other to raucous rockers. In the former
dept, he offers his gripping, dramatic ballad tech-
nique in “Sentimental Me,” “There’s Always Me”
and “Gently”; the latter side contains “I’m Cornin’
Home,”
“Judy”
and
“I
Slipped,
I
Stumbled,
I
Fell” from the flick “Wild In the Country.” Huge
sales imminent.
“VIVA!”—Bobby Montez
and
his
Orch.—World
Pacific WP-1404
The Bobby Montez quintet features instrumen-
tation and ensemble sound similar to the Martin
Denny and Arthur Lyman
groups.
In
this
vein
they play
eight extended Montez
originals. The
music
is most-times attractively melodic and the
beat
is of the gently-persuasive, undulating kind
that compels at least toe-tapping
if not outright
dance participation to the cha cha rhythm. Album
has
already
hit
the
stereo
chart and promises
much more sales action.
“GET HAPPY”—Ella Fitzgerald—Verge V-4036
Another collection
of
fine songs honored with
the impeccable taste and artistry of an Ella Fitz-
gerald performance. Here, the
first lady of song
offers personal essays of such goodies as “Some-
body Loves Me,” “Blue
Skies,” “Cheerful
Little
Earful” and “St. Louis Blues.” Arranging chores
are shared by Riddle, Garcia, DeVol and Weston,
a particularly distinguished group
of chartsmen.
As
is
expected,
this
set maintains
the
singer’s
respected tradition and should do extremely well
at the counters.

“SING OUT WITH PETE!”—Pete Seeger—Folk-
ways FA 2455
There’s hardly a Pete Seeger concert at which
he doesn’t at least once prod his audience to as-
sist him in a community sing. These sessions are
usually indicative of the enthusiasm which greets
Seeger at every stop on his itinerary. Here Folk-
ways has preserved a dozen of these sing-alongs
from concerts
at Yale, Chicago
Univ., Carnegie
Hall and the Village Gate, and
it’s a joy to ob-
serve how Seeger manipulates
his audience
into
responding. Songs include “Down By The River-
side,” “Oh, Mary Don’t You Weep,” “I’m On My
Way” and “The Hammer Song.”
Lyrics
are
in-
cluded for home audiences.
“THE FOLK MUSIC OF THE NEWPORT FOLK
FESTIVAL, 1959-60”— Vols. 1 & 2—Folkways FA
2431, 2432
With the main attractions of the
’59-’60 New-
port Folk Festivals already released on other la-
bels,
Folkways
has
picked
up
the
performance
tapes
of many
of
the
lesser-known
folk
artists
and released them here in a two volume set. It is
the most engrossing
collection
of
disk perform-
ances
to come
out
of the
Festivals. Performers
include
Brownie McGhee &
Sonny
Terry,
Pete
Seeger, New
Lost
City
Ramblers,
Pat
Clancy,
Guy Carawan, Alan Mills and several outstanding
blues singers. Among the names are some of the
only authentic
folk
artists
to perform
at New-
port and the entire set should be of high interest
to the more astute folk enthusiasts.
“THE SOUND
OF MY OWN
VOICE AND
OTHER NOISES”—Severn Darden At The Sec-
ond City—Mercury OCS-6202
Severn Darden
is one of the leading members
of The Second
City, a group
of young Chicago-
based satirists who work improvisationally. Here,
he offers a sampling of his comedic wares (from
“live” performance),
including
a
16 minute
dis-
sertation on
Metaphysics
that’s thoroughly con-
fusing and
hilarious. Other Second
Citizens sup-
port
in
various
minor
roles.
It’s
part
of
that
“new” wave of comedy.
“CATERINA
.
.
. THE GREATEST IN ANY
LANGUAGE”—Caterina Valente—Decca DL 4052
With six languages at her command, Caterina
Valente
has
charmed

by
switching singing language as frequently as pos-

to

with showmanship flair and talent.

al. but

“LA PLATA JUMPS THE CHARANGA”—La
Plata Sextette—Seeco CELP-472
La Plata, an industrious sextette of Latin musi-
cians (& vocalists) with a strong following in the
east
(especially
the
Catskill
resort
area), now
hops on the charanga/pac-hanga bandwagon with
this LP.
In
it they perform
a
lineup
of mostly
authentic Latin tunes in pachanga rhythm with a
couple
of cha cha chas and a merengue thrown
in. Lively dance date here.
“LOVE SONGS OF THE MEDITERRANEAN”
—Charles K. L. Davis—Everest LPBR 5122
The concert/operatic tenor who’s been concen-
trating on the pop song, offers interpretations of
Italian,
French
and
Spanish
love
songs.
He’s
aided by David Terry’s arrangements in perform-
ances of such material as “Non Dimenticar,” “So-
lamente Una Vez,” “Sou Le
Ciel
de Paris” and
. the very American “Song From Moulin Rouge.”
Pleasing
vocal
entertainment.
“MI ULTIMO TANGO”—Sarita Montiel—Colum-
bia EX 5048
International
film
star
and
nitery
attraction
Sarita Montiel
is heard in a program of Spanish
popular songs. The album is titled after her latest
film
success and
contains
songs from
this
film,
plus
others,
including
the
traditional “A Media
Luz.” Has a natural appeal to the Spanish-speak-
ing markets.
“SONGS OF JUAN VALDEZ
Music of Colom-
bia—Jose Duval—RCA Victor LSP-2367
Native
Colombian music
is
presented
here
in
arrangements palatable to American record mar-
ket
tastes. The
singer
is Jose
Duval,
the Juan
Valdez
of
the TV
commercials,
hence
the
LP’s
title
tie-in. Ray Martin’s
ork and
chorus
assist
the
varying moods
of
the music
appropriately.
It’s a tuneful, lively session
in which the colorful
Colombian music is essayed in easy-to-take terms.
“KNOW WHAT WILL HAPPEN TOMORROW”
—Maurice Woodruff—Warner Bros. 1414
Woodruff, billed as “the world’s foremost clair-
voyant” by
dint
of
several
reportedly uncanny
observations,
plies
his
trade now
via
this WB
disk. In
it he offers a whole array of political and
social
predictions
which
will
take
place
before
June
1, 1962. For disbelievers, the predictions are
guaranteed 79% accurate or the purchaser
is en-
titled to another WB LP. We predict Mr. Wood-
ruff
will
not
sell
too many
albums.
(Accuracy
not guaranteed.)
“PARTY MAGIC”—Harry Blackstone—Pathe 701
The famed magician presents several card and
mathematical
tricks that should appeal
to many
adults as well as the youngsters they’re intended
for.
In
addition, musical
interludes are
supplied
by
Glenda
Paris
and
an
ork. The
Blackstone’s
“magic”
can
be
fascinating
but
the
music,
of
amateurish
quality,
serves no purpose.
“GROOVIN’ BLUE”—Curtis Amy & Frank But-
ler-Pacific Jazz PJ-19
Tenor saxist Curtis Amy has become a leading
figure in the new “return to roots” movement on
the west coast, speaking a
virile, muscular blues
language. His previous Pacific Jazz album
(with
Paul Bryant) went a long way in establishing his
popularity and this set, on which he shares leader
chores with drummer Frank Butler, will well add
to
his
audience. Trumpeter
Carmell Jones
also
distinguishes
himself
in
this
idiom.
It’s
truly
a
“groovin’ ” session.
“LET’S SWING!”—The Budd Johnson Quintet—
Prestige/Swingville 2015
Through a long and distinguished career Budd
Johnson has always been noted for his warmth, a
natural, easy flow
of musical
ideas, and uncom-
promising taste. This set
is no exception.
It fea-
tures the tenor saxist
in easy-swing
stylings
of
several
standards and
a few
originals.
Cohesive
support
is provided by
a Flanagan-Persip-Duvi-
vier rhythm section and brother Keg Johnson con-
tributes
some
interesting trombone
licks.
High
points of the set are “Falling In Love With Love,”
“Serenade
in Blue” and “Uptown Manhattan.”
“FUSION”—The Jimmy Giuffre 3—Verve V-8397
In
his
search
for new
musical
vistas Jimmy
Giuffre comes up with
several
interesting
ideas
for
his
trio
setup. Within a
slight framework of
written arrangements
(at beginning and end
of
piece),
the
three
musicians work
almost
inde-
pendently
of
each
other
in
improvising. When
their ideas
coincide there
is
“fusion”
of various
sorts, otherwise there
is dissonance—but a seem-
ingly
planned
dissonance
that
titilates
the
ear
with
all
kinds
of
intriguing
combinations
of
sounds. Another step in the Giuffre development.
“UNDERCURRENT”—Kenny Drew—Blue Note
4959
Having “paid his dues” for years as a sideman,
Kenny Drew emerges here
in his
first Blue Note
LP as
a group
leader. The LP
title “Undercur-
rent”
(also the name of the
fiery first track)
is
indicative
of
the
unifying rhythm
piano
Drew
plays to back up the front
line of Hank Mobley
and Freddie Hubbard, but Drew
is
also
a
tech-
nically
proficient and mature
soloist
in
his own
right. Six Drew originals are performed in a full-
voiced, virile style by the sextet.
“NEW GROOVE”—Bud Shank, featuring Carmell
Jones—Pacific Jazz PJ-21
Caught
up
in
the west
coast
“blues
groove”
movement, Bud Shank has adjusted his sights to
bear down harder in his playing to meet the de-
mand. It’s highly debatable whether Shank’s “new
groove”
is more desirable than his previous
fluid,
subtle
style which always found
a
sympathetic,
attentive
ear. But on
face
value, Shank
acquits
himself
here
admirably. He
has
the
support
of
trumpeter Carmell Jones, a fast rising, versatile
young man with a rich, open tone, and a vigorous
rhythm section headed by drummer Mel Lewis.
“JAZZ AIN’T NOTHIN’ BUT SOUL”—Norman
Mapp Sings—Epic BA 17014
Just
as
its
co-label, Columbia, has introduced
Oscar Brown,
Jr., Epic now has
its own
triple-
threat writer-arranger-singer
in Norman Mapp,
who bows here
in
a lineup
of originals
(except
“Moanin’”). His songs are melodically sure and
have intelligent lyrics. He sings with an intimate
warmth
in
a relaxed, natural
gait. Instrumental
support by Clark Terry, Seldon Powel and others
is well written and gently swinging. Mapp’s got
a future and this debut LP will certainly help.
CLASSICAL
“EXOTIQUE”—Whittemore & Lowe—Capitol SP
8550
The duo pianists in a program of “exotic” mu-
sic from the classics. They have culled works from
such
composers
as
Ravel,
Debussy,
Cyril
Scott
and
Rachmaninoff
and
have
adapted
these
ex-
cerpts
into compelling mood
pieces. Their piano
work
is technically proficient and the wrap-up of
Capitol’s
fine
stereo sound make for a
desirable
album
of light
classical entertainment.
“NEW DIMENSIONS

Jamal Opens New
Chicago Nitery
CHICAGO—Argo recording star Ah-
mad Jamal hosted a gala press party
here
last Thursday afternoon
(22)
in
his exotic new nitery, Alhambra, which
is located in the heart of Record Row.
Jamal,
who
has
many
successful
albums
on the Argo
label
for many
years with his trio, boasts of the fact
that his new club—designed in a mid-
dle
eastern

the
finest

available
for
enter-
tainers
to perform
with. He
said
he
went out into the field to find the best
experts possible
to
set up the acous-
tical arrangements
in
the Alhambra.
He further
stressed
the
fact
that,
although
there
are
no

bev-
erages served in Alhambra, there are
“90 different, exciting drinks available
to
patrons.” He
selected
the
concoc-

month project.
“Another

we

“is that we

in

serve Middle Eastern

(Pakis-
tani and Indian) as well as American
delicacies. Also, every ethnic group
is
represented
in
cuisine at the Alham-
bra.”
Argo
and
Jamal
have
made
ar-
rangements
to
record Ahmad Jamal
And His Trio at the Alhambra.

Conniff Breaks Record
At Hollywood Palladium
WOODLAND HILLS, CALIF.—Maes-
tro Ray Conniff took his orchestra and
chorus into the World Famous Holly-
wood
Palladium
on
Friday and
Sat-
urday (June 16 & 17), played his first
public dance date in the United States,
and went on to break all existing rec-
ords at the Palladium for a two night
stand.
9614
paid
admisions
for
the
two
nights
brought
in
a
total
gross
gate
of $24,035.
(Price
of admission:
$2.50 per person.)
Conniff
by-passed
the
customary
band-stand
set
up
at
the
Palladium
and installed his own stage and plat-
form at the west end of the ballroom.
Sound
engineers
located
in
the mid-
dle of the ballroom balance the sounds
of
the
orchestra and
chorus
for
the
“Dance in Stereo.”
Conniff
is
currently
at
work
ar-
ranging
a new
album
for
Columbia
Records which he will record back in
New York the
first week in July.

ALL THAT JAZZ
After months of being romanced by Miles Davis,
J.
J. Johnson
finally gave
in and joined Davis’ Quintet. The association should benefit both greatly. Davis
was
in
dire need
of a good man
to
share
the
front-line. Hank Mobley
just
didn’t
fit
into
the pattern. Johnson, who, though winning poll
after
poll, has
been floundering around for the past few years. (He’s
still trying to live down
his association with Kai Winding.) A long stint with Davis should set him back
on
his feet with the public; and Miles will certainly reap benefits from
J.J.’s
inventiveness. With
this
addition, the group continues
to be one
of the most
effective small groups in jazz.
WLIB becomes the
first full-time AM
jazz
station
in the New York
area,.
The forward-looking general manager of the station, Harry Novik, appointed
Billy Taylor music coordinator to oversee the new format. In addition, Billy’s
Saturday jazz show now becomes a daily feature, running from
5 PM
until
sign-off. Commenting on
the appointment and new format, Taylor
said
that
he now will be able to bring the FM quality concept of radio to AM
listeners.
While programming jazz full-time, the station also plans to concentrate com-
pletely on
service
to the IV2
million Negroes
in the New York
metropolitan
area
through
public
service
projects,
educational
programs
and
news
and
special events coverage.
At a press conference to welcome him back from an extended Latin American
tour, guitarist Charlie Byrd reiterated several of the complaints of other jazz
musicians touring under
State
Dept, auspices. Byrd’s
biggest complaint was
that
the USIS
is
not thoroughly coordinated
in
these
events. Although
his
group was travelling under diplomatic immunity, they repeatedly had to check
all 28 pieces of luggage through customs. This held them up considerably and
put a pinch
in their close-timed schedule.
Then there’s the matter of officious
officials—American embasy officials who
frequently demanded too much of Byrd’s time to play at private parties. Many
of these
officials, said Byrd, felt as
if the tour was a personal benefit to them
and disregarded the demands made upon his time. Byrd also commented that
at many of the
concerts, which were supposed
to be
for the general
public,
were filled mainly with embassy officials and representatives of the political and
cultural factions of the countries. The “plain people” didn’t have much oppor-
tunity in some places to hear Byrd. Of course there were notable exceptions on
the tour, but these were few and far between. In some stops, the embassy was
not even aware
of
his
arrival and
failed
to coordinate the
concert with
the
American State Dept. In these places, producing the concert was
left up to a
local promoter
or jazz
club. An
incident
in Mexico
City proved the
biggest
violation
of the
tour. A jazz concert had been
set up there
to
coincide with
Byrd’s performance
in
the
city. But the embassy had
not
even
bothered
to
associate Byrd’s name with the
concert. Nevertheless,
it was
in Mexico
City
that the guitarist received his most enthusiastic public reception. And despite
these
flagrant mistakes, Byrd made many friends on
the
tour.
In
Bogota,
a
jazz club was formed on the night of his departure—in his honor. In summing
up, Byrd
felt that the proper way
to conduct
State
Dept, jazz was
to
send
young musicians to spend time
in one place working with
local musicians and
fermenting friendships. On a tour such as his, Byrd thinks a four-day minimum
in each
city should
be
established.
This would
allow the
musician
to make
friends and really influence the local populace. All in
all, he thinks that Presi-
dent Kennedy’s favorable outlook on the arts will eventually remedy many of
his
complaints.
JAZZ JOTTINGS.
.
.
. The MJQ will both open and close the Berkshire Music
Barn
season. As
disclosed here two weeks
ago, the quartet
will open July

concert
with
the

Quartet.
They’ll
close
the

Sept. 3 in an all-jazz concert with guest soloists. ... A special Randall’s Island
Jazz Concert will be held June 28 for the benefit of C.O.R.E. and the Freedom
Riders. Performing for the occasion will be Louis Armstrong, Cannonball Ad-
derly and Gerry Mulligan and their respective groups. Naturally, the
special
buses leaving from Harlem for the concert that evening will be fully integrated.
.
.
. Bob Hope bowed out of Newport because of a conflict of a taping schedule
for July
1. Additions to the Newport fest include the Jon Hendricks-narrated
“Evolution of the Blues” presentation featuring Jimmy Witherspoon, Hannah
Dean and Big
Miller.
Also, Mel Torme
will be added
to
the
closing
night’s
festivities,
as
will
the Quincy Jones
ork.

.

will
be
appearing at the Antibes Jazz Festival in France, July 16 through 25.

WB Pushes "Fanny/'
"Parrish" Sound Tracks
NEW YORK—Warner Bros,
is doing
“extensive” advertising and
exploita-
tion work
on two
important
sound-
track LP’s, “Fanny” and “Parrish.”
Both albums are
being
issued
this
week (28)
to coincide with the nation-
al release of the pics.
“Fanny,”
the
pic
version
of
hit
Harold Rome Broadway musical, stars
Leslie Caron and Maurice
Chevalier.
Voice tracks by Miss Caron and Chev-
alier
and
producer-director
Joshua
Logan,
are being prepared
for
disk-
jockeys.
“Parrish,”
starring Troy
Donahue,
Connie
Stevens,
Diane
McBain
and
Sharon Hugueny,
is being released
in
a four-color book-type package, with
the
front cover and
side
one
of
the
LP
featuring
the
soundtrack
music
by Max Steiner, and the other side of
the LP features George
Greeley and
his
piano-concerto
interpretations
of
the
film’s music.
Both
LP’s
will
be
distributed
to
some
500 members
of the
entertain-
ment press. In addition, special screen-
ings
for
deejays,
and
dealers
have
set-up for both films, and the albums
are being made
available
for
sale
in
theatre
lobbies throughout
the coun-
try, and die-cut window displays and
window streamers have been prepared
for dealer
distribution. Many AM &
FM outlets will receive the packages.
WB has also tied-in with the Fair-
child Camera Company’s current mer-
chandising campaign, “So You Want
to be A
Star” and “Parrish” albums
are
being made
available
as
contest
prizes through Fairchild.
Film
trailers,
radio-TV
spot com-
mercials make liberal use of the music
from both attractions.

Youth Figures Big
In New
Chancellor Expansion Moves
PHILADELPHIA—Robert
Marcucci,
President of Chancellor Records, has
announced
an
expansion
and
re-or-
ganization program for the label—ac-
centing
youth.
One objective of the expansion has
been
a
concentrated
effort
by
Mar-
cucci and his A & R chief, Russ Faith,
to recruit actors to make
their debut
as
singers.
It’s
a
switch
for
Chan-
cellor
since
its
top
two
artists,
Fa-
bian and Frankie Avalon gained fame
first
as
singers and then became
ac-
tors.
Marcucci and
Faith, who
will
pro-
duce
all
of
Chancellor
sessions, have
been seeing some of filmland’s young
talents.
Additionally,
Marcucci
still
will be looking for new singing talent
in
all
categories,
male
and
female
teen
singers,
groups and
instrumen-
talists.
Besides interviewing and
audition-
ing new
talent,
Marcucci
has
been
concentrating
on wrapping up
deals
with
pic
studios
to
produce and
re-
lease scores from features. Currently,
he has penned
(with collaboration by
Faith),
produced,
recorded'
and
re-
leased
“You’re
Only
Young
Once,”
from
“Love
In
A
Goldfish
Bowl,”
“Opposites Attract” from Columbia’s
“Sail A Crooked
Ship,” and
“If You
Knew” for “North
to Alaska.”
New
talent
signed
to
the
label by
Marcucci
so far
is Lada Edmund,
of
Broadway’s “Bye Bye
Birdie,” Carlo
Gerace, a new Marcucci
find, who cut
“Wild About That Girl” from Colum-
bia’s
“Gidget
Goes
Hawaiian.”
The
Fabulous
Four, who
previously had
been used to vocally backstop Fabian,
also have
cut an
individual
LP.
The
record company
reshuffled
too
by
Marcucci
and
its
organizational
breakdown
will be
as
follows:
Joyce
Weston,
public
relations
for
Fabian
and
Frankie
Avalon
in
the
East;
Marti
Jewel, head
of
the Promotion
department and
also promoted
to the
top
of Chancellor’s new Literary
de-
partment,
with
duties
that
include
finding
film and
television properties
which can be used as starring vehicles
for the label’s artists; Rocco B. Ochu-
ida, top man in the foreign
sales and
distribution department and assistant
to
Marcucci;
Peter
Girardi,
also
ex-
ecutive
assistant
to
Marcucci;
Chic
Laganella,
chief
of
advertising
and
art;
Barbara
Cartassi,
foreign
pub-
licity and promotion.
Lastly,
Chancellor’s
personal man-
agement arm, MDB, has hired for ex-
ecutive
training
in
the management
field, two Philadelphians, Thomas Ma-
rotta
and
Tony
DeSantis.
Marcucci
stated
in summing up
the new
pro-
gram, “I merely am looking for fresh
and new ideas.
I believe that only the
young or the young at heart can give
()
us
this.
It’s
part
of
a
campaign
I
started in management and recording
to give youth
its say.”

SCANDINAVIA
SWEDEN
Scandinavian Record Co.
(Sonet,
Storyville, Roulette, Gazell, Colpix, Debut,
Bel Air, Collector and Hispavox record labels) presents a bi-monthly magazine-
news bulletin, with Bjorn Fremer (head of publicity)
as editor.
Its
first issue
presents an editorial article which no doubt has caused some discussions here.
Fremer
refers
to
the
problems
of promoting
records and record
artists
in
Swedish Radio and TV. “When an artist is contracted for a radio or TV show,
the non-commercial Radio-TV-company refuses him/her to sing a song from
the
latest record made by the
artist, the Radio-TV
Co. being
so
afraid
for
all the noise caused by a column writer in the daily evening paper Aftonbladet
(social-democratic) who seems
to have
got
this
thing
called
‘promotion’
on
his brain,” writes Fremer. He also refers to the fact that Swedish Radio-TV
recently had
a chance
to present Connie
Francis
but they
refused
since
it
expected her to sing one or two songs from her latest record, and knowing all
the noise that followed after Bobby Rydell’s visit, when he sung “Sway” twice
or three times in two days, it expected the same
if they accepted a show with
Miss Francis. The
policy of the Swedish government radio and TV company
does not stimulate cooperation between the record companies and the Radio,
and
with more and more
best-selling
artists bound
to
record
companies
it
seems as
if SBC-TV might be short of artists for
its entertainment programs
if
it doesn’t change
its policy. Exceptions to
its
rules are made from time
to
time, particularly when
it concerns a few of the top
selling Swedish
artists,
such as Povel Ramel, Martin Ljung,
etc. from Knappupp and
Siv Malmquist
from
Metronome,
artists who
are
badly wanted by radio and TV
but who
refuse to appear there unless they are allowed to do the numbers they want.
Other artists who do not have the same
possibilities become more and more
interested (and forced)
to look for cooperation with the so called pirate radio
stations, operating on commercial basis.
Nordiska
Musikforlaget’s
record
dept,
presents
three new jazz
LP’s
and
one 45 RPM single on Blue Note. The LP’s are “Flight To Jordan” with Duke
Jordan,
“Goin’ Up” with
Freddie Hubbard
and
“Grant’s
First
Stand” with
Grant Green. The same company also released four new jazz LP’s on
Pacific
Jazz. Nordiska Musikforlaget represents some 15 different labels in the Swedish
market.
Latest releases from Knappupp are Pat Boone’s “Moody River” on Dot and
a new EP with Robertino on Triola. The latter has, among others, “Jamaica”
and “Pappagallo” among the numbers. Knappupp also informs that Robertino’s
“O
Sole Mio”
(It’s Now Or Never)
has
sold
100,000
in
Scandinavia and the
artist received a gold disk when he appeared
in Sjomarken, near Gothenburg
in western Sweden on June 23.
Bjorn Fremer, publicity head
of Sonet Grammofon AB, reports that
Bertil
Englund has
signed
a new contract with
Sonet
for another two
years. The
popular singer Ping Ping
(“Sucu Sucu”)
will tour
in Sweden
at
the end
of
July and beginning of August.
EMI
has
contracted
the
couple
Solveig
Linner
and
Bengt
von
Knorring
(they are married)
for recordings. The couple has become very popular after
some TV shows here
recently. Another
artist the company
is doing much
to
promote these days
is Jay Epae on Mercury.
New
sheet
music
from
Gehrmans
includes
“Salome”
by
Robert
Stolz,
a
German song, “Buzz-Buzz A-Diddle-It”/“Opportunity” both with Swedish lyrics
by Ulf Klefelt, and “Two Sleepy People” by Hoagy Carmichael with Swedish
lyrics by A1 Sandstrom.

ARGENTINA
The visitor of the week was Miguel Aceves Mejia, the world-famous Mexican
singer. Mejia
plans
to stay
in Buenos Aires for some time, but without per-
forming. Recently, RCA released
his LP “The Voice of Mexico.” Other artists
of
international
prestige
currently
in
Argentina
are
Bobby
Capo,
Antonia
Prieto and Daniel Riolobos. We were told Prieto would wax tangos with Juan
D Arienzo’s orchestra—he has always been a bolero and rock singer—and also
record “Cara de Payaso” (Face of a Clown), the Brazilian tune.
Pat Henry—the Chilean rock’n roller—may become a big hit in the northern
part of Argentina. Some dealers have written Odeon asking for special promo-
tion
in Tucuman, where Pat’s “Poetry
in Motion” has shown very good
sales.
Ray Anthony has recorded “Moliendo Cafe” (Grinding Coffee)
in the States.
The
tune
is number
one
on
our
charts
this
week. Domenico Modugno—the
author of “Volare”—cut “La Novia,” sung in Spanish and
Italian.
Columbia has finished the recording of
its
first stereo LP for release here.
It contains tango music played by Osvaldo Fresedo, well known arranger and
director. Columbia
has been
recording
in
stereo
for
the
States
for about
a
year and a
half, but these records weren’t released here, because the market
for this type of disk was too small.
RCA announced
it
will
start releasing
single
33’s, considering the
success
they have had. The label will make combinations of 33, 45 and 78 releases for
each record, according to the type of music. The “Compact 33” will also appear
very soon. The first single 33 will be “Exodus” (movie soundtrack) and will be
presented with a special
sleeve.
Los Cuatro Duendes—Chiliean vocal group—arrived here recently and
will
perform on radio and television.
The fire that destroyed part of Channel 9 TV caused, besides material losses,
big trouble
for people who have
to produce shows because
of lack
of space
and time. One of them
is Rodriguez Luque, who had to start his “Musica en
el
Aire” show in July, and now has his program delayed.
Los TNT will go to Venezuela next July, after they finish their second LP.
According
to RCA,
the
first one
is
selling pretty
well
in
that country.
Los
Santos,
as
part of
their world-wide
trip,
will perform
at
the Pessaro Song
Festival,
in
Italy. This contest
will be
telecast by Eurovision. After
it, they
will
go
to
Spain,
United
States and
France.
Billy
Cafaro
is
also
going
to
Venezuela, contracted by Venevision. July 10 he will go to Spain, to take part
in the Benidorm Song Festival, and then to Peru (Panamericana TV, Channel
13) and Chile (Bim Bam Bum Theatre-Buddy Day).
Famous SRL—ABC Paramount representative—has an agreement with EMI
of England and
its local representative, Odeon, for releasing part of Odeon’s
French
catalog. This was
possible because both
parts
considered
it was big
enough to permit both companies operations. Famous has also started releasing
Brazilian
label
Musidisc and American
Colpix.
Colpix
has
a
good
seller
in
“Blue Moon” by The
Marcels.
Musidic’s
best
seller
is
the
“Romanticos
de
Cuba” LP.

Virgilio Exposito has decided to wax his compositions with his own orchestra.
He’ll
also
start a record producing company. He hasn’t decided yet on which
label he will release them.
“II Nostro Concerto” has reached
24 waxings, Gigo
Gallo
(the
publisher)
announced. The tune
is on the charts this week mainly because of the Roberto
Yanes, Umberto Bindi and Pino Calvi recordings.
Palette
will
release
ten
Disc
Jockey
recordings
this
year,
according
to
Rodriguez Luque,
Disc Jockey’s
topper. Disc Jockey had
a good
hit recently
with Palette’s recording of “Never on Sunday” made by Makadopoulos and his
orchestra.
“Eso”
(one
of Argentina’s 1960 best
sellers)
has been contracted by Tulio
Gallo for publishing in Italy. “El Momento” and “Bailemos, Bailemos” will also
be published in that country.
Ruth
Durante—tango
songstress—recorded
“Esclavo
de
tu
piel” and “La
Noche de Anoehe”—formerly boleros—with Roberto Casal’s orchestra.
Inter Bas has put to sale its first “Petit LP’s,” that
is, seven inch 33’s with
three tunes on each side. The price
is slightly higher than EP’s.
Ariel
Records
released
Paul
Anka’s “Songs
for Young
Lovers”
with
big
acceptance. Anka’s
last single, “Tonight My Love, Tonight,”
is
selling pretty
well.
“Angelica”—currently number three in the
list—is being recorded in nearly
all companies. TK released
it, sung by Los Andariegos; Odeon, by Los Chilico-
tes, and RCA, by Bienvenido Cardenas and the Trio Lima.
Jolly Land
has
just
finished
her
first LP
for
Vik,
sung
in
Spanish
and
L:
English. Fernando Borges
is starting a tour of Mendoza and Peru. Lalo Fran-
sen
is
returning from
Colombia
very
soon.
Columbia’s
promotional LP
is
receiving big air play. Rafael Hidalgo cut “Ciceron Cha Cha Cha,” which may
become a
hit. “Ja
da,” by Johnny and
the Hurricanes
is also sounding
loud.
Paco Amor
will wax “Flamenco Rock” and “Argentina.” Capitol
is releasing
a “La Pachanga” LP recorded by Rene & Orch
in Spanish. Clebanoff’s “Cha
Cha Cha Flamenco” was just released here on Mercury.

E. Abner Named Vee Jay Prexy
CHICAGO—Ewart Abner was named
president of Vee Jay Records follow-
ing the company’s distributor meeting-
at the ARMADA Convention. Abner,
who headed
the
firm’s
delegation
to
the convention, was formerly general
manager
of Vee
Jay. The announce-
ment
of
the new
post was made
to
the assemblage immediately following
the actual business session at the Dip-
lomat Hotel.
Abner was one
of the founders
of
ARMADA
and
served
as
president
until succeeded by Art Talmadge last
year. He
is
a member
of the execu-
tive
committee and
served
as
chair-
man of the nominating committee this
year.

as new

of nineteen the number

“YELLOW BIRD”—Roger Williams—Kapp KL-
1244
The Williams keyboard
flair in a lineup of as-
sorted melodies that includes “Yellow Bird,” “Two
Different
Worlds,”
“Greensleeves,”
“A
Lover’s
Symphony”
and
“Gigi.”
Orchestral
accompani-
ment, in the lush manner,
is supplied by the orks
of Frank Hunter, Marty Gold and Gene Von Hall-
berg.
It’s the usual flavorful Williams sound and
has a large pre-sold market.
“THE WEIRD AND THE BEARD”—Jack Clem-
ents and Dale Stevens—Fraternity F-1012
A chance meeting some time ago between
col-
umnist-radio interviewer Dale
Stevens (WNOP-
Cincinnati) and comedy writer Jack Clements may
prove to have produced the freshest and funniest
new comedy
team. Using
material—delightfully
original and unhackneyed—written by Clements,
the two delve into normal comedy areas but come
up with absolutely abnormal situations. This deck
could be the big stepping stone to national fame.
“GREAT BAND WITH GREAT VOICES”—The
Si Zentner Orch. & the Johnny Mann Singers
Liberty LSS-14009
There
are numerous
ork-chorus
disks
on
the
market
but few
as
virile
as
this. The pungent
swing of the Zentner band
sets the intense pace
for such vehicles
as “Serenade
In
Blue,”
“Little
White
Lies,”
“Tain’t What You
Do”
and
“St.
Louis Blues” and the Mann voices are woven
in
various
inventive
ways—sans
lyric,
ensemble
voicings, solos, etc. Its penetrating zest should be
a much sought after upbeat change from the fa-
miliar
sterile
quality
of many
other ork-chorus
sets.
“APACHE!”—Sam
Butera
and
the
Witnesses
Dot DLP 3381
The rowdy, rampaging Witnesses, who proved
such effective pace-setters for Louis & Keely, reel
off a dozen pop items here led by the powerhouse
tenor sax blowing of Sam Butera. Leadoff tune
is
the
Butera
single,
“Apache!,”
followed
quickly
by
“Spanish
Harlem,”
“One
Mint
Julep,”
“Jo-
sephine” and
a
couple
of vigorous Butera
orig-
inals. For those inclined
to
virile ork music.
“SEEING ISRAEL WITH GEORGE JESSEL”—
Strand SL 1031
Jessel
proves
an
articulate
and
well-versed
guide
(historically)
in
this rocking-chair
trip
to
the Holy Land. To a background of appropriate
music and sound
effects Jessel provides a mono-
cled-eye view of the country’s three major cities
Haifa, Tel-Aviv and Jerusalem—that reveals the
adoring twinkle in his eye for this land. As Israel’s
unofficial public relations counsel, he
is bound to
increase tourism through this album.
“STREET SCENE”—Felix Slatkin—Liberty LSS-
14008
Slatkin’s
“street scene” encompasses
such
fa-
miliar
boulevards
as
“Pigalle,”
“Streets
of
La-
redo,” “On the Street Where You Live,” “Lullaby
of Broadway” and the title tune, “Street Scene.”
As can be seen from the selections, the moods are
widely varied
(though mostly
in the blue-tinged
area) and Slatkin has outfitted them with flowing,
colorful arrangements. Good commercial
appeal.
“EBB TIDE AND OTHER INSTRUMENTAL
FAVORITES”—Earl
Grant,
organ—Decca
DL
7416.5
Singer-pianist-organist Grant concentrates here
on organ stylings
of twelve evergreens. He
dis-
plays a technical
skill on the instrument, especi-
ally with unusual gimmick sounds
(as
on “Ebb
Tide”), and over-all handles what could be a cum-
bersome instrument with lightness and dexterity.
Other tunes are “Stormy Weather,” “That’s All,”
“My Foolish Heart” and “Misty.” There’s lots of
interesting inventiveness
in the Grant style that
many people will enjoy.
“SONGS OF THE BLUE & GREY”—The Way-
farers Trio—Mercury SR 60634
The Wayfarers Trio
is similar to the Kingston
Trio
in that
traditional folksongs
are revamped
to
a
pop-acceptable,
arranged,
gimmick
sound.
Here, songs recalling the Civil War are performed
in this likeable manner. Side one, devoted to the
North, contains “John Brown’s Body” and “March-
ing Through Georgia”;
side two, the South, has
“Dixie,” “Stonewall” and “The Hammer
Song.”
Could do a brisk trade.

BRAZIL
June
is proving
to be
a
very important month
for the
Brazilian
records
'
industry. Philips released its
first 33 compacts in both Brazilian and Interna-
tional
fields. Carlos Lyra, young composer and singer, waxed two sambas of
his own: “Quern Quiser Encontrar O Amor” (Who Wants To Find Love) and
“Mister Golden”; Sonia Delfino, teenage singer, appears in a compact with two
Brazilian versions of American
hits: “Emotions” and “Tonight My Love To-
night.” The International repertoire
is represented by Henry Jerome’s “Man
With The Golden Arm,” Brenda Lee’s “Emotions,” Paul Anka’s “Tonight, My
Love Tonight” and by a Paraguayan
singer Luis Alberto
Del
Parana
with
^
“Princesa Soraya”
(Princess Soraya).
Philips is also responsible for a new album which should cause great sensa-
tion: “Sylvia Telles U.S.A.,” made in the United States by the Brazilian singer,
accompanied by such American musicians as Barney Kessel, Calvin Jackson,
Joe Mondragon, A1 McKibbon and Bill Hitchcock Orchestra. Sylvia
is married
to Aloysio de Oliveira, Philips
artistic director and well known in the United
States, where he lived for several years. Aloysio said the album
is an attempt
to break rhythmical barriers between two
different musical
idioms. And, we
^
may add a successful one since the combination of Brazilian music and Amer-
ican rhythms seems perfect.
Brazilian public opinion will be shaken soon by a new LP released a few
days ago by Copacabana Records. The album,
entitled “A Musica Do
Seculo
XX De Joey” (Joey’s 20th Century Music) was entirely cut with popular com-
positions interpreted by Joey De Oliveira—pianist-writer-composer and now,
singer—wife
of maestro Eleazar De Carvalho, one of the
closest friends
of
the late maestro Serge Koussevitzky, with whom he worked
in Tanglewood.
Joey’s style is completely new and critics have said that she’s years ahead of
'
her time. She
is a very famous pianist with an international background, hav-
ing given concerts in Europe and the U.S. with great success. And though the
fact isn’t known, when a classical musician turns to pop music here, the public
here is puzzled.
There
is another new Brazilian record company: Fermata Do
Brasil Ltda.
This company has three
labels: Fermata, Premier and Young, and represents
another
six:
Atlantic-Atco—New
York;
King
Records—Cincinnati;
Cameo-
Parkway—Philadelphia;
Jamie
Records—Philadelphia;
Hispa-Vox—Madrid,
^
Spain,
and
Jupiter
Records—Munich,
Germany.
Fermata’s
head
office
is
Avenida Ipiranga, 1123-Sao Paulo, Brazil. The executive line-up
is:
President—Enrique Lebendiger
General Manager—Juvenal Fernandes
Sales Department—Miguel Politi
Public Relations—Francisco Florencio Da Silva.
Fermata is also one of the most active publishers in South America.

######## 1961-07-15 p23  [blue\s*note\s*40\d\d]
Album
Reviews
JAZZ
NEWPORT?
cnaaiis mmms
\
MBX RORCH
ERIC DOLPHY
ROY ElORI&GSl
NEWPORT REBELS”—Candid
8022
The rebellious Cliff Walk Manor concerts at the
1960 Newport
fest grew
into
the
militant Jazz
Artists
Guild, which now
results
in
this
session.
Fortunately,
the
most
impressive
aura
of
Cliff
Walk—the
thoroughly
relaxed
atmosphere—has
been
retained
in
these
studio
dates.
Also,
the
mingling of old and new jazz faces has resulted
in
an
ingratiating
benevolence
among
the mu-
sicians, and grips
all
in
a bond of cohesiveness.
Participating
are
Charlie
Mingus,
Max
Roach,
Roy
Eldridge,
Eric
Dolphy,
Jo
Jones
among
others. Tunes, like the men, are old and new. An
achievement
of
sorts
that
results
in worthwhile
listening.
“WHISTLE STOP”—Kenny Dorham—Blue Note
4063
The
sweeping,
persuasive Dorham trumpet
is
reunited here with the vigorous charging of Hank
Mobley’s tenor and together form a striking front
line for seven Dorham tunes of somewhat connec-
tion. Dorham and Mobley surge through such en-
thusiastic
pieces
as
“Philly
Twist,”
“Buffalo,”
“Whistle
Stop” and Dorham’s Epitaph”
(a
one-
minute
dirge)
and
get
vital
assistance from
a
Philly
Joe-Paul
Chambers-Kenny
Drew rhythm
section.
It’s a neatly tied-up jazz package of tre-
mendous strength.
“JAZZ REUNION”—Pee Wee
Russell, Coleman
Hawkins—Candid 8020
In the reuniting of oldsters Russell and Haw-
kins
it
is
immediately
evident
that
neither has
been
left behind, and both
still command respect
and
admiration
from
the
modernists. They
are
accompanied by sidemen Jo
Jones,
Milt
Hinton,
Nat Pierce, Emmett Berry and Bob Brookmeyer
in readings
of “If
I Could Be With You,” “Tin
Tin
Deo,”
“All Too
Soon” and
“28th and
8th.”
There is a naturalness and unhurried approach to
the playing here that makes
it
all the more en-
joyable. Another
fine example
of the care which
goes into every Candid album.
“THE GREATEST OF DIZZY GILLESPIE”—
RCA Victor LPM-2398
An
indication
of
the
vast
early
influence
of
Dizzy Gillespie in both small combo and big band
sessions
is revealed here in recording dates from
’46
and
’47. The
’46
small combo
dates
feature
Gillespie,

Gold Vinyl Disks
In MGM/Verve Experiment
NEW YORK—MGM/Verve
Records
is experimenting with the use of gold
vinyl compound
to
place
special
ac-
cent on certain promotional disks sent
to radio stations. The first such record
to get this treatment will be an Ella
Fitzgerald
single
of “Mr.
Paganini”
on
the
Verve
label.
Single
is
from
Ella’s upcoming fall album release of
“Ella
In Hollywood”.
Diskery execs feel that the gold col-
ored vinyl would catch the eye of disk
jockeys,
record
librarians,
producers
and program
assistants quicker than
the
usual
black
material.
Close
to
4,000 of the Ella Fitzgerald gold vinyl
disk samples will be shipped this week
as part of the experiment. The label’s
distributors
salesmen
and
promotion
men
will query
stations for reaction.

f@) ALL THAT JAZZ
REPORT FROM NEWPORT
As Music At Newport rang down the curtain Sunday night on Duke Ellington,
primary interest centered on how effective a policing job was done. At a cost
of about $20,000, producers Sid Bernstein and John Drew guaranteed an orderly
affair. They got one!
.
.
. and taught a too-late lesson to the old Newport Jazz
Festival producers. Police were imported from throughout New England and
told
to
keep
order under any
conditions. They were
so
effective
that
even
parking tickets were heavily distributed.
In
all,
there were few
disturbances
in
the
town,
and
they were
quickly
extinguished. For example,
a 19-year-old boy ended up
in the cooler
(plus
a
substantial fine) for carrying beer on the beach. Automobile traffic was expertly
supervised and cars moved freely through the main thoroughfares—in
direct
contrast
to the interminable jam-ups
in previous years. Youthful enthusiasm
was allowed to express itself, but within bounds and at a reasonable tenor. An
excellent idea was the searching of youths for liquor upon entering Freebody
Park.
But
if Bernstein and Drew were
able
to teach
the
old producers
a
lesson,
they didn’t bother
to learn from past mistakes
in programming. Despite the
inroads
in mature selection of talent and balancing concert
bills that the
old
Newport
tried
to do—and
finally
did
last year
despite
the
riots—Music At
Newport
resorted
to
booking
only
the
most
attractive
popular
stars
and
jammed each concert to the brim with music without regard for balance and
blend. Apparently now that the Newport festival
is out of the hands of a non-
profit
organization
and
under
stress
to produce
a
sizable
profit,
jazz
as
a
whole will suffer but the weekend reveleers
will
rejoice.
It was apparent that
not many serious jazz fans were on hand
for the weekend
(except for some
press) when, what we think were the most provocative and engrossing groups
laid
a bomb with
the
patrons. Among
these were
such
interesting
acts
as
Carmen
Delavallade’s
“Portrait
of
Billie”
music
and
dance
sequence;
John
Coltrane, the Jazztet, Horace Silver, Stan Getz, Art Blakey and the Jazz Mes-
sengers, Oscar Peterson and A1 Mims and Leon James. These are fairly big
names and represent many popular concepts of jazz. But they were even too
“far
out”
for
the
obviously
uninformed
audience,
which
responded
to
such
tired veterans as George Shearing, Louis Armstrong, Duke Ellington, and
al-
most
all the vocalists, without reservation. Of course, the matinees were very
poorly attended
despite the
brilliance
of John
Hendricks’
“Evolution
of
the
Blues” program
(with Maynard
Ferguson, Hannah Dean, Ben Webster and
others), and
the
inquisitive
attraction
of
the
jazz
vocal
styles program by
Jackie
Paris, Mark Murphy
and
Carol
Sloane—who
scored
such
a triumph
Saturday afternoon that she was brought back for the Monday night
affair
and “knocked ’em dead.” She was one of the bright spots of the event.

LP
In

Seal

NEW YORK—RCA Victor Records

ever” as a

In answer to numerous requests for
such
an
all-Sousa

al-

of Gould’s

Seal catalog.
In addition to “Sousa Forever,” Vic-
tor had previously announced another
recording by Morton
Gould,
for July
release, “Beyond The Blue
Horizon.”
Included were such pop
“classics” as
the
title
song,
“Stardust,”
“Stormy
Weather,” and 8 other tunes.

via

hops, TV
band-
stand shows and p.a.’s.
But despite the absence of esthetic quality from Newport last weekend, the
people paid their money knowing in advance what they wanted and responded
overwhelmingly for their popular favorites. And Sid Bernstein and John Drew
must be hailed for their success in preserving order in an incendiary situation.
With Newport in the bag, conduct-wise, the Randall’s Island Jazz
Festival
now proceeds
to an
orderly
goal. Frank
Geltman, producer
of
the
festival,
has announced
his talent lineup for the three-night event and
it’s interesting
to note
that most
of the faces
at Newport
will
be
seen
again
at
Randall’s
Island. Dates have been set for Aug. 25, 26 and 27. Curiously, Lambert, Hend-
ricks & Ross will perform each night. Out for some sort of a record, probably.

GARY (U.
S.) BONDS (Legrand 1009)
Bonds, who catapulted to the top with “New Orleans” and repeated with
the current phenomenon, “Quarter To Three,” has another that’s already
tearing up the charts. Side, tabbed “School Is Out” (pulled from his new
LP, “Dance
‘Til A Quarter To Three”),
is a
similarly-styled gang-sing,
happy-handclapping mashed potatoes entry. Looks like another #1 out-
ing. The haunting coupler
(also from the LP has a winning “Stand By
Me” Latin beat format.

Powerful

already

“LOVE SWINGS”—Bobby Darin—Atco 33-134
Bobby Darin runs
the gamut
of a musical
love
affair. He opens with the joyful buoyancy of “I
Didn’t Know What Time It Was” and “How About
You,”
proceeds
to
the
deep
devotion
of
“No
Greater Love,” then the painful breakup with “In
Love
In Vain” and then the
final
futility
in
“I
Guess I’ll Have To Change My Plan.” Other songs
in-between
further
illustrate
the
events.
The
songster
is excellently equipped
to purvey these
varied emotions convincingly. Arranger-conductor
Torrie Zito is a surprise “find” on the date. Rates
a secure chart niche.
“YELLOW BIRD”—Lawrence Welk—Dot DLP
3389
Again the “new” Welk ork sound dresses up pop
melodies in interesting teen/adult appeal fashion.
Here
the
orkster
performs
his
single,
“Yellow
Bird,” along with such
other
solid
favorites
as
“Heartbreak Hotel,” “Runaway,” “Don’t Worry,”
“Harbor Lights” and “Mockin’ Bird Hill.” As with
his previous LP dates, this one has a big chart
future.
“SPANISH
HARLEM”—Ben
E.
King—Atco
33-133
Taking
a
cue
from
the
immense
success
of
“Spanish Harlem,” Ben E. King freshly tailors an
LP-full of pseudo and authentic Latin American
tunes.
The
Stan Applebaum
arrangements
are
invigoratingly
alive and
in
his charming
inter-
pretations, King proves a major new pop talent.
Along with the title tune are “Perfidia,” “Frene-
si,”
“Besame
Mucho,”
“Amor”
and
“Quizas.”
Impressive and definitely commercial LP bow for
the songster.
“STARLIGHT,
STARBRIGHT”—Linda
Scott—
Canadian-American CALP 1005
Young “new star” thrush Linda
Scott debuts
in
her first package. In
it she gathers a handful of
“stars,”
such
sturdies
as
“Stars
Fell On
Ala-
bama,”
“Stardust,” “When You Wish Upon A
Star” and
her own intro
single
hit,
“I’ve
Told
Ev’ry Little Star.” Hutch Da'vie has supplied the
lark with a
solid footing of teen-beat backdrops
and she follows them diligently. Should meet with
strong teen acceptance.
“THE GUNS OF NAVARONE”—Original Film
Soundtrack—Columbia CL 1655
Apparent from the rave
opening
notices
it
re-
ceived, “Navarone” should rank among the best
action
flicks
of
the
year.
Dimitri
Tiomkin
has
accorded
it a compelling
score
that matches
it
scene
for
scene
in dramatic impact and
turbu-
lence. In addition, for the pop music fans, incorpo-
rated in the package is the Mitch Miller single of
the title theme. Set has a solid future.
“TRY
A
LITTLE
TENDERNESS”—Frank
D’Rone--Mercury SR 60174
D’Rone is one of the few who rightly deserve the
reference of “a singer’s singer.” He sings for Isrric
impact alone and in the process ties together an
immaculate
performance
that few
can
not
ap-
preciate. In this third Mercury LP he investigates
the varied romantic moods of pop songs choosing
such delectable vehicles as “Long Ago,” “There’s
A Small Hotel,”
“I Wish
I Knew” and
“Invita-
tion.” Rewarding listening here.

“THE FANCIFUL WORLD OF OGDEN NASH”
—Capitol SW 1570
The whimsical
poetry
of Ogden Nash,
-with
its
ridiculously unbalanced meter, its forced rhymes,
its uproarious social commentary have long been
a
delight for
the
informed. Here
the
poet has
selected some 27 of his short poems for his o^wn,
reading. But Mr. Nash’s poems, above all modern'
poetry, have their greatest comic impact visually,
and this
is unfortunately lost in recital. Too, Mr.
Nash does not have the vocal prowess to bring
off his poems with the dash of fancy they would
require.
Still, the album has
its
delightful mo-
ments and
is worth hearing for Mr. Nash’s
in-
terpretation alone.
4

for

up includes the national anthem as well as such

of the
Ocean,’!
“This My
Country”
and “God
Bless
America."*^’
Has a place in the catalog.

“STRAIGHT AHEAD”—Abbey
Lincoln—Candid
8015
As
first
demonstrated
in
the
“We
Insist!”
Candid
album,
Abbey
Lincoln
is
an
extremely
forceful singer. Now that she’s “learned” to com-
municate
directly, she expresses
a mature pride
in her
lyric descriptions of the directions
of her
race. (Several of the songs here feature lyrics by
Miss
Lincoln.)
Collaboratively
accompanied
by
such masters
as Max Roach, Coleman Hawkins,
Mai Waldron among others, she delves into “Blue
Monk,” “When Malindy Sings,” “Retribution” and
“African
Lady.”
Gratifying vocal entertainment
that deserves a wide hearing.
“DJANGOLOGY”—Django Reinhardt—RCA Vic-
tor LPM-2319
One
of the most
influential
guitarists
in jazz
history and the most influential of
all European
jazz musicians, Django Reinhardt was an estab-
lished
legend
at the time
of
his death
in
1953.
Here he
is heard
in
a
series
of
late recordings
from 1949-50 cut at a private studio in Rome and

######## 1961-07-22 p31  [star\s*bright]
Kapp: Good Product, Sound Biz Practices
Cure For “Profitiess Prosperity”
NEW YORK—Good
product,
sound
business
practices
and an
avoidance
of
“profitless
prosperity”
can
cure
much of the financial woes of the rec-
ord industry, according to Dave Kapp,
president of Kapp Records.
These
points form
the
label’s new
“Kapp Concept” policy, and were an-
nounced by Kapp
to
a
gathering
of
the
firm’s
distribs
over
the weekend
(15)
at
New
York’s
Savoy-Hilton
Hotel.
“With
all of
its current
problems,
the record business
still offers a fabu-
lous potential for profits,” said Kapp.
The way
is not through
bigger and
better
deals, which eventuate
in
dis-
counts at the retail level, diminishing
profits
for
manufacturers
and
dis-
tribs, and ultimately leave nothing to
look
forward
to
but
larger
volume,
viewed
Kapp
“Sometimes
it
works,
but
the
business
graveyard
is
filled
with
companies
for whom
it
didn’t
work!”,
said Kapp
“.
.
. the answer
is simple
.
.
. We Must Sell Our Rec-
ords At A
Profit!”
“Profitless
Prosperity,”
according
to
the
recording
exec.,
is
too
often
present,
in which
large numbers
of
records
are
sold
without
the manu-
facturer and distrib realizing a profit
on the merchandise.
The Kapp Concept—“make a prod-
uct which is a good product and which
we
can
sell
at
a
profit”—indicates,
Kapp
explained,
self
appraisal
of
goals and methods, and has been “suc-
cessfully”
applied
at Kapp
enabling
the company to make great progress
in the past six months, in the way of
efficient operation and better arrange-
ments with
its
distribs.
Back
in 1947 at Decca, Kapp
said,
he had
been
in a
position
of having
a huge demand for records, a demand
coming
in
faster than
records
could
be made. “Production was stepped up
to 8 million 400 thousand for a month
yet we
lost money,”
said Kapp, “on
the
last
114
million because
of addi-
tion
costs
in
hitting that
figure.
.
.
.
It was
then
that
I
learned
the
full
meaning of the words ‘profitless pros-
perity’.”
Kapp went on
to
say, “The manu-
facturer
and
distributor
must
look
ahead and think of his business as a
continuing
operation
projected
into
years rather than days or weeks.
.
.
.
We must understand that we cannot
live
if we do not
sell at a reasonable
profit
both
in
Good
times
and Bad
times.”
Dave Kapp further told the gather-
ing:
“I
firmly
believe that there are
not
enough
of us
in
the
record
in-
dustry who actually take the time and
effort to find the road to profits.
I be-

RIAA To Fight
All Kinds
Of Disk “Duplication”
NEW YORK—A
full-scale
program
aimed
at
halting
the
spread
of
un-
authorized
duplication
of
sound
re-
cordings
has
been
approved
by
the
board
of directors
of
the Record
In-
dustry
Association
of
America
(RIAA),
it was announced
last week
by Henry Brief, Executive Secretary.
Unauthorized
duplication
includes
not
only
counterfeiting,
which
the
RIAA
said
it
will
“continue
vigor-
ously”
to
investigate,
but
also:
The
transfer
of
phonograph
records
to
tapes which are leased, sold or broad-
cast for the sole profit of the duplica-
tor,
including
the
use
of
such
unauthorized
reproductions
for back-
ground
music
services;
piracy
of
records both here and abroad; and the
dubbing
of parts
of
different phono-
graph
records
in
the
production
of
so-called
“mosaic”
records.
In
all
such
cases, RIAA
contends,
such
entrepreneurs
are
infringing
upon
the
legitimate
record manufac-
turers’
property
rights.
In
addition,
they
are
probably
also evading pay-
ments to performance rights societies,
copyright
owners,
artists
and
mu-
sicians.
During the course of
its probe into
counterfeiting,
RIAA’s
investigatory
branch uncovered numerous instances
of other types
of unauthorized dupli-
cation
of phonograph
records. RIAA
is making
this information
available
to
its members for consideration and
appropriate action.
In
addition, RIAA
will
press
for
corrective
legislation
in
areas where
it is found that inadequate laws or no
laws at
all exist.
Ernest
S.
Meyers, RIAA
general
counsel, pointed
out that the growth
of
activities
involving
the
unauthor-
ized duplication of
all types of sound
recordings
presents
an
increasing
threat to record manufacturers. While
the
ethical nature
of the business of
some of the people who are duplicat-
ing sound recordings is not comparable
to that of counterfeiters, their conduct
must inevitably damage the business
of record manufacturers, he declared.

Stafion Offers Plan To
Share Sales, Programming
Ideas
NEW YORK—A plan for U.S.
radio
stations to share
sales and program-
ming ideas, similar to the plan utilized
by
six leading Canadian
outlets, has
been
advanced
by WLEE-Richmond,
Va.
Each month, the sales manager and
the program
director
of each
partic-
ipating
station
would
prepare
a
de-
tailed report of all unusual or success-
ful sales ideas, sales or station promo-
tion schemes, contests, and program-
ming
ideas
inaugurated
during
the
preceding
month.
This
report would
be mimeographed
and
mailed
to
all
other
participating
outlets
for
their
benefit.
No cash
is involved
in the scheme,
WLEE
says.
In
order
to
participate
each station would have to prepare its F
own report each month. Any
station
which
fails
to mail a monthly report
would
be
dropped from
the
mailing
lists
of other participants
until such
time as a report is submitted.
Stations which
would
like
to
par-
ticipate
in
such
a
plan
can
contact
WLEE
program
director
David
E.
Lyman.

ENGLAND
The holiday season
is with us once again and, accelerated by a prolonged
heatwave, the accustomed
lull seems to have started earlier than usual. Holi-
day
plans
have
been
announced by
the major
labels
and
the
factories
of
Decca, E.M., Philips and Pye will be closed completely over a period July 28-
August 14.
The highlight of the week
is the arrival of Johnny Mathis making his
first
visit to Europe.
In London,
his working holiday includes three concerts
fol-
lowed by a nation wide tour,
all with Ted Heath and
his Orchestra. He
will
also
tele-record a show for Granada for transmission
later
in the
year. His
latest single, “You Set My Heart To Music,” and LP
“I’ll Buy You A Star”
are released here on Fontana.
Also arriving in England this week
is Peggy Lee for her four-week cabaret
appearance at A1 Burnet’s Pigalle Restaurant. Fears that Miss Lee might run
into trouble with the Musicians Union following the recent debacle over Steve
Lawrence & Edyie Gorme’s accompanists, have been
alleviated. The Ministry
of Labour has granted working permits for Miss
Lee’s British born
pianist,
Victor Feldman, drummer Stan Levey, guitarist Dennis Boudimier, and bassist
Max Bennett. Peggy Lee’s latest disk, “Yes Indeed,” is released here on Capitol.
The
first
Soviet Trade
Exhibition opened
in London
this week. The
only
record company exhibiting is Associated Recordings. On their elaborate stand,
A.R.
is displaying recordings by Soviet
artists which they issue here on the
M.K.,
Artia
and
Parliament
labels.
Associated
Recordings
recently
invited
dealers to the first of a monthly series of recitals to introduce their latest re-
leases
at
the
newly
opened
Centre
of
Sound.
Russian
pianist,
Sviatoslav
Richter, whose recordings are released here exclusively on the Parliament label,
is currently in London for concerts at the Royal Festival Hall.
Further proof
of the improved
cultural
relations between East and West
comes with the release of a new Russian Language Course, “Elementary Rus-
sian,” by Nina Potapova, available from the retail and import firm of Colletts.
Comprising four 10" LP’s together with a 78-page text book, the
set
retails
at
£4.
10.
0. Another
fifteen
shillings
secures two more books
compiled by
Nina Potapova.
Ricky Valance who jumped
into the
spotlight with
his controversial cover
version of “Tell Laura
I Lover Her,”
is hoping that his latest Columbia ver-
sion of “Bobby”—also
in the death idiom—will put him back into the charts.
Original American recording of “Bobby” is by Neil Scott on Pye with a second
cover by Johnny & Chaz on
Decca. Although the B.B.C. has not banned the
disk, they are not too keen to give
it airplay.
John Barry, the man responsible for arrangements and backings of all Adam
Faith’s hits, has combined his talents with those of ace writer Johnny Worth
for Adam’s latest Parlophone release, “My Last Wish.”
Prolific song
writer, Lionel
Bart,
this week hosted
a
party to launch
his
latest composition “Hide And
Seek,”
specially
written
for and
recorded by
Marty Wilde on
Philips.
Bart
considers
this
his
biggest
hit
potential
since
Cliff Richard’s million
selling “Livin’
Doll”. The song
is published by
Bart’s
Apollo Music Company.
Bart has also penned a new number for another Philips artist, Anne Shelton,
entitled “Don’t Forget”. A & R Manager Johnny Franz
is convinced this will
be an
even
greater
success than
Anne’s
recent
chart
entry,
“Sailor”. The
number
is also published by Apollo Music.
John Kennedy, joint manager for Tommy Steele and many other top
stars,
leaves for New York on July 16 for ten days to negotiate cabaret dates for
Shani Wallis currently starring in the London production of “Irma La Douce,”
and in cabaret at the Hungaria. Her latest waxing, “Something In The Air”
an English version by Hal David of the
Italian
hit “Cera
Sella”—is released
by Philips and published by Shapiro-Bernstein. Kennedy also plans to
tie up
with
a good independent management
firm
for
reciprocal
representation
of
artists.
I

for three weeks
vacation
is
popular

|

on July

all her
i
hour-long TV programmes
to be screened both here and
in America later

Peter Sellers.

Levy Exits Epic
NEW YORK—Bill Levy told The Cash
Box
last week
that
he was
leaving,
effective
last Friday
(21), his post as
A&R director of Epic Records. He said
an
impending
consolidation
of
the
A&R
departments
of
Columbia
and
Epic
would
eliminate
his
function.
Columbia and
Epic
had no comment
to make
on
the Levy announcement.
Levy
said
he
will
be
discussing
sev-
eral
offers
and
would
announce
his
plans shortly.
"Nashville Concerto" Being
Cleffed For Atkins
NEW YORK—Composer/pianist
Bill
Pursell
is
writing
a
concerto
for
guitar and orchestra for RCA Victor’s
guitarist/A&R man Chet Atkins.
Pursell and Atkins were both guest
soloists
at a recent concert
in Nash-
ville with the National Symphony Or-
chestra under the
direction
of Willis
Page.
Despite
rain,
over
8,000
fans
attended
this outdoor program
in the
city’s Centennial Park.
Pursell’s
composition,
to
be
called
“The
Nashville
Suite
for Guitar and
Orchestra,” was
suggested
by
Page.
Atkins has also appeared as
soloist
with the Atlanta Symphony, at New-
port’s
jazz
festival, and
in
a
special
recent concert for President Kennedy.
As
manager
of
Victor’s
Nashville
popular A&R productions, he has also
contributed
his
talents
to
such
cur-
rent Victor singles successes as Floyd
Cramer’s “San Antonio
Rose”; Ann-
Margret’s “I Just Don’t Understand”;
Don Gibson’s “Sea of Heartbreak” and
Jim Reeves’ “What Would You Do?”
May To Provide Music
For New Sinatra Pic
HOLLYWOOD — Conductor-arranger
Billy May has been
signed by Frank
Sinatra to compose, arrange and con-
duct
the music
score
for
his
Essex-
UA
production, “Soldiers
3.”
May
has
previously
worked
with
Sinatra
on
four
albums
and
five
singles
for
Capitol Records and
Sin-
atra’s
Reprise
Records.
His new
as-
signment will begin in mid-September
following
the
final
editing
of
“Sold-
iers 3,” which John Sturges
is direct-
ing with
stars Sinatra, Dean Martin,
Peter Lawford, Sammy Davis, Jr. and
Joey Bishop.
