Last week saw the
first concert of the annual season of Henry Wood Prom-
enade
Concerts
at
the Royal
Albert
Hall.
Sponsored by
the BBC under
the
guidance of Sir Malcolm Sargent, the season continues for eight weeks with!
,
nightly performances by
leading Symphony
Orchestras and
the
world’s
top
classical
soloists.
The
low
price
of
admission
affords many
teenagers
an
opportunity to become acquainted with the best in classical music and together
I
with
extensive TV
and
Sound
coverage
by
the
BBC,
these
concerts
un-
doubtedly encourage the
sale of classical LP recordings.
Equire Records has extended
its rhythm and blues catalog by
signing an
exclusive contract with Bandera Records of Chicago. First releases due shortly!
on the
Starlite
label
will
be
singles by
artists
such
as Bobby
Davis, Dusty
Brown, Jimmy Lee and The Diatones. The catalog also contains several country
j
,
items to be issued in due course.
After
several years
in
the
iron
curtain
countries,
British
songstress Gery
Scott has returned to England. A recording contract with Supraphon Records
of Prague has established her as one of Russia’s top female vocalists with disk
sales well over the
4,000,000 mark. Last week Gery had her
first release on
the Parlophone
label—“The Dum de Dum Song” specially written for her by
top Russian composer Ludmilla Ladova. Gery hopes to encourage more British
artists and bands to visit Russia on an exchange
basis.
The MGM film “A Matter of Who” starring Terry Thomas and Alex Niche!
,,
had
its London preview
last week. Roy Castle, who sings the
title song over
the credits, has recorded the number for Philips—an instrumental version by
John Barry on Parlophone is due in August. Published by Southern Music.

to
Alan
Holmes
of
Robbins
Music
publisher
of

No.
1
hit “Temptation”—incorrectly
credited

Chappells
in The

charts
last week.

is

.
acquire material with a Scottish, Irish or national flavor. In London, he visited h

At a recent meeting, The Gramophone Record Retailers Association elected
London dealer James Robinson as President of the Association and Reg Reed
(former Chairman)
as vice president.
Board
of Trade
figures
for May show that 28% more
records were
sold
than in the same month last year. Export sales were also up by 4%.
The latest recording star to expand his publishing interests
is
Cliff Richard
with the opening of Joanaline Music Co. Handling the company
is
Franklyji
Boyd
of Aberbaeh,
a
close
associate
of
Cliff’s
since
his
early days
in show
ft
business. Boyd
also handles
the publishing interests of other stars
including
The Shadows, Johnny Mathis (Cathryl Music and Nomat Music);
Elvis Pres-
ley (Gladys Music Inc. and Elvis Presley Music
Inc.) The Aberbaeh group are
currently riding high with Del Shannon’s “Runaway,” Presley’s “Surrender,”
|
Buddy
Holly’s “Baby
I Don’t Care” and “High Voltage by Johnny and
the
Hurricanes.
Karusel, major Swedish label whose international stars include Nora Brock-
stedt and Lil Babs, plans to release its product here in September. The placing
and subsequent promotion of material will be handled by consultant P. A. L.
Skinner.

CLIFFIE STONE PRESENTS THE ORIGINAL
COUNTRY SING-A-LONG”—Capitol SKAO 1555
Cliffie
Stone has assembled
32 country
favorites
and
rounded up
a
group
of male
voices
for
a
cheerful, home-cooked
sing'-along. The songs are
all
taken
at
a
gentle,
easy-to-follow
pace
and
will be greatly appreciated by many country mu-
sic
fans.
Among
the
tunes
are
“Bouquet
Of
Roses.”
“I Walk The
Line,” “Slipping Around,”
“Walking
The
Floor
Over
You,” “A
Satisfied
Mind,”
“I
Don’t Hurt Anymore” and “Bummin’
Around.” Lyrics are included.
"BUTTON
SHOES,
BELLY
LAUGHS
AND
MONKEY BUSINESS”—The Duke of Paducah—
Starday SLP 148
The rustic, corn-fed humor of the Duke of Padu-
cah
has
been
a
southern
nitery
attraction
for
years. He’s now brought to disk by Starday and
has
been
recorded
in
a
typical
performance
of
his finely-timed, drawled, sometimes-risque mate-
rial.
It’s good fun and
could experience
the
re-
sponse given Dave Gardner a while back.
“ROBERT CLARY
LIVES
IT
UP AT THE
PLAYBOY CLUB”—Atlantic 8053
The
diminutive
French
songster
is
heard
in
a
program cut in an appearance at Chicago’s Play-
boy Club. He
is an exuberant song
stylist and
a
charming interpreter of both French and Amer-
ican
tunes. Here he performs
his two stage
tri-
umphs (“New Faces Of 1952”)—“Lucky
Pieri-e”
and “I’m In Love With Miss Logan”—plus “Love
Is A Simple Thing”
(from the same show), “He
And She” and sevei al French delights. A package
bursting with vocal charm.
“THE OL’ CALLIOPE MAN AT THE FAIR”—
The
Sande &
Greene
Fun-Time
Band—Reprise
R-6004
Summertime music
is
calliope music, what with
amusement
parks
and
fairs
in
all
their
glory.
Here, the calliope
is in full swing demonstrating
its
universal
appeal
with
such
tasty

as
“The
Carousel
Waltz,” “And The Band
Played
On,” “It’s A Grand Night For Singing” and oth-
ers of this
ilk. A real fun-time package.
“MAZEL TOV, MIS AMIGOS”—Juan Calle and
His Latin Lantzmen—Riverside RLP 97510
Merging the elements
of
Latin rhythms
(infec-
tious)
with Jewish melodies
(warm and univer-
sally appealing)
is not new but as done here by
the pseudonymed Juan
Calle, promises
a bagful
of dancing and
listening enjoyment.
Vocals are
in Yiddish.
Selections include such popular tunes
as
“Belz,” “Hava
Nagila,”
“Bei
Mir
Bist Du
Shein” and “Yossel,
Yossel,” mated
to such va-
ried
rhythms
as

cha
cha,
mambo and samba.
“ON THE BRINK”—Will Holt & Dolly Jonah—
Atlantic 8051
The
husband-wife comedy
team,
newly
arrived
on the scene, could be categorized with the new,
semi-sick “in” group. Their sketches, rather than
provoking belly-laughs,
elicit a kind of knowing-
chuckle.
In
addition.
Holt
has
a
pleasing
voice
and uses
it for two folkish songs. The kind of al-
bum that
will appeal
to the “new sophisticates.”
“EL CONJUNTO TIPICO LADI”—The
Musical
Folklore of Puerto Rico—Alegre LPA 806
Puerto Rico has
a
rich
musical
heritage dating
to the 16th and 17th Centuries of Spanish
occu-
pation,
evolving now
into
a
curiously
enticing-
combination
of European and
native
influences.
Here, Ladi
Martinez, a leading exponent of this
genre, performs with a small group a dozen ex-
amples of this music. It
is melodic and constantly
surprising
in
its
classical-like
subtlety.
Though
limited
in appeal, a fascinating listening experi-
ence.

—Pacific Jazz PJ-26

Mercury Inks Little Richard,
Josh White, Danny Jordan
CHICAGO—Mercury
Records
has
added
Little Richard and Josh White
to
its
roster
and
newcomer
Danny
Jordan
to
its subsid Smash stable,
it
was announced
last week.
Little Richard was an early pioneer
in rock
’n’
roll with a long string of
hits on the
Specialty
label,
including
“Tutti Frutti,” “Long Tall Sally” and
“Slippin’
and
Slidin’.”
Following
a
self-imposed
religious
retirement,
he
joined
the
End/ Gone
set-up
for
a
short time. He has been
inactive for
the past two years.
Sessions are cur-
rently being readied for
Little Rich-
ard by Mercury music director Quincy
Jones.
Josh White
is considered to be one
of
the
country’s
leading
“authentic”
folk
artists, specializing
in blues and
work
songs.
He
was
formerly
on
Elektra. A
single and an album
re-
lease is in the works by A&R director
Shelby
Singleton.
Danny Jordan is from the Van-Pock
artist stable and is being groomed for
appeal
to
the
teen market. His
first
single,
“Jeannie” b/w “Boom
Diddy
Boom,” was released last week.

will

appear in 1962 unless other stations in Tokyo assume
its right of telecasting.

“THE MANY KEYBOARDS OF THE AMAZ-
ING PAUL RENARD”—Riverside RLP 97507
Renard’s
keyboard
proficiency
encompasses
the
piano, Hammond
organ,
Wurlitzer
pipe
organ,
harpsichord
and celeste. He takes
it yet another
step by combining several combinations of these
instruments
in
various
tracks
by
multi-track
methods
(a
sort
of Les
Paul
of
the keyboard).
But keyboard
virtuosity
is
only
a means
to
a
scintilating
musical
end
in
which
Renard
per-
forms a program of evergreens in different styles.
Selections include “The Boy Next Door,” “Drums
In My
Heart,”
“Deep
Purple”
and
“Darktown
Strutters Ball.”
“THE SOUND OF THE ASPHALT JUNGLE”—
Joe Harnell & his Orch.—Medallion ML-7518
The myriad sound and moods of the city
ai'e mu-
sically portrayed by
a big swinging band under
the direction of Joe Harnell. The scene
is set by
the Ellington-cleffed TV theme, “Asphalt Jungle,”
followed by such
carefully chosen
selections
as
“Blues
In
The
Night,”
“Take
The
‘A’
Train,”
“In The Wee Small Hours Of The Morning” and
“Solitude.” A
bold,
exciting program
that
also
serves as a workout for the
stereo
rig.
“THE
YOUNG
SAVAGES”—Original
Movie
Soundtrack—Columbia CL 1672
The Burt Lancaster-starred
flick
of juvenile
de-
linquency
features
a
jazz-oriented
score penned
by David Amram. Latin themes
are
also
exten-
sively used to comply with the Italian vs. Puerto
Rican gang theme of the
film. Though the
film
was not
too well
critically
received,
it’s
subject
matter
promises
good
box
office
and
resulting
disk sales.
“BILLY ROWLAND PLAYS BOOGIE WOOGIE”
—Grand Award GA 259SD
Boogie woogie in a polished, pop-acceptable form
is
enticingly
essayed by
pianist
Billy
Rowland.
Three guitarists pick up the rolling bass figures
while Rowland neatly explores each tune’s melodic
potential. Additional drums and bass are rhythmic
essentials to the whole picture. Selections include
“Rhumboogie,”
“Cow Cow
Boogie,”
“Bye
Bye
Blackbird” and “Scrub Me Mama.”
“YES
I SEE”—Bob Gibson—Elektra EKL-197
Young folk singing
talent Bob
Gibson has been
witnessing
a big following springing up among
the younger folk enthusiasts. Reason
is
his own
enthusiasm for
his work and
his
effective
direct
communication with his audiences. In this album
he
performs
a
collection
of
both
old and new
items,
several
of
his own
composition. On
sev-
eral
tracks
he
is
accompanied
by
the
Gospel
Pearls.
Selections
include
“Sprighill
Mine
Dis-
aster,” “Trouble In Mind” and “Copper Kettle.”
“BETTY
BLAKE
SINGS
IN
A
TENDER
MOOD”—Bethlehem BCP
6058
New thrush debut here. Betty Blake falls into the
Anita-Chris-June school of singing but does have
a special warmth and lyrical intuitiveness of her
own. Then, choice of material reveals thoughtful-
ness:
seven
of
the
twelve
tunes
are
by
Alec
Wilder, and there
occurs
a
beautiful match
be-
tween Miss Blake’s vocal tenderness and Wilder’s
melodic
sensitivity. Accompaniment
is by several
top notch jazz names.
Selections include
“I’ll Be
Around,”
“It’s So Peaceful In The Country” and
“While We’re Young.” Album rates exposure.
“CONTINENTAL HOST”—Raoul Maynard
and
Orch.—Warner Bros. W1424
Suave,
continental
musical
moods
essayed
in
typical
continental
fashion by
the
orkster. One
side, devoted to the French Riviera, contains such
Parisian melodies as “Under Paris Skies” and “La
Vie En Rose.” The other half
is
Italian and
in-
cludes “Arrivederci Roma” and “Come Back To
Sorrento.” Good Instrumental offering.
“AJA! PACHANGA”—Randy
Carlos
and
his
Orch.—Fiesta FLP 1317
The Randy Carlos band joins the fold for the pa-
changa fad. A solid musical organization,
it pre-
sents here
a program
that
includes
besides
pa-
changas, a couple of cha chas and mambos. Vo-
calists
Chivirico
Dauila
and
Willy
Torres
lend
an
air
of
authenticity
to
the
proceedings. Fine
disk for the Latin dance crowd.
“HOLIDAY IN BRAZIL”—Kurt Edelhagen and
his Orch.—Decca DL 74038
The
internationally popular German orkster
en-
gages a handful of original Brazilian songs and
comes up with an
inspiring
Latin
musical
pro-
gram suitable for dancing and listening. Rhythms
move
between
the
exuberant
and
sublime
and
melody is always foremost. Good package for the
burgeoning
int’l market.
“FLIPPIN’ ”—Flip Wilson—Imperial LP
9155
New comic Flip Wilson is intro’d here in his first
disk.
Unlike most new
comics
today,
Flip
is
a
story-teller spending up
to a couple of minutes
on one
episode. He
also
utilizes a
flavorful
dia-
lect
in
his
conversations.
Dubbed
in
laughter
could have been dispensed with for Flip
evokes
enough real chuckles in
his work.
“EXPLOSIVE VOCAL PERCUSSION”—Myrna
March—Strand SLS 1033
The
clever
employment
of
unusual
stereo-ized
vocal
effects
introduces
thrush
Myrna
March
Throughout the
session
both
her
voice and
the
accompanying ork sounds are subjected to tricky
effects
with
emphasis
on
echo
and
between-
speaker bounces. Some novel ideas are used.
Se-
lections
include
“Mademoiselle
De
Paris,”
“It
Was Written In The Stars” and “You Don’t Know
What Love Is.”
JAZZ
PICK
OF THE WEEK
“MEET YOU AT THE JAZZ CORNER OF THE
WORLD”—Vol. 1—Art Blakey and the Jazz Mes-
sengers—Blue Note 4054
Once more Blue Note has gone
into Birdland to
cut Art Blakey and again the result
is a superb
recording. This, volume one of a two disk series,
opens with the familiar Pee Wee Marquette
in-
troduction and then swings into a vigorous, com-
pelling performance
featuring
collaborative
en-
semble work, excellent solos by the maturing Lee
Morgan and Wayne Shorter, Bobby Timmons and
long stretches of showmanship by Blakey. Tunes
include
“ ’Round About Midnight,” “The
Breeze
And I” and “The Opener.” Top jazz disk.
“AFRO-JAWS”—Eddie “Lockjaw” Davis—River-
side RLP 9373
The complementing combination of Lockjaw Da-
vis’ earthiness and Afro-Cuban music meet head
on here. Jaws’ tenor sax
is backed up by a
six
man combo plus Ray Barretto and his Latin Per-
cussion. They perform “Tin Tin Dee,” “Star Eyes,”
a Davis title tune original and four by arranger
Gil Lopez. A pulsating,
fiery jazz date
of large
interest.
“CY COLEMAN PLAYS HIS OWN COMPOSI-
TIONS FROM WILDCAT”—Indigo GBM-502A
Composer/jazz
pianist Cy
Coleman
in
a
dual
threat
role
here, playing
his
score from
“Wild-
cat.” The
score
is
already
well enough known.
Coleman’s keyboard technique
is light and fresh,
with
an
enthusiastic
zip
that
lends
additional
sparkle to a
lively lineup of songs. Dave Bailey
(drums),
Bill
Takas
(bass)
and
Ralph
Dorsey
(conga), contribute rhythmic bounce to the effort.

NEW YORK—Roulette

has

a specialized line of juke-box singles.
The line, “Juke Box Favorites,” issued
for juke-box use only,
is a result, the
label said last week, of numerous re-
quests
at
the recent Roulette
distrib
meet for such a
line.
The

able
in

outlets,
will be sold
to
one-stops and
operators
through
the
regular network
of Roulette
distribs
in both
45’s and
33’s.
According to Joe Kolsky, the label’s
exec veep, the label went direct to
its
distribs for suggestion on the launch-
ing of the series and even accepted a
list of titles and artists from a num-
ber of distribs
to make-up
its
initial
release.
Twelve
singles
bow
the
line,
10
from
Roulette
LP’s
two
from

affiliate.

are
Pearl
Bailey, Joe Williams, Maynard Fergu-
son
Orchestra, Harry “Sweets”
Edi-
son, guitarist Johnny Smith and alto-
ist Sonny
Stitt.
All
labels and
title
strips
supplied
for
these
issues
indicate
the
album
from which
the
selections have been
made.
Promotion
head
Bud
Katzel
said
that
quantities
of
specially prepared
order
blanks
have
been
shipped
to
distribs
to
aid
in writing
orders
for
the
singles
and
a
direct
promotion
campaign aimed at one-stops and op-
erators
is planned. Katzel added that
initial distrib orders indicated an “un-
qualified
success” for the
line.

Capitol’s
Fiscal Year Sales
Show $2
Million
Increase
HOLLYWOOD—Sales of Capitol Rec-
ords,
Inc.,
for
the
fiscal
year
ended
June 30 increased to $48,364,719 from
$46,368,096
in
the
preceding
year,
according to the firm’s annual report
issued
last week.
Sales were
second highest
in com-
pany
history,
exceeded
only
by
the
$94,266,860
registered
for
the
fiscal
year ended June 30, 1959.
In
a
letter
to
shareholders,
Capi-
tol’s
president and co-founder, Glenn
E. Wallichs, revealed that the $2 mil-
lion increase in sales enabled the com-
pany
to
show
a
slight
increase
in
profits,
despite
a
highly-competitive
industry situation that has resulted in
reduced
profit
margins.
Net
income
was
$1,815,523,
equivalent
to
$3.93
per share on
the 461,409
shares
out-
standing at the end of the year. This
figure compared with a net of $1,796,-
233
($3.77 a share)
in the
fiscal year
ended June
30,
1960.
In
his
report,
Wallichs
reviewed
highlights of the company’s operations
for the
fiscal year just closed:
“Important events during the year
included the signing of new contracts
providing
continuance
for
long
peri-
ods of three artists in the best-selling
category—Nat King
Cole,
Tennessee
Ernie Ford and Judy Garland, whose
sensational performance
at
Carnegie
Hall and Capitol’s album recorded ‘on-
the-spot’
skyrocketed
her
popularity.
New artists signed by Capitol included
the singing
star, Vic Damone.
“Capitol
continued
its
Broadway
activities with
the
acquisition
of
al-
bum rights to Noel Coward’s first mu-
sical
in
recent
years,
‘Sail
Away.
:
‘Gay
Life,’
produced
by
Kermit
Bloomgarden
(‘Music
Man’),
and
‘Kwamina,’ an
Alfred DeLiagre
pro-
duction, are two other top shows
for
the
fall
season which
will be
issued
by Capitol in album form.
“ ‘The
Unsinkable
Molly
Brown,
for which
Capitol
provided
financing
as well as producing the original casf
album, proved
to be
a most
success-
ful show, and there is every indication
of
a
prolonged Broadway
run.
‘Fio-
rello,’ another Capitol album property
continues
in
its second year to be an
outstanding
attraction.
Albums
of
both shows remain on the
list of best
sellers.
“During the year a greater numbei
of Capitol singles were placed on the
best-seller
lists
of
trade magazines
Expansion of the educational and
re-
ligious
markets
continues
to
show
great
promise
for

Future

Capitol’s
children’s
record
line
at
a
competitive price.
“The
improvement
in
the
general

that
is

in the year ahead should have a bene-
ficial

on
the

and your Company is in a strong posi-
tion
to participate

concluded.
Mercury To French
Philips;
Ends Long Barclay Ties
NEW YORK—Because of the upcom-
ing Mercury-Philips
tie, Mercury and
Barclay Records have agreed
to
ter-
minate
their
12-year
representation
agreement, which
still had three-and-
half years to run, with Mercury mov-
ing over
to George
Meyerstein, head
of Societe Phonographique Philips
of
France.
The
termination
agreement, which
Barclay
felt would be
to
the mutual
advantage
of
all, thus ends an
asso-
ciation
in which Barclay represented
Mercury
in France and Mercury had
the
rights
to
Barclay
dates
for
re-
lease in the U.S.
In
addition,
Barclay and
Mercury
had
collaborated
in many
areas
re-
garding
sales
outlets throughout va-
rious countries of the world, and many
Mercury artists were cut in Barclay’s
Paris studios, including Quincy Jones,
Clebanoff,
David
Carroll
and
The
Platters.
Jones
also
served
as
musical
di-
rector
of
the
Barclay
organization,
cutting
such European
stars
as
Da-
lida, Eddie Constantine and Bob Az-
zam.
French Philips has such top attrac-
tions as Sasha
Distel, Yves Montand,
Juliet
Greco,
Michele
LeGrand
and
Patachou. These and other artists will
appear
in the U.S. under the
Philips
tag when the label bows here in Sep-
tember.
First Mercury product
to be
released in France under Philips
will
take
place
next month.
Release
and
sales plans will be debuted at a meet
of the entire Philips sales
staff at its
fall meet in Paris on August 25.
Capitol Extends Holdings
In Toshiba Musical Industries
HOLLYWOOD—Capitol
Records
has
entered
into
an
agreement
to
“sub-
stantially”
increase
its
interests
in
Toshiba Musical Industries of Tokyo,
according
to
an
announcement
last
week by Lloyd W. Dunn, the
label’s
marketing
veep.
Capitol
has
already
purchased 10%
of TMI’s outstanding
shares and has the option to increase
its holdings up
to a
total
of 49%
of
the
stock.
(Tokyo
Shibaura
Electric
Co.
(Toshiba)
owns
the
remaining
shares.
The agreement between Capitol and
Toshiba, which
handles
Capitol
Rec-
ords in Japan, calls for Capitol to pro-
vide TM with advice and counsel
re-
garding
the
record
business
and
to
contribute to the management of the
Japanese firm. Towards this end, Cap-
itol
has
designated Warren
Burken-
head,
Tokyo,
and
G.
N.
Bridge,
England, to
fill two vacancies on the
TM board of directors.
Among
specific business operations
under
immediate
consideration
by
Capitol and TM
are improvement
of
record manufacturing and expanding
sales and merchandising activities.
The
agreement
also
calls
for TM
personnel
to
visit
Capitol’s
plant,
studios and offices in the U.S.
The
agreement
was
confirmed
in
writing on June
5 by Glenn E. Wal-
lichs,
Capitol
president,
and
Motoji
Kuno,
senior
managing
director
of
TM. TM’s shareholders approved
the
deal at a general meeting in Tokyo on
July
28.
Since shortly after
its formation in
October
of
i960, TM
has
manufac-
tured and distributed Capitol disks in
Japan,
pressing
them
from
master
disks
provided
by
Capitol.
Prior
to
that, Japanese distribution and press-
ing
of
Captol
disks was handled by
TM’s
parent
firm,
Toshiba.
Under
the terms
of the agreement,
Capitol
will continue
to provide TM with
its
pressing catalog of recordings.

ALBUM REVIEWS
M)TMACKS B^iADS
“DANCING ON SUNDAY”—United Artists UAS
6146
The interest in Greek music aroused by the popu-
larity of “Never On Sunday”
is capitalized on by
the label
in this sort-of-sequel to the best-selling
soundtrack disk. The songs are by Greece’s lead-
ing composers, including “Sunday’s” Manos Had-
jidakis, and are etched with inviting color by typi-
cally
Greek
instruments.
Charming
set;
could
click.
“THE IMMORTAL VICTOR HERBERT”—Robert
Shaw
Chorale &
Orchestra—RCA
Victor LM/
LSC-2515
Schmaltzy or what have you, the melodies of Vic-
tor Herbert continue to charm—and how can any-
one
resist
these
lovely readings
of some
of the
composer’s most popular numbers! The excellent
group, including
fine solo turns, are backed by a
full
ork, with arrangements by vet musical-com-
edy
orehestrator
Robert
Russell
Bennett. Tunes
include “In Old New York,” “When You’re Away,”
“Thine
Alone,”
“Sweethearts”
and
“Ah!
Sweet
Mystery of Life.”
“RADIO’S GREAT OLD THEMES”—Frank De-
Vol and the Rainbow Strings—Columbia CL 1613
Theme songs from 36 radio programs are appro-
priately
lushly
essayed
by
the
DeVol
Strings,
evoking a wealth of memories of the sentimental
“good
old
days”
of
radio.
All
the
soap
operas
and comedy favorites are here, as well as numer-
ous others that will be remembered, among them
“Dr.
Christian,” “The
Contented
Hour,” “Amos
and
Andy,”
“Eddie
Cantor
Show,”
“Bob
Hope
Show,” “Our Gal Sunday” and “The Romance
of
Helen Trent.” Great nostalgia
set.
“MAGGIE’S THEME”
Emanuel
Vardi
and
the
Medallion Strings—Medallion ML-7527
Flick theme’s of recent vintage are read with rich
lushness by the Medallion ork. Vardi lead off with
his single outing, “Maggie’s Theme,” and follows
through vibrantly with “Goodbye Again,” “Exo-
dus,” “La Dolce Vita” and other listenable tracks.
Good stereo effects complete a pretty instrumental
picture.
"EXCITING SOUNDS OF THE SOUTH SEAS”
—Leo Diamond,
His Harmonica
and
Orch.—Re-
prise R 6002
The
romantic
aura
of
Island
enchantment
is
flavorfully expressed through the medium of Leo
Diamond’s
virtuoso harmonica
stylings.
In
addi-
tion
there
are
the
usual
assortment
of
steel
guitars and
other
gentle rhythm and
string
in-
struments
to
enhance
the
mood. Tunes
are
the
familiar “Beyond the Reef,” “Pagan Love Song,”
“Now
Is
the
Hour”
and
“Far Away
Places.”
Enticing mood
setter.
“BAWDY
BARRACKS
BALLADS”—Vol.
2—
The Four Sergeants—ABC-Paramount ABC-381
The
lusty,
uncensored Four
Sergeants
are back
with
another volume
of bawdy songs
to
titilate
the senses. This time out they do suggestive jus-
tice
to
such
ribald gems
as “No Hips At
All,”
“How the Money Rolls In,” “She Had To Go And
Lose
It At The Astor” and
nine
others.
They’ll
get no air play—but plenty of home play!
“SONGS
I WISH
I HAD PLAYED
.
.
. THE
FIRST TIME AROUND”—Sammy Kaye and his
Orch.—Decca DL 74154
The sweet swaying rhythms of the Sammy Kaye
band embrace a tuneful dozen evergreens that are
associated with famed names
of the
past. They
include “My Reverie,”
“I’ll Never Smile Again,”
“I Understand” and “Got A Date With an Angel.”
They’re essayed in the sentimental Kaye manner,
with
vocals by Ray
Michaels, Laura
Leslie and
the Kaydets.
BIBULOUS
SONGS Of THE
30S
“C’EST MAGNIFIQUE”—Dance Time
In
Paris
With Chauncey
Gray
and
His
Orch.—Riverside
RLP 9705
Continental
flavored dance music
in the familiar
society-beat
style
is
offered
here by the
sweet-
sounding Chauncey Gray
band.
Fourteen
selec-
tions
in
all,
including
the
more
familiar
“La
Seine,” “La Vie en Rose,” “April In Portugal” and
“Lar Mer.” Enjoyable adult dance fare.
“FABULOUS SONGS OF THE
30’s”—Charlie
McKenzie and his Twin Piano—Dot DLP 3377
A
pleasing
listening/dancing package
is
offered
by McKenzie’s
pianistic
travels. At an
easy,
re-
laxed pace he surveys the 30’s thru such tunes as
“September In the Rain,” “Body And
Soul,” “It’s
Only A Paper Moon,” “Time On My Hands” and
nine
others. Good
songs,
fine technique,
saleable
package.
JAZZ
PICK
OF THE WEEK
“GIL EVANS AND
HIS ORCHESTRA”—Fea-
turing Budd Johnson & John Cole—Pacific Jazz
PJ-28
One
of
the
more
adventurous
arrangers
today,
Evans
fills
his
charts
with imagination and
in-
dividuality. Here, fronting a big band, he cleverly
unfolds
new
looks
at
five
jazz
standards,
one
original and Tommy Wolf’s
“Ballad
of
the
Sad
Young Men.” Solo
spotlight
is on Budd Johnson
(tenor,
clarinet), John
Coles
(trumpet), Jimmy
Cleveland
(trombone)
and
Steve Lacy
(soprano
sax),
an
odd
combination
that
also
indicates
Evans’ original thinking. A very modern big band
set with enormous appeal.
“EXPOOBIDENT”—Lee
Morgan—Vee
Jay
LP
3015
The warm, intelligently lyrical style of Lee Mor-
gan
continues
to
evoke more
public
awareness.
In
this
outing
he’s
teamed
with
Cliff
Jordan
(tenor)
and Art Blakey
(drums) among
others,
in performances of seven mixed-origin tunes that
allow Morgan freedom
in expressing several
dif-
ferent
moods.
There’s
the
bristling
“Fire”
(by
Wayne Shorter), the sensitive “Easy Living,” and
the “down home”
“Lost
and
Found”
(by
Cliff
Jordan). Versatile display of talent.
carrot- yuio-
fiterwi jazz- isa hr inarrfcsi soiai
“DOIN’ ALLRIGHT”—Dexter Gordon—Blue Note
4077
Influential
jazz
style-setter
of
the
40’s,
Dexter
Gordon returns to the scene exhibiting again
his
big
fat
tone,
his relaxed yet
intensely
inspiring
manner. Surrounded by sympathetic support from
Blue Note regulars Freddie Hubbard, Horace Par-
ian,
George
Tucker
and
A1
Harewood,
Gordon
plays
excellently here and with
a knowledge
of
what’s been happening the years
of
his
absence.
It’s a
virile, mature jazz date that indicates Gor-
don’s back
in top form again.
“MARTIAL SOLAL”—Capitol ST 10261
Disk debut of Parisian jazz pianist Martial Sola!.
Side one
is the
trio
set up with
Solal rendering
five originals
in a quick, precise Oscar Peterson-
like manner.
Side two he
solos on
six standards
drawing
at
times
on
Tatumesque
figures.
To
quote,
he’s got rhythm,
lots of
it, and
a
definite
view towards jazz that maintains
his playing at
a
consistent
level. A
proficient,
talented
new-
comer to jazz piano ranks.
WAGNER:
“The
Flying
Dutchman”—George
London,
Leonie Rysanek, Giorgio Tozzi, Richard
Lewis,
Rosalind
Elias, Karl
Liebl, Antal Dorati
conducting
the
Orch. and
Chorus
of
the
Royal
Opera House, Convent Garden—RCA Victor LSC-
6156
Only
the
third
complete “Flying Dutchman”
in
the catalog,
it
is the
first in stereo and features
the most distinguished “names” of the three. The
broad, sweeping vistas of the opera come to full
realization in stereo and Dorati’s experience (and
huge success)
in stereo recording enables him to
take
full advantage
of the medium.
CLASSICAL PICK OF THE WEEK

######## 1961-08-26 p29  [star\s*bright]
^b|<^USTRAUA>
Jim Sutton, general sales manager of Australian Record Company,
advises
that ARC
will
launch
the
United
Artists
label
right
across
the
nation
on
September
1. The launching
will
be accompanied by
special
trade
functions
in each State towards the end of August to review the premiere release. The
initial release—all Ultra-Audio albums in both mono and stereo will consist of
“Cozy” by Steve Lawrence and Eydie Gorme; “Golden Piano Hits” with Fer-
rante and Teicher; “Mr. Percussion” by Terry Snyder and “Echoing Voices
and Trombones, Guitars Woodwinds and Bongos” by A1 Caiola. At
first, ARC
planned to release the “Sound
Series” in stereo only but as Jim pointed
out,
this material has
such tremendous
potential
airplay-wise,
it was
decided
to
make dual mono and stereo releases. All United Artists albums
will
retail
at
52/6 in line with ARC’s Coronet and Warner Bros, albums. The Sydney launch-
ing of the UA label will take place on board the Royal Dutch Mails liner “Johan
van Oldenbarnevelt,” which will be moored at Sydney’s Circular Quay on Au-
gust
24. The UA disks
will be premiered before
press,
radio, TV and
retail
bodies at a cocktail party on board
the
ship and
after
a
buffet
dinner,
the
United Artists film “Goodbye Again,” starring Ingrid Bergman,
will be
pre-
viewed in the
ship’s theatrette.
The
soundtrack album from “Goodbye Again”
will
be
ready
for
release
as soon as a film date is set for Australia and ARC also has the Ferrante and
Teicher
hit single
of the
film’s theme which
it
will present—with
a
special
souvenir label—to each guest at the launching functions. All in
all, Jim Sutton
and the ARC
staff
in each State are
set
to
give the UA
label
a
first-class
introduction to the Australian scene.
Roy Atkinson,
public
relations
officer with
Festival
Records,
has
advised
Cash Box of some important moves in the Festival group. Festival announced
that Johnny O’Keefe—one of Australia’s top personalities in the recording, TV
and entertainment world—has just signed two new contracts with their organ-
ization. The contracts are for a period of five years and encompass O’Keefe’s
talents
as both a recording
artist and producer and
in
particular related
to
the release of O’Keefe’s
efforts through
Festival’s Leedon
label. Johnny has
just finished recording a top production ballad entitled “I’m Counting On You”
c/w “Right Now,”
his
first
actual
recording
for more
than
twelve
months.
The Festival organization
is hoping for big things with this disk which
is due
for national release
shortly.
Elaine McKenna, winner of last year’s TV Logie Award as “Australia’s most
popular female singer on television,” left Australia on August 20 for a lengthy
overseas
visit which will take her
to the United
States, where she plans
to
spend quite a deal of time.
On its Columbia label, EMI released the new single by England’s
Cliff Rich-
ard, “A Girl Like You” c/w “Now’s The Time To Fall In Love.” Cliff Richard
is scheduled to tour Australia soon and as a result of a string of hit singles
it should be
a
successful
venture.
It
is believed that music publishers
J. Albert & Son Pty. Ltd. created pub-
lishing history in this country by issuing a reprint of “Tammy” with a four-
color title page featuring Elaine McKenna. It is understood that this is the first
time that a four-color title page has been produced in sheet copy form for an
individual title
in Australia. “Tammy”
is the subject of a big revival
in
this
country with new disks by Noeline Batley on
Festival and
Elaine McKenna
on W&G.
Radio
Corporation,
which
has
the
Mercury
catalog
for
this
area,
just
launched a
series
of
low-priced
singles
on
the Wing
label
retailing
at
6/9
(around 75 cents)
as against the regular
singles price
of
10/.
(approx.
$1).
Among the artists featured in the
first release of the low-priced Wing singles
are Damita Jo, Jivin’ Gene, The Big Bopper and The Derbys.
The Belinda Music boys are rolling along
in fine style with a batch of hits
on its slate including “I’m Gonna Knock On Your Door,” “Runaway” and “Hats
Off To Larry” and its subsid Aaron Schroeder Music (Australia)
Pty. Ltd. has
“Hello Mary Lou” going great guns and another Belinda
associate,
Trinity
Music, is making an all-out drive on “Come September” Bobby Darin’s instru-
mental single.
Pye Records made a rush-release of “That’s What Girls Are Made For” by
The Spinners. This one
is showing out strongly on the Cash Box Top 100 and
the Pye boys
are hoping for
similar
success
here. Included
in
other newies
released by Pye are “Bobby” by Neil
Scott, which
is enjoying current chart
ratings in the US; “Triangle” by Jamie Grant; “Daddy’s Home” by Shep and

Leeds Music created quite an amount of interest in their new songs as a re-
sult
of a telegram

“You’re Driving Me Mad” but don’t worry
“I

Time” my “Sweet Dreams” of you
all
will
drive away the “Big Cold Wind”

in the Leeds group. “You’re Driving Me Mad”
is

by Judy Stone on Festival;
“I
Still Love You All”
is Kenny Ball’s Pye single
published by Leeds;
“In Time”

publication
recorded by

Lawrence; “Sweet Dreams” is a Leeds item recorded by Col Joye for Festival

is another Pincus-Gil song soon to be released by
Pat Boone and
of course
“Starlight,
Starbright”
is
Linda
Scott’s new chart
item—published by Dominion Music. It would seem that Jack Argent
is set for
success over the next few weeks.
Don Gibson’s RCA single of “Sea Of Heartbreak” is getting away to a good
start here,
it’s already shaping
like a
strong challenger
for the No.
1
spot
and if the present action continues it will be Don’s biggest hit in this country.

######## 1961-08-26 p32  [pacific\s*jazz]
There should be more words
of praise for a young record company which
is building very seriously and successfully in this industry. Ri-Fi Records, the
house managed by Mr. Ansoldi which has the sensational voice of Cocki Maz-
zetti. The most recent hit product of this songstress features the
first version
sung of the old “Cumparsita” arranged by Maestro Soffici, with lyrics by Cala-
brese (known here as one of our best lyrics-writer after he wrote the texts of
“Arrivederci’ 'and “II Nostro Concerto”). Just a short while before, Cocki Maz-
zetti cut a hit disk with “Cha Cha Cha Pepito,” already played a
lot in our
juke boxes and, perhaps, to become even more popular.
“Pera Matura” (Ripe Pear)
is the
latest tune by Pino Donaggio who
also
recorded
it. His “Come Sinfonia” (backed by “Cane Di Stoffa”) which he pre-
sented
first on the stage of San Reno, and
also
his “Tu
Sai”
(You Know),
are selling well.
Italy had only one disk jockey, and now he has
left
his job
at our
radio
station
for new
duties
at the
second
channel
of
our TV
set-up
just
being-
opened. Vittorio Zivelli recently stopped broadcasting a new record each day
on his show “Discobolo,” on the
air daily early in the afternoon and
listened
to by a very large audience of teenagers. Vittorio
started his daily broadcast
nine years ago, always revealing an excellent “good taste” in music. His show
will be replaced daily by a new program
titled
“II
Disco Del
Giorno”
(The
Record Of The Day) which, instead of being handled by a single man, will be
managed by an anonymous committee with the help of labels which will peri-
odically submit
to
the committee a
certain number
of new recordings from
which will be selected those to be broadcast.
At the end of July, the fourth international festival of light music at Pesaro
took place, bringing to our audience a new song penned by Galassini and Di
Marco and
interpreted by Jolando
Rossin
(Carisch)
and by
Luciano
Tajoli
(Juke Box), who stated that rarely had he had the pleasure, over his very long
career, of finding a tune so
fine. The song
is titled “Eclissi” and won the
first
prize. Besides Italy, eight other foreign countries took place
in
this competi-
tion:
Argentina,
France, Germany,
Iran,
Yugoslavia,
Holland,
Sweden
and
Switzerland. The
second
prize was won by
Yugoslavia with
the song “Non
Sciupate L’Amore” performed by Dragan Tokovic and,
in an
Italian
version,
by Nilla Pizzi (Titanus). The third place prize went to Argentina, which
sent
the song “Voy Caminando.” Hungary was
to
participate
in
the
festival
but,
unfortunately, the consul’s ok came too
late and consequently the Hungarian
representative
had
not
sufficient
time
to
reach
Pesaro. As
for
Belgium,
it
sent a song and a singer, Gaby Varny, but Nunzio Gallo, who had to perform
the Italian version of the tune at the
last moment gave
it up because he was
not well and since no other Italian singer wanted to attempt to learn the tune
in a few hours, Belgium preferred to withdraw. France presented
a tune by
Georges Moustaki, the same author of world-wide known “Milord.” This new
Moustaki composition
is
titled “Le Jugement Dernier” and was
liked by the
audience.
Frank Sinatra, whose trip to Italy was expected very shortly, will not come
here. His latest LP released in Italy by V.C.M.
is “Sinatra’s All The Way.”
Percy Faith told us, on his short stay in Milan, that his success here last year
of his “Theme From A Summer Place” was really a pleasant surprise which
he did not expect from Italy.
Germano
Ruscitto,
formerly
with
Bluebell,
wrote
to
us
announcing
that
Interdisc has opened its independent office in Italy, of which he is the manager.
Interdisc Italiana has settled
in Milan Via
Settala 20—tel. 22
13 29 and han-
dles
the
following record
lines:
Riverside; Good Time
Jazz;
Contemporary;
World Pacific; Jazz Land; Hi Fi; and Gene Norman. Some of their labels
will
be distributed across Italy by Bluebell, some by Ricordi and some by whole-
sale dealer KARIM of Genova.

Three hundred and

ALBUM REVIEWS
‘•THE NEW
‘I LOVE PARIS’ ’’—Michel Legrand
and his Orch.—Columbia CL 1640
Michel Legrand’s
first
“I Love
Paris” LP
intro-
duced him to American disk audiences and resulted
in one of the label’s biggest hit sets. The original
songs have been
retained,
as have many
of
the
original
arrangements,
but now
newly-recorded
in stereo a new sales vista
is open for
it. A tiib-
ute to the Legrand touch is that the modernity he
achieved in the first set
is just as up to date now
with just some minor changes for
stereo’s
sake.
Among the tunes are “I Love Paris,” “Under The
Bridges Of Paris,” “La Vie En Rose” and “The
Last Time
I Saw Paris.”
“GUITAR LAMENT”—A1 Viola—World
Pacific
WP-1408
A
lot of of artistry and care has gone
into
the
production
of this album.
Viola, basically
a pop
guitarist,
takes
on
a new
look
as
he
combines
influences
from
classical,
flamenco
and
jazz
in
restyled
interpretations
of
twelve
pop
songs
played on the simple but eloquent classical guitar.
Intriguing
listening
as
Viola
performs
“Lover
Man,” “Black Coffee” and “End Of A Love Af-
fair,” among others.
“THE MAGIC ISLANDS REVISITED” — Axel
Stordahl and
his
Orch.
and
Chorus—Decca DL
79096
A “return to paradise” musical offering in which
Stordahl gathers up his ork, the Gene Rains chor-
isters, the seagulls and tastefully essays a dozen
Island-influenced
tunes. A
10-page
colorful
pic-
ture panorama
of Hawaiian
sights
accompanies
the disk in booklet form.
Selections include “Re-
turn To
Paradise,” “The Hukilau
Song,” “Fare-
well” and “Forevermore.”
“GUS BIVONA DEALS IN MILLIONS”—War-
ner Bros. W 1361
Echoes
of
the Swing Era
here
as
Gus
Bivona
twists
his way
through
line-up
of
the
period’s
big
hits
in the
original
styles
of
their
creators.
Included
are Woody
Herman’s
“Woodchopper’s
Ball,” Artie
Shaw’s “Summit Ridge
Drive,” Ba-
sie’s
“One
O’clock
Jump”
and
Glenn
Miller’s
“Tuxedo Junction.”
“BABES
IN TOYLAND”—Narrated
by
Little
Boy Blue—Disneyland ST-3913
Also preceding the forthcoming soundtrack LP
is
this “storyteller” of the Disney adaptation of the
Victor Herbert musical, which contains the same
15 selections as the
$1.98
set but with an
addi-
tional narration
of the story
line by
Little Boy
Blue (Ginny Tyler). An 11-page color booklet
is
bound
into
the
book-fold
jacket.
Musical
per-
formances
are
excellent
and
the
narration
has
tremendous kiddie appeal.
“PROFESSOR LUDWIG VON DRAKE” — Dis-
neyland DQ-1222
New Walt
Disney
character.
Professor Ludwig
von
Drake,
star
of
the NBC-TV’er “Wonderful
World Of Color,” is introduced on disks in
all his
comical
self-esteem.
Children
should
delight
in
his vaudevillian German accent and
the manner
in which he imitates Elvis and others. Good
dis-
play cover.

“THE
FIRST
COUNTRY
COLLECTION
OF
WARREN SMITH”—Liberty LST 7199
Fast
rising
young newcomer
to
country
music
ranks,
Warren
Smith
bows
on
his
first
album
for the
label.
In
it he performs
his two big
hits,
“I
Don’t
Believe
I’ll
Fall
In
Love
Today”
and
“Odds And Ends,” and
lends a
talented voice
to
the recreation
of several country items of recent
vintage, including “Foolin’ Around,” “Kissing My
Pillow,” “Pick Me Up On Your Way Down” and
“I
Fall To
Pieces.”
Should
get
a
solid country
field reception.
“DONALD BYRD AT THE HALF NOTE CAFE”
—Volume
1—Blue Note 4060
The relaxed, superbly sympathetic atmosphere of
NY’s Half Note Cafe has resulted in several out-
standing location recordings. Here, Blue Note has
taken
its equipment into the spot for a two-vol-
ume session with the newly-formed Donald Byrd
group and there’s no doubt as
to the consistency
of the outcome. Byrd’s sweetly surging trumpet
work is supported by Pepper Adams, Duke Pear-
son, Laymon Jackson and Lex Humphries
in a
spirited exhibition of jazz fireworks.
Since there
are
only four
cuts
there
is
plenty
of room
for
each to stretch out.
“A DATE WITH THE MASTERSOUNDS”—Fan-
tasy 3316
Disbanded
except
for
Fantasy
LP
dates,
the
Mastersounds
still maintain the high
level
of in-
dividuality
that
first marked
their
ascendancy
Here, Buddy Montgomery
is back on v'bes
(he’s
been concentrating on piano with the Montgom-
ery Brothers)
and
he’s a delight
of
tasteful
in-
genuity, leading the group through
intelligently
constructed readings
of “Whisper Not,” “Surrev
With The Fringe On Top,” “Noreen’s Nocturne”
and five others.
“FREEDOM SOUND”—The Jazz Crusaders—Pa-
cific Jazz PJ-27
The
Jazz
Crusaders
are
four young men from
Houston who through years
of playing together
have developed
into
a
cohesive, purposeful
jazz
unit. On their debut disk there
is a bristling en-
thusiasm that propels them headlong into a stim-
ulating display of jazz knowledge. Selections, ex-
cept for the “Theme From Exodus,” are
all orig-
inals by grou]) members. Solid jazz listening here.
“GERRY MULLIGAN WITH CHET BAKER”—
GNP-56
No liner notes to reveal circumstances of this date
but
it
is apparent that
it was made some time
ago. Nonetheless, Mulligan and Baker work
col-
laboratively here in a relaxed, easy-going manner
and provide substantial interest for even the cas-
ual
jazz
fan. The
addition
of Buddy DeFranco
and the Herman McCoy Swing Choir on side two
gives a “pop” sheen to the proceedings and makes
it even more accessible to non-jazz buyers. Pleas-
ant listening package.
CLASSICAL
RAVEL: Concerto in D for the Left Hand; PRO-
KOFIEV:
Concerto #3
in
C—John
Browning,
piano,
Erich
Leinsdorf
conducting
the
Philhar-
monica Orchestra—Capitol SP 8545
The young Browning continues
to grow rapidly
into one of our leading virtuosos. Here, the
intri-
cate Ravel concerto seems to present no obstacles
to Browning and he disposes of
it with dash and
spirit yet with the utmost artistic integrity. An-
other
virtuoso
work,
Prokofiev’s
3rd
concerto,
also quickly succumbs to the young pianist’s
at-
tack. A major accomplishment for the artist.

“WORKS FOR CHAMBER ORCHESTRA”-^on.
ducted by Bruno Maderna and Luciano Berio —
Time S/8002
Three young Italian composers who are working
in the new electronic music idiom are represented
in
Time’s
latest
classical
venture. The
English
Chamber
ork
under
Bruno
Maderna’s
direction
performs
the
conductor’s
“Serenata
_ #2”
and
Luigi Nono’s “Polifonica-Monodia-Ritmica”; Berio
conducts
an ensemble
in
his own
“Differences.”
Earl Brown has done a highly commendable
re-

Mew Capitol Ed. Guide
HOLLYWOOD — The
1961-62 edition
of Capitol’s Educational Music Guide,
a 72-page booklet containing 15
arti-
cles by some of the nation’s foremost
musicians
and
music
educators,
is
being readied for publication on Sept.
1 .
In addition to articles covering the
entire
spectrum
of
music
education,
the new guide carries complete, illus-
trated descriptions and evaluations of
more than 300 Capitol and Angel
al-
bums especially selected for use in all
areas of musical and audio-visual in-
struction. The albums were
screened
and
selected
by
a
special
panel
of
music educators from the more than
2,000 LP’s
in the Capitol and Angel
catalogs.
The
guide
covers
15
specific
fields
of music
and
demonstrates how
re-
cordings may be integrated into vari-
ous general and musical curricula.
According to Art Duncan,
director
of Market Development for CRDC and
head
of
the
educational
department,
Capitol’s share of the expanding edu-
cational market is steadily increasing.
Many
dealers,
Duncan
said,
report
that the educational market amounts
to from 5 to 30 per cent of their total
sales volume. In some instances, Dun-
can
reported,
the
Capitol-Angel
vol-
ume forms as much as 70% of dealer’s
educational sales.

Nat Goodman Joins Sunset
In Exec Post; Brings Talent
NEW YORK-Nat Goodman has been
named vice president and general
manager of Sunset Enterprises, the
personal management firm. Goodman
will helm Sunset and operate out of
the firm's New York and Los Angeles
office with Clyde Otis, founder of the
firm, and arranger Belford Hendricks.
By joining Sunset, Goodman, for-
mer west coast A&R rep for Mercury
Records, also merges the talent in his
own management stable under the
Sunset banner. Goodman brings with
him
the
Diamonds,
the
Smothers
Brothers, the Parmours and Jay Epae.
Sunset already has Brook Benton and
Timi Yuro.
Goodman said that we will continue
the type of operation Sunset was set
up as, not only to manage the talent
but to arrange and produce all their
sessions and to build new talent
through
extensive
exploitation and
promotion. He also indicated that sev-
eral "big names" are being negotiated
for the Sunset stable.
Starday Sets German Pubbery,
Foreign Releases; Extends Sale
NASHVILLE-Martin Haerle,
sales
and production exec at Starday Rec-
ords, returned recently from a trip to
Germany, France
and
Switzerland
where he negotiated the forming of a
Starday publishing company in Ham-
burg, Germany and arranged for the
release of Starday product in Ger-
many, France, Holland and Sweden.
Haerle also met with execs of Top
Rank, which distributes Starday in
Europe, and conferred with Starday
publishing affiliates in Europe.
Starday topper Don Pierce also dis-
closed that the firm's "Country Music
Spectacular" package goods sale re-
ceived such an overwhelming response
that production had been backed up.
Therefore, the sale has been extended
to a Sept. 15 expiration date.
New Starday distributor in Los An-
geles is Jack Frost's new Sunset Sales
operation.
Command Unveils 35mm Film Recording;
Releases "Stereo 35" LP
NEW YORK-After months of engi-
neering effort and at a cost in excess
of $300,000, Command Records last
week issued its initial "Stereo 36" al-
bum, the first in a series of Command
disks recorded on 35mm film and
hailed by the company as the greatest
advance in the field of stereo in re-
cent years.
The first release, called "Stereo 35
MM," features Enoch Light and a 60
piece orchestra playing a dozen stand-
ards arranged by Lew Davies. It was
recorded at Carnegie Hall.
Enoch Light, head of Command, in-
troduced his new line at a press con-
ference and demonstration in Studio
B of the Great Northern Hotel.
In presenting plans for the "Stereo
35" line Light explained the advan-
tages he and his engineers discovered
in 35mm film over the tapes he and
other companies had been using. In
attempting to achieve a still better
sound in the recording of large or-
chestras, it was found that even the
most advanced tape techniques were
faced with two mechanical limitations
which create minor distortions-hiss
and flutter. Light claims that the tight
holding of the film by sprockets elimi-
nated flutter and the extra width of
the film eliminated hiss, adding up
to a more faithful recorded sound
and the complete elimination of any
3rd Series Of Victor
Distrib Advisory Meets
NEW YORK-RCA Victor Records
last week announced the third series
of Distributor Advisory Council meet-
ings to be held during late September
and early October in Dallas, Pitts-
burgh, Newark and Seattle. Directing
the meetings will be David Finn, Vic-
tor's manager of record distributor
relations, and in attendance will be
the regional delegates elected to rep-
resent all Victor distributors at these
informal sessions.
The first meetings of the Councils
were in March, 1961; followed by a
second series in June. The location of
the meetings change with each new
schedule to permit different distribu-
tors to act as regional hosts. Reports
of all regional meetings are later
made available to every distributor.
The meetings are designed as an
opportunity in which mutual prob-
lems and programs can be studied
and discussed in order to create bet-
ter relations and more profitable op-
erations for the benefit of dealers as
well as the distributors and the manu-
facturer. J. Y. Burgess, Jr., division
vice-president, Commercial Sales, has
described the meetings as a "forward
look which enables all of us to as-
sume a more practical approach on
the planning of new product and mer-
chandising programs."
ASCAP To Fete
Int'l Composer Group
NEW YORK-Stanley Adams, presi-
dent of ASCAP announced last week
that ASCAP will hold a reception on
Tuesday, September 5, at the Low
Library Rotunda, Columbia Univer-
sity, from 4 to 6 PM, in honor of the
International
Musicological
Society.
Members of the ASCAP board of di-
rectors, as well as composer mem-
bers as William Bergsma and Nicolas
Slonimsky, will be among the famous
composers of the Society who will act
as hosts.
The Eighth Congress of the Inter-
national
Musicological
Society
will
convene in New York City from Sep-
tember 5 to 11. Dr. Friedrich Blume
of Germany is the President of the In-
ternational Musicological Society.
This year will mark the twenty-
seventh annual meeting of the Ameri-
can Musicological Society, of which
Professor Donald J. Grout of Cornell
University is President.

Also, the cost of recording on film,
reportedly ten times that of recording
on tape, presented a monetary prob-
lem. But Light now feels that the
overall results achieved through many
tests and the first recording will reap
benefits to overcome the additional ex-
pense involved.
Other advantages found in 35mm
film were: The thickness of the film
reduced the possibility of contamina-
tion by print -through; excellent fre-
quency response assured by the fast
speed -18 ips-the film travels; the
wider track allows for maximum sepa-
ration and a wider range of dynamics
without
distortion;
greater
tensile
strength and sprocket drive eliminates
pitch change due to tape stretch;
signal to noise ratio is far superior.
A special dealer preview hearing of
yet unreleased Command albums on
35mm film is set for the Starlight
Roof of the Waldorf Astoria Hotel,
Sept. 6. At this time Light will unveil
the first Command classical record-
ings on film.

Webb Pierce Renews
Decca Pact
NEW YORK-Following an uninter-
rupted decade as a consistent top -
selling Decca recording artist, Webb
Pierce has signed a new exclusive
long-term contract with the label, ac-
cording
to an announcement from
executive vice-president, Leonard W.
Schneider.
Pierce, who first joined the Decca
roster in March 1951, catapaulted to
fame on the heels of such hits as
"There Stands The Glass," "In The
Jailhouse Now," "Why Baby Why,"
"More And More," "I Ain't Never"
and "Lovers Leap." Pierce has toured
coast -to -coast
in
personal
appear-
ances and frequently is featured on
leading television shows.
Currently, Webb is represented on
record with a new single, "How Do
You Talk To A Baby" coupled with
"Walking The Streets." His latest al-
bum is "Fallen Angel."
In addition to his success as a re-
cording artist,
Pierce
is
a
prolific
song writer with many hits
to
his
credit, recorded both personally and
by other leading artists.
Pierce is under the direction of the
Jim Denny Artist Bureau.

weeks
in

ENGLAND
John Leyton this week becomes the third successive British artiste to claim
the No. 1 slot in the British charts. The song, "Johnny Remember Me," was
written by Geoffrey Goddard who is under contract to the publishers Southern
Music and recorded by independent A & R Manager Joe Meek for release on
the Top Rank label. Within three weeks of release the waxing won a Silver
Disk for sales exceeding a quarter million. In fact British artistes John Leyton
(Top Rank), Helen Shapiro (Columbia), Eden Kane (Decca), Shirley Bassey
(Columbia), Billy Fury (Decca) and Petula Clark (Pye) this week occupy the
first 6 places in the British charts and with Cliff Richard's "A Girl Like You,"
Britain claims 7 out of the top 10 places.
Eden Kane's second disk for Decca, "Get Lost," is out this week. Specially
written for him in the hully-gully idiom by Johnny Worth (who wrote his chart
topper "Well I Ask You"), it again has the backing of Johnny Keating and his
orchestra. With 8 TV shows and 3 broadcasts lined up Kane will give the disk
maximum exploitation. David Platz of Essex Music, who publishes both num-
bers, informs us that "Well I Ask You" is fast becoming an international hit
with 2 recordings in Germany, 3 in Scandinavia and 3 in the United States in-
cluding one by Kay Starr on Capitol.
Another bright star from Decca, Mark Wynter, has gathered his biggest ad-
vance to date with his latest waxing "Girl For Ev'ry Day" published by Marlyn
Music. Following his successful Australian tour earlier this year Mark returns
"Down Under" in September for 6 weeks of TV, stage and broadcasting en-
gagements.
Decca confidently expects a double sided hit with the latest Elvis Presley
disk released on the RCA label. Although "Wild In The Country" by A & R
men Hugo & Luigi, which Presley sings in the film of the same title, is the
"A" side maybe, as in the States, the rocking flip side "I Feel So Bad" will
rove the biggest seller.
Neil Gallaghan, vice president of Canadian American Records, in London with
the label's star Linda Scott, impressed by the warm reception accorded her by
the British Press. Also delighted to see her latest L.P. "Starlight Starbright"
enter the Cash Box Best Selling Album charts. Linda made a great impact with
her cabaret act at the dinner hosted by E.M.I. Records at the close of their
annual sales conference where she appeared with Matt Monro and Danny Wil-
liams. Paul Anka and manager, Irving Feld, were also present.
R. N. White, general marketing manager for EMI Records, reports that this
year's annual sales conference has been the most successful to date. Highlight
of the event, attended by company executives and the complete sales force,
was the presentation of releases for the coming season, with recorded messages
from many EMI stars including Nat King Cole, Tennessee Ernie Ford, the
Four Freshmen, etc. Innovation for the autumn is the introduction of colour
sleeves for certain of the single jazz releases in the famous Landsdowne Jazz
Series retailing at 7/3d. ($1) against the usual 6/9d. (940).
Visitor to the Cash Box office this week Ron Kass, controller of the Interdisc
European Organisation, here for conferences with Ed Michel, recently appointed
director to the London office, concerning expansion plans for the fall season.
Kass has now left for Paris where he will attend the Vee-Jay Records Euro-
pean Distributors Convention. Interdisc is currently in the British Jazz charts
with two entries from Riverside by Cannonball Adderley "Them Dirty Blues"
and "At The Lighthouse." Leading factors, Thompson Diamond & Butcher
have recently been appointed to the Interdisc Distribution network for all lines
in the U.K.
Lee Pincus, Vice President of Gil -Pincus Publishing Co. New York, has
arrived in London to take over the company's operation in this country and to
coordinate the activities of the Pincus Associated companies on the continent.
Lee gets off to a good start with the current Stateside hit "Big Cold Wind" by
Pat Boone released here on September 22nd on London.
Apologies to Bill Ward of publishers Lawrence Wright who points out that
their best selling "Theme From The Apartment" was omitted from the list
in the Anniversary Issue of British copyrights to enter the American charts
this year. In fact "Theme From The Apartment" by British composer Charles
(Dream of Olwen) Williams entered Cash Box Top 100 charts on July 9th 1960
and stayed there for exactly six months climbing as high as No. 9 and was No. 1
in the British Best Selling Sheet Music lists for many weeks. Wright is cur-
rently in the British Top Twenty with "That's My Home" by Acker Bilk on
Columbia.
Following an agreement between United Artists America and EMI Records
London, disks by top British vocalist Shirley Bassey will be released in the
States on the U.A. label. First single release comprises her British hits "Reach
For The Stars" and "You'll Never Know" as well as her L.P. "Shirley." Sep-
tember 13th is the date set for Shirley's cabaret opening at The Persian Room,
New York.
50 minutes after telerecording "The Anka Show" for Granada TV, Paul Anka
and his Manager, Irving Feld, flew to Paris where shooting starts on Paul's
latest film. Before leaving they announced plans for bringing Clarence Henry
and Duane Eddy here for a duel package tour in November.
Sammy Davis Jr. opened this week his 7 -week season for Bernard Delfont at
The Prince of Wales Theatre playing to capacity houses. Sammy is seeing a
lot of Britain's ace song and show writer Lionel Bart who plans to write a
musical for him. This will not be until 1962 as Bart is busy putting the finish-
ing touches to his next show, "Blitz," scheduled for production next Spring.
Following their recent agreement with Seeco Records, Ceneral Record Dis-
tributors, September releases include LPs by La Plata Sextet (Seeco), Bimbi
and his Trio Oriental and Pupi Campo and his Orchestra (Tropical). C.R.D.
3
also has some impressive releases from Bluenote, 77 and Folklore Records for
whom they have sole distribution rights and from Riverside, Harlequin, Pres-
tige, Alpha-Rhythmn and Ember labels.

Wedding bells this month for Decca Promotion Manager Tony Hall who mar-
ries Mafalda Hunter. Having recently left Audio Enterprise Ltd. where she
worked on the promotion of Eden Kane's "Well I Ask You," Mafalda Hunter
has now set up her own P.R.O. office handling individual American artistes and
records.
A new trade group, the Mike Cotton Jazzmen, formed in February this year,
make their debut disk on the Columbia label with "Senora" coupled with
"Colonel's Tune" written by Johnny Dankworth. Johnny also has a new disk
out this week "Avengers Theme" from the TV Series.
Two current Stateside hits from Cash Box Top 100 released here on the
Mercury label -this week: "I'll Never Smile Again" by The Platters and "I'll Be
There" by Da mita Jo.
Gene Vincent has abandoned his current national tour owing to ill health.
Following a complete breakdown he has returned to America for a prolonged
rest. His latest single "I'm, Going Home," is released this week on Capitol.

“WONDERLAND OF SOUND”—The New Andre
Kostelanetz—Columbia CL 1657
For years a leader in the mood
field, Andre Kos-
telanetz
does a Welk turn
here—going with the
modern sound for this instrumental date. There’s
still plenty of meat here for the moodists but the
beat has been strengthened and the arrangements
fortified with modern day
cleverness. The “new
look” could mean
a wealth
of new and younger
admirers.
Selections
include
“Wonderland
By
Night,”
“Are
You
Lonesome
Tonight?”,
“Un-
chained Melody” and
“It’s Not For Me To Say.”

JAZZ PICKS OF THE WEEK
“THE JAZZTET AND JOHN LEWIS”—Argo
LP 684
Improbable as it may at first seem it really makes
musical sense for John Lewis to write an
entire
album for the Jazztet. Art Farmer’s and Benny
Golson’s group
has
since
its
inception
trod
the
line
between
free-wheeling
blowing
and
com-
pletely written
out

al-
ways been
its

the group image by supplying one new tune and
arrangements
for
5
older ones
that draw upon
the group’s cohesion and yet allows sufficient solo
expression space. It comes

tions
include
“Django,”
“Odds
Against Tomor-
row” and “Milano.”
“DOIN’ THE THING”—The Horace Silver Quin-
tet At The Village Gate—Blue Note 4076

in

to catching the

Silver session. Cut at the Village Gate (NY) the
package introduces to disk fans several new Silver
compositions that he has been featuring at nitery
engagements and festivals. The title tune, “Doin'
The Thing,” the lead-off track, “Filthy McNasty,”
and the three others burn up the grooves with the
honest
“soul” music
that had
catapulted
Silver
to prominence. Deck has
a guaranteed
sale.

“GROOVE YARD”— The Montgomery Brothers
—Riverside RLP 9362
Familiarity doesn’t breed contempt for the Mont-
gomery Brothers; it breeds an instinctive rapport,
a

that
only
the most

achieve.
With

Buddy Thomas

Outwardly

the group
has
a
solid
blues
base and a firm

######## 1961-09-16 p47  [star\s*bright]
FRANCE
Here’s possibly the most important issue of the year or of the last 20 years
in the French record world. Johnny Hally day, nicknamed the “Prince of Rock
’n Roll,” and who
is under contract with Vogue, has signed a contract with
Philips! His first recording for Philips
is of “Salome” but up to the present he
has failed to terminate his contract with Vogue and
it has not yet expired. Let
it be said that in addition, Hallyday received upon signing with Philips a sum
of money which reached
into the millions and Philips agreed
in the contract
to pay any costs and charges resulting from the law
suit which Vogue
shall
_ certainly not fail
to bring against Hallyday. To complete the
story, Hallyday
* was a minor in the eyes of the law when he signed with Vogue and
his con-
tract with that firm was therefore countersigned by his father. Before deciding
definitely
to
sign with
Philips, Johnny had
also
started
negotiations
(which
were quite advanced) and rumor has
it that he even signed an agreement, with
still a third company!
It
is
completely normal and
current,
especially
for
a
“star,”
to
discuss,
negotiate and even “play one company against the other” when his old conti-act
,-is expired and he
is ready to sign a new
one. This
is how things happen
in
the record and other
fields. But the whole problem with Hallyday
is that
all
the operations mentioned above took place while he was
still legally and nor-
mally under contract with Vogue! His agreement with that firm seemed a valid
one for he has recorded with Vogue now for more than two
years, received
regular royalties,
etc., and the duration of the
said contract was for another
three years. During the Vogue
period, Hallyday became the “Prince of Rock
’n Roll” not only because of his talent but also because of the consistent work
of Leon Cabat and his staff.
<
Well, we would hate to be in the shoes of the judge who must hand down
; the decision
in this
case, for his judgment will certainly become a precedent
[
in French law and the result of his decision will serve to slow up or accelerate
;
the process by which the French record market
is being monopolized by the
i
big, international companies which might, unbridled, absorb
or eliminate the
;
independent, national companies.
The world of records, music and song
is beginning to show a
little activity
I 'after
the summer
slack,
the leading manufacturers, dealers and
artists
are
back
in town, the factories have reopened, the market
is
livening
up, names
of new songs and new issues are being heard. The last recording which Edith
Piaf made just before she suffered such a serious relapse a few months back
are now on the market. Coupled on the disks with
Piaf’s interpretations are
, performances by Charles Dumont,
Edith’s
personal and
preferred composer.
This may be the best way for Dumont to get known, but he would also need
i a voice. The tune to watch among the Piaf songs
is “C’est Peut-Etre Ca” for
which publishing rights belong
to Barclay Editions. By the way,
P.
Boutet,
director of the latter publishing firm,
is also back from

ALBUM REVIEWS
“THE VOICES OF BOB BALLARD”—Dot DLL
25383
Girls
from
the
left
(speaker),
men
from
the
right, blending
in sparkling harmony
in a
lively
chorale
session
guided
by
Lawrence
Welk
ar-
ranger Bob Ballard.
Stereo
is used
to maximum
advantage
in various ways, and
it
all comes out
as a musically sound vocal-orchestra date. Among
the
tunes
are
“These
Foolish
Things,”
“People
Will Say We’re In Love,” “Me And My Shadow”
and “Fools Rush In.”
“STORY SONGS”—Pete
Seeger—Columbia
CL
1668
Pete
Seeger’s
first album
for Columbia was
cut
in performance
at NY’s
Village Gate
before an
appreciative audience which, at Seeger’s familiar
urging,
helps
out
occasionally
on
the
choruses.
The
songs
are
compiled from
the
repertory
of
American
folk
ballads,
including
“Washington
Square,”
“Pretty Boy Floyd,” “Buffalo
Skinner”
and “The
Foolish
Frog.” Somehow
the
electric
excitement that marks most of Seeger’s past work
is missing
here and
the
singer appears
less
re-
laxed
than
usual.
Still,
he’s
the
acknowledged
leader
in
his
field and
the album
should
find
a
receptive market.
“GREAT HAWAIIAN HITS”—The
Mills
Bro-
thers-Dot DLP
25368
Soft swaying harmony
glossily
essayed by
the
Mills
Brothers
nicely do up
a
collection
of Ha-
waiian songs. Pleasant vocal mood listening that
includes readings of “Blue Hawaii,” “Keep Your
Eyes On The Hands,” “Trade Winds” and
“Be-
yond The
Reef.” The
group
still
has
its
loyal
fans.
“TO YOU AND YOURS ”—George Hamilton IV
—RCA Victor LPM-2373
The
soft-voiced
songster
turned
country
singer
and is doing well in the idiom. In his
first Victor
album he offers a varied
collection
of songs
that
includes
his
current
hit
“Three
Steps
To
The
Phone,” some new
songs:
“I Want A
Girl”
and
the
title
tune,
and
several
oldies:
“Rainbow,”
“East
Virginia.”
Easy
listening
collection
that
shows strength in pop as well as country markets.

“SONGS OF THE FAMOUS CARTER FAMILY”
—Lester
Flatt &
Earl
Scruggs—Columbia
CL
1664
For
this
collection
of songs
associated with
the
famed Carter Family, Flatt & Scruggs
(and the
Foggy Mountain Boys)
have
altered their
inter-
nationally
famous
Bluegrass
style
to
conform
more
to
the
traditional memory
of
the
Carter
Family style. Much of this alteration
is achieved
through
the
addition
of
Mother
Maybelle
Car-
ter’s
autoharp,
which
accompanies
the
boys
on
such
cherished
items
as
“Keep On
The
Sunny
Side,” “Jimmy Brown The Newsboy,” “Forsaken
Love”
and
“Worried Man
Blues.”
Outstanding-
album for country and folk markets.
“EVERYTHING
GOES!”—The
Music
of
Cole
Porter—George
Siravo and
his
Orch.—Epic LN
3803
Siravo
calls upon
a fresh blending
of
usual
in-
strumentation
to
accord
the
momentous
Cole
Porter
songs
the
fitting
settings
they
rate. He
also
uses
extra
helpings
of
stereo
effects
(bon-
gos,
etc.)
-which
help
at
times,
but
also
hinder.
Musically,
it’s
a
pleasing
compilation
of
such
melodies as “So In Love,” “Anything Goes,” “I’ve
Got You Under My Skin” and six more.

Kenton’s West Side Story
“KENTON’S WEST SIDE STORY”—Stan Ken-
ton and his Orch.—Capitol ST 1609
This
is by far the most exciting album by Ken-
ton
in many
years!
It’s
his
first attempt
at
a
Broadway show
score
(probably
the
only
score
that
fits
so well into
his
idiom)
and he has
ac-
corded the Leonard Bernstein masterpiece a
bril-
liant new jazz
look. Each
piece’s mood
is
thor-
oughly
explored
for
every
subtle
nuance
(and
there are many)
in an invigorating splash of or-
chestral
color.
The
album
is
outstanding
from
start
to
finish. Should revive a big disk
interest
in Kenton.
“SUMMIT MEETING”—Vee Jay LP-3026
This
is not just a sampler but a sampling of the
best that’s to be found
in the
excellent, growing
Vee Jay jazz
catalog. Among the names
repre-
sented
are
such
stars
as
Cannonball
Adderley,
Art Blakey, Lee Morgan, Wynton Kelly, Bill Hen-
derson,
Paul
Chambers,
Philly
Joe
Jones,
and
more. Of course Eddie
Harris’
best-selling “Ex-
odus”
single
is
included. Among
the
remaining
7
tracks
are
Bill
Henderson’s “Bye Bye
Black-
bird,”
and
the
MJT-f-S’s
“Sleepy.”
Could
be
a
big jazz item.
“UP AT MINTON’S—Stanley
Turrentine^—Blue
Note 4069,
Vol.
1
The legendary Play House
(Minton’s)
serves as
a falsely glamorous but quite appropriate setting
for
the
hard-driving, powerhouse
tenor
playing
of
Stanley
Turrentine.
Along
with
Blue
Note
regulars
Grant
Green
(guitar),
Horace
Parian
(piano), George Tucker (bass), and A1 Harewood
(drums), Turrentine moves
spiritedly through a
set
that
includes
“But Not
For
Me,”
“Yester-
day’s,”
“Broadway”
and
“Stanley’s
Time.”
There’s
lively
swinging,
gut-bucket
blues,
and
generally
all-around
top
notch
jazz
performing
here.

Light,

“PARADISE REGAINED”—Leo Addeo and
his
Orch.—RCA Victor LSA-2414
The weaving, swaying motions of south seas mu-
sic,
evocatively essayed
here by
the Leo Addeo
ork, are also translated into speaker movements
via the “Stereo Action” formula. It’s an engaging
session for those who favor
this
flavor
in
their
mood music.
Selections are “Ka-Lu-A,” “Now
Is
The Hour,” “Beyond The Reef” and 8 more.
STRAUSS:
“Ein
Heldenleben”—Sir
Thomas
Beecham
conducting
the
Royal
Philharmonic
Orch.,
Steven
Staryk,
solo
violin—Capitol
SG
7250
Richard Strauss’ imposing tone poem, considered
to be
his best orchestral work, was
fittingly one
of
Beecham’s
last
recorded
pieces
and,
as
ob-
served here, he had risen to the occasion in
bril-
liant,
richly
rewarding
results.
Staryk’s
violin
solo
is very capable but
it
is Beecham’s
stirring
direction of the difficult piece that remains upper-
most. A lasting last bow.

Musidisc just released four Connie Francis’ albums at the same time. They
are: “More Italian Favorites,” “Songs To A Swinging Band,” “Connie Francis
Sings Jewish Favorites” and
“Connie
Francis At The
Copa.”
Connie’s
first
releases here were marked by big
public’s enthusiasm and
Musidisc
expects
very good sales on
all these releases.
After a successful experience in the 33 Compact’s
field, Musidisc issued last
month many of 7 inch 33 records. The fight around here
is against the 45 RPM
records, singles or EP’s, sales of which never reached a high
level, with some
exceptions, of course.
RGrE Records August releases includes a new album by the Brazilian singer
Miltinho, entitled “Miltinho E Samba” (Miltinho
is Samba)
with twelve very
well selected sambas. The main quality of Miltinho,
is undoubtedly his rhythm,
clearly proved
in this new album. Under the Dot label, RGE issued Lawrence
Welk’s “Yellow Bird” LP. Naturally they’re trying for better sales than Welk’s
“Calcutta” received a few months ago. We’re talking about the album, since
the single reached the highest positions in our Best Sellers charts.
RCA Victor’s releases of the month brought to the Brazilian public an album
with
the
vocal
group
Titulares
Do
Ritmo—a
very
unusual
sextet
formed
by six blind men, with an extraordinary musical sense. The Titulares Do Ritmo
are very well known throughout Brazil and some other Latin American coun-
tries, which they visited in successful tours. All vocal arrangements are made
by the group. Another album with great possibilities
is Elvis Presley’s “Some-
thing For Everybody,” -with the original soundtrack of 20th Century Fox
pic-^
ture “Wild In The Country.” Elvis has an enormous popularity here and
thisj
new album will sure be another hit.

New Ray Charles LP
In Atlantic Release
NEW YORK—Atlantic Records
is re-
leasing six LP’s this month, including
a new
vocal album by Ray
Charles,
whose LP
releases
for
Atlantic have
had consistent chart success.
The new Charles’ package is tagged
“The Genius Sings the Blues’’ and
is
available
in mono
only. The new
re-
leases are: John Lewis’ “The Wonder-
ful World
of
Jazz;’’
Herbie
Mann’s
“ The Family of Mann;’’ Ornette Cole-
man Double Quartette’s “Free Jazz;’’
“The
Blues
in Modern
Jazz,’’
includ-
ing dates by Ray Charles, Art Blakey,
Thelonious
Monk &
The
Jazz
Mes-
singers;
The
Modern
Jazz
Quartet,
Lennie
Tristano,
Dizzy
Gillespie,
Charlie
Mingus,
Milt
Jackson
and
Jimmy Giuffrex (mono only).
This
is
the
first LP
release
since
Atlantic’s
“highly
successful”
sum-
mer plan
in which Atlantic
distribu-
tors
reportedly
more
than
doubled
their
quotas. An important result of
this plan, which was accompanied by
distribution
of a new sales book and
other aids, was that the catalog “sold
'
in depth,” according to Lennie Sachs,
LP merchandising director. “This has
continued
vigorously
since
the
plan
period ended.”
Col.’s “Sound of Music” LP Hits Million Mark
NEW YORK—The
original
cast
re-
cording of “The Sound of Music” has
become the second Rodgers and Ham-
merstein
Broadway
show
score
on
Columbia Records
to pass the
1

lion album
sales mark,
according
to
Goddard

president
of
the
label.
“The
Sound
of
Music” album has
attained
the
rarely-equalled
one
mil-
lion sales mark in less than two years
after
the Broadway
opening
of
the
show (November, 1959). Rodgers’ and
Hammerstein’s “South Pacific” album,
also recorded by Columbia,
is now ap-
proaching the 2 million mark in sales.
A
national
touring
company
has
played
to
standing-room-only
audi-
ences
since
February
27,
1961
and
commences its Chicago run on Novem-
ber
14. The London company has also
played since May 18, 1961, to capacity
audiences.
Star
Mary
Martin
has
given
over
700
performances
in
the
role of Maria Trapp
in the
still-run-
ning Broadway
version.
. The announcement was made
at
a
luncheon
which
took
place
at
the
Twenty-One Club here last week
(19),
during
which
Lieberson
presented
composer
Richard
Rodgers
with
a
gold
record
symbolizing
the
album’s
sales. Rodgers presented the gold rec-
ord
to Harold Spivacke, Chief of the
Music
Division
of
the
Library
of
1
Congress,
Washington,
D.C.,
for
in-J
elusion
in
the
Library’s
Richard
Rodgers
Collection,
comprising
the';
composer’s manuscripts and memory-
,(
bilia. Also present were Miss Martin
{
and
Mrs. Oscar Hammerstein, Ham-
\
merstein’s widow.

“SOME LIKE IT YIDDISH”—The Feder
Sisters
—United Artists UAS 6160
Sister vocal team,
vet
of the Yiddish
entertain-
ment
field
(vaudeville, theatre, radio), has an in-
side
track
on
the
familiar
traditional
Yiddish
harmonies a
la the Barry
Sisters. First time out
for the UA label they engagingly perform a pro-
gram
comprised
of
both
Yiddish
chestnuts
and
newer
melodies;
among
them
“A
Zemerel,”
“Chassidic
In
Rhythm,”
“Yossel,
Yossel,”
“Oy
Mama” and “Mazel.” Abe
Ellstein, leading com-
poser-conductor
in
the
Yiddish
idiom,
conducts
sympathetic ork settings. Big draw for the mar-
ket.
“THE FOLK LORE OF JOHN LEE HOOKER”
—Yee Jay LP 1033
This
is the guts of the blues performed by one of
the last remaining links to the revered, old coun-
try
blues.
Hooker
has
one
of
the most
persua-
sively individual blues
styles and every perform-
ance
comprises
a
unique deep
personal
involve-
ment with the
subject. To say
his work
is com-
pelling
is an understatement. Here Hooker sings
“Tupelo” and “The Hobo”
(recorded
at the
1960
Newport Folk Festival)
and
10 more earthy ex-
amples
of some
of the
best current
blues
avail-
able.
Strong
jazz,
blues,
folk
and r&b
interest.
“LOLLIPOPS FOR
BIG BRASS BAND”—The
Deutschmeister Band
conducted
by
Julius
Herr-
mann—Westminster WST-15058
The famed Deutschmeister brass band
of Vienna
is
heard
in
another
varied
program.
Here,
the
line-up
ranges
from
Strauss’
“Tritsch-Tratseh
Polka,”
to
“Dixie,”
“Can
Can,”
the
traditional
“Gaudeamus
Igitur” and
the
Hallelujah
Chorus
from
Handel’s
“Messiah.”
Quite
an
interesting
array for band
aficionados.
“MORE LATIN AMERICAN HITS”—Trio
Los
Panchos—Columbia EX
5061
Favored Mexican trio offers
its romantic stylings
of
a
dozen
Latin
evergreens, among
the
most
famed
in
the
field.
It’s
a
very
pleasant
outing,
with
appeal
to
pop
buyers
as
well
as
Spanish-
language markets. Tunes include “Historia de un
Amor,” “Quiereme Mucho,” “Solamente Una Vez,”
“Besame Mucho,” “Amor,” “Perfidia” and “Aquel-
los Ojos Verdes”
(Green Eyes).
“OLD TIME FIDDLE TUNES”—Curly Herdman
—Arcade CR-LP-1002
Old-time
country
music
fiddler
Curly Herdman
wields an authentic bow and with
his West Vir-
ginia Boys instrumental quartet turns out a
ses-
sion with appeal to the mountain markets. Eleven
of
the
twelve
tunes
are
Herdman
originals,
penned
in the traditional manner; the twelfth
is
the
chestnut,
“Orange
Blossom
Special.”
Folk
music enthusiasts should
find an
attraction here
too.
"PARIS BLUES”—Film Soundtrack composed by
Duke
Ellington,
featuring
Louis
Armstrong
United Artists UAL 4092
The
soon-to-open
flick
story
of
an
expatriate
American jazz musician in France (starring Paul
Newman, Joanne Woodward, Sidney Poitier, Dia-
hann Carroll) features an Ellington cleffed score
and
the always
likeable
playing
of
Louis Arm-
strong.
The
score
has
some
Ellington
sturdies
(plus
Strayhorn’s
“Take
the
‘A’
Train”)
and
several
newly
tailored
themes
of
apparent
big
interest. Playing
is top drawer though musicians
remain unidentified. Should find hot pop and jazz
reception.
“MIGHTY LIKE A ROSE”—Eddie Harris—Vee
Jay LP 3025
The alto-saxophonist who recently came to chart
attention via single (“Exodus”) and LP (“Exodus
To Jazz”)
dates turns out here another friendly
swinging session. No shrillness in Harris’ playing,
yet
he
avoids
the
other
extreme — saccharine
sweetness.
It’s a middle-of-the-road trek through
such
tunes as “My Buddy”
(new
single), “God
Bless The Child,” “Fontessa” and “Willow Weep
For Me.” Possible chart material.

SENGERS”—Impulse A-7
The pile-driving Blakey rhythms propel the Mes-
sengers
to
fiery heights
in the
group’s
Impulse
date
here. Though
familiar enough
to
jazz
au-
diences,
Blakey
still
generates
more
than
the
usual
excitement
in
each LP
session
and
finds
new devotees each time
out. Group makeup
still
includes
Lee
Morgan,
Wayne
Shorter,
Bobby
Timmons and Jymie
Merritt but with
the
addi-
tion of Curtis Fuller, a
full
(don’t laugh) sound
is achieved in the close ensemble work. Tunes are
“I Hear A Rhapsody,” “Alamode,” “Circus” and
three more.
“BRILLIANT!”—Don
Goldie—Argo LP
4010
Don Goldie’s trumpet style is difficult to pin down
—his playing encompasses years of jazz trumpet
styles and touches down
occasionally on various
mentors. His full-bodied, rich-toned, “sweet” read-
ing of Gershwin’s “Soon”
is a
la Buddy Hackett,
and
there
are
other
familiar
recalls. He
some-
times works with mute and with modern rhythms,
r
but
is at his best in the “mainstream” manner as
on
“I’ll Be Around,” “They
Didn’t
Believe Me,”
“Look For the
Silver Lining” and the aforemen-
tioned
“Soon.”
Good,
enjoyable
jazz
listening.
“THE
REMARKABLE
CARMELL
JONES”—
Pacific Jazz PJ-29
The
stir being
caused
by
Carmell Jones
is not
unlike the Don Goldie commotion. Both are tech-
nically
proficient young trumpeters with
an
in-
dividual approach and a clear mind. But here the
comparison
ends,
for
while
Goldie
occupies
the
mainstream, Jones
is forging ahead in directions
initiated by Miles Davis et al. In his first PJ date
as a leader, Jones nimbly fingers through Elling-
ton’s
“I’m Gonna Go
Fishing,” “Come Rain Or
Come Shine,” “Full Moon and Empty Arms” and
his own “Sad March.”
“FREE JAZZ”—A
Collective
Improvisation
By
The
Ornette Coleman
Double
Quartet—Atlantic
1364
Controversy over
the
direction
of
Ornette
Cole-
man will be further heightened by the release of
this album.
It features the
alto saxophonist and
a “double quartet”—two reeds, two trumpets, two
basses, two drums—in one continuous 36 minute
studio take, unedited. To many people
it
will be
just
a more
intense cacaphony
of meaningless,
unrelated noises. To others,
it will be the “gospel
truth.”
But
controversy
breeds
commercialism,
and
album
sales
should
be
good.
Outstanding
cover
is a die-cut through to a reproduction of a
Jackson
Pollock painting.

HOLLYWOOD—Liberty Records has

1961.

said
first half earnings after taxes rose to
$129,466 from $101,900 in the previous
period. Sales, including royalties from
overseas
operations,
were
up
24%,
from
$1,980,000
to
$2,450,000
in
the
more
recent
