net
rose from
17
to
21
cents,
based
on
199,356 common and 407,921
class B
shares now outstanding.
Bennett
said he
expects

of

year’s
levels.
He
explained
that,
aside from
the
industry’s
sea-
sonal
first half slack, second half op-
erations should improve as the result
of several new programs.
In the year ended January 31, 1961,
Liberty
recorded
sales
of

traordinary charges of $160,071.

said,
should receive a boost from a nation-

New RIAA Rule Allows
For Multi-LP "Gold" Award
NEW YORK—The
Record
Industry
Association
of America (RIAA)
has
revised its regulations governing the
certification
of
Gold
Record
Album
Awards
to
enable
multi-disk
sets
to
qualify.
The
standards
for
such an award
that previously called for a minimum
unit sale of 500,000 LP’s and a mini-
mum factory billing of $1 million has
been changed to a minimum factory
billing of $1 million only.
In
voting
the
change,
the RIAA
board noted the fact that some best-
selling
multi-disk
sets,
whose
price
might be two or three times that of a
single LP
release, might
not
reach
the required unit
sales volume while
attaining
the
necessary
dollar
sales
figure.
Such may
well
be
the
case
with
Judy
Garland’s
2-LP
Carnegie
Hall
release
on
Capitol, which
this week
tops both the mono and stereo
sales
charts.
Gold
records
for
a
singles
release
still require a sale of a million copies.

HOLLAND
Dureco L.C. excited about having four records on Holland’s Best Sellers
list:
“Pepito” (Los Machucambos/Omega, number 5), “Batje Vier” (Cocktail Trio/
Omega, number 12), “Brigitte Bardot” (Jorge Veiga/Omega, number 13) and
“Danke Schon Fiir Die Blumen” (Wedding Cake)
(Siw Malnikvist/Metronome,
number 19). Mr. Maessen, a&r manager of Dureco L.C., told Cash Box that, in
fact, Dureco
is doing the biggest business in
its history.
Mr. Wim van Vught of Musicpublishers Editions Altona reports big activities
on two South American titles: “Brigitte Bardot” and “La Novia”. On “Brigitte
Bardot”, Phonogram made an overnight recording with The Butterflies on
its
Philips-label and others
will follow, among them The Emeralds on the CNR-
label. Best selling “B.B.”—platter is the version of Jorge Veiga on the Barclay-
label, closely followed by the version of Digno Garcia on Palette. As for “La
Novia,” this title hits the market in the Tony Dallara version (after two weeks
on release,
it’s already on the number 29 spot of the Dutch Best Sellers
list),
released in Holland by Delta-records and plugged strongly by so-called pirate-
station Radio Veronica. Famous Willy Alberti covered the title on the Philips-
label and on the same label songstress Mieke Telkamp
is going to sing a fine
Dutch
version.
Great success on the Dutch Fontana label
(L.C. Phonogram)
is popular teen-
age singer Ria Talk’s first LP, “El Rancho Grande.” This 10 incher has the title
song
(also known as “Give Me My Ranch”), “I’m An Old Cowhand,” teenbeat
versions of “Poor Old Joe,” “Home On The Range,” and “My Bonnie
Is Over
The Ocean,” also some Dutch sung numbers of the same kind. Eddy de Roever,
who hails from Rotterdam and plays piano dance music in a very pleasing and
danceable way, has a “Piano-Medley No. 1” out on the Fontana-label. Included
are
recent
hits
like
“Hello Mary Lou,” “Are You
Sure” and “Wheels.” We
suppose no one here had ever heard of fine Greek singer Yiannis Voyadjis. His
versions of the two best and most popular songs from the Greek film “Dream-
land Of Desire” will make him known very soon. These must be the very best
sung versions by any male singer of this wonderful Hadjidakis music. High
class work on Fontana.
First showings of the motion picture version of “Exodus” have just begun
here. Million selling version of the main theme by piano duettists Ferrante &
Teicher is doing very, very fine over here on the United Artists label, released
by L.C. Phonogram.
Big new single
hits on the London-label are “Should
I”
(String-A-Longs),
“Heart And Soul” (Jan & Dean), “A Tear” (Gene McDaniels), “Amor” (Ben E.
King) and “Take Good Care Of My Baby” (Bobby Vee).
Reportedly on top
of the
charts
in
Singapore
is “Asmara” by Indonesian
born Dutch teenage singer Anneke Gronloh, on
Philips. Recording was made
in Holland.
A new Dutch author, Oscar Remeeus, has been discovered
in the South
of
Holland. Remeeus
lives
in Eindhoven and
is 26 years
old. Basart contracted
four songs
of
this new
talent,
of which “Crazy Love” has already been
re-
corded by John Lamers, accompanied by Cees and his Skyliners. The CNR-label
(distributed by
C. N. Good
L.C.)
reports
a
big
sale
and
are
sure
that
it
has a big hit on
its hands. “Crazy Love” has
not only been recorded
in the
Dutch, but also in the English language, and a German recording for the Ger-
man market
will
be
released
soon.
Paul Anka’s recordings “Tonight My Love, Tonight” and “Dance On
Little
Girl,” released by Artone, have become top-scorers
in Holland. Likewise, Ar-
tone’s Funckler department
is building Clarence “Frogman” Henry into a con-
sistent seller. His first hit “But I Do” reached the top twenty charts in Holland
and Belgium. His
follow-up “You Always Hurt The One You Love”
is
also
doing well, while Frogman’s
third etching “Lonely Street” has been eagerly
awaited by the trade, and was released recently. New LP releases from Argo’s
Jazz Line by Artone are very well received, especially “A Night At The Village
Vanguard” by the Kenny
Burrell
Trio and “Meet The
Jazztet” by the Art
Farmer-Benny Golson Group.
Delta Records contracted for a long-term period the Gold Coast Combo and
vocal star Edwin Rutten. Eighteen years young Edwin, son of filmmaker Gerard
Rutten,
is a very swinging singer with a touch of Sinatra, a bit of Torme, and
a fling of Eckstine, but
still has individuality. First recordings were made last
week; Edwin was accompanied by the Gold Coast Combo, directed by pianist
Rogier van Otterloo, talented son of the world famous conductor of the Resi-
dentie Orchestra, Willem van Otterloo.
BELGIUM
Belgian teenage singer number one Will Tura
left the army;
his
first ap-
pearance after his release was a real triumph. Tura has big success with
his
Palette
platter “El
Soldado De
Levita.” Two
other Spanish numbers
will be
recorded soon and these will be released in Spain
too. New talent on
Palette:
Carlo Roma, discovered only some months ago. His first recordings: “Mia Bella
Rosie” and “Oh! Oh! Rina”. Carlo Roma
is a young Italian miner, working in
Jemappes. He makes his songs himself and plays guitar.
Gramophone
L.C.,
already representing
H.M.V.,
Columbia,
Pathe,
Capitol,
Electrola, Fonit, Parlophone, MGM and Odeon, has a new label on the market:
Trianon. Thus Gramophone joined the low-priced labels on the Belgian market:
prices will be 54 francs (EP), 99 francs
(10" LP) and 168 frs
(12” LP). New
releases of Gramophone L.C. include: “Star Eyes”/“I Would Do Anything For
You”
(Jackie
Davis—Capitol), “American Beauty Rose”/“Sentimental
Jour-
ney” (Frank Sinatra—Capitol), “I’m Going Home”/“Love Of A Man” (Gene
Vincent—Capitol), “Kon Tiki”/“36-24-36” (The Shadows-—Columbia). Further-
more, Gramophone
L.C.
released
a very funny
version
of
the
big
seller
of
Jacques Brel “La Valse A Mille Temps.” The new words were made by Jean
Poiret, who sings the new version on records himself under the title “La Vache
A. Mille Temps.” Gramophone
also released
the French
version
of the
Cliff
Richard
success “D In Love” under the
title “Trois En Amour”
(Les Chats
Sauvages on Pathe). Kroner’s Duo are playing rock-versions of “Amapola” and
“Blue
Guitar” on H.M.V.
New artist under contract with “Will” records
is Robert Hancre, formerly
with H.M.V. He recorded the Vico Torriani hit “Sieben Junge Madchen” (Seven
Young Girls). This composition has been published by Sab Music.
Best selling LP in Flemish Belgium: “Bravo Bobbejaan Schoepen”. This
is a
selection
of Bobbejaan’s biggest successes
of the
last years, with
a.o. “Cafe
Zonder Bier” (Pub With No Beer). In October, Bobbejaan will open his “Bobbe-
jaanland” in Lichtaarde. Visitors are able to do really everything they want:
swimming, fishing, horseriding,
eating, sunbathing, waterskiing and assisting
big shows. “Bobbejaanland”
will be
a very unique enterprise for Belgium!
Belgian radio and tv have big plans to start with FM transmissions. They
will start at the occasion of the “Exhibition Of Charleroi.” There will be a num-
ber
of programs broadcast and
televised from
this
exhibition. The
Cousins,
Will Tura, The Harmonica Boys and others are already signed.

Like many of their contemporaries,

Initial

Getting together

Records,
was
arranged.
He
signed

“A
CHILD’S INTRODUCTION TO THE
IN-
STRUMENTS OF THE ORCHESTRA”—Joseph
Cooper and the Sinfonia of London—Wonderland
1443
Children
are
introduced
to
the
orchestra
on
a
much
higher plane
of
intelligence here than
in
the
Capitol
deck.
It
will
serve a
useful
educa-
tional purpose
to an older
child.
British concert
pianist and musical
educationist Joseph Cooper
narrates the
detailed
explanations
meticulously,
and
the
musical
examples
are
flawlessly
per-
formed. Side two traces the history of the piano
from
its predecessors the harp, clavichord, harp-
sichord, etc.
“FOR DOCTORS ONLY”—Oscar Brand—Elek-
tra EKL-204
It’s
the
medical
profession’s
turn
to
be
good-
naturedly disemboweled by Oscar Brand’s candid
comments.
Drawing
on
his
huge
repertoire
of
traditional
folk
melodies
he
outfits them
with
choice
satirical
lyrics and pokes an
effectionate,
sometimes harsh finger at the profession in such
titled songs as “The Old
G.P.,” “How To Be A
Doctor
-,”
“Miracle
Drugs,”
“Here
Comes
The
A.M.A.” and “Medical Life Calypso.” An hilarious
spoof that’ll turn many heads.
“MELODIE
d’lTALY—The
DiMara
Sisters —
Roulette R 25151
The bi-lingual DiMara
Sisters keep
close
to the
Italian flavor even
in American songs: throwing
in an Italian phrase, working with continental fla-
vored ork arrangements,
etc.
Here,
songs from
both
sides of the ocean provide the impetus for
an
enjoyable
vocal
program.
Selections
include
“24
Mila Bad,”
“Santa
Lucia,”
“If
I
Give My
Heart To You” and “Smile.” Has a place
in the
market.
“COMO ESTA”—Nora Morales—Tico LP 1068
Ever since he proved instrumental in creating the
Latin dance craze
in
the
U.S.
years
ago, Nora
Morales
has remained one
of
the more popular
Latin music purveyors here. In this new Tico out-
ing, the familiar melodic warmth and the flavor-
ful, gently persuasive rhythmic swing
is heard in
a
collection
of varied-tempo
originals and
ever-
greens. An
enticing
entry
for
the
Latin
dance
market.
“STAIRWAY TO THE STARS”—Jack Weigand
at the Organ—Cameo SC 1012
Organist Weigand
handles
the
instrument
with
overpowering
gusto, working up
to
a
self-pro-
pelled speed. In this first set for Cameo he offers
such-styled readings
of “Tara’s Theme,”
“Satin
Doll,” “Street
Scene,” “Pompton Turnpike” and
six more. OK session for organ fans.
“CALYPSO
PARTY”—Lloyd

stand BLP 102
Bermudian Simmons puts on no airs for calypso

offers some traditional calypso items and several
originals,
notably
“Back
To
Back—Belly
To
Belly,” “The Fly Song,” “Don’t Calypso On Me”
and “Lloyd Sweet Lloyd.” Much of

is off-color
and that should attract the buyers.

“HIGH
FLYING
WITH
LAMBERT,
HEN-
DRICKS & ROSS”—With the Ike Isaacs Trio—
Columbia CL 1675
The
trio’s third Columbia album
is a lot of fun.
More so than previous
dates, for the deep
seri-
ousness which marked much of their early work
has relaxed
into a swinging
naturalness and
a
half-cocked wink toward humor.
It
is most
evi-
dent
in
the
choice
of
material,
especially
such
items
as
Slim
Gaillard’s
“Popity
Pop,”
Art
Farmer’s “Farmer’s Market” and three by Hor-
ace
Silver: “Come On Home,” “Cookin’ At The
Continental”
and “Home
Cookin’.”
Ike
Isaacs’
threesome
is good accompaniment. Big package
for jazz fans.
“A
STUDY
IN
FRUSTRATION — THE
FLETCHER HENDERSON STORY”—Columbia
C4L 19
The man who
literally launched big band
jazz
in
the
early
twenties
(his
own
arrangements
made Benny Goodman a “king” ten years later)
finally gets his story told on disk. Columbia has
secured from its archives 64 sides cut by the vari-
ous Henderson bands
(enough material for four
full disks)
and with an accompanying extensive
documentation by Frank Driggs the package is of
tremendous jazz
history
interest. Almost
all
of
the famed early jazz names are represented here
too.
“AFRICA/BRASS”—The John
Coltrane Quartet
—Impulse A-6
The
intensive
probing,
searching
Coltrane
sax
style reaches a high point in the 16% minute
(all
of
side
one)
“Africa,”
in
which
the
quintet
achieves a Mingus-like fury of neatly thought-out
abandon. It’s a wild thing with Coltrane standing
out as a giant on his instrument. This same idea
is
carried
out
in
the
two
tracks
on
side
two,
“Greensleeves”
and
“Blues
Minor.”
Interest
abounds here.
“THE WONDERFUL WORLD OF JAZZ—John
Lewis—Atlantic 1375
Devotees
of John
Lewis’
musical
mystique
will

N.Y. Philharmonic Strike
Ends Sessions At Columbia
NEW YORK—The strike of the musi-
cians
of the New York Philharmonic
Orchestra
against
the
Philharmonic
Society—-which has delayed the open-
ing
of
the
orchestra’s new
season
has
ended,
for
the
duration
of
the
strike,
all
sessions
of Leonard
Bern-
stein-conducted
group
for
Columbia
Records.
A spokesman for the label said last
week that the orchestra’s regular Mon-
day sessions could not continue unless
a settlement was reached. Last Mon-
day’s scheduled
studio work was not
held.
The musicians’ union, Local 802
of
the American Federation of Musicians,
is holding out for a one year pact, a
$32.50
raise
in
the minimum
salary
of 180, two days off a week instead of
one, overtime at any concert over two
hours, and better tour conditions.
The
Philharmonic
Society
has
of-
fered
a
three-year
pact
with
a
$10
raise above the minimum salary, with
$10
more
in
the
1963-64
season,
a
guarantee
of
a
longer
season,
and
other benefits.
At presstime, no meetings between
the
union
and
the
society
had
been
scheduled.

NEW
YORK—Following

Mathews, who has been
associated
with the recording
field for the past
10 years as a promotion director and
independent
producer,
will

all activities in the A&R division, and
will concentrate on singles and artists
relations.
The two

also
follow

recent

by

madge naming Lieber and Stoller, who
will
produce new
artists
exclusively
for UA, and H. W. “Pappy”
Dailey,
Houston, as head of the Country de-
partment of the label, to the UA pro-
ducing team.
Perito has been actively engaged as
a
musician,
arranger
and
conductor
since his graduation from Juilliard in
1946. An acomplished musician, Perito
has, for the past year been featured
as an instrumental recording artist on
UA
and

Audio,
and
has
also
served as conductor for such artists as
Ferrante and Teicher, A1 Caiola, Terry
Snyder, Eydie Gorme and Steve Law-
rence, Sauter-Finegan and others.
Prior

with

artist and

the major labels. In his new capacity
with UA
he

Mathews,

on

product, especially in the motion pic-
ture
Sound
Track
and
theme
area
where his musical background can be
of special value.
Mathews, as an indie producer, was
responsible for such hits as “The Wed-
ding” by June Vali, and a number of
others in the pop
field. In addition to
his A&R background, he has served
as promotion director for several large

as an
indie
in that

He
will continue to supervise promo-
tion for UA.

standing job for UA in the past, and

Perito’s

July Stereo Phono Sales
Down, Mono Sales Up
NEW YORK—The
sales
of
stereo
phonos
in
July
dropped
to
143,920
from
152,950
in June, according to a
report
last week
in The Wall
Street
Journal.
Mono
set
sales
during
the
same month increased to 59,839 from
49,183 in June. The report noted that
mono sales were at the same level as
in July, 1960, while stereo sales were
sharply below that of the same period
last year.

1
Billionth Victor
Disk
Is
Pressed
INDIANAPOLIS — The one billionth
disk
produced
by RCA
Victor
was
pressed
last week
(3)
at
the
label’s
plant
here.
The
deck
that
achieved
this milestone was a 45
single, Eddie
Arnold’s “One Grain of Sand.”
Attending
the
ceremonies marking
the
event, which
included an
on-the-
scene radio broadcast over WFBM
di-
rect from
the production
area, were
City
Comptroller,
A1
Losche,
repre-
senting
Mayor
Charles
F.
Boswell,
Fred Beyer of the Indianapolis Cham-
ber of Commerce, plant manager and
spokesman Roy Price and Arnold, as
well as plant personnel.
The
platter was
presented
to
Ar-
nold by
Losche, who had
accepted
it
from
record
press
operator
Anna
Franks.
All
record
division
employ-
ees,
1,300
in
number,
were
given
a
duplicate
of
the
one
billionth
record
as a momento.
Along with Losche and Beyer, Price
congratulated
and
paid
tribute
to
“each and every person who helped in
achieving
this
outstanding
success.”
Price underlined the magnitude
of
the achievement. “We are the world’s
largest manufacturer
of phonograph
records,”
he
stated,
“yet
it required
over 22 years to attain the one billion
mark. Our
record plant produced
its
first record
here
on August
5,
1939,
and
currently manufactures 65
to
70
million
records
per
year.
If
all
the
records produced here
in the past 22
years were
spread
out,
one
by
one,
they would
cover
a
total
area
of
23
square miles, more than one-third the
area
contained
in
the
city
limits
of
Indianapolis.
Also,
if
you
were
to
play
all the
records manufactured
in
Indianapolis
one
after
another,
twenty-four
hours
a
day
for
seven
days a week,
it would take more than
23,834
years
of
listening
time.”
Following the ceremonies, the com-
munity
officials
and
Arnold
were
guests
at
a
luncheon and
then were
conducted on an inspection tour of the
plant by
Price.
Joining
in the festivities were rep-
resentatives of four other Victor rec-
ord
division operations
in
Indianapo-
lis; the RCA record merchandise and
administration group, the RCA mag-
netic tape
plant, and
record
division
E.D.P. and the RCA record engineer-
ing group.

At Connie Francis’ cocktail party, held recently in Milan, Mr. Sugar told us
he is on the verge of entering the film field as a producer. Beginning next year,
he will start producing one film a year and
it will be a musical film, of course,
crammed with songs he publishes.
Alberto Carisch, the director of Southern Music
here,
said he
is going
to
make a business trip through some countries behind the iron curtain, visiting
Russia, Hungary and Roumania. He recently sold some pieces from his Italian
catalog (“Guarda Che Luna,” a big hit here, “Tua” and “Scusami,”
all penned
by Maestro Malgoni)
to some communist countries and
said he
got back
a
remarkable amount
of money in payment for the music
rights. Remarkable
because there
is no law inside the communist countries as
to the amount of
money publishers
can
receive for music
rights. They
take
a
chance, when
selling their catalog pieces, because they can either receive no money at
all,
or whatever money the people inside the iron curtain decide to send them.
Mr. Rapetti of Ricordi phoned us to announce the figures of the best selling-
records of the company. They are: “Non Arrossire”
(Don’t Blush) by Giorgio
Gaber—80,000 copies; “Riviera” by Umberto Bindi—50,000 copies; “La Ballata
Del Cerutti” (Cerutti’s Ballad) by Giorgio Gaber—40,000 copies; “Senza Fine”
(Endlessly) by Gino Paoli—20,000 copies.
Following the fashion of the old Neapolitan and Roman
songs, which have
been seen at the highest spots in our charts and also abroad,
is the revival of
old tunes from Florence,
like “Firenze Sogna”
(Florence Dreams) performed
successfully by Narciso
Parigi
(V.C.M.), and most
broadcasted
on
the
air.
Singer Narciso Parigi
is our sensitive and tender hearted
interpreter
of
old
songs from Florence. He is due in South America early this month.
While “Mule Skinner Blues”
is
still
selling pretty
well
here, Durium has
released Soma’s new follow-up by the Fendermen
titled “Heartbreaking Spe-
cial.” In two weeks,
15,000
copies were
sold,
as reported by Mr.
Scussel
of
Durium. Durium also released Vogue’s version of “Brigitte Bardot,” interpreted
by Roberto
Seto. This
disk
will
feature
a
special
cover,
while
the
original
version on Barclay by J. Velga was published just a short time ago. Both are
number one in France.
Peppino Di Capri’s in great demand currently with one of his latest record-
ings, of an old Neapolitan song
titled, “Piscatore E Pusilleco” (A Fisher At
Pusilleco), which has been on the chart for a few weeks. The same company
that handles Di Capri has another name worth being considered with interest,
songstress
Jolanda
Rossin, who won
the
Pesaro
Festival
with
“Eclisse
Di
Sole” (Eclipse Of The Sun). The record has been available for some time. She
then won another
first
prize,
also
this
year,
at
Ventimiglia
with “Quando
L’Alba Verra” (When Dawn Will Come). Recently, she did “Jealous Of You”
on TV and this is her record that sells best.
His
Master’s
Voice-Columbia-Marconiphone
(V.C.M.)
will
be
represented
in
the Canzonissima
(The
Songest)
music TV
shows by the
following
hit
names: Pino Donaggio, who will sing “II Mio Sotterraneo” (My Tunnel); Luci-
ano Virgili, “La Tempesta” (The Storm);
Sergio Bruno, “O Cappotto,”
(The
Overcoat); Corrado Lojacono, “Vienimi Vicino” (Get Close To Me); Lelio Lut-
tazzi, “Chiedimi Tutto” (Ask Me For Anything).
Mr. Ruscitto announced that Interdisc has acquired the rights to the
distri-
bution of the Vee Jay
label across
Italy, Switzerland, Austria and Germany.
Negotiations are being held here to transfer the charge of the distributorship
to a big Italian distributor. Ruscitto also told us that the first LP’s on Pacific

THE
EVERLY BROTHERS
For more than four years, The Ev-
erly Brothers have been among the top
attractions
in the teen-beat business.
The boys’ latest click vehicle is “Don’t
Blame
Me,’’ one
of
their
rare
stints
on a standard, which this week holds
the #35
spot
on
the Top
100. They
began
their remarkable Top
100
ca-
reer in 1957, when, after looking for a
break in Nashville, publisher-manager
Wesley Rose liked the way they sang,
and introduced them to Archie Bleyer,
head of Cadence
Records, who added
the duo to his
label.
That same year, Don and
Phil
of-
fered “Bye Bye Love’’ to the teeners,
who responded to the distinctive coun-
try-styled sound of the boys in a gold-
record manner. Other hits, many mil-
lion-sellers, on Cadence, both
singles
and LP’s, came one after another. In
1960, the boys left Cadence for Warner
Bros. Records—and continued making
chart dates.
The Kentucky-born
artists
(Phil
is
22, Don
24)
now
live
in
Hollywood,
where
they
study
acting,
not
as
a
team, but on an individual basis.
The
Dreamlovers
are
yet
another
example of the willingness of young-
sters to readily accept new talent. The
five
vocalists bowed both themselves
and
the
Philly-based
Heritage
(dis-
tributed by Cameo)
label on the Top
100 with their disking of “When We
Get Married,” and are now going for a
second-in-a-row
success
with
“Let
Them Love” and “Welcome Home.”
Their background should be famil-
iar
to
those who have
followed
the
careers of today’s teen-market stand-
outs. The boys were friends and
fel-
low-classmates at Philly’s North East
High
School,
where
they
formed
a
singing
team,
in
1956,
for
a
talent
show at the
school.
After
four years
of
talent
shows,
charity benefits and an occasional lo-
cal club date, the songsters were
se-
lected
to provide
the vocal backdrop
on
last
year’s
smash
by
Chubby
Checker
(Parkway),
“The
Twist.”
While most were listening to Checker
on the date. Heritage execs Jerry Ross
and Murray Wecht spotted a “unique
style” from the group. Donny Hogan,
a former member of the group, sup-
plies all
its material.

HOLLAND
On September 29 the Month-Of-The-Record Action, which has been organized
by the Commission of Collective Grammophonerecords Campaign started
to a
brilliant classical show in the Concertgebouw, Amsterdam. On September
30,
a popular show took place in the Kurzaal, Scheveningen. The highlights of the
“Grand Gala Du Disque” events, on which more than 20 top national and inter-
national attractions were featured, was the “Solemn Hour Of Edisons” Awards
for the best performances on records in 1961 in every musical
field. Here is the
list of artists and records which got an “Edison”;
Classical Music
Robert Casadesus
for
his recording
of
Beethoven’s
“Eifth
Piano
Concerto.”
(Philips).
Filomusica
Of
London
for
their
recording
of
Handel’s
“Water
Music”
(L’Oiseau Lyre).
George Szolti for his recording
of Wagner’s “Tristan Und
Isolde”
(Philips).
Joan Sutherland for her recording of “The Art Of The Primadonna” (Decca).
Elisabeth Schwarzkopf for her recording of “Goethe Lieder” (Columbia).
The Amadeus Quartet for their recording of Beethoven’s “Quartet” (DGG).
Bernard Haitink
for
his
recording
of Andriessen’s “Etudes Symphoniques”/
Bartok’s “Concerto For Orchestra”
(Philips).
Honorable mention was given to the recording of “Musique Insolite”
(Pathe).
Popular Music
Wim Kan for his recording of “Uithuilen en Opnieuw Beginnen” (Philips).
Rita Keys for her recording of “Mai’riage In Modern Jazz” (Philips).
Captain H.
F. W. van Diepenbeek for
his recording
of “Marching Together
Holland/U.S.A.” (CNR).
The Blue Diamonds for their recording of “Ramona” (Decca).
Henk Bakker for his recording of “Ali Baba En De Veertig Rovers” (Artone).
Jack Marshall for his recording of “Soundsville”
(Capitol).
John Coltrane for his recording of “Giant Steps” (London).
Harry Belafonte for his recording of “Belafonte At Carnegie Hall” (RCA).
Actor Ko van Dijk received an “Edison” for his recording of “Tribunal Scene”
from “Danton’s Death” (Pythia).
The Edison Award performances were closed by a pleasantly informal
ball,
(at the Kurzaal, Scheveningen) which lasted until the small hours of Sunday
morning.
Edison Awards have now international recognition and importance. Closely
following the commercial importance of Oscars in the motion picture industry.
The Edison Awards
is becoming more of a big highlight
in the international
recording industry every year. The big
stars, applauded during both “Grand
Gala Du Disque” shows
(classical— and popular music), were top artists like
Elisabeth Schwarzkopf and Robert Casadesus
(classical music), and Caterina
Valente, Siw' Malmkvist, Valerie Masters, Lys Assia, Svend Asmussen & Ulrik
Neumann and Charles Aznavour.
Dutch singer of Italian songs, Willy Alberti,
is the first over here to record
the now famous and well loved Mexican song “La Sposa,” better known under
its Italian title: “La Novia.” Willy’s new single disk may prove a double win-
ner, for
it has the latest Rocco Granata song “Irena” on the other side.
Ray Conniff records never
fail to be good
sellers. Two new EP records
in
the series, “Ray Conniff Presents The Classics,” have just been released. They
feature compositions by masters like Liszt, Chopin and Puccini, presented in a
special way by The Ray Conniff Orchestra and chorus, on
Philips.
The boys of The Dutch Swing College Band of Peter Schilperoort are real
world travellers these days. Fortunately, they find time now and then to make
records in the Hilversum Phonogram studio. Their dixie-versions of pop songs
have made the band popular by an even larger public than before. Latest single
release has “Old Amsterdam,” counled with pre-war German
hit “Bel Ami,”
which comes from the Willi Forst film of the same name.
Soundtrack EP from “Dreamland Of Desire” (“Traumland Der Sehnsucht”),
with Greek music and songs by Manos “Never On Sunday” Hadjidakis, is meet-
ing with great success here (Fontana, L.C. Phonogram).
Decca-London’s new
label manager John Ros
told Cash Box he has great
expectations of Bobby Darin’s new rendering of oldie “You Must Have Been A
Beautiful Baby,” on London. New season
started with
three big
hits: “Take
Good Care Of My Baby” (Bobby
Vee), “The
Mountain’s High”
(Dick And
Deedee) and “Hurt” (Timi Yuro), Liberty recordings that are issued here on
the London label. At the time you read this, Mr. John Ros will be
in England
to talk to Decca people in London.
Dutch song
“Gloedrode Rozen”
(“Glowing Red
Roses”),
written
by Theo
Warrens,
has
been
assigned
to
Germany
by
Storz
Musikverlag,
Osterode
(Harz). Storz informed Basart, that the German lyrics are
in the making and
that a release
is

label.
Basart, who represents
the Storz catalog for Benelux, also has some very good songs on hand, from
which “De Trouwe Herder” (“The Old Shepherd”)
has been recorded by the
popular Limbra Sisters on the Polydor label.
Conny Froboess, Bovema’s His Master’s Voice teenage star from Germany,
recorded some English versions of late, of which the
titles are “Lovable” and
“No One Can Tell Me I’m Too Young.”
Ricky Nelson’s “Hello Mary Lou”—hit recently passed the
100,000
sales in
Holland. Rick
is the big American
star of the Imperial
label, represented by
L.
C. Bovema, Holland.
In the meantime, William Voerman
of Bovema
said
that there is a rapidly increasing interest for Fats Domino LP’s in Holland so
that more Fats LP’s than ever before will be released on the Dutch market in
the near future.
German publisher Peter Meisel and Dutch publisher Joop Portengen made
an exchange deal with successful results for both of them: Meisel gave Dutch
rights
of top hit “Schade, Schade, Schade”
to Joop Portengen, who
in some
days obtained a Philips record of the Dutch version of this new Siw Malmkvist
success. Peter Meisel obtained a Lys Assia record to be released by German
Philips of “Ay, Ay, En Bilbao,” of which Joop Portengen
is original publisher.
C. N. Rood L.C. just released “Runaround Sue” by Dion on the
'Top Rank

of Europe. Hum-
phrey Lyttelton, Chris Barber, Cy Laurie and the (Dutch) New Orleans Syn-

Robertino, CNR’s fast selling young Italian singer, will come to Holland this
month, for radio and TV performances. Robertino’s “Mama” and “O Sole Mio”
ai’e selling extremely well.
First Dutch sung version of “Brigitte Bardot” by The Emeralds got a big
promotion by Dutch TV.
C. N. Rood L.C.
is making very good business with
country & western LP’s and EP’s on the Starday label.
First jazz concert of this season
in Holland
is by The Modern Jazz Quartet
(20th October). Others to follow are The Dave Brubeck Quartet (10th Novem-
ber), the groups of Dizzy Gillespie and John Coltrane

Over Night”
well over the

second award was
for “Rock

“TRAV’LIN
LIGHT”—Anita
O’Day—Verve
V-2157
That this album
is a
sort of tribute to the late
Billie Holiday
is obvious from the selections, but
that’s where the comparison
ends. Though both
are among the greats in true jazz singing, stylist-
ically
they’re
miles
apart. Here
Anita’s rough-
hewn voice takes on
its recently-acquired polish
and
she
directs
hei’
boundless
vocal
energy on
carefully
chosen
paths
through
“Remember,”
“God
Bless The
Child,”
“I Hear Music,” “Some
Other Spring” and 8 others. Johnny Mandel and
Russ Garcia have orchestrated admirably.
She’s
a rarity among today’s crop of singers; jazz buffs
should respond.
“THELONIOUS
MONK
WITH
JOHN
COL-
TRANE”—Jazzland JLP 946S
When Monk and
Coltrane
get
together
there’s
fireworks. Add such figures as Coleman Hawkins,
Art Blakey, Shadow Wilson and Gigi Gryce and
you have a real head-on collision. Needless to say,
there are some very unsual moments in this rec-
ord.
Generally, the package
will
appeal
greatly
to the most modern
of jazz fans. Sessions date
from
1957
(when
Monk
and
Coltrane
were
teamed at the Five Spot) and there will be his-
torical interest here
too,
especially for the
late
Shadow Wilson’s parts.

MOBILE—H. C. Kain, topper of the
HARM
Questionnaire
Rack Jobbers
Wili
Obtain
Facts And Figures
NEW YORK—A questionnaire
is be-
ing sent to rack-jobber members of the
National Association of Record Mer-
chandisers (NARM)
in order
to
get
a detailed picture of the rack-jobbing
field.
Jules Malamud, NARM’s
executive
secretary stated: “The growth
of the
record rack merchandiser
in the
last
five years has been a phenomenal one.
One of the prime purposes in circulat-
ing
the
questionnaire
will
be
to
ac-
cumulate
accurate,
authenticated
figures
of
rack
jobber
business
in
phonograph records. We feel that the
estimates
that
have
been
made
up
until now will prove appreciably
less
than the actual figures which we will
gather through
the
questionnaire.
It
is our aim to have secured by the end
of
1961,
a
complete
and
accurate
statistical picture of record rack mer-
chandising
in the United
States. Re-
sults
of
this
survey
will
be
issued
early
in
1962
via
the
trade
publica-
tions, and
will
be evaluated by both
record
merchandisers
and
manufac-
turers
during
the NARM
1961
con-
vention program
in April.”
The
rack
jobbers
will be asked
to
give
the
exact number and
type
of
their phonograph record locations, and
the rate of increase of those locations
in the past year.
It will then be pos-
sible
to determine how many
super-
markets,
department
stores,
drug-
stores,
service
PX’s,
phonograph
equipment
outlets,
discount
outlets,
and variety stores are serviced by the
rack
jobber.
The
rate
at which
the
number of each of these types of out-
lets are being added to those already
serviced by the rack jobber,
will
in-
dicate the trends
in rack merchandis-
ing,
and
demonstrate
the growth
of
the rack jobber
in these various out-
lets.
Included
in
the
survey
is
a
com-
plete breakdown of the type of record
product
sold
through the
racks. The
breakdown
is requested both
in units
sold and
in percentage
of total
busi-
ness
for
each
type
of
phonograph
record product. Figures are requested
on
percentage
of
total
sales
and
in
units of singles, EP’s, kiddie records,
and album product
sold on the racks.
The
percentage
of mono
and
stereo
will
also
be
taken. A
survey
of
the
type
of LP
unit
sold
will
also
be
taken,
in
which
a
percentage
figure
is
requested
for
Original
Cast
and
Sound Track LP’s, sound LP’s, comedy
LP’s, classical LP’s, and pop Albums.
The
record
merchandisers
are
in-
cluding
a
survey
of
the
problems
which
they
face
in
their
outlets.
When
the prevalency
of these
prob-
lems
is determined, the course which
NARM will take in solving them, will
be
outlined.
Among
the most
vital
poi’tions
of
the survey,
is the one which
will
re-
quest
dollar
gross
figures
for
rack
sales. Thereby, a total industry figure
can
be
estimated,
a
figure
useful
to
labels,
advertising
agencies,
statisti-
cal
organizations,
public
relations
firms,
etc.;
and,
of
course,
the
rack
jobbers
themselves.
NARM
has
guaranteed
that
the
questionnaire
will
be
a
completely
confidential one, the figures to be used
in
a
total, composite form
only. No
individual company figures are mean-
ingful
alone,
but merely
as
part
of
the entire rack jobber picture, the or-
ganization
feels.

Rodgers, Williams & Rose
First
In CMA’s
“Hall
of Fame”
JIMMIE RODGERS
HANK
WILLIAMS
FRED
ROSE
NASHVILLE—Jimmie Rodgers, Hank
Williams
and
Fred
Rose,
three
late
greats in country music, are the
first
three occupants of the Country Music
Association’s
new
“Country
Music
Hall of Fame.”
Bronze
plaques
testifying
to
their
memories were
unveiled
last
Friday
night,
(3)
during the Third Anniver-
sary Banquet
of
the Country Music
Association held during WSM’s Coun-
try Music Festival in Nashville.
Ken Nelson, Capitol Records execu-
tive
and CMA
president,
announced
the names of Rodgers, Williams and
Rose to the hundreds of industry per-
sonnel who were present.
Nelson
also
presented
certificates
bearing
the
exact
wording
on
the
plaques to members of the immediate
families
of
the
three men
honored.
The widows, Mrs. Jimmie Rodgers,
Mrs. Hank
(Audrey)
Williams
and
Mrs. Fred Rose accepted
certificates,
as did Wesley and Lester Rose, Fred
Rose’s
sons.
The choice of these three men was
arrived
at
through
a
secret
vote
weeks
ago
by
a
committee
of
100
veterans
of the country music
indus-
try.
For
the
time
being,
the
bronze
nlaques will be kept on exhibit in the
Tennessee
State
Museum,
Memorial
Building,
in
Nashville. Plans
call for
a permanent Country Music
building
to be
constructed
in
Nashville
later,
and the
plaques
will
then
be
placed
there.

“ENZO STUARTI”—Roulette—R25163

is dramatic and powerful as he

“I’d Cry No

“THE SWINGIN’ PETERS SISTERS”—Capitol
ST 10290
Singing

of standards, the

Girls

“ALONE”—David
Whitfield—London PS
212
One of the few
fine concert voices
in pop music,
Whitfield endows this collection of love songs with
his customary meticulousness. Many of the songs
here are
of an

perfect
for
Whitfield’s
rich,
well-rounded

Accompani-
ment, by the Paul Conrad ork, is in the appropri-
ate
full
string manner.
Sides include “Ramona,”
“I Believe,” “Look For The
Silver Lining,” “You
Are
Too
Beautiful”
and
“You’ll
Never
Walk
Alone.”

“MIS’RY AND THE BLUES”—Jack Teagarden

The

“BLUE LIGHTS”—Vol. 1—Kenny Burrell—Blue
Note 1597
This second deck,
like the
first,
is a compilation
of some jam sessions indulged in by several Blue
Note regulars with guitarist Burrell at the helm.
Others
present
include Tina
Brooks, Duke
Jor-
dan,
Bobby
Timmons, Sam
Jones,
Art
Blakey,
Junior Cook. It was dates
like these that shaped
the beginnings of modern jazz and much can be
learned
(and
appreciated)
by
the
uninhibited
“blowing” going
on.
Burrell
displays
a
capacity
for both rhythm and solo work. Relax and
listen
to
first rate modern jazz.
“JAZZ ABSTRACTIONS”—John Lewis Presents
Contemporary Music—Atlantic 1365
Gunther
Schuller has proved himself one
of the
most adventurous “third stream” jazz composers.
Here, three of his pieces, originally premiered at
a 1960 concert, are presented in all their boldness
of freedom from
conventional
forms.
Musicians
include
Ornette Coleman
and
various
first-rate
jazzmen. Jim Hall’s “Piece For Guitar & Strings”
also
gets an
inspired
airing.
There’s
a
musical
sensitivity
in
this
writing
and
many
uniquely
exciting moments.

Anthony Newfey
Britisher Anthony Newley, London
disk
star,
is on
his way
to
his third
U. S. hit with “Pop Goes the Weasel,”
which made its premiere entry on this
week’s top 100
in the number 77
slot.
Newley made his professional debut
at the age of eight, playing tent shows
and music
halls before making

in
his
starring role as the r&r actor
in “Idle on Parade.” Since then, Tony’s

row.
Stateside,

and “If She Should Come To You.”

is presently serving in a triple threat
capacity
as

of this season’s London hit play “Stup
the World,
I Want to Get Off,” which
David Merrick may bring to Broadway
next year.

Big news of the week emanates from impresario Vic
Lewis. Following
his
recent visit to the States, he has announced that plans are
in hand for Elvis
Presiey to come
to Britain. Presley has agreed to do a concert on the condi-
tion that everything
is donated to
charity. He
will pay
all
his own expenses
and the
services
of everyone
connected
with the
show,
including
the
arena,
must be given free of charge. Presley is not interested in playing a commercial
date but wants to reciprocate the British support of
his disks and
films,
it
is
expected that the concert
will
take
place some time during
the summer
of
1962.
Other
American
artists
being
brought
over by
Lewis
include The
Four
Freshmen,
Jeri
Southern
and Mel Torme who
will
have
the
backing
of
a
British group during
their ten-day
visit
in
March. Johnny Mathis has been
booked for a two-week tour in May. No confirmation has yet been received for
Frank Sinatra and Nat King Cole
to appear here.
Agent Tito Burns, who handles many
artists, including Billy Fury and The
Allisons
is
currently on a two-week
visit
to America
taking
in New York,
Philadelphia and Los Angeles. He nlans talks with record company executives
in connection
with
his own Lindon Record Company
as well
as
negotiating
American appearances for his artists.
Two
record
companies who
are
normally
competitors
are
to
link up
in
South Africa.
It was announced
that Pye Records
is
to be pressed and
dis-
tributed in South Africa by the Johannesburg affiliate of EMI under the Parlo-
phone
label.
Artists such as Lonnie Donegan, The Brook Brothers, Clarence
‘Frogman’ Henry and Benny Hill have already had disks released and further
releases are planned.
Newcomer Danny Davis has signed a long term contract with Pye Records
and makes his bow with
“Tell All The World” published by Robbins
Music.
On the same label Adele Leigh, who
is currently appearing at Zurich’s Stadt
Theatre, has a single release “Marie Marie.” Latest Reprise
single
is Frank
Sinatra’s “Coffee Song” backed with “A Foggy Day.” Piccadilly issue “Don’t
Get Around Much Any More” by A1 Saxon while on the Pye Jazz Series Bob
Wallis and his Storyville Jazzmen have “Come Along Please.”
Continuing
its expansion policy. Oriole Records has signed a contract with
London Records of America. This was announced by managing director Morris
Levy
following
his
recent
visit
to
America. Levy
told Cash Box
that
this
agreement, which
is on a selective
basis, will ensure the exposure and
distri-
bution of the
Oriole
label throughout North America.
It
will
also
afford an
excellent opportunity for British talent on that label to succeed in the Ameri-
can market.
_ Sam
Costa, who
is better known nowadays
as
a
disk
jockey, was
at
one
time one of this country’s leading vocalists. He has now turned the clock back
and
signed with
Palette Records
as a
singer. His
first disk just released
is
“I’m Changing My Hat To A Bowler” on which he
is accompanied by Tommy
McQuater and The Trad Hatters.
Straight from her American triumph, Shirley Bassey appeared in The Royal
Variety Show and topped the bill of Val Parnell’s “Sunday Night At The Lon-
don Palladium.”
Also
making
his
fourth
appearance
in
The
Royal
Show
was
Frankie
Vaughan, whose latest disk “Tower Of Strength” is getting a lot of exposure.
Frankie
flies to Cologne on Nov. 23 where he will represent Britain in the big
NATO show being organized by German
Radio.
Versatile Roy Castle has a tour of South Africa and America lined up for
early in 1962. His many talents are featured on his Philips L.P. “Castle Wise.”
John Barry has returned from the States with the news that he has concluded
an agreement with film producer Marty Melcher to write the music for both
film
and
theatrical
productions
in
America.
This
will
necessitate
frequent
visits
to the
States—at
least four a year. Plans are

for a
music publishing outlet to be handled here by Melcher’s European representa-
tive Leslie Conn.
Cameo Records European rep Harry Walters tells us that Chubby Checker
is to make a European tour and will arrive
in England on December 21 for
TV, radio and personal appearances. “The Twist” dance craze sparked
off by
Checker
is currently swinging here and
is having
a great impact on dance
halls up and down the country. Pop singer Bobby Rydell
is
also expected
to
visit Europe some time in February.
Latest names to be added to Milton Subotsky’s film “It’s Trad Dad” are dj’s
Alan Freeman and Brian Matthew.
From EMI comes news that David Whitfield has been signed up
to record

UA's First Promo Conference
NEW YORK—United Artists Records
last Friday
(17) inaugurated a series
of
special
Promotion
Conferences
in
which
executives
of the record com-
pany
will meet
Informally with
dis-
tributor
promotion men
at
the New
York
headquarters
of
the
firm
to,
firstly, allow
the men
in
the
field an
opportunity
to meet
personally
with
those
with whom
they
are
in
tele-
phone
or
mail
contact
at
the
label
and, secondly, to give the UA person-
nel an opportunity to learn first-hand
the
situation
in various
parts
of the
country.
In
attendance
at
the
initial
meet-
ing,
with
Art
Talmadge,
president,

Distributors,
Boston:
Larry
Cohen, Marnel Distributing
Co., Phil-
adelphia,

Licata, Cosnat

uting

Bernie
Block,
Marnel
of
Baltimore,
Ray
Free,
Big
Town
Distributors,
New York, and A1 Valente, Arc
Dis-
tributing
Co., Detroit.
Meeting
with
the
promotion men
were Eddie Mathews, A & R
super-
visor and national promotion director;
Jerry Raker, national
sales manager,
and
Norman
Weiser,
vice-president,
each of whom held individual sessions
with
the
group
following

breakfast

individual
department
meet-
ings,
a
luncheon
session
took
place,
with a general meeting of
all parties
involved completing the day.
The
visitors
were
also
introduced
to
all home
office
personnel
at UA,
and were able to meet with the heads
of the various divisions to obtain any
special information they
desired.
Talmadge,
a
staunch

of
this method
of record
exposure,
said
that UA will hold several other simi-
lar
seminars

to

Southern
and Western
personnel.
In

that
in

much closer liaison with the distribu-

promotion

“THE MUSIC FROM MILK & HONEY”—Wild

FRANCK: Symphony in D Minor—Chicago Sym-
phony Orchestra conducted by Pierre Monteux
RCA Victor LM 2514
Pierre

Panel
Debates
''Is Stereo Necessary?"
NEW YORK—An audience estimated
at between 300 and 400 persons heard
a debate, “Is
Stereo Necessary?”, at
the
Great Northern
Hotel
here
last
week
(28).
The debate, sponsored by NARAS,
the
disk
awards
organization,
pro-
duced
the
general
conclusion
that
stereo was not yet perfected, but had
a future, and that it had already made
a great deal of money.
Those on the “pro” side of the panel
felt
that
stereo was
“not
true”
and
that
it was done just for effect, while
the “con”
side felt that
it “enhanced
music” and was commercially success-
ful. The “pro” panelists were Enoch
Light, Skitch Henderson, Bill Milten-
berg,
of
Apex,
and
Manny
Albam.
The
“con”
panel
consisted
of
Dave
Kapp, Francis Robinson, an assistant
at
the
Metropolitan
Opera,
Woody
Herman and Gerry Mulligan.
Also
discussed were
the
problems
and
difficulties
encountered by
engi-
neers
in
recording
in
stereo,
and
whether the
stereo
effect was
at the
expense of the material.
Panel moderator was WNEW-New
York deejay William
B. Williams.

Kramer To Manage
Gospel
Stars
NEW YORK—Gary Kramer resigned
last

commissioned
famed

right Langston Hughes
to

for

Dec.

Theatre
in New

the

Prof.

&

of

Singers, and on a

Singers.
Kramer
also
manages Billy Dee Williams, the actor
last seen on Broadway in “Taste Of
Honey.”
Williams’
first
vocal
LP,

“Let’s

been

Kramer

DORSEY BURNETTE (Dot 16305)
This is a tug-at-your heartstrings tale of “A Country Boy In The Army,”
who had a 3-day Christmas pass, was broke and thousands of miles from
home.
It’s a happy-ending
lilter that Dorsey Burnette delivers
(in part
talk-sing fashion) with warmth and
sincerity. Also keep an eye on the
feelingful cha cha beat lover’s lament, “Dying Ember.” Can
also make
the hit grade. Chalk up two grade “A” assists by the Billy Vaughn outfit.

MGM/Verve Rushes
4
LP's
For Xmas Sales
NEW YORK—MGM/Verve Records is
rushing four LP’s to market in time
to cash-in on the Christmas gift buy-
ing rush. Two sets are on the MGM la-
bel and two on Verve.
Highlight of this
special release
is
a
twist album
titled
“Let’s Do
The
Twist For
Adults’’
on MGM,
which
features A&R
staffer
Danny
Davis
and The
Twisters. The second
set, a
deluxe two record package,
is
a
col-
lection of MGM million sellers featur-
ing
such
all time
hits
as
“It’s
Only
Make Believe,” Conway Twitty;
“It’s
All In The Game,” Tommy Edwards;
“Teen
Angel,” Mark
Dinning;
“The
Purple
People
Eater,”
Sheb Wooley
and others.
One
of
the
Verve
releases
offers
“Chicago And All That Jazz” featur-
ing selections from the NBC-TV net-
work special project series “America’s
Music” and stars such jazz personali-
ties as Eddie Condon, Bud Freeman,
Bob
Haggart,
Gene
Krupa,
Jimmy
McPartland,
Pee Wee
Russell,
Joe
Sullivan,
Jack
Teagarden,
Lil Arm-
strong and Blossom
Seeley.
The other Verve
set
is a jazz ver-
sion of the smash Broadway musical
“How To Succeed In Business With-
out
Really
Trying”
with
Gary
Mc-
Farland and his Orchestra.

Capitol Adds Top Singles
To Starline Series
NEW YORK—Capitol
Records
has
added to its Starline series the reissue
of its top singles over its 21-year his-
tory. The
first
such
release,
consist-
ing
of
25
singles,
50
sides,
is
being
made Dec. 18. The label’s Starline se-
ries
has
previously
consisted
of
re-
issues
in LP form.
Each
disk
will

NEW YORK—Bob Neal, talent man-

effec-
tive Jan.
1, 1962.
Neal, who has been owner of radio
station KCIJ
in

for the
past year, has sold the station in order
to join Wil-Helm.
Neal
is
responsible
for
the
early
development of Elvis Presley’s career,
and later worked with such artists as
Roy
Orbison,
Warren
Smith,
Carl
Perkins and Johnny Cash. The move
was made on the part of the agency
to
strengthen
its
roots,
feeling
that
Nashville, more than any other
city,
needs
strong
forces
in

its
available talent.
Wil-Helm
now
represents
Joe
Dowell, Bobby Helms,

and The Wilburn
Brothers,
and
an-
nouncement will be made soon of other
acts to be represented by the agency.
Neal,
in charge
of talent
develop-
ment, will join Joe D. Taylor, director
of talent in co-ordinating the manage-
ment,
booking
and
development
of
clients of agency.

Jack
Mills On
His 70th
Birthday
NEW YORK—Jack
Mills,
head
of
Mills Music, celebrated his 70th birth-
day Tues.
(5), an
occasion
that was
marked by a surprise party given by
the staff of the New York office.
After entering the
office where the
fete was held. Mills remarked that “I
can’t make a speech, but this
is won-
derful— I feel
like I’m
living my
life
over again.”
The
vet
publisher
was
presented
with a plaque of appreciation and ac-
complishment, and he was
also given
a
birthday
card
signed by
the New
York
staff.
A light-hearted congratulatory tele-
gram was
read
from
Mills’
London
office in which the hope was expressed,
in
verse, that by the time
Mills was
71,
the
London
branch
would
have
come-up with another “Stardust,” the
top Mills copyright.
Mills
also
was
given
a
surprise
party on
Sat.,
Dec.
2,
at the Drake
Hotel, and included among the guests
were
Leroy
Anderson,
Jesse
Block,
Red
Buttons,
Irving Caesar, Sammy
Cahn,
Jack
Carter,
Morton
Gould,
Ted
Lewis,
Mitchell
Parish, Jimmy
Van Heusen and Jack
Yellen.
Instead
of
birthday
gifts.
Mills’
friends
are making
contributions
to
form a music library at Brandeis Uni-
versity
in
Waltham,
Mass.,
to
be
known
as
the Jack
Mills
Music
Li-
brary.
Mills
has
been
greatly
inter-
ested for many years in Brandeis Uni-
versity,
the
first
Jewish-sponsored
non-sectarian university in the U.S.

JAZZ
PICKS
OF THE WEEK
“BOOKER LITTLE OUT FRONT”—Candid 8027
A great tragedy to the jazz world was the silenc-
ing
of
the promising trumpet
of
Booker
Little
some two months
ago. He had shown
in
his 23
years a command
of harmony and original
self-
expression that
is
the mark
of
a mature
artist.
Through
this
Candid album,
Little’s
talents
are
captured for his legion of fans. His sound
is big,
impressive
and
invigorating
as
he
reads “We
Speak,” “Man
Of
Words,”
and “A New
Day.”
Album
should be a welcome asset
for
all
Little
buffs.
“A JAZZ VERSION OF KEAN”—Riverside Jazz
Stars—Riverside 397
With a strong emphasis on the melodic
qualities
of the
score, the Riverside Jazz Stars consisting
of Blue
Mitchell
on
trumpet, Jimmy
Heath
on
tenor
sax and the Bobby Timmons
Trio
read a
firmly-constructed LP
of the Alfred Drake
star-
rer. The 8 selections played are not distorted
or
mutilated
but
rendered
as
a
valid,
lyrical
jazz
treatment
of
the
original
score.
Disk’s
authen-
ticity makes
it a stimulating musical experience.
“ON THE SPUR OF THE MOMcfNT”—Horace
Parian Quintet—Blue Note 4074
The flowing piano of Horace Parian
is beautifully
matched with the
skills of Tommy Turrentine on
trumpet, Stanley Turrentine on tenor sax, George
Tucker
on
bass and
A1 Harewood
on drums
in
this buoyant, swinging offering from Blue Note.
The boys start things moving with “On The Spur
Of The Moment,” a Parian original with a rhyth-
mic blues
tack that
is
aptly accentuated by the
hot piano. “Pyramid”
is another fine example of
the group’s superb sound. LP ranks as easy, top-
notch jazz listening.

“HAVE A GOOD TIME WITH JOE WILLIAMS”
—Roulette R52071
Joe Williams is in his usual top form as he reads
a
group
of
Ernie
Wilkins-arranged

in

re-
laxed, easy Williams

of “Old

and his ork provide a well-molded musical back-
ground
for

Disk
should
attract attention with
Williams’
fans.
“MARTYN GREEN SIGNS THE GILBERT &
SULLIVAN SONG BOOK”—MGM E 3980
The magnificent impish quality of Martyn Green
brings a touch of genius to this fine collection of
melodies from the light operas of Gilbert &
Sul-
livan. Perhaps no other singer in the world today
is more closely associated with G & S than Gi-een.
His
steadfast
devotion
to
his
craft
has
earned
him an
endless
string
of
laurels
and
this
disk
must rank as
still another honor for the talented
Britisher. The Green reading of “I Am The Very
Modern Of Modern Major General”
is the high-
point of the album and must be classed as super-
lative lung work. Jane Bronhill and Andrew Gold
assist
in
other
selections.
Disk
should
attract
mobs of Green and Gilbert & Sullivan fans.
“15 COUNTRY GREATS BY

105

ing Margie Bowes, Roy Acuff, and Rusty & Doug.
The tunes are sturdies with proven records of pub-
lic acceptance. LP should draw attention in coun-
try circles.

ar-

on bass, and Purnell Rice on drums. All the tunes

mons give the set a polished free-flowing touch.

Versatile

over a hundreds

Born

Solomon
Burke
Solomon
Burke, who
is
currently
riding the charts with “Just Out Of
Reach” (#27
in the week’s top
100),
received
his
principal
vocal
training
in
his home town
church. He was
a
soloist in a chuch at 9, and at 12 had
his own church called “Solomon’s Tem-
ple.” From
the
Temple,
which
was
located
in
South
Philadelphia,
he
broadcast his own radio show.
While
still in his teens, the wife of
a prominent Philly spinner discovered
him, and was instrumental
in having
young
Burke
signed
at
Apollo
Rec-
ords.
It was
at that time that Burke
was
seen
on
the
Steve
Allen
Show.
From then on things started
to hap-
pen.
Late
in
1960
he was
signed by
Atlantic Records where his career sky-
rocketed when
he
cut
“Just Out Of
Reach.”
Burke
has appeared on many top-
rated TV shows as well as important
night clubs
all over the country.
Chuck
Foote
Chuck Foote came into the national
limelight
with
“Running
Out
Of
Kisses,” which
is
in the #87
slot
in
the
week’s
chart. The
Soncraft Rec-
ords
star was born
in Manhattan on
March
10, 1942 and attended
P.S.
12
on
New
York’s
Lower
East
Side.
While attending the Metropolitan Vo-
cational
School,
his vocal
talent won
him the lead singer spot in a neighbor-
hood group
called
the
Five
Reasons.
A
series of wedding, and dance dates
followed.
A few years later a chance meeting
with a friend led to a successful audi-
tion for a
fill-in spot with the Crests
(“Sixteen Candles”). A deal for Foote
was made to join the group and that
very same night he was on
the bus
westbound
for
a
one-nighter
tour
playing theatres, arenas, auditoriums,
etc.
Most of Foote’s spare time on the
road was spent in writing and rehears-
ing
in
an
effort
to
develop
his own
style
of
signing
and
performing.
Many
tours
and many groups
later,
he
made
that
all-important
demo.
From that came a management deal,
a record
contract and eventually
his
hit deck of “Kisses.”

BIOGRAPHIES BENELUX ARTISTS
THE COUSINS
(PALETTE)
Four
boy-friends
discovered
at
the
club
‘*Les
Cousins,
Grand’Place
in
Brussels.
Their
first record
for
Palette,
“Kili
Watch,**
reached
the
charts
im-
mediately.
*‘Kili
Watch’*
remained
number one
In
the Top Ten
for several
weeks.
Today, The Cousins
are
one
of
the
hottest
teen-ager
combo's
on
the
Continent. A few months
after
the
release
of
‘'Kili
Watch,”
they
received
a
Golden
Record
for
this
disc.
Their
current
hit
is
”Dang
Dang”/Stodola.
The Cousins appeared on TV and Radio
in Belgium,
Holland,
France,
Sweden,
Germany
and
Italy
(Caterina
Valente
Show).
An
EP
is
iust
out:
“The
Cousins
Celebrate
Christmas.”
Every
new
release
of
The
Cousins
appears
on
the
charts.
They
are
favourite
best-sellers
in
record
shops.
This
is
quite
unusual
for a Belgian group.
THE TRAMPS
(FONTANA)
Five boys from Antwerp, who got undoubtedly their
taste
for
Rock
and
Roll
underneath
the
harbour
lights
of
their famous town. These young boys'
first
record
“Maharadia’’/“Tomawak”
made
o
world-
tour and
this
record
will
soon
be
out
in
America.
To
maintain
a
position
on
a
hit-parade
is
not
so
easy,
especially
not
for
a
local
product,
but
The
Tramps made
it and
this proves
their
quality.
Their
next
one
was
“Murder”
and
“Macacafoo”
that
also touched America and you
will
hear
of
this
re-
lease
shortly.
THE JOKERS
(PHILIPS)
One
of the most popular rock-combo’s
of
Belgium,
recording
for
Philips.
First
record was a
topper:
a
traditional
song,
adapted
for
teeners:
“Cecilia
Rock.”
The
combo
is
composed
of
six
boys
of
a
different profession
each:
a student, an
engineer, a
storekeeper,
an
electrician,
a
car-driver
and
a
cadet
of the
Military Academy.
The
senior has
23,
and
the
junior has
16 years.
Their
latest record
just
came
out
and
looks
even
more
promising
than
their
first:
“Kwezelke”
(a
traditional) and “Congo
Rock”
(a
very
actual
title).
THE BLUE DIAMONDS
(DECCA)
Brothers Rudi
(20) and Riem
(18) de Wolff came
to
Holland
from
Indonesia
in
1949.
Started with
Ha-
waiian
band,
later
were
inspired
by
the
Everly
Brothers,
but found
style
of
their own.
First
record
had
“Till
I
Kissed
'fou”
c/w
“I’m
Gonna
Get
Married,”
released autumn
1959, and was
an
im-
mediate
success.
Radio
and
TV
appearances.
Made
two
albums,
“Always
.
The
Blue
Diamonds” and
"Till We Meet Again,” wiih mod-
ernized
standards.
“Ramona”
recording
become
worldwide
hit.
Version appeared
In “Cash Box Too
100,”
sold
quarter
of a
million
in
Holland
(which
had
never
happened
before
over
there)
and
one
million
in Germany.
Guest appearances
in
all
parts
of the world. Sang
In German
film
in
1961. Ameri-
can
songwriters
teom
Pomus
&
Shuman
wrote
“Little Ship”
for Blue Diamonds,
their
current
best
seller.
1961
hits:
"Ramona,”
“In A
Little
Spanish
Town”
and
“Little
Ship.”

Team made

up
til)

JOHNNY HOES
(PHILIPS)
Singer,
composer,
lyric
writer,
music
publisher,
talent scout and promoter.
Born 1917
in Rotterdam.
Now
has
own
publishing
firm
in
Weert
(south
of
Holland). Sang for allied troops in 1945. Since 1954
his
songs
became
great
hits.
Very
prolific
song
writer.
Of
his
own
recordings,
“Och
Was
Ik
Maar” became one
of biggest Dutch
hits
in
1961.
Also
very popular
in Belgium. Song
just mentioned
originally was
a
carnival
song some
time
ago
in
southern
part of Holland, but became a nationwide
hit
in
Dutch
version
by
Johnny
Hoes.
Hoes
also
made a German version.
Caterina Velente recorded
the song
as “Ich Mach'Mir Nix.” More than
250,-
000
copies
of
the
Dutch
Hoes
version
have
been
sold
now.
Was
presented
with
a
platinum
record
with
ten
diamonds
(and
a
gold
watch
with
in-
scription)
November
30th.

ail

i

Laurie & Affiliates Report 50*^0
Net Sales Increase For ’61
NEW YORK—Laurie Records and
its
associate
labels
last week reported
a
strong sales year in 1961, with gross
sales
increased by over 30% and net
profits by over 50%.
The year saw the establishment of
Dion as top teen attraction, with such
smashes as “Runaround Sue” and the
current “The Wanderers.”
Other
big
successes
scored by
the
label
in
’61
included
dates
by Gary
Bonds,
“Quarter
to
Three,”
“School
Is
Out,” “School
Is In” and
his
cur-
rent
hit, “Dear Lady Twist,” on the
Laurie-handled
Legrand
label,
and
The Jarmels’ “A
Little Bit of Soap,”
on
the
Rust
label,
also
handled by
Laurie.
Recognizing
the
increased
impor-
tance
of the world
disk market,
the
label’s
Bob
Schwartz
spent
four
weeks in Europe visiting most of the
countries
there.
Changes were made
in
a number
of countries
in order to
get the “most effective and hard-hit-
ting
distributors”
in these
areas.
In
1962,
the
label
will
continue
to
re-
lease
foreign
product
here, and
ses-
sions along this line have been set for
release
soon.
1961 also showed increased activity
by
the
Laurie
publishing
operations.
Just Music and Schwartz Music.
In the coming year, Laurie expects
to
continue
the
development
of new
talent, the
first such attraction to be
a duo. Dean and Jean, to be followed
by a new young singles’ artist.
Victor Ups Stereo Sales
For Xmas; Other ’61 Successes
Victor Launches Dealer
Special Order Service
The RCA
Victor
“Record
Dealer
Special Order Service” will enable
all
dealers
to
assure
themselves
and
their customers
of
quick
delivery
of
any
album
which
is
out
of
stock
either
in
their own
or their distribu-
tor’s
inventory.
“Dealer Special Order Service” cer-
tificates are similar to the carbonless
forms which are now used for Amer-
ican Express, Diner’s Club, and other
charge
accounts,
will
permit
an
ef-
ficient and streamlined ordering
sys-
tem.
When
a customer wishes
to
order
an
out-of-stock
record,
the
dealer
simply fills in the album number, date
of order and the address of the cus-
tomer on the
certificate.
It
is already
addressed for mailing, with
a
“post-
age prepaid” imprint on one
side.
The
certificates
come
in
two
de-
nominations,
equivalent
to
Victor’s
nationally
advertised
prices
of
$4.98
and
$5.98.
Victor
distributors
across
the country receive on memo
billing,
a quantity
of these
certificates,
pre-
coded
for
identification
and
billing
purposes.
Apostoleris Buys Out
Halonka
In Alpha Distribs
NEW YORK—Harry Apostoleris has
purchased Johnny Halonka’s
interest
in Alpha
Distributing
Corp., the ma-
jor distributor here.
The
deal,
for
an
undisclosed

a nine-year

tion
of Alpha.

MRIA Forms
Standards Committee
NEW YORK—In
a
step
to
“insure
consistent high standards” in the tape
industry, an
11 man standards com-
mittee has been
set-up by the Mag-
netic Recording Industry Association
(MRIA).
The
committee
will
be
chaired by John Ihrig, executive veep
of Webcor,
Inc.
Ihrig
said
that
the
chairmen
of
the
11
sub-committees
will
form
their
groups
by
enlisting
not only MRIA members, but others
who have special talents in their par-
ticular fields.

Command’s ’61 Sales 20% Over ’60
NEW YORK—Command Records, the
strong
“sound” LP
label,
increased
sales 20%
in
’61 over
’60, according
to Enoch Light, executive director.
Light also reported
a
“significant”
increase in the average number of al-
bum
sales per
release, claiming that
the
label’s
average
sale
per
release
was
higher
than
that
of
any
other
label.
Command’s
overall
breakdown
shows 85% of sales in stereo and 15%
in mono.
Looking forward to a “banner year”
for stereo this year. Light noted that
stereo
set
manufacturers
had
their
biggest year
in
’61.
Gershwin Package Show
Sef
For
U.S., Canada
NEW
YORK — “A
Night
With
Gershwin” starring Rhonda Fleming,
Earl
Wrightson,
the
Ray
Charles
Singers
and
Skitch
Henderson,
con-
ducting a small symphony orchestra,

presi-
dent.
The show, which will commemorate
the 25th anniversary
of the death of
the great
cleffer,
will

a

week tour on March
9, and will cover

United
States
and

Among the cities already lined up are
Boston,
Montreal,
Pittsburgh,
Phila-
delphia,
Hershey
and
Washington.

set.
Per-
formances will be given in arenas and
auditoriums.
This
will
be
the
first
concert
for
Miss
Fleming.
Although
she
first
achieved stardom as a motion picture
actress, she has also appeared in con-

in

and
in

stock.

appear

on

televi-
sion program.

“With so many more stereo sets in
homes this year, the potential market

stereo albums

as
well

leaning
towards
buying
albums
instead of singles, and can be counted
on
for
a
substantial amount
of
this
year’s album sales.”
Light’s
current
project
is

fiick
theme-music LP on Command,

on 35mm
film. His
“Stereo
35” LP of showtunes—^first Command

seller last year.

“ARE YOU READY FOR PHYLLIS DILLER?”
—Verve V 15031
Phyllis Diller launches her second LP outing with
ten extremely funny monologs which ranks as a

beat humor and professional

many yocks. Some highpoints of the disk
are. the
Diller
bits
titled
“The Way

And Turkey,” and “Small

could step out sales-wise.

DENMARK
Several
Swedish
recording
artists
have
been
contracted
to
the
summer
restaurant Kystens Perle, where among others Anita Lindblom, Siv Malmquist,
Lill-Babs and Monica Zetterlund will be seen and heard this coming summer.
350
contributions have
been
received by
the
local
Danish
song
Festival,
which takes place on Feb. 11th. The winning song will represent Denmark in
this year’s Eurovision Song Festival from Luxembourg in the middle of March.
Ola Mortensen, Chris Dane, Dario Campeotto, Gitte, Birthe Wilke and Ellen
Winther
will present the songs
in this
year’s
local Festival over Denmark’s
radio and TV.
German
recording
artists were
recently on
tour
in Denmark. They were
Freddy, Bill Ramsey, Helmut Zacharias, and others. Great success is reported.
.At the same time, the Danish artists Dario Campeotto and Gustav Winckler
visited Germany, doing a TV show with Werner Muller.
Liberty people here from Stockholm on their promotion tour for the Liberty
label, which debuted here on Feb.
1. While in Denmark, Bobby Vee made a TV
program for Denmark’s TV Co.
Helge Roundquist of Cupol, Stockholm, in Copenhagan for biz talks. He might
leave for a biz visit in Vienna.

local Song

11.

ducer Snuffy Garrett, press manager Arnie Mills and press man A1 Hunt, who
flew in from his London
office. Handling the Liberty label in Finland will be
Oy R. E. Westerlund Ab, which also distributes HMV and Mercury in Finland.
Vee made a TV show while in Finland.
NORWAY
The Key Brothers, three young men from
Oslo, have now made their
first
English language
record
for
Triola
here. The
songs
are “Happy
Birthday,
Sweet Sixteen” and “Candle of Faith.” The latter song
is a Norwegian com-
position with lyrics in English by Norwegian-American Per W. Schulze. The
trio has already been recording in Norwegian and Swedish, and their Geiunan
debut record
is expected within a couple of weeks.
Eilif Meyer of A/S Nera (RCA in Norway) reports great success of “Grynet”
Molvig, who this week enters the charts with her Nomvegian version of “Wings
Of A Dove,” in Norwegian “Det Var Du Som Sa Nei” (“You’re The One Who
Said No),” with Norwegian lyrics by C. C. Boyesen. Publisher of the song is
Belinda
(Scandinavia) AB
in
Stockholm.
This
is
the
first time Miss Molvig
appears on the best selling charts.
Young Noi’wegian singer Ray Adams, who has been doing very well in Swe-
den recently, is now getting very international. His recording of “Violetta” is
reported as having sold more than 300,000
in some European countries and in
the near future the record will be released in England, United States and New
Zealand.
Melody Grand Prix in Norway
(the
local Song Festival)
starts on Feb.
5.
The 101 song contributions are now being studied by the jury, who will choose
the songs which will be presented in the competition. Carsten Kloumann will
be handling the arrangements for NRK-TV, and
did
so
last year. However,
there was some controversey here when he published the songs in the Festival
at his own publishing house.
SWEDEN
Anders Holmstedt, head of EMI
off for biz visit to London. Composer and
music publisher Stig Anderson expected back from biz visit in London over the
weekend. Helge Roundquist, head of Cupol, on biz trip at the Continent.
Lennart Reuterskiold of Reuter & Reuter told Cash Box that during his trip
to Italy, Switzerland and Germany recently he was very successful in looking
for new songs as well as placing Swedish songs
in these
countries. Reuter-
skiold has among others the world wide copyrights for ten songs by American
composer Spencer Williams and so far Essex Music in England has taken those
songs for Great Britain.
Cupol presented Gosta “Snoddas” Nordgren with a diamond record for the
sale of 250,000 of his 10 year old “Flottarkarlek.”
It was on a radio program
on Jan. 26, 1952, he sang the song the first time, and it started something of a
sensation
in Swedish music
life. The
first 100,000 records were
sold
in a few
weeks and another 100,000 during the next two months. The record
is
still a
good
seller, according to Cupol, and
it seems to have become something of a
standard.
In Stockholm for two days during their present promotion trip for Liberty
were Bobby Vee, Al Bennett, Snuff Garrett, Arnie Mills and A1 Hunt. At the
press party at the Apollonia Hotel, Bennett told Cash Box that he was very
happy with the trip as
it had started very successfully and he was sure that
Liberty would be doing very well at the European market, where EMI started
the distribution on Feb.
1. While in Sweden, SBC-TV made an interview
(on
radio)
with Bobby Vee, which the TV refused due
to
its “non-commercial”
policy. The non-commercial TV was afraid that he would sing songs from one
of
his
current
recordings,
which
would
be
“record
promotion,”
something
SBC-TV wants to stay out of. With Vee making TV shows in both Finland and
Denmark, Swedish TV viewers were the only Scandinavians who missed him
this time.
What’s wrong with jazz in Sweden these days? Sweden, not long ago con-
sidered one
of the most jazz-minded
countries
in the
world, seems
to have
lost
all
its interest in jazz
records. From being a nice and
profitable
affair
here, handling jazz records
is now far from
profitable. People and companies
handling jazz records are confused. An exception from this rule
is the Dixie-
land jazz records, which
still have a market here.
Pelle Nystrom, press and public relations man of Metronome, married Elisa-
beth
Lilliestiarna on Jan. 27th in the Djurgarden Church in Stockholm. The
couple left for Egypt, where they will spend their honeymoon.
Bernt Baune
of Gehrmans
told Cash Box that he
is very happy with the
success of “Dance With A Dolly”
all over Scandinavia. The Damita Jo record
has been on the charts in most Scandinavian countries. The sheet music is also
selling very good.
Hans Westerberg of Oy R. E. Westerlund Ab in Helsinki in Stockholm for
biz talks with EMI last week.

Chad Mitchell
Trio
The
Chad
Mitchell
Trio, who
are
currently riding the charts with “Liz-
zie Borden,” started singing together
two years ago in the Gonzaga Univer-
sity glee
club.
Their professional
ca-
reer was launched by their first “book-
ing agent,”
Rev. Reinard W. Beaver
of St. Augustine’s Church in Spokane.
Father Beaver heard the boys perform
many times on campus and persuaded
them
to come to New York with him
and take a crack at show business.
The
trio
secured
a booking
at
the
Village
Barn when
they
arrived
in
Gotham—thanks to the efforts of their
manager.
Within
a
short
time,
they
were under contract
to a
large man-
agement firm, and guest appearances
on
television
and
radio
followed
in
quick
succession.
They
appeared
on
the Pat Boone TV Show and were reg-
ulars on the Arthur Godfrey daytime
radio shows, while their public appear-
ances have included dates at the Blue
Angel with Shelley Berman, and with
Harry Belafonte at Carnegie Hall.
Since then the Kapp recording stars
have
never
looked
back,
and
their
popularity steadily increases. The Trio
consists
of
Chad
Mitchell,
Mike
Kobluk and Joe Frazier.
Paris
Sisters
The
Paris
Sisters
big break came
in 1954 when they came to the War-
field Theatre in San Francisco to hear
their
idols,
the
Andrews.
Between
shows the youngsters went back stage
to
meet
the
long-established
head-
liners. The Andrews
like what they
heard and saw
so much that at the
next show they asked them to come up
from their seats
in the audience and
perform. The reaction was so enthusi-
astic that the next day the girls were
swamped with offers from agents.
As they grew
into
their
teens
the
girls
developed
a harmony
style
all
their own, one which was
to launch
their first records into immediate big-
sellers, beginning with “Be My Boy”
and more recently with “I Love How
You
Love
Me.”
Currently,
they
are
pulling coin with “He Knows
I Love
Him Too Much.”
The trio-’s acts, (and they have more
than a
couple)
includes
routines
be-
yond the singing which has made their
Gregmark
records
best-sellers.
The
girls
play
instruments,
piano
and
guitar, and dance in either tap, ballet
or modern.

NEW YORK—Louis
Bernstein,
the
longtime
(since
1911)
president
of
Shapiro-Bernstein
Music,
died
last
week
(15)
at his home
in Manhattan,
about a month before he would have
reached
his
89th birthday.
Bernstein, who was
active as head
of the firm until just
six weeks ago,
was also a vice-president and director
of ASCAP since 1914.
In
mourning
the
death
of
Bern-
stein,
Stanley
Adams,
president
of
ASCAP,
said
that Bernstein “guided
and helped the careers
of many men
and women
of music ... he
will be
sorely missed.”
Bernstein, born
in New
York,
en-
tered
the
music
business
in
1898
in
partnership with Harry Von Tilzer as
Bernstein & Von
Tilzer Music. Their
first success was “My Old New Hamp-
shire Home.”
In 1911, Bernstein formed Shapiro-
Bernstein with Morris Bernstein, who
died a year later. Morris Bernstein’s
son, Elliot, also active in the pubbery,
died
five years ago.

John W.
Griffin
Dies;
Former RIAA Exec. Sec.
NEW YORK—John
W.
Griffin,
a
music business
vet and formerly ex-
ecutive
secretary
of
the
Record
In-
dustry
Association
of
America
(RIAA), died suddenly here last week
(15)
at the age of
68.
After
serving
as
a
1st
Lieut,
in
France
during World War
I,
Griffin
worked as a reporter and ad man in
New York.
In
1922,
he
founded
his
own music store here. He was named
sales manager of RCA Victor Records
in
1932,
and was
later named
sales
vice-president
for
the American and
Columbia labels, when the former firm
was merged with
Columbia.
During World War
II, he acquired
a
substantial
interest
in
a
Scranton
pressing
plant,
later
sold
to
Capitol,
with the firm becoming the east coast
pressing
affiliate
of
the
label,
and
Griffin being named a director of the
firm.
He
became
executive
secretary
of
RIAA
in
1951, holding the post
until
several years ago.
Griffin was a graduate of Holy Cross
(1916) and served as president of the
school’s
alumni
association
for
the
past two years. Long active in Cath-
olic lay circles, he was made a Knight
of Malta in 1951. He was also a mem-
ber
of
the
Athletic
and
University
clubs
in New York.
A Mass for Griffin was set for Mon-
day (19) at the Temple of Faith, Hope
&
Charity
at
59th
Street and
Park
Ave. He will be buried
in Watertown,
N.Y.,
his birthplace.

“JERRY
KENNEDY’S
DANCING
GUITARS
ROCK ELVIS’ HITS’’—Smash SRS 67004
Jerry Kennedy pays an attractive musical tribute
to Elvis Presley on this Smash album containing
instrumental
versions
of
the
chanter’s
previous
triumphs. With an able assist from a chorus, that
joins in sans-lyric, the Kennedy group offer first-
string arrangments of “Love Me Tender,” “Heart-
break Hotel,” and “All Shook Up.” Set looms as
powerful package for teens.
“A
SLICE OF LIFE”—Porter Wagoner—RCA
Victor LP 2447
Porter Wagoner’s top-drawer country talents are
beautifully
showcased
in
this
Victor album
of
ballads and weepers. The chanter
is in fine form
as he injects the necessary
feeling and emotion
to the tunes that he renders. Some extremely
lis-
tenable tracks on the set are “My Name Is Mud,”
“Sugarfoot
Rag,”
“Cryin’
Loud,”
and
his
cur-
rent
hit “Misery Loves Company.” Disk
should
attract a posse of the songster’s fans.
“MEXICO
WITH
LOVE”—Jo
Basile^Audio
Fidelity AFSD 5946
Jo Basile dishes up a collection of popular Mexi-
can
melodies
on
this
extremely
appealing
disk
from Audio
Fidelity.
Basile gives proof positive
of
accoi’dion
virtuosity by
rendering
the
selec-
tions
here
with
tremendous
range and
melodic
scope. Backed by his ork, the accordionist comes
through with some exciting arrangements of “La
Bamba,” “La Raspa,” and “El Rancho Grande.”
LP looms
as a sure noisemaker for
Basile.
“THE SOUND OF SPIRITUALS”—Echoes
Of
Zion—Smash SRS 67006
The
Echoes Of
Zion
were founded twenty-four
years
ago
in
Atlanta,
Georgia. Throughout
the
past quarter of a century
the group has toured
the
U.S.
winning
countless
admirers
for
their
moving, inspirational rendering
of gospel favor-
ites. The Smash disk showcases the voices singing
gospel
tunes
like “When
Jesus
Comes,”
“Tell
God,” and “Walk Right In.” LP could prove pop-
ular in many markets.

is a generous helping of the relaxed, easy
side
of the

coin. Charles

Twisters should find terpsichorean delights in this
disk of twistin’ favorites by Chubby Checker. The
songster has earned many laurels for his past wax
efforts and
this new LP should garner loads
of
honors and coin for the talented

offers such blockbuster geared-for-dancing
selec-
tions
as “Slow
Twistin’,”
his newest
hit
entry,
“The Fly,” and “Dear Lady Twist.” Disk should
spark very strong sales.
“TWISTIN’ ROUND
THE WORLD”—Chubby
Checker—Parkway P 7008
Chubby Checker comes on strong on this new LP
which
is destined
to move quickly to the upper
reaches
of chartdom. This time out the
chanter
reads songs in seven languages including English,
Hebrew and
Greek. Chubby’s
distinctive,
potent
vocal style
is showcased on such items as “Hava
Nagila,” “Never On Sunday,” and “Tea For Two.”
Disk should score heavily.

dahl, who

ork, has come up
with
some quality arrangements for the sturdies that
the crooner reads. The chanter
is

Ventures
Don Wilson and Bob Bogle met four
years ago when they were both work-
ing
in
the
construction
business
in
Seattle, Washington. The boys quickly
realized
that
they
both
played
the
guitar and soon were getting together
for daily jam
sessions.
The
twosome
continued
practicing
for many months and by the Summer
of 1959 they were able to interchange
parts, playing either
lead, rhythm
or
bass
guitar. They were booked
in
a
Tacoma
night
club but
continued
to
work
days
as
they
still
needed
the
security of steady jobs.
Don and Bob began to build a potent
instrumental group including “Nokie”
Edwards on guitar and “Howie” John-
ston on percussion which became the
basis for the Ventures. The boys big
break
came
when
they
cut
“Walk,
Don’t Run” for their own Blue Hori-
zon
label. Bob
Reisdorff, Dolton
top-
per, took notice of the tune’s growing
popularity
and
offered
to
distribute
the record nationally through the re-
sources of Liberty. The rest is history.
The Ventures have appeared at the
Hollywood Bowl and have drawn
ca-
pacity crowds
in
all major
cities
in
the U.S., Canada, Australia, New Zea-
land and Hawaii.

Manufacturers are going to agree with the Government’s “price cut” plan
on their products.
Earlier, taxation
officials proposed a 5%
cut in the
retail
price on all disks
(of smaller than 7" in diameter)
based on the 10% cut in
commodity tax which goes on effect April
1. Reaction from diskeries and their
organization, JPRA (Japan Phonograph Record Association) was on the nega-
tive side at first (Mar. 3 issue). But thru several meetings with
officials and
face-to-face gatherings of industry people themselves, they admitted the need
for a retail price-cut in order to keep up with our Government’s policy. Never-
theless,
final decision
will come after more

(see

“CHUCK BERRY TWIST”—Chess LP 1465
Chuck Berry jumps on the twist bandwagon full-
blast
with
the album
of
his
previous
hits and
noisemakers
that
lend
themselves
to
a
twistin’
beat. There’s plenty of solid rockin’ sounds as the
chanter offers “Maybelline,” “Roll Over Beethoven”
and
“Reelin’ And Rockin’ ” while accompanying
himself with a
spirited
electric
guitar. Most
of
these Berry-penned items are
several years
old
but session should
still pick plenty of loot.
“COUNTRY
AND
WESTERN
GOLDEN
GREATS”—Rusty Draper—Mercury SR 60657
Country fans should come out in droves for this
spinnable,
listenable
package
which
highlights
Rusty Draper belting out a flock of best-sellers of
other artists. The chanter is in his expected good
voice
as
he
renders
some
impressive
arrange-
ments of “Please Help Me, I’m Falling,” “When
Two Worlds Collide” and “Signed Sealed And De-
livered” with verve and polish. Top-flight country
“JIMMY McCRACKLIN SINGS”—Chess LP 1464
The
versatile r&b talents of Jimmy McCracklin
are swingingly showcased on this spinnable
ses-
sion
of a dozen popular
self-penned
tunes. The
chanter’s delivery
is
sincere and feelingful with
enough listening pleasure to attract a wide variety
of record buyers. Disk includes the songster’s past
smash of “The Walk,” “I Know,” and “I Am The
Blame.” Session’s contagious tempo coupled with
some hot instrumental bridges rank
it as a top-
rung r&b-blues disk.
“GYPSY
ROSE
LEE
REMEMBERS
BUR-
LESQUE”—Stereooddities CG 1
Gypsy Rose Lee re-creates all the excitement and
color of her by-gone burlesque days on this origi-
nal musical revue written by Eli Basse, with music
composed by Bobby Kroll. Disk consists of a group
of funny blackouts and tsrpical vaudeville routines.
There’s
plenty
of

here and
Gypsy and crew go through

Definitely
not
a

is

“JOSE MELIS PLAYS HIS TV FAVORITES”—
Mercury SR 60683
The 88’er, in a subtle blending of pop tunes done

ing for both types of music as he plays the stur-

along

Among the

Melis’ quality performance makes the

excellent programming fare.

(released by Artone’s Funckler Dept, on the Funckler label in Benelux,

slot
as

solid
start.

in

of “Norman,” an EP

in

FRANCE
Top-seller at Pathe-Marconi is Richard Anthony’s “Lecon de Twist (Twistin’
the Twist),” the tune that holds the Number 3 spot on this week’s Best Seller
list.
Johnny Hallyday waxing of “Bebop a Lulah” in
its original form promises
to be a big hit. It will be interesting also to see the eventual reaction in other
countries to the operation which consists of “internationalizing” Hallyday, who,
it must be said, has crashed through all the barriers in France. And to be fair,
we note that Hallyday owes much to Leon Cabat, who was the first to back his
career.
Two events ought to warm the hearts of those who believe in the true French
“chanson”: one
is the success that Gilbert Becaud
is having
at the Olympia
Music Hall. On opening night, the crowd was so dense that the police and
